questions.stem: Marcus and Tanya were legally married on December 31, 2024, at 5:00 p.m. They have no children and lived apart for most of the year. For the 2024 tax year, which filing status options are available to them?
options: They must each file as Single because they married late in the year
They must file Married Filing Jointly because they are now married
They may file Married Filing Jointly or Married Filing Separately
One spouse files Single and the other files Head of Household
questions.rationale: Filing status is generally determined by marital status on the last day of the tax year. A couple married on December 31 is considered married for the whole year and may file jointly or separately.

questions.stem: Diana is unmarried and pays more than half the cost of keeping up a home where her 70-year-old mother lives in a separate nursing facility. Diana provides over half of her mother's support, and her mother qualifies as Diana's dependent. Which filing status may Diana use?
options: Single, because her mother does not live in Diana's home
Qualifying Surviving Spouse, because she supports a parent
Married Filing Separately, because she maintains two households
Head of Household, because a dependent parent does not have to live with the taxpayer
questions.rationale: For Head of Household, a dependent parent need not live with the taxpayer as long as the taxpayer pays more than half the cost of maintaining the parent's main home, including a nursing home.

questions.stem: Raymond's wife died in March 2023. He has one dependent son who lived with him all of 2024, and Raymond paid all costs of keeping up their home. He did not remarry. What is the most advantageous filing status Raymond may use for 2024?
options: Qualifying Surviving Spouse
Married Filing Jointly
Head of Household
Single
questions.rationale: Qualifying Surviving Spouse status is available for the two tax years following the year a spouse died, if the taxpayer has a dependent child and maintains the household and has not remarried. It provides joint-return rates.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally required for a taxpayer (and spouse, if filing jointly) to be claimed on a U.S. individual income tax return and to be eligible for most tax benefits?
options: Proof of U.S. citizenship for every taxpayer
A current passport
A Social Security number or other valid taxpayer identification number
A valid driver's license number
questions.rationale: Taxpayers, spouses, and dependents must generally have a valid taxpayer identification number (such as an SSN or ITIN) to be reported on a return and to claim related tax benefits.

questions.stem: A single taxpayer under age 65 who is not someone else's dependent had gross income of $13,200 in 2024 (none from self-employment). Considering the 2024 filing thresholds tied to the standard deduction, what is the taxpayer's filing obligation?
options: Not required to file because income is below the $14,600 threshold for single filers
Required to file because any income over $10,000 triggers a filing requirement
Required to file because the threshold for single filers is $5,000
Not required to file only if the taxpayer had no withholding
questions.rationale: For 2024, the income filing threshold for a single taxpayer under age 65 equals the basic standard deduction of $14,600. With $13,200 of gross income, this taxpayer is below the threshold and not required to file, though filing could yield a refund of withholding.

questions.stem: To claim someone as a qualifying child, the child must meet a residency test. Which statement correctly describes that test for 2024?
options: The child must have lived with the taxpayer for at least three months
The child must live in the same state as the taxpayer at year end
The child must have lived with the taxpayer for the entire tax year without exception
The child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year, with certain temporary absences treated as time lived together
questions.rationale: The qualifying child residency test requires the child to live with the taxpayer for more than half the year. Temporary absences for reasons such as school, illness, or vacation are treated as time the child lived with the taxpayer.

questions.stem: Carla wants to claim her cousin's daughter, age 19, as a qualifying relative. The child is not Carla's qualifying child or anyone else's. To meet the gross income test for 2024, the dependent's gross income must be:
options: Less than $5,050
Less than $4,700
Less than $14,600
Zero
questions.rationale: A qualifying relative must have gross income below the annual limit, which is $5,050 for 2024. This limit is indexed for inflation and differs from the standard deduction.

questions.stem: Under the support test for a qualifying relative, who must provide more than half of the dependent's total support for the year?
options: No one needs to provide support; the test is based only on residence
A government agency must provide more than half of the support
The taxpayer claiming the dependent generally must provide more than half of the dependent's support
The dependent must provide more than half of their own support
questions.rationale: For a qualifying relative, the taxpayer must generally furnish more than half of the dependent's total support during the year, unless a multiple-support agreement applies.

questions.stem: Nadia received the following in 2024: $40,000 in wages, $300 in municipal bond interest from her state, $1,200 in qualified dividends, and a $2,000 federal income tax refund (she took the standard deduction last year). How much is includible in her gross income?
questions.rationale: Wages and qualified dividends are taxable. Municipal bond interest is tax-exempt, and a federal income tax refund is not taxable income (and a state refund is only taxable if the taxpayer itemized and got a benefit). Includible income is $41,200.

questions.stem: Greg sold 100 shares of stock he had held for 8 months at a $3,000 gain. He also sold a vacant lot held for 5 years at a $1,000 loss. How are these treated on his 2024 return?
options: The loss cannot offset the gain because they are different asset types
The $3,000 is short-term capital gain and the $1,000 is long-term capital loss, netted across categories to a $2,000 net gain
Both transactions are long-term because the lot was held over a year
The $3,000 gain is ordinary income because the stock was held under one year
questions.rationale: Holding period determines short-term (one year or less) versus long-term (more than one year). Gains and losses are netted within each category and then across categories; here the result is a $2,000 net gain.

questions.stem: In 2024, Priya had a net capital loss of $7,000 (all long-term) with no capital gains. She is single. How much of the loss can she deduct against ordinary income this year, and what happens to the rest?
options: She may deduct $1,500 this year and carry forward $5,500
She may deduct $3,000 this year and carry forward $4,000 to future years
She may deduct the full $7,000 this year
She may deduct nothing this year because she has no capital gains
questions.rationale: Individuals may deduct net capital losses against ordinary income up to $3,000 per year ($1,500 if married filing separately). Excess losses carry forward indefinitely, retaining their character.

questions.stem: Leo inherited his late aunt's painting in 2024. The aunt had bought it for $2,000, and on the date of her death it was worth $9,000. Leo sold it three months later for $9,500. What is Leo's basis and the character of his gain?
options: Basis $9,000; long-term gain of $500
Basis $9,000; short-term gain of $500
Basis $9,500; no gain
Basis $2,000; short-term gain of $7,500
questions.rationale: Inherited property generally takes a basis equal to its fair market value on the date of the decedent's death, and any gain or loss on its sale is automatically treated as long-term.

questions.stem: When a taxpayer receives property as a gift and later sells it at a gain, what basis does the taxpayer generally use to compute the gain?
options: The donor's adjusted basis (carryover basis)
The sales price reduced by selling expenses
The fair market value of the property on the date of the gift
Zero, because the property was free to the recipient
questions.rationale: For computing gain on gifted property, the donee uses the donor's adjusted basis (carryover basis). A special dual-basis rule applies only when figuring a loss if FMV at the gift date was below the donor's basis.

questions.stem: A single taxpayer owned and used a home as a principal residence for 3 of the last 5 years and sells it in 2024 for a $310,000 gain. The taxpayer has not excluded gain on another home in the past two years. How much of the gain is taxable?
options: $0; the entire gain is excluded
questions.rationale: Under the home-sale exclusion, a single taxpayer who owned and used the home as a principal residence for at least 2 of the last 5 years may exclude up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 for married filing jointly). Gain above the limit is taxable.

questions.stem: Hassan, age 45, took an early distribution of $10,000 from his traditional IRA in 2024 to pay general living expenses. He had deducted all contributions. Ignoring any exceptions, how is this distribution generally treated?
options: Fully tax-free because it is his own money
Included in income but never subject to any penalty
Subject only to the 10% additional tax but not income tax
Included in gross income and subject to a 10% additional tax on early distributions
questions.rationale: A distribution from a traditional IRA of deductible contributions and earnings is taxable. If taken before age 59½ without a qualifying exception, an additional 10% tax applies on top of ordinary income tax.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the taxation of a qualified distribution from a Roth IRA that meets the 5-year rule and is made after the owner reaches age 59½?
options: Tax-free, including both contributions and earnings
Taxable and subject to a 10% additional tax
Fully taxable as ordinary income
Only the earnings are taxable
questions.rationale: Qualified Roth IRA distributions are completely tax-free. To be qualified, the distribution must occur after the 5-year period and after the owner reaches 59½ (or due to death, disability, or a first-time home purchase).

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a Form 1099-INT showing $850 of interest from a bank certificate of deposit. How should this be treated?
options: Reported as a capital gain
Reported only if it exceeds $1,500
Reported as taxable interest income
Excluded because CD interest is tax-exempt
questions.rationale: Interest from a bank certificate of deposit is taxable interest income reported on the return. The $1,500 threshold only determines whether Schedule B must be filed, not whether the interest is taxable.

questions.stem: Olivia bought 200 shares of XYZ stock for $6,000. She later received a nontaxable 2-for-1 stock split, leaving her with 400 shares. What is her per-share basis after the split?
options: $6,000 per share
$15.00 per share
$60.00 per share
$30.00 per share
questions.rationale: A nontaxable stock split does not change total basis; it reallocates the original basis across the increased number of shares. Here $6,000 over 400 shares equals $15 per share.

questions.stem: Marisol received $24,000 in Social Security benefits and had $50,000 of other income in 2024. Which statement is most accurate regarding the taxation of her Social Security benefits?
options: Social Security benefits are never taxable
Up to 85% of her benefits may be taxable because her combined income is high
All Social Security benefits are fully taxable for everyone
Exactly 50% of benefits are always taxable
questions.rationale: The taxable portion of Social Security benefits depends on combined income (AGI plus tax-exempt interest plus half the benefits). It ranges from 0% to a maximum of 85%; higher-income taxpayers reach the 85% cap.

questions.stem: For 2024, what is the basic standard deduction amount for a single taxpayer who is under age 65 and not blind?
questions.rationale: For 2024, the basic standard deduction is $14,600 for single filers, $21,900 for Head of Household, and $29,200 for Married Filing Jointly. Additional amounts apply for taxpayers 65 or older or blind.

questions.stem: Theo, single and age 67, is not blind. What is his total 2024 standard deduction, including the additional amount for being 65 or older?
questions.rationale: For 2024, an unmarried taxpayer who is 65 or older receives an additional standard deduction of $1,950. Added to the $14,600 basic amount, Theo's total standard deduction is $16,550.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an itemized deduction subject to the rule that only the portion of expenses exceeding 7.5% of adjusted gross income is deductible?
options: Unreimbursed qualified medical and dental expenses
State and local income taxes
Charitable cash contributions
Home mortgage interest
questions.rationale: Medical and dental expenses are deductible as an itemized deduction only to the extent they exceed 7.5% of adjusted gross income. Other itemized deductions have their own separate rules and limits.

questions.stem: For 2024, what is the maximum amount of combined state and local taxes (the SALT deduction) that a married couple filing jointly may deduct as an itemized deduction?
options: Unlimited
questions.rationale: The combined deduction for state and local income (or sales) and property taxes is capped at $10,000 ($5,000 if married filing separately) under current law.

questions.stem: The Patel family has three qualifying children under age 17 with valid SSNs and modified AGI of $90,000 (married filing jointly). For 2024, what is the maximum Child Tax Credit before considering any tax liability limits, and is it phased out at this income?
options: $3,000 total, and it is fully phased out
$6,000 total, with a partial phaseout
$6,000 total, with no phaseout because income is below the threshold
$9,000 total, with no limit per child
questions.rationale: The Child Tax Credit is $2,000 per qualifying child under 17 with a valid SSN. The phaseout begins at $400,000 MAGI for joint filers ($200,000 otherwise), so a $90,000-income couple with three children gets the full $6,000.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC) from the Lifetime Learning Credit (LLC)?
options: Both credits are fully refundable
The AOTC is partially refundable and limited to the first four years of postsecondary education; the LLC is nonrefundable
The LLC requires at least half-time enrollment in a degree program; the AOTC does not
The AOTC is available for an unlimited number of years; the LLC is limited to four years
questions.rationale: The AOTC covers the first four years of postsecondary education, requires at least half-time degree enrollment, and is up to 40% refundable. The LLC has no year limit, no enrollment minimum, but is nonrefundable.

questions.stem: Jamal and Aisha (married filing jointly) both work and paid $7,000 in 2024 for daycare for their two children, ages 3 and 5. Their AGI is $60,000. For the Child and Dependent Care Credit, what is the maximum amount of qualifying expenses they may use?
questions.rationale: The Child and Dependent Care Credit limits qualifying expenses to $3,000 for one qualifying person and $6,000 for two or more. The applicable percentage (20%–35%) is then applied to that capped amount.
questions.source: Part 1 – Child and Dependent Care Credit

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally required for a taxpayer to claim the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)?
options: The taxpayer must have a child who is a dependent
The taxpayer must have earned income and investment income below the annual limit
The taxpayer must itemize deductions
The taxpayer must be at least 35 years old
questions.rationale: The EITC requires earned income and limits investment income (the limit is $11,600 for 2024). It is available to certain taxpayers with or without qualifying children and does not depend on itemizing.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the key difference between a tax deduction and a tax credit?
options: Both reduce the tax liability by the same amount
A deduction reduces taxable income; a credit reduces the tax liability dollar-for-dollar
A deduction reduces tax dollar-for-dollar; a credit reduces taxable income
A credit is always less valuable than a deduction of the same amount
questions.rationale: A deduction reduces taxable income, so its benefit equals the deduction times the marginal rate. A credit reduces the tax liability dollar-for-dollar, generally making credits more valuable than equal-sized deductions.

questions.stem: For 2024, what is the maximum contribution to a traditional or Roth IRA for an individual who is under age 50, assuming sufficient compensation?
questions.rationale: For 2024, the IRA contribution limit is $7,000 for individuals under 50, with an additional $1,000 catch-up (total $8,000) for those 50 or older, subject to having enough compensation.

questions.stem: Renata is covered by a 401(k) at work. She wants to deduct her traditional IRA contribution for 2024. Which factor primarily determines whether her contribution is fully deductible, partially deductible, or nondeductible?
options: Whether she also has a Roth IRA
Whether she files electronically
Her modified adjusted gross income relative to the active-participant phaseout range
The total balance in her IRA at year end
questions.rationale: When a taxpayer is an active participant in an employer retirement plan, the traditional IRA deduction phases out over a MAGI range that depends on filing status. The contribution can still be made (and is nondeductible) above the range.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the U.S. federal individual income tax rate structure?
options: A regressive structure where higher income is taxed at lower rates
A flat tax where everyone pays the same rate
A single rate that changes each month
A progressive structure with graduated tax brackets that apply higher rates to higher income ranges
questions.rationale: The federal individual income tax is progressive: income is taxed in brackets, with each successive band of income subject to a higher marginal rate. A taxpayer's average rate is lower than the top marginal rate.

questions.stem: Which of the following types of income is generally NOT subject to self-employment tax?
options: Interest and dividends from a personal investment portfolio
A general partner's distributive share of partnership trade or business income
Net earnings from a single-member LLC operating a business
Net profit from a sole proprietorship reported on Schedule C
questions.rationale: Self-employment tax applies to net earnings from a trade or business carried on as a sole proprietor, independent contractor, or partner. Passive investment income such as interest and dividends is not subject to SE tax.

questions.stem: Which item is most likely to be an adjustment (preference) that increases income in computing the Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) for an individual?
options: Charitable contributions of cash to a public charity
Home mortgage interest on acquisition debt for a primary residence
The standard deduction and certain state and local tax deductions
Qualified dividends taxed at capital gains rates
questions.rationale: AMT disallows certain regular-tax benefits. Common add-backs include the standard deduction and the state and local tax deduction. Items like cash charitable gifts and acquisition-debt mortgage interest are generally still allowed.

questions.stem: A self-employed taxpayer with net earnings from self-employment computes self-employment tax. What deduction related to that tax may the taxpayer take in arriving at adjusted gross income?
options: The full amount of self-employment tax paid
One-half of the self-employment tax
Twice the self-employment tax as an incentive
None; self-employment tax is never deductible
questions.rationale: Self-employed taxpayers may deduct one-half of their self-employment tax as an adjustment to gross income, reflecting the employer-equivalent portion of payroll taxes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a refundable credit, meaning it can produce a refund even if it exceeds the taxpayer's tax liability?
options: The Saver's Credit (Retirement Savings Contributions Credit)
The Lifetime Learning Credit
The Earned Income Tax Credit
The Foreign Tax Credit (general limitation)
questions.rationale: A refundable credit can exceed the tax liability and generate a refund. The Earned Income Tax Credit is refundable, while the Lifetime Learning Credit, Foreign Tax Credit, and Saver's Credit are nonrefundable.

questions.stem: The Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) of 3.8% applies to certain taxpayers. Which statement about the NIIT is correct for 2024?
options: It applies to all wage income above $200,000
It applies to the lesser of net investment income or the excess of MAGI over a threshold ($250,000 MFJ, $200,000 single)
It replaces the regular income tax on dividends
It applies only to taxpayers with no earned income
questions.rationale: The 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax applies to the lesser of net investment income or the excess of modified AGI over the threshold ($250,000 for joint filers, $200,000 for single and Head of Household).

questions.stem: A taxpayer expects to owe $4,500 of tax for 2024 after withholding. To avoid an underpayment penalty using the prior-year safe harbor, what is generally required of an individual whose prior-year AGI was $120,000?
options: Pay at least 100% of the prior-year tax liability, since AGI did not exceed $150,000
Pay through withholding and estimates at least 90% of the current-year tax only
Make no payments because the balance is under $5,000
Pay at least 110% of the prior-year tax liability because AGI exceeded $150,000
questions.rationale: To avoid an underpayment penalty, individuals generally must pay the smaller of 90% of the current-year tax or 100% of the prior-year tax (110% if prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000). With $120,000 prior AGI, the 100% safe harbor applies.

questions.stem: A client did not receive a corrected Form W-2 in time and the regular April filing deadline is approaching. What is the best advice for obtaining more time to file the return?
options: File Form 4868, which also extends the time to pay the tax
Wait until the corrected form arrives, even if it is years later, with no consequences
Simply file late; extensions are not available for individuals
File Form 4868 for an automatic extension of time to file, but pay any tax owed by the original due date
questions.rationale: Form 4868 provides an automatic extension of time to file an individual return, but it does not extend the time to pay. Taxpayers should estimate and pay any balance by the original due date to minimize penalties and interest.

questions.stem: A taxpayer asks how long to keep records supporting income and deductions on a filed return. What is the most accurate general guidance regarding the basic period of limitations for an assessment?
options: Records must be kept for exactly one year
Records may be discarded as soon as the return is filed
Keep records generally at least three years from the date the return was filed or due, since that is the usual assessment period
Records never need to be retained because the IRS keeps copies
questions.rationale: The general period of limitations for the IRS to assess additional tax is three years from when the return is filed or due. Taxpayers should keep supporting records at least that long, and longer for basis records or special situations such as substantial omissions.

questions.stem: A married couple filed a joint return. One spouse later discovers the other significantly understated self-employment income without their knowledge, and they meet the conditions for relief. Which provision may relieve the innocent spouse of joint liability for the resulting tax?
options: Innocent spouse relief
Married Filing Separately amendment after the deadline
Head of Household reclassification
Injured spouse allocation
questions.rationale: Innocent spouse relief may relieve a spouse of joint and several liability for an understatement of tax attributable to the other spouse, where the requesting spouse did not know and had no reason to know. Injured spouse relief is a different remedy involving refund offsets.

questions.stem: A taxpayer realizes after filing that they omitted a deductible IRA contribution that would increase their refund. Which form is used to correct a previously filed individual income tax return?
options: Form 1040-X
Form W-4
Form 1099-R
Form 4868
questions.rationale: To correct or change a previously filed individual return, the taxpayer files Form 1040-X, the Amended U.S. Individual Income Tax Return. A refund claim generally must be filed within three years of the original return or two years of paying the tax.

questions.stem: A client cannot pay the full balance due with their return but can pay over time. Which option is the most appropriate to advise the taxpayer to pursue with the IRS?
options: Do not file the return until they can pay in full
File using a different Social Security number to delay collection
Ignore the balance because the IRS will eventually forgive it
File the return on time and request an installment agreement to pay the balance over time
questions.rationale: Taxpayers should file on time even if they cannot pay, because the failure-to-file penalty is much larger than the failure-to-pay penalty. An installment agreement allows the balance to be paid over time.

questions.stem: A U.S. citizen worked abroad all of 2024 and met the bona fide residence test. Which provision may allow this taxpayer to exclude a portion of foreign earned income from U.S. taxation?
options: The Foreign Earned Income Exclusion
The standard deduction for expatriates
The home-sale exclusion
The dependent care exclusion
questions.rationale: Qualifying U.S. citizens and residents working abroad may use the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion to exclude foreign earned income up to an annual limit ($126,500 for 2024), provided they meet the bona fide residence or physical presence test.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received $1,200 of unearned income (interest and dividends) and no earned income in 2024. The child is 16, a dependent of the parents, and a full-time student. Which statement about the kiddie tax is most accurate?
options: All $1,200 is taxed at the parents' marginal rate
A portion of the child's unearned income up to the annual threshold is taxed at the child's rate, and amounts above it may be taxed at the parents' rate
The kiddie tax never applies to a 16-year-old
Unearned income of a dependent child is always tax-free
questions.rationale: The kiddie tax applies to certain children's net unearned income. For 2024, the first $1,300 is generally offset by the dependent's standard deduction and the next $1,300 is taxed at the child's rate; unearned income above $2,600 is taxed at the parents' marginal rate.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the federal income tax treatment of a nonresident alien individual?
options: Nonresident aliens are exempt from all U.S. income tax
Nonresident aliens are taxed the same as U.S. citizens on worldwide income
Nonresident aliens are generally taxed only on U.S.-source income and income effectively connected with a U.S. trade or business
Nonresident aliens must always file a joint return with a U.S. spouse
questions.rationale: Nonresident aliens are generally subject to U.S. tax only on U.S.-source income and income effectively connected with a U.S. trade or business, reported on Form 1040-NR, rather than on worldwide income.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally true about the U.S. estate and gift tax annual exclusion as it affects an individual donor for 2024?
options: Gifts to anyone are always fully taxable to the recipient
The annual exclusion applies only to gifts to charities
A donor may give up to $18,000 per recipient in 2024 without using any lifetime exemption or filing a gift tax return
Every gift, regardless of size, must be reported on a gift tax return
questions.rationale: For 2024, a donor may give up to $18,000 per recipient (the annual exclusion) without filing a gift tax return or using lifetime exemption. Gifts are not taxable income to the recipient.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who is a member of the U.S. Armed Forces serving in a designated combat zone received basic pay while there. How is qualifying combat pay generally treated for federal income tax purposes for an enlisted member?
options: Subject to double taxation
Fully taxable like ordinary wages
Taxable only if it exceeds $50,000
Excludable from gross income, though it may still count as earned income for certain credits
questions.rationale: Combat pay for enlisted members serving in a designated combat zone is excludable from gross income (officers have a monthly cap). Taxpayers may elect to treat excluded combat pay as earned income to qualify for or increase certain credits such as the EITC.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to be claimed as a qualifying child by a relative. Which of the following is NOT one of the four tests (relationship, age, residency, support) that a qualifying child must meet?
options: The age test
The relationship test
The residency test
The gross income test
questions.rationale: A qualifying child must meet the relationship, age, residency, and support tests (and not file a joint return except to claim a refund). The gross income test is a qualifying relative test, not a qualifying child test.

questions.stem: Two unmarried parents both supported their child, who lived with the mother for 7 months and the father for 5 months of 2024. Both want to claim the child as a qualifying child. Under the tiebreaker rules, who is entitled to claim the child?
options: Whichever parent files first
The parent with the lower adjusted gross income
The parent with whom the child lived the longer period during the year
Neither parent; they must split the dependency
questions.rationale: Under the tiebreaker rules, if two parents could claim the same qualifying child, the child is treated as the qualifying child of the parent with whom the child lived longer during the year. If time is equal, the parent with the higher AGI prevails.

questions.stem: Four siblings together provide all of their elderly father's support: 12%, 18%, 30%, and 40%. No single sibling provides over half. The father otherwise qualifies as a dependent. Under a multiple support agreement, which sibling may be eligible to claim the father?
options: Only the sibling providing 40%, because they provided the most
Any sibling who provided more than 10% of the support, if the others who provided more than 10% agree in writing
All four siblings may each claim a one-fourth share
None of them, because no one provided more than half
questions.rationale: A multiple support agreement (Form 2848 is not used; Form 2120 is) lets one person who paid more than 10% of a dependent's support claim the dependent when no one paid more than half, provided the other 10%-plus contributors agree in writing not to claim that person.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old single dependent earned $3,200 in wages and had $500 of interest income in 2024. What is the dependent's standard deduction for 2024?
questions.rationale: For 2024, a dependent's standard deduction equals the greater of $1,300 or earned income plus $450 (not to exceed the regular $14,600 single amount). With $3,200 earned income, the deduction is $3,200 + $450 = $3,650.

questions.stem: A married couple normally files jointly. One spouse wants to ensure they are not held responsible for the other spouse's questionable deductions. Which filing status would generally make each spouse responsible only for the tax on their own separate return?
options: Married Filing Separately
Head of Household
Qualifying Surviving Spouse
Married Filing Jointly
questions.rationale: Married Filing Separately makes each spouse responsible only for the tax on their own return, avoiding the joint and several liability that arises on a joint return, though it often results in higher overall tax and loss of certain benefits.

questions.stem: Which of the following individuals can be claimed as a dependent, assuming all other tests are met?
options: A person who files a joint return with their spouse solely to claim a refund of withheld tax, with no tax liability on either separate return
A person who provided more than half of their own support
A person who is a resident of a country with which the U.S. has no relevant treaty and is not a U.S. citizen, national, or resident
A married child who files a joint return to reduce the couple's total tax liability
questions.rationale: The joint return test allows a dependent who files jointly only to claim a refund of withheld or estimated tax, provided neither spouse would owe tax on a separate return. The dependent must also meet the citizen/resident test and not provide over half their own support.

questions.stem: A married taxpayer lived apart from their spouse for the entire last half of 2024 and paid more than half the cost of keeping up a home that was the main home for their dependent child all year. The spouses did not file jointly. Can this taxpayer be 'considered unmarried' to file as Head of Household?
options: No, because Head of Household is only for single or divorced taxpayers
Yes, if the spouse did not live in the home during the last six months of the year and the other Head of Household requirements are met
No, because any married person must file jointly or separately
Yes, but only if the couple has been separated for more than two years
questions.rationale: Under the 'considered unmarried' rules, a married taxpayer may file as Head of Household if the spouse did not live in the home for the last 6 months, the taxpayer furnished more than half the cost of the home, and a qualifying child lived there more than half the year.

questions.stem: A taxpayer needs a taxpayer identification number for a dependent who is a resident alien not eligible for a Social Security number. Which form is used to apply for an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN)?
options: Form W-7
Form W-9
Form SS-5
Form SS-4
questions.rationale: An individual who needs a U.S. taxpayer identification number but is not eligible for a Social Security number applies for an ITIN using Form W-7. SS-5 is for an SSN, SS-4 is for an EIN, and W-9 furnishes an existing TIN.

questions.stem: By what date must most individual taxpayers file their 2024 Form 1040 or request an extension, assuming the date does not fall on a weekend or holiday?
options: October 15, 2025
April 15, 2025
March 15, 2025
questions.rationale: Calendar-year individuals must generally file Form 1040 (or request an extension) by April 15 of the following year. An extension moves the filing deadline to October 15, but not the payment due date.

questions.stem: A self-employed single taxpayer under 65 had net earnings from self-employment of $600 and no other income in 2024. Is this taxpayer required to file a federal income tax return?
options: No, because $600 is below the standard deduction
Yes, because net earnings from self-employment of $400 or more triggers a filing requirement
No, because self-employment income under $1,000 is exempt
Yes, but only if the taxpayer received a Form 1099-NEC
questions.rationale: Even when total income is below the general filing threshold, an individual must file if net earnings from self-employment are $400 or more, because self-employment tax is owed. This applies regardless of whether a 1099 was received.

questions.stem: Which of the following payments is generally taxable and must be included in the recipient's gross income for 2024?
options: A qualified scholarship used solely for tuition and required course fees
Child support payments received under a divorce decree
Jury duty pay received for serving on a jury
Workers' compensation for a job-related injury
questions.rationale: Jury duty pay is taxable. Child support, workers' compensation, and qualified scholarships used for tuition and required fees are excluded from gross income.

questions.stem: Under a divorce finalized in 2024, one former spouse pays the other $1,500 per month labeled as alimony. How are these payments treated for federal income tax purposes?
options: Neither deductible by the payer nor taxable to the recipient
Deductible by the payer and taxable to the recipient
Deductible by both spouses
Taxable to the payer and deductible by the recipient
questions.rationale: Under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, for divorce or separation agreements executed after December 31, 2018, alimony payments are neither deductible by the payer nor taxable to the recipient.

questions.stem: A taxpayer sold investment land for $50,000. The buyer paid $10,000 down in 2024 and will pay the remaining $40,000 in equal installments over the next four years. The taxpayer's basis in the land was $30,000. Under the installment method, how is the gain generally reported?
options: The entire $50,000 is taxable as ordinary income in 2024
All $20,000 of gain is reported in 2024 when the sale closes
A portion of each payment is treated as gain based on the gross profit ratio, recognizing gain as payments are received
No gain is reported until the final installment is collected
questions.rationale: The installment method recognizes gain as payments are received. The taxable portion of each payment equals the gross profit ratio (here $20,000 gain ÷ $50,000 contract price = 40%) times the payment. Basis recovery and gain are spread across years.

questions.stem: A taxpayer sold 100 shares of stock at a $2,000 loss on November 10, 2024, and repurchased 100 shares of the same stock on November 30, 2024. What is the tax consequence of this transaction?
options: Only half the loss is deductible because of the short holding period
The loss is disallowed permanently and lost forever
The $2,000 loss is fully deductible in 2024
The loss is disallowed under the wash sale rule, and the disallowed amount is added to the basis of the new shares
questions.rationale: The wash sale rule disallows a loss when substantially identical securities are purchased within 30 days before or after the sale. The disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement shares, and the original holding period carries over.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a state income tax refund of $1,200 in 2024 for the 2023 tax year. The taxpayer itemized deductions in 2023 and deducted state income taxes, receiving a full tax benefit. How is the refund treated in 2024?
options: Included in 2024 income to the extent the taxpayer received a tax benefit from deducting the tax in 2023
Fully excluded because tax refunds are never taxable
Included only if the taxpayer took the standard deduction in 2023
Always fully taxable regardless of the prior year's deductions
questions.rationale: Under the tax benefit rule, a state income tax refund is includible in income to the extent the prior-year deduction reduced tax. If the taxpayer took the standard deduction or was limited by the SALT cap, some or all of the refund may not be taxable.

questions.stem: Which of the following distributions or amounts is generally treated as a return of capital rather than as taxable income when received?
options: An ordinary dividend reported in box 1a of Form 1099-DIV
Interest credited to a savings account
A nondividend distribution that exceeds the corporation's earnings and profits but is within the shareholder's stock basis
A taxable distribution from a traditional IRA
questions.rationale: A nondividend distribution is a return of capital: it is nontaxable to the extent of the shareholder's stock basis, reduces that basis, and produces a capital gain only when it exceeds basis. Dividends, interest, and taxable IRA distributions are income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received qualified dividends of $4,000 in 2024 and is in the 12% ordinary income tax bracket with taxable income that keeps them within the 0% qualified dividend rate range. What rate applies to the qualified dividends?
questions.rationale: Qualified dividends and net long-term capital gains are taxed at 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on taxable income. A taxpayer whose taxable income falls within the lowest range qualifies for the 0% preferential rate on those dividends.

questions.stem: A taxpayer disposed of virtual currency (cryptocurrency) held as a capital asset for 14 months, realizing a gain. How is this gain generally characterized for federal income tax purposes?
options: It is a long-term capital gain because the asset was held more than one year
It is tax-free because cryptocurrency is not recognized by the IRS
It is exempt unless converted to U.S. dollars
It is always ordinary income regardless of holding period
questions.rationale: The IRS treats virtual currency as property. When held as a capital asset for more than one year, gain on its sale or exchange is long-term capital gain. Disposing of crypto, including exchanging it for other property, is a taxable event.

questions.stem: Where on Form 1040 must an individual taxpayer respond regarding their involvement with digital assets during the tax year?
options: It is optional and may be left blank
By answering the digital asset question that appears near the top of Form 1040, which all filers must answer
Only nonresident aliens must answer the digital asset question
Only on a separate schedule if they sold cryptocurrency
questions.rationale: Form 1040 contains a digital asset question near the top of the form that every individual taxpayer must answer 'Yes' or 'No.' This requirement applies to all filers regardless of whether they engaged in digital asset transactions.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a Form 1099-R for a $30,000 distribution from a traditional IRA. They redeposited the full $30,000 into another traditional IRA 45 days after receiving it, and they have not done another rollover in the past 12 months. How is this treated?
options: Taxable because rollovers must be completed within 30 days
Fully taxable because any IRA distribution is income
A valid tax-free 60-day rollover, so none of the $30,000 is included in income
Subject to the 10% early distribution penalty only
questions.rationale: A distribution that is rolled over to another IRA within 60 days is generally not taxable. Only one IRA-to-IRA rollover is allowed in any 12-month period; since that condition is met here, the entire $30,000 is excluded from income.

questions.stem: An employee received $5,000 in dependent care assistance through their employer's qualified plan in 2024 and excluded it from income. How does this affect the expenses they may use for the Child and Dependent Care Credit?
options: It has no effect; they may still use the full expense limit
It doubles the available credit
They must include the $5,000 in income to claim the credit
The excluded employer-provided benefits reduce the dollar limit of expenses eligible for the credit
questions.rationale: Dependent care benefits excluded from income (up to $5,000) reduce the expense limit available for the Child and Dependent Care Credit. This coordination rule prevents claiming both an exclusion and a credit on the same expenses.

questions.stem: Which of the following retirement plan amounts is generally subject to required minimum distributions (RMDs) during the original owner's lifetime?
options: A health savings account (HSA)
A Roth IRA in all circumstances
A Roth IRA owned by the original account holder
A traditional IRA owned by an individual who has reached the applicable RMD age
questions.rationale: Traditional IRAs require minimum distributions beginning at the applicable RMD age (73 under the SECURE 2.0 Act for those reaching that age currently). Roth IRAs have no lifetime RMDs for the original owner.

questions.stem: A taxpayer failed to take a required minimum distribution (RMD) from a traditional IRA for 2024. Under current law (SECURE 2.0), what is the general excise tax penalty on the amount that should have been distributed but was not?
options: 50% of the shortfall
25% of the shortfall, potentially reduced to 10% if timely corrected
There is no penalty for missing an RMD
10% flat with no reduction
questions.rationale: SECURE 2.0 lowered the excise tax on a missed RMD from 50% to 25% of the amount not distributed. The penalty can be further reduced to 10% if the missed RMD is corrected within the prescribed correction period.

questions.stem: A landlord rented out a residential property all of 2024, collecting $18,000 in rent. They also received a $1,500 security deposit they intend to return at the end of the lease and a $300 payment for the tenant breaking a lease. Which amount is included in rental income for 2024?
questions.rationale: Rental income includes rent received and payments for canceling a lease. A security deposit intended to be returned is not income when received (it becomes income only if kept). Includible rental income is $18,000 + $300 = $18,300.

questions.stem: Which of the following fringe benefits provided by an employer is generally excludable from an employee's gross income?
options: A gift card given as a holiday present
Employer-paid premiums for the first $50,000 of group-term life insurance coverage
A year-end cash bonus of $1,000
Reimbursement of personal commuting costs in cash
questions.rationale: Employer-provided group-term life insurance up to $50,000 of coverage is excludable from income. Cash bonuses, cash gift cards, and cash commuting reimbursements are taxable compensation.

questions.stem: A taxpayer cashed in a Series EE U.S. savings bond and received interest. Under what circumstance may the bond interest be excluded from income?
options: If the proceeds are used to pay qualified higher education expenses and the taxpayer meets income and other requirements (the education savings bond exclusion)
Never; savings bond interest is always fully taxable
Only if the bond was held less than one year
Always, because U.S. savings bond interest is tax-exempt
questions.rationale: Interest on Series EE and I U.S. savings bonds is generally taxable federally, but it may be excluded under the education savings bond program when the redemption proceeds pay qualified higher education expenses and the taxpayer meets income limits and other requirements.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received property in a like-kind exchange of real property used in a trade or business. They exchanged land worth $100,000 (basis $60,000) plus $10,000 cash received as boot, for replacement land worth $90,000. How much gain is recognized?
options: $0, because like-kind exchanges are always fully tax-deferred
$40,000, the full realized gain
$10,000, limited to the boot received
questions.rationale: In a Section 1031 like-kind exchange of real property, realized gain is recognized only up to the boot (cash or non-like-kind property) received. Here, although $40,000 of gain was realized, only the $10,000 boot triggers recognized gain.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received $8,000 in gambling winnings and incurred $10,000 in gambling losses during 2024. The taxpayer is not a professional gambler and will itemize deductions. How are these amounts reported?
options: Report net winnings of $0 because losses exceed winnings
Neither winnings nor losses are reported
Report $8,000 as income and deduct the full $10,000 of losses
Report $8,000 of winnings as income and deduct gambling losses only up to $8,000 as an itemized deduction
questions.rationale: Gambling winnings are fully taxable. A casual gambler who itemizes may deduct gambling losses, but only up to the amount of winnings reported; excess losses provide no benefit and cannot be carried forward.

questions.stem: A taxpayer had $200 in ordinary dividends and $50 in tax-exempt interest in 2024 and no other interest or dividends. Which schedule, if any, must they file solely because of these amounts?
options: Schedule B is required because they have dividends
Schedule C is required to report the interest
No Schedule B is required because neither taxable interest nor ordinary dividends exceed $1,500
Schedule D is required for the dividends
questions.rationale: Schedule B is generally required only when taxable interest or ordinary dividends each exceed $1,500 (or in certain other situations). With $200 of dividends, no Schedule B is required, though the dividends are still reported on Form 1040.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a gift of stock from a friend. The donor's basis was $5,000 and the fair market value on the date of the gift was $3,000. The taxpayer later sold the stock for $2,500. What is the recognized loss?
options: $2,000 loss
$2,500 loss using the donor's basis
$500 loss, because the loss basis is the $3,000 fair market value at the gift date
No loss because gifts cannot generate a loss
questions.rationale: When gifted property's FMV at the date of gift is less than the donor's basis, a special dual-basis rule applies: gain is figured using the donor's basis, but loss is figured using the lower FMV. Here, the loss is $3,000 − $2,500 = $500.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $20,000 distribution from a 401(k) after leaving their job at age 50, separating from service. They did not roll it over. Besides ordinary income tax, what additional tax generally applies?
options: No additional tax because separation from service at any age is an exception
A 6% excise tax on excess contributions
A 25% additional tax
A 10% additional tax on the early distribution because the taxpayer is under 59½
questions.rationale: Distributions before age 59½ are generally subject to a 10% additional tax. The separation-from-service exception applies only if the employee separates during or after the year they turn 55 (50 for certain public safety employees), which does not help a 50-year-old here.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an 'above-the-line' deduction (adjustment to income) rather than an itemized deduction?
options: State and local property taxes
Home mortgage interest
Charitable contributions
Educator expenses up to the annual limit for eligible teachers
questions.rationale: Adjustments to income (above-the-line deductions) reduce AGI and are available regardless of whether the taxpayer itemizes. The educator expense deduction is such an adjustment; mortgage interest, property taxes, and charitable gifts are itemized deductions.

questions.stem: For 2024, what is the maximum educator expense deduction an eligible K-12 educator may claim as an adjustment to income?
questions.rationale: For 2024, the educator expense deduction is up to $300 per eligible educator. On a joint return where both spouses are eligible educators, the limit is $300 each (up to $600 combined).

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $2,800 in student loan interest in 2024 and has modified AGI below the phaseout range. What is the maximum student loan interest deduction they may claim?
questions.rationale: The student loan interest deduction is capped at $2,500 per year as an adjustment to income, available without itemizing. It phases out over a modified AGI range that depends on filing status.

questions.stem: A taxpayer made a $5,000 cash contribution and donated appreciated stock held over one year worth $8,000 (basis $3,000) to a public charity in 2024. Their AGI is $100,000. Considering only the AGI percentage limits, what is the maximum amount deductible this year, assuming they elect no special reductions?
options: $13,000, the full amount of both gifts
$5,000 only
$8,000 only
$13,000, because cash is limited to 60% of AGI and appreciated long-term capital gain property to 30% of AGI, both well within limits
questions.rationale: Cash gifts to public charities are deductible up to 60% of AGI, and appreciated long-term capital gain property is deductible at fair market value up to 30% of AGI. Here both gifts ($13,000 total) are well within those ceilings.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to deduct a $400 cash contribution made to a qualified charity. What documentation is generally required to substantiate this deduction?
options: A bank record or written communication from the charity showing the name, date, and amount
No documentation is required for cash gifts
A signed appraisal regardless of amount
Only an oral statement to the preparer
questions.rationale: To deduct a cash contribution, the taxpayer must keep a bank record or written communication from the charity. Contributions of $250 or more additionally require a contemporaneous written acknowledgment from the organization.

questions.stem: A homeowner took out a $900,000 mortgage in 2024 to buy their main home. Under current law, on how much of the acquisition debt is the home mortgage interest generally deductible?
options: Interest on up to $750,000 of acquisition debt
No mortgage interest is deductible on loans over $500,000
Interest on the full $900,000 of debt
Interest on up to $1,000,000 of acquisition debt
questions.rationale: For home acquisition debt incurred after December 15, 2017, mortgage interest is deductible on up to $750,000 of debt ($375,000 if MFS). The older $1,000,000 limit applies only to grandfathered pre-December 16, 2017 debt.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a nonrefundable credit that helps low- and moderate-income taxpayers who contribute to a retirement account?
options: The American Opportunity Tax Credit
The Earned Income Tax Credit
The Child Tax Credit
The Saver's Credit (Retirement Savings Contributions Credit)
questions.rationale: The Saver's Credit (Retirement Savings Contributions Credit) is a nonrefundable credit of 10%, 20%, or 50% of up to $2,000 in retirement contributions ($4,000 if MFJ), based on AGI. It rewards eligible lower-income savers.

questions.stem: A taxpayer claims the Child Tax Credit but cannot use the full $2,000 per child because their tax liability is too low. Which related credit may allow a refundable portion, and what is the maximum refundable amount per child for 2024?
options: The Earned Income Tax Credit, up to $2,000 per child
The Additional Child Tax Credit, up to $1,700 per qualifying child
There is no refundable portion of the Child Tax Credit
The Saver's Credit, up to $1,000 per child
questions.rationale: When the nonrefundable Child Tax Credit exceeds tax liability, the Additional Child Tax Credit can refund part of it, up to $1,700 per qualifying child for 2024, generally based on 15% of earned income over $2,500.

questions.stem: A taxpayer supports a 25-year-old dependent who does not qualify for the Child Tax Credit because of age. What credit may the taxpayer claim for this dependent if all requirements are met?
options: No credit is available for an adult dependent
The Credit for Other Dependents of $500
The Earned Income Tax Credit of $500
The Child Tax Credit of $2,000
questions.rationale: The Credit for Other Dependents is a $500 nonrefundable credit for each dependent who does not qualify for the Child Tax Credit, such as dependents age 17 or older or qualifying relatives, subject to the same income phaseouts.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is deciding whether to itemize deductions or take the standard deduction. Which approach generally produces the lower tax?
options: Always take the standard deduction
Take the average of the two amounts
Always itemize regardless of amounts
Take whichever is larger: total itemized deductions or the standard deduction
questions.rationale: Taxpayers should compare their total allowable itemized deductions to the standard deduction and claim whichever is larger, since that produces the lower taxable income and tax (some taxpayers, however, are required to itemize).

questions.stem: A self-employed taxpayer paid $9,000 in health insurance premiums for themselves and their family in 2024 and had a net profit from the business. They were not eligible for employer-subsidized coverage through any employer. How is the premium generally treated?
options: Deductible as a self-employed health insurance adjustment to income, up to net self-employment earnings
Deductible only as an itemized medical expense subject to the 7.5% floor
Not deductible at all
Deductible as a business expense on Schedule C reducing self-employment tax
questions.rationale: A self-employed individual not eligible for subsidized employer health coverage may deduct health insurance premiums as an adjustment to income, limited to the net profit from the business. It reduces income tax but not self-employment tax.

questions.stem: A single taxpayer with self-only high-deductible health plan coverage all year wants to make the maximum 2024 Health Savings Account (HSA) contribution. They are age 45. What is the maximum HSA contribution for 2024?
options: $4,150 plus a $1,000 catch-up
questions.rationale: For 2024, the HSA contribution limit is $4,150 for self-only HDHP coverage and $8,300 for family coverage. An additional $1,000 catch-up is allowed for those age 55 or older, which does not apply to a 45-year-old.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $3,000 of qualified tuition for their dependent's first year of college and wants to maximize the education benefit. Which credit generally provides the most favorable result for an eligible first-year, half-time degree-seeking student?
options: The American Opportunity Tax Credit, which provides up to $2,500 per eligible student and is partly refundable
The tuition and fees deduction, which is still available
The Lifetime Learning Credit, because it is refundable
The student loan interest deduction
questions.rationale: The American Opportunity Tax Credit provides up to $2,500 per eligible student for the first four years of postsecondary education and is 40% refundable, generally outperforming the nonrefundable Lifetime Learning Credit for a qualifying first-year student.

questions.stem: Which form does a taxpayer typically receive from an educational institution reporting qualified tuition and related expenses to support an education credit?
options: Form W-2
Form 1099-Q
Form 1098-E
Form 1098-T
questions.rationale: Form 1098-T is issued by eligible educational institutions to report qualified tuition and related expenses, helping taxpayers claim the American Opportunity or Lifetime Learning Credit. Form 1098-E reports student loan interest.

questions.stem: A married couple filing jointly has three qualifying children and earned income of $30,000 with no investment income in 2024. They have no disqualifying factors. Which statement about their Earned Income Tax Credit is most accurate?
options: Only one child counts toward the EITC
The EITC is capped at $500 regardless of the number of children
They may claim a substantial EITC, as the credit increases with earned income up to a maximum and the largest credit applies to three or more children
They cannot claim the EITC because their income is too low
questions.rationale: The EITC increases with earned income up to a maximum, then phases out. The credit amount grows with the number of qualifying children, reaching its largest value for taxpayers with three or more qualifying children.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $600 in foreign taxes on dividends from a foreign mutual fund in 2024. Which option generally allows the taxpayer to claim a credit for these foreign taxes without filing Form 1116?
options: Foreign taxes can never be claimed without Form 1116
If total creditable foreign taxes are below the de minimis threshold ($300 single / $600 MFJ) and reported on a payee statement, the credit may be claimed directly without Form 1116
The taxpayer must deduct the taxes as an itemized deduction instead
Only corporations may claim the foreign tax credit
questions.rationale: Individuals may claim a foreign tax credit without Form 1116 when their total creditable foreign taxes are $300 or less ($600 or less for joint filers) and are reported on a qualified statement such as Form 1099-DIV.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's adjusted gross income is $80,000, and they have $9,000 of unreimbursed qualified medical expenses. How much of the medical expenses are deductible as an itemized deduction in 2024?
questions.rationale: Medical and dental expenses are deductible only to the extent they exceed 7.5% of AGI. Here, 7.5% of $80,000 is $6,000, so $9,000 − $6,000 = $3,000 is deductible if the taxpayer itemizes.

questions.stem: Which of the following expenses qualifies as a deductible medical expense for itemizing purposes?
options: Health club dues to maintain general fitness
Cosmetic surgery to improve general appearance with no medical necessity
Nonprescription vitamins for general health
Premiums paid for qualified long-term care insurance, subject to age-based limits
questions.rationale: Qualified long-term care insurance premiums are deductible medical expenses up to age-based limits. Cosmetic surgery without medical necessity, general-health vitamins, and health club dues are not deductible.

questions.stem: A self-employed taxpayer had net earnings from self-employment of $100,000 in 2024. Approximately what self-employment tax rate applies before considering the Social Security wage base, and what are its two components?
options: 7.65%, consisting of income tax and Medicare
15.3%, consisting of 12.4% Social Security and 2.9% Medicare
2.9%, consisting of Medicare only
10%, consisting of Social Security only
questions.rationale: Self-employment tax is 15.3% on net earnings from self-employment (after the 92.35% adjustment), comprising 12.4% Social Security (up to the annual wage base) and 2.9% Medicare (no cap). An additional 0.9% Medicare tax may apply at higher incomes.

questions.stem: A single taxpayer has Medicare wages of $240,000 in 2024. The Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% applies to wages above a threshold. On how much of the wages does the Additional Medicare Tax apply?
options: $40,000, the amount above the $200,000 threshold
$0, because the Additional Medicare Tax only applies to self-employment income
questions.rationale: The 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies to wages, self-employment income, and certain compensation exceeding the filing-status threshold ($200,000 single, $250,000 MFJ, $125,000 MFS). For this single filer, it applies to $40,000.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the difference between a taxpayer's marginal tax rate and effective (average) tax rate?
options: The marginal rate is the rate on the last dollar of income; the effective rate is total tax divided by total income
They are always equal
The marginal rate applies only to capital gains
The effective rate is always higher than the marginal rate
questions.rationale: The marginal tax rate is the rate applied to the next dollar of income (the top bracket reached), whereas the effective or average rate equals total tax divided by total income. In a progressive system the effective rate is usually lower than the marginal rate.

questions.stem: Which schedule is used to report additional taxes, such as self-employment tax and the additional tax on early distributions, on Form 1040?
options: Schedule 1
Schedule 2
Schedule A
Schedule 3
questions.rationale: Schedule 2 reports additional taxes such as self-employment tax, the alternative minimum tax, and the 10% additional tax on early distributions. Schedule 1 handles additional income and adjustments, and Schedule 3 handles additional credits.

questions.stem: A taxpayer must compute the Alternative Minimum Tax. Which form is used to figure the AMT for an individual, and what general concept underlies it?
options: Form 6251, which recalculates income with certain preferences added back and an exemption applied to determine whether a minimum tax is owed
Form 4868, which extends the AMT due date
Form 8949, which reports AMT capital gains
Form 8862, which claims the AMT exemption
questions.rationale: Form 6251 is used to compute the individual Alternative Minimum Tax. It recalculates taxable income by adding back preference items and disallowed deductions, subtracts the AMT exemption, and imposes the AMT to the extent the tentative minimum tax exceeds the regular tax.

questions.stem: A taxpayer had a long-term capital gain of $5,000 from selling collectibles (such as coins) held for three years. How is this gain generally taxed compared to other long-term capital gains?
options: Tax-free because collectibles are personal-use property
At the same 0/15/20% rates as other long-term gains
At a maximum rate of 28% for the collectibles gain
At ordinary income rates only
questions.rationale: Net long-term capital gain from collectibles (such as coins, art, antiques) is taxed at a maximum rate of 28%, rather than the 0/15/20% rates that apply to most other long-term capital gains.

questions.stem: A taxpayer sold rental real estate at a gain. Part of the gain is attributable to depreciation previously deducted. How is the unrecaptured Section 1250 gain portion generally taxed for 2024?
options: At ordinary income rates up to 37%
At 0% as part of the home-sale exclusion
At a maximum rate of 25%
Tax-free because it is real estate
questions.rationale: When depreciable real property is sold at a gain, the portion attributable to prior straight-line depreciation is 'unrecaptured Section 1250 gain,' taxed at a maximum rate of 25%. The remaining gain is taxed at regular capital gains rates.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how a tax credit reduces a taxpayer's liability compared to gross tax?
options: It only affects payroll taxes
It reduces the computed tax liability directly
It reduces gross income before computing tax
It increases the standard deduction
questions.rationale: A tax credit reduces the computed tax liability dollar-for-dollar after the tax is figured, unlike a deduction, which reduces taxable income before the tax is computed.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has wages subject to federal income tax withholding plus self-employment income. Which statement about how their total tax is assembled on Form 1040 is most accurate?
options: Income tax on taxable income and self-employment tax are both computed and added together to determine total tax
Only one of the two taxes can apply in a given year
Self-employment income is exempt from income tax
Self-employment tax replaces the income tax on the business income
questions.rationale: Total tax on Form 1040 combines the regular income tax on taxable income with other taxes such as self-employment tax. Net self-employment earnings are subject to both income tax and self-employment tax.

questions.stem: A taxpayer realized a $4,000 short-term capital loss and a $10,000 long-term capital gain in 2024. After netting, what is the character and amount of the net result?
options: $6,000 net long-term capital gain
$14,000 of capital gain
$4,000 net long-term capital loss
$6,000 short-term capital gain
questions.rationale: Short-term and long-term amounts are netted. A net short-term loss offsets net long-term gain, so $10,000 long-term gain minus $4,000 short-term loss yields a $6,000 net long-term capital gain eligible for preferential rates.

questions.stem: An individual taxpayer expects to owe $6,000 in tax for 2024 with no withholding because all income is from self-employment. To avoid an underpayment penalty, how are estimated tax payments generally made?
options: Monthly to the Social Security Administration
In four quarterly installments during the tax year, generally due in April, June, September, and the following January
Only at year end in December
In a single lump sum on April 15 of the following year
questions.rationale: Individuals with income not subject to withholding generally must make four quarterly estimated tax payments using Form 1040-ES, due about April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15, to avoid an underpayment penalty.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to change the amount of federal income tax withheld from their paycheck. What should they do?
options: File Form 1040-ES with the IRS
Nothing can be changed during the year
File an amended return
Submit a new Form W-4 to their employer
questions.rationale: An employee adjusts the federal income tax withheld from wages by giving the employer a new Form W-4. This is separate from making estimated payments with Form 1040-ES for non-wage income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to claim a refund for an overpayment on their 2021 return, originally filed on time on April 15, 2022. Under the general refund statute of limitations, by when must they file the refund claim (assume no special extensions)?
options: By April 15, 2024
By April 15, 2025, which is three years from the original filing/due date
There is no deadline to claim a refund
By December 31, 2024
questions.rationale: A refund claim must generally be filed within three years from when the return was filed or its due date, or two years from when the tax was paid, whichever is later. For a 2021 return due April 15, 2022, the deadline is April 15, 2025.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a notice that their refund was applied to their spouse's past-due child support, even though the income and withholding belonged mostly to the taxpayer on their joint return. Which relief may allow the taxpayer to recover their share of the refund?
options: An offer in compromise
A penalty abatement request
Injured spouse allocation (Form 8379)
Innocent spouse relief
questions.rationale: Injured spouse allocation, claimed on Form 8379, allows a spouse to recover their portion of a joint refund that was offset to pay the other spouse's separate past-due debts, such as child support, defaulted student loans, or back taxes.

questions.stem: Generally, what is the smallest balance of tax due that triggers a potential underpayment penalty for an individual who did not pay enough through withholding and estimates?
questions.rationale: An individual generally avoids the underpayment penalty if the balance due after withholding and refundable credits is less than $1,000, or if they meet a safe harbor (90% of current-year or 100%/110% of prior-year tax).

questions.stem: A taxpayer files a return that omits more than 25% of their gross income. Under the special statute of limitations rule, how long does the IRS generally have to assess additional tax?
options: Three years, the normal period
No limit, because any omission means an unlimited period
Two years
Six years from the date the return was filed
questions.rationale: The normal three-year assessment period is extended to six years when a taxpayer omits more than 25% of gross income. The statute is unlimited for fraudulent returns or when no return is filed.

questions.stem: A taxpayer cannot pay their full tax bill and has limited assets and income. They believe they will never be able to pay the full amount. Which IRS program may allow them to settle the liability for less than the full amount owed?
options: An offer in compromise
An installment agreement
Innocent spouse relief
An extension to file
questions.rationale: An offer in compromise lets a taxpayer settle a tax debt for less than the full amount, typically based on doubt as to collectibility, doubt as to liability, or effective tax administration. An installment agreement instead spreads full payment over time.

questions.stem: What is the best advice for a taxpayer who wants to receive their federal refund as quickly as possible?
options: Request the refund be applied to next year only
Wait until October to file
File a paper return and request a paper check
File electronically and choose direct deposit
questions.rationale: Electronic filing combined with direct deposit is the fastest way to receive a refund, typically within a few weeks, compared to mailing a paper return and waiting for a paper check.

questions.stem: A taxpayer filed late and owes tax. They had no extension. Which combination of penalties generally applies, and which is typically larger per month?
options: The two penalties are always equal
Only the failure-to-file penalty applies
Both failure-to-file (generally 5% per month) and failure-to-pay (generally 0.5% per month) penalties apply, with failure-to-file being larger
Only the failure-to-pay penalty applies
questions.rationale: The failure-to-file penalty is generally 5% of unpaid tax per month (up to 25%), while the failure-to-pay penalty is generally 0.5% per month. When both apply, the failure-to-file penalty is reduced by the failure-to-pay penalty, but filing on time still avoids the larger penalty.

questions.stem: A first-time taxpayer with a clean compliance history was assessed a failure-to-file penalty for one late return. What relief might a preparer suggest to remove the penalty?
options: There is no way to remove a penalty once assessed
File an amended return to remove the penalty
Convert to Married Filing Separately
Request first-time penalty abatement based on a clean prior compliance history
questions.rationale: First-time penalty abatement (FTA) can remove failure-to-file, failure-to-pay, and failure-to-deposit penalties for a taxpayer with a clean compliance history (no significant penalties in the prior three years) who has filed required returns and arranged to pay.

questions.stem: A client received an IRS notice proposing additional tax (a CP2000) because income reported on a Form 1099 was not on the return. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Immediately pay the full proposed amount without review
Review the notice, verify whether the income was correctly reported, and respond by the deadline agreeing or disagreeing with documentation
File a brand-new original return for the year
Ignore the notice; it will resolve itself
questions.rationale: A CP2000 notice proposes changes based on income or deductions that do not match third-party information. The taxpayer should review it against their records and timely respond, agreeing or disagreeing with documentation, rather than ignoring it or blindly paying.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who works abroad qualifies for the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion. They want to claim it. Which form must they file with their return to elect and figure the exclusion?
options: Form 8862
Form 1116
Form 8889
Form 2555
questions.rationale: The Foreign Earned Income Exclusion is claimed on Form 2555, which also computes the foreign housing exclusion or deduction. Form 1116, by contrast, is for the Foreign Tax Credit.

questions.stem: A U.S. citizen wants to use the physical presence test to qualify for the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion. How many days must they be physically present in a foreign country to meet this test?
options: At least 90 days in a foreign country
The entire calendar year without exception
At least 330 full days during any 12 consecutive months
At least 183 days in a calendar year
questions.rationale: To meet the physical presence test for the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion, a taxpayer must be physically present in a foreign country or countries for at least 330 full days during any 12 consecutive months. The bona fide residence test is an alternative.

questions.stem: A taxpayer reports income from a farming operation. Which schedule is generally used to report profit or loss from farming on an individual return?
options: Schedule SE
Schedule F
Schedule E
Schedule C
questions.rationale: Profit or loss from farming is reported on Schedule F. Schedule C is for nonfarm businesses, Schedule E for rentals and pass-through income, and Schedule SE computes self-employment tax.

questions.stem: A decedent's estate is below the federal estate tax exemption, but the deceased had income earned but not yet received at death (such as a final paycheck and accrued interest). How is this 'income in respect of a decedent' (IRD) generally treated?
options: It receives a stepped-up basis and escapes income tax
It is never taxable to anyone
It is taxed only on the decedent's final individual return
It is taxable to the recipient (estate or beneficiary) and retains the same character it would have had to the decedent
questions.rationale: Income in respect of a decedent (IRD) is income the decedent earned but had not received at death. It is taxable to whoever receives it (estate or beneficiary), keeps its original character, and does not receive a basis step-up.

questions.stem: When must a final income tax return (Form 1040) be filed for a taxpayer who died during 2024?
options: Only the estate's Form 1041 is filed and no Form 1040
A final Form 1040 covering income through the date of death is generally due by the normal filing deadline for that year
It is always due within 30 days of death
A final return is never required for a deceased person
questions.rationale: A decedent's final Form 1040 reports income from the beginning of the year through the date of death and is generally due by the normal filing deadline. A separate Form 1041 may be required for income earned by the estate after death.

questions.stem: Which form is used to report income, deductions, and credits of an estate or trust that has income after the decedent's death?
options: Form 1065
Form 1041
Form 1040
Form 1120
questions.rationale: Form 1041 is filed by estates and trusts to report their income, deductions, and credits. The decedent's final individual income is reported on Form 1040.

questions.stem: A donor gave a single recipient $25,000 in cash in 2024. The annual gift tax exclusion is $18,000. Which statement is most accurate regarding the gift tax consequences?
options: The recipient must pay income tax on the $25,000
The full $25,000 is immediately subject to gift tax
The donor must file a gift tax return (Form 709), and $7,000 reduces the donor's lifetime exemption (no gift tax is likely due)
No gift tax return is required because gifts are always exempt
questions.rationale: When a gift to one person exceeds the annual exclusion ($18,000 for 2024), the donor must file Form 709. The excess ($7,000) reduces the donor's lifetime unified credit/exemption; actual gift tax is owed only after the large lifetime exemption is exhausted.

questions.stem: Which of the following gifts is generally NOT counted against the annual gift tax exclusion or the donor's lifetime exemption?
options: A gift of stock worth $30,000 to a friend
A $50,000 gift to a sibling
A $20,000 cash gift to an adult child
Tuition paid directly to a university on behalf of a grandchild
questions.rationale: Tuition paid directly to an educational institution and medical expenses paid directly to a provider are excluded from gift tax entirely (the qualified transfers exclusion), with no dollar limit, and do not use the annual exclusion or lifetime exemption.

questions.stem: A member of the U.S. Armed Forces on active duty receives a permanent change of station (PCS) move order. Which statement about moving expenses is correct for 2024?
options: Active-duty members moving due to a military order may still deduct unreimbursed moving expenses, unlike most other taxpayers
Moving expenses are never deductible by anyone
Only retirees may deduct moving expenses
All taxpayers may deduct moving expenses
