questions.rationale: The moving expense deduction is suspended for most taxpayers through 2025, but active-duty members of the Armed Forces who move due to a permanent change of station under military orders may still deduct qualifying unreimbursed moving expenses.

questions.stem: A nonresident alien who has U.S.-source wages effectively connected with a U.S. trade or business generally files which return?
options: Form 1041
Form 1040
Form 1040-SR
Form 1040-NR
questions.rationale: Nonresident aliens with U.S.-source income or income effectively connected with a U.S. trade or business file Form 1040-NR. Form 1040 (or 1040-SR for seniors) is used by U.S. citizens and resident aliens.

questions.stem: A foreign national was physically present in the U.S. for 130 days in 2024, 120 days in 2023, and 120 days in 2022. Under the substantial presence test, is this person treated as a U.S. resident for 2024? (Count all 2024 days, 1/3 of 2023 days, 1/6 of 2022 days.)
options: Yes, but only if they hold a green card
Yes, because the weighted total is at least 183 days and they were present at least 31 days in 2024
No, because foreign nationals can never be U.S. residents
No, because they were present fewer than 183 days in 2024 alone
questions.rationale: The substantial presence test counts all current-year days plus 1/3 of prior-year and 1/6 of second-prior-year days. Here 130 + 40 + 20 = 190 days meets the 183-day threshold, and with 31+ days in the current year, the person is a U.S. resident for tax purposes.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a distribution from a 529 qualified tuition program. The earnings portion was used for the beneficiary's qualified education expenses. How is the earnings portion taxed?
options: Fully taxable as ordinary income
Taxed at capital gains rates
Tax-free, because the earnings were used for qualified education expenses
Taxable plus a 10% penalty
questions.rationale: Distributions from a 529 plan are tax-free to the extent used for qualified education expenses. If a distribution exceeds qualified expenses, the earnings portion of the excess is taxable and generally subject to a 10% additional tax.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a Form 1099-C reporting $6,000 of canceled credit card debt. They were solvent both before and after the cancellation. How is the canceled debt generally treated?
options: Included in gross income as cancellation of debt income
Excluded because the taxpayer was solvent
Excluded from income because canceled debt is never taxable
Treated as a capital gain
questions.rationale: Forgiven debt is generally taxable as cancellation of debt income. Exclusions exist for bankruptcy, insolvency, qualified principal residence indebtedness, and certain farm or business debt. A fully solvent taxpayer with credit card debt forgiveness must include the $6,000.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's debt was canceled while they were insolvent (their liabilities exceeded the fair market value of their assets) by $10,000. The canceled debt was $4,000. How much of the canceled debt is excludable from income under the insolvency exclusion?
options: Only $2,000
$0; insolvency does not allow exclusion
$4,000, because the insolvency amount ($10,000) exceeds the canceled debt
questions.rationale: Canceled debt is excludable from income to the extent the taxpayer is insolvent immediately before the cancellation. Since insolvency ($10,000) exceeds the canceled debt ($4,000), the entire $4,000 is excluded (reported on Form 982).

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally excluded from gross income?
options: Severance pay received after a layoff
Bonuses paid by an employer
Qualified disaster relief payments for personal living expenses not otherwise compensated
Back pay awarded in a lawsuit
questions.rationale: Qualified disaster relief payments for personal, living, and funeral expenses not otherwise compensated are excluded from gross income. Severance pay, bonuses, and back pay are all taxable compensation.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $50,000 life insurance death benefit as the named beneficiary of a deceased relative's policy, paid in a lump sum. How is this generally treated for income tax purposes?
options: Fully taxable as ordinary income
Taxable to the extent it exceeds $25,000
Taxed at capital gains rates
Generally excluded from gross income when paid by reason of the insured's death
questions.rationale: Life insurance proceeds paid by reason of the insured's death are generally excluded from the beneficiary's gross income. Any interest paid on installment payouts, however, is taxable.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a settlement: $30,000 for physical personal injuries from a car accident and $5,000 of punitive damages. How are these amounts treated for income tax purposes?
options: Both amounts are fully taxable
Both amounts are fully excludable
The $30,000 for physical injuries is excludable, but the $5,000 of punitive damages is taxable
Only the punitive damages are excludable
questions.rationale: Damages received for physical personal injuries or sickness are excluded from gross income. Punitive damages, however, are generally taxable, even when awarded in connection with a physical injury claim.

questions.stem: A taxpayer with qualified business income (QBI) from a sole proprietorship has taxable income below the threshold where limitations apply. What is the general maximum QBI deduction percentage they may claim?
options: 50% of QBI
10% of QBI
20% of qualified business income
There is no QBI deduction for sole proprietors
questions.rationale: The Section 199A qualified business income deduction is generally up to 20% of QBI from pass-through businesses, including sole proprietorships. Above certain taxable income thresholds, wage and property limitations and SSTB rules may reduce or eliminate it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about the deductibility of personal casualty losses for individuals for 2024?
options: Personal casualty losses are generally deductible only if attributable to a federally declared disaster (subject to limits)
Only business casualty losses count
Personal casualty losses are never deductible under any circumstances
All personal casualty losses are fully deductible
questions.rationale: Through 2025, individuals may deduct personal casualty and theft losses only if they result from a federally declared disaster. Such losses are subject to a $100 reduction per event and a 10%-of-AGI floor.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to deduct a contribution of used clothing and household items to a qualified charity. What is the general requirement for the condition of these items to be deductible?
options: Only new items with tags qualify
Clothing donations are never deductible
The items must generally be in good used condition or better
Any clothing qualifies regardless of condition
questions.rationale: To deduct donated clothing and household goods, the items must generally be in good used condition or better. A deduction for an item valued over $500 that is not in good condition is allowed only with a qualified appraisal.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a Form 1099-NEC reporting $8,000 of nonemployee compensation for freelance work. Which statement about reporting this income is most accurate?
options: It is reported only if it exceeds $20,000
It is tax-free because no taxes were withheld
It is reported as wages on the wage line of Form 1040
It is reported as self-employment income on Schedule C, and net earnings are subject to self-employment tax
questions.rationale: Nonemployee compensation reported on Form 1099-NEC is self-employment income, generally reported on Schedule C. The resulting net earnings are subject to both income tax and self-employment tax when $400 or more.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has a passive rental real estate activity that generated a $15,000 loss in 2024. They actively participated and have modified AGI of $110,000. Under the special $25,000 allowance, how much of the loss may they generally deduct against nonpassive income?
options: The full $15,000
A reduced amount because the $25,000 allowance phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of MAGI
$0, because rental losses are never deductible
questions.rationale: Taxpayers who actively participate in rental real estate may deduct up to $25,000 of passive loss against other income. This allowance phases out 50 cents per dollar of MAGI between $100,000 and $150,000, fully disappearing at $150,000. At $110,000 MAGI, the allowance is reduced to $20,000.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's qualifying child for the Child Tax Credit must meet an age requirement. What is the age limit for a child to be a qualifying child for the Child Tax Credit (not the Credit for Other Dependents)?
options: Under age 24 if a student
Under age 17 at the end of the year
Under age 13 at the end of the year
Under age 19 at the end of the year
questions.rationale: For the Child Tax Credit, the qualifying child must be under age 17 at the end of the year (along with the other dependency tests and a valid SSN). The under-13 limit applies to the dependent care credit.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old is a full-time student for five months of 2024, earns $8,000, and lives with their parents all year. The parents provide more than half the student's support, and the student does not provide more than half of their own support. Can the parents claim the student as a qualifying child?
options: No, because the student is over 18
Yes, because as a full-time student under 24 who did not provide more than half their own support and meets residency, the student is a qualifying child
Yes, but only as a qualifying relative
No, because the student earned more than the gross income limit
questions.rationale: A child under age 24 who is a full-time student for at least five months, lives with the taxpayer more than half the year, and does not provide more than half of their own support is a qualifying child. There is no gross income test for a qualifying child.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is unsure which form to use. They have only wages, interest under $1,500, and want to take the standard deduction. Which form do nearly all individual taxpayers now use to file their federal income tax return?
options: Form 1065
Form 1040 (or Form 1040-SR for seniors)
Form 1040-EZ
Form 1040-A
questions.rationale: The IRS consolidated individual filing onto Form 1040 (with Form 1040-SR as a senior-friendly version). The older Forms 1040-EZ and 1040-A were discontinued.

questions.stem: A married couple lived in a community property state for all of 2024 and chose to file separately. Generally, how is their community income reported on the separate returns?
options: Community income is generally split equally between the two spouses
Each spouse reports only the income paid in their own name
All income is reported by the higher earner
Community property rules do not affect income reporting
questions.rationale: In community property states, married taxpayers filing separately generally each report half of the community income and half of community deductions, with separate property income reported by its owner. Special rules can apply when spouses live apart.

questions.stem: Which of the following itemized deductions is claimed on Schedule A?
options: Self-employment tax deduction
Home mortgage interest on a qualified residence
Student loan interest deduction
IRA contribution deduction
questions.rationale: Schedule A reports itemized deductions such as home mortgage interest, state and local taxes, charitable contributions, and medical expenses. IRA contributions, student loan interest, and one-half of SE tax are adjustments to income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is subject to the income phaseout for the American Opportunity Tax Credit. For a single filer, over what modified AGI range does the AOTC phase out for 2024?
options: It never phases out
questions.rationale: The American Opportunity Tax Credit phases out for single filers with MAGI between $80,000 and $90,000 ($160,000 to $180,000 for married filing jointly), and is unavailable above the top of the range.

questions.stem: How long must a capital asset be held to qualify for long-term capital gain treatment?
options: More than two years
More than one year
More than 6 months
Exactly one year
questions.rationale: To be long-term, a capital asset must be held for more than one year (the day after acquisition begins the holding period). A holding period of one year or less results in short-term treatment.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a state income tax refund but had taken the standard deduction in the prior year. How is the refund treated in the year received?
options: Taxable only if it exceeds $1,000
Not taxable, because no tax benefit was obtained from deducting state taxes
Fully taxable
Half taxable
questions.rationale: A state income tax refund is taxable only to the extent it produced a tax benefit. A taxpayer who took the standard deduction in the prior year received no benefit from deducting state taxes, so the refund is not taxable.

questions.stem: A taxpayer exercised a nonqualified stock option (NSO) from their employer. The fair market value of the stock exceeded the exercise price by $12,000 (the bargain element) at exercise. How is the bargain element generally treated for a regular-tax taxpayer?
options: It is never taxable
It is treated as ordinary compensation income in the year of exercise and is generally reported on Form W-2
It is not taxable until the stock is sold
It is a long-term capital gain at exercise
questions.rationale: When a nonqualified stock option is exercised, the bargain element (FMV minus exercise price) is ordinary compensation income reported on Form W-2 in the year of exercise. Later sale of the stock produces capital gain or loss based on the stepped-up basis.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $1,000 distribution from a Coverdell Education Savings Account (ESA), and the entire amount was used for the beneficiary's qualified elementary education expenses. How is the distribution treated?
options: Fully taxable to the beneficiary
Subject to a 10% penalty only
Taxable to the contributor
Tax-free, because it was used for qualified education expenses
questions.rationale: Distributions from a Coverdell Education Savings Account are tax-free to the extent used for qualified education expenses, which include elementary, secondary, and higher education costs. Nonqualified earnings are taxable and may incur a 10% additional tax.

questions.stem: Marcus, age 24, was a full-time student for 7 months in 2024, did not provide more than half of his own support, and lived with his parents all year. Which dependency test does the 7-month full-time student status most directly affect?
options: The age test for a qualifying child
The joint return test
The gross income test for a qualifying relative
The relationship test
questions.rationale: A child under age 24 who is a full-time student for at least part of 5 calendar months can satisfy the age test for qualifying-child status.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: Three siblings together provide 100% of their mother's support: Ann 12%, Beth 40%, and Carl 48%. Their mother is otherwise a qualifying relative. Under a multiple support agreement, who is eligible to claim her as a dependent?
options: Only Carl, because he provided the most
Either Beth or Carl, because each provided more than 10%
All three siblings may split the dependency
Ann only, by signing Form 2120
questions.rationale: Under a multiple support agreement, a contributor who paid over 10% of support may claim the dependent if the group paid over half and the others sign Form 2120.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: Dana and Eli divorced in 2024. Their child lived with Dana (the custodial parent) for 8 months. Eli wants to claim the child tax credit. What is required for Eli to do so?
options: A court decree dated after 2008 attached to the return is sufficient
Eli must have paid more than half the child's support
Dana must sign Form 8332 releasing the dependency claim to Eli
Nothing; the noncustodial parent always gets the child tax credit
questions.rationale: A noncustodial parent may claim a child and the child tax credit only if the custodial parent signs Form 8332 releasing the claim.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: Frank is single, age 40, not anyone's dependent, with 2024 gross income of $14,200 (all wages). Based solely on the gross-income filing threshold, is he required to file a 2024 return?
options: Yes, all wage earners must file
Yes, because $14,200 exceeds $13,850
No, because $14,200 is below the $14,600 single filing threshold
No, because withholding makes filing optional
questions.rationale: For 2024, a single taxpayer under 65 must file when gross income reaches $14,600; $14,200 is below that threshold.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A married couple lived apart the entire last 6 months of 2024. Their qualifying child lived with the wife, who paid more than half the cost of keeping up the home. They will not file jointly. Which filing status may the wife use?
options: Married filing separately only
Qualifying surviving spouse
Head of household
Single
questions.rationale: Under the abandoned-spouse rules, a married taxpayer living apart for the last half of the year who maintains a home for a qualifying child can file as head of household.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: George received an IRS notice that someone already filed using his Social Security number. What is the appropriate action to report the suspected tax-related identity theft to the IRS?
options: File Form 14039, Identity Theft Affidavit
File Form 8857, Innocent Spouse Relief
Amend the prior return with Form 1040-X
File Form 911, Request for Taxpayer Advocate Service Assistance
questions.rationale: Form 14039, Identity Theft Affidavit, is filed to report tax-related identity theft to the IRS.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of obtaining an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN)?
options: To qualify for Social Security benefits
To establish state residency
To provide a tax processing number for individuals not eligible for an SSN
To allow employment authorization in the U.S.
questions.rationale: An ITIN is a tax processing number for people required to have a U.S. taxpayer ID but who are not eligible for an SSN.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer's spouse died in March 2024. They have a dependent child. For tax year 2024 itself, what is the most favorable filing status generally available?
options: Qualifying surviving spouse
Married filing jointly
Head of household
Single
questions.rationale: In the year a spouse dies, the surviving spouse can usually file a joint return; QSS status applies to the following two years.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: Hannah is a U.S. citizen married to a nonresident alien. She wants to file jointly and treat her spouse as a resident for the whole year. What is required?
options: No election; marriage to a citizen makes the spouse a resident automatically
Form W-7 only, with no income reporting changes
The nonresident spouse must first obtain a green card
A written election under IRC §6013(g) attached to the joint return, reporting worldwide income
questions.rationale: A citizen and nonresident-alien spouse may elect under §6013(g) to file jointly, treating the NRA as a resident and reporting worldwide income.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally NOT considered support when applying the support test for a qualifying relative?
options: Federal income taxes the dependent paid on their own income
Medical and dental care provided
Lodging valued at fair rental value
Clothing and recreation expenses
questions.rationale: Items like income taxes paid, Social Security taxes, life insurance premiums, and funeral costs are excluded from the support computation.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: Ines had $9,000 of credit card debt canceled in 2024. Immediately before the cancellation, her total liabilities were $40,000 and the FMV of her assets was $36,000. How much of the canceled debt may she exclude under the insolvency exception?
questions.rationale: Canceled debt is excludable only to the extent of insolvency (liabilities minus asset FMV); the excess is taxable income.

questions.stem: Jamal, single, sold his main home in 2024 for a $310,000 gain. He owned and used it as his principal residence for 2 of the last 5 years. He has no prior §121 exclusion in the look-back period. How much gain is taxable?
questions.rationale: Section 121 lets a single taxpayer exclude up to $250,000 of gain on a main home; gain above that is taxable.

questions.stem: Kira received Social Security benefits of $20,000 in 2024. Her other income (including tax-exempt interest) produced provisional income of $40,000, and she files single. What is the maximum portion of her Social Security benefits that could be taxable?
questions.rationale: Up to 85% of Social Security benefits is taxable once provisional income exceeds the upper threshold ($34,000 single).

questions.stem: Which of the following fringe benefits is generally TAXABLE to the employee?
options: Employer-provided cell phone for business use
De minimis occasional snacks
Qualified employee discounts within limits
Cash bonus of $500
questions.rationale: Cash and cash-equivalent fringe benefits, including bonuses, are taxable wages even when small.

questions.stem: Leo won $5,000 gambling and had $3,200 of documented gambling losses in 2024. He does not itemize. How are these reported?
options: Gambling winnings under $5,000 are not taxable
Losses offset winnings automatically on Schedule 1
Net $1,800 is reported as other income
The full $5,000 is included in gross income; losses are deductible only if he itemizes
questions.rationale: Gambling winnings are fully taxable; losses are deductible only as itemized deductions up to the amount of winnings.

questions.stem: Maria inherited stock from her father, who died in 2024. His basis was $10,000; the FMV at the date of death was $45,000. Maria sells it for $47,000 three months later. What is her gain and its character?
options: $2,000 short-term gain
$2,000 long-term gain
$37,000 short-term gain
$37,000 long-term gain
questions.rationale: Inherited property takes a date-of-death FMV basis and is always treated as long-term when sold.

questions.stem: Nora received a $12,000 distribution from her traditional IRA in 2024 at age 52. She had made $20,000 of nondeductible contributions, and the total value of all her traditional IRAs at year-end was $80,000. Using the pro-rata rule, what portion of the $12,000 is nontaxable?
options: $2,609 approximately
questions.rationale: The IRA pro-rata rule recovers basis proportionally: nontaxable portion equals basis divided by total IRA value (including the distribution).

questions.stem: Owen received $1,500 of municipal bond interest and $800 of interest on a federal income tax refund in 2024. What is taxable on his federal return?
options: $800 only
$1,500 only
Neither amount
Both amounts
questions.rationale: Municipal bond interest is federally tax-exempt, but interest the IRS pays on a refund is taxable income.

questions.stem: Priya, a cash-basis taxpayer, received a $4,000 advance in December 2024 for services she will perform in 2025. When is the $4,000 taxable?
options: Split evenly between 2024 and 2025
Not taxable because it is a deposit
2025, when services are performed
2024, when received
questions.rationale: Cash-basis taxpayers generally report income, including advance payments for services, in the year of receipt.

questions.stem: Quinn exchanged a rental apartment building (FMV $500,000, adjusted basis $300,000) for another rental building (FMV $470,000) plus $30,000 cash in a properly structured §1031 exchange in 2024. How much gain is recognized?
questions.rationale: In a like-kind exchange, recognized gain equals the lesser of realized gain or boot received.

questions.stem: An employee received $200 worth of company logo merchandise as a length-of-service award (tangible personal property) under a qualified plan. How is it generally treated?
options: Treated as a nontaxable gift
Always fully taxable as wages
Excludable within the employee achievement award limits
Taxable only if over $25
questions.rationale: Qualified employee achievement awards of tangible personal property are excludable within statutory limits, not treated as gifts.

questions.stem: Tomas and Uma file jointly with one qualifying child age 6. Their modified AGI is $180,000. How much Child Tax Credit (before any other limitation) may they claim for 2024?
questions.rationale: The Child Tax Credit is $2,000 per qualifying child under 17, phasing out only above $400,000 MAGI for joint filers.

questions.stem: Vera paid $5,000 of qualified tuition for her first-year college student in 2024. Her MAGI is $82,000 (single). The maximum AOTC is $2,500 and the single phaseout range is $80,000 to $90,000. What is her allowable AOTC?
questions.rationale: The AOTC phases out for singles between $80,000 and $90,000 MAGI; at $82,000, 80% of the $2,500 maximum ($2,000) remains.

questions.stem: Walt withdrew $6,000 from a 529 plan in 2024 but only $4,000 went to qualified education expenses. The $2,000 nonqualified portion includes $700 of earnings. What is the federal consequence of the nonqualified portion?
options: The entire $6,000 is taxable
The full $2,000 is taxable plus a 10% penalty
No tax because 529 distributions are always tax-free
Only the $700 earnings are taxable, plus a 10% additional tax on the $700
questions.rationale: For nonqualified 529 distributions, only the earnings portion is taxable and subject to a 10% additional tax.

questions.stem: Xavier, age 45, has self-only HDHP coverage all of 2024. What is his maximum HSA contribution, and is there a catch-up?
options: $8,300 with a $1,000 catch-up
$3,850 with a $1,000 catch-up
$4,150 with no catch-up (catch-up begins at 55)
$4,150 plus a $1,000 catch-up
questions.rationale: For 2024, the self-only HSA limit is $4,150; the $1,000 catch-up starts at age 55.

questions.stem: Yara incurred $12,000 of unreimbursed qualified medical expenses in 2024 with AGI of $80,000. What is her allowable itemized medical deduction (before considering whether she itemizes)?
questions.rationale: Only medical expenses exceeding 7.5% of AGI are deductible as an itemized deduction.

questions.stem: Zoe paid $9,500 in state income taxes, $4,000 in property taxes, and $1,000 in sales tax in 2024. What is her maximum deductible state and local tax (SALT) itemized deduction?
questions.rationale: The combined deduction for state and local income (or sales) and property taxes is capped at $10,000.

questions.stem: Aaron and Bri adopted a child in 2024 with $20,000 of qualified adoption expenses. The maximum adoption credit for 2024 is $16,810. Their MAGI is below the phaseout. How much adoption credit may they claim, and what type of credit is it?
options: $13,810, nonrefundable
$20,000, refundable
$16,810, fully refundable
$16,810, nonrefundable with carryforward
questions.rationale: The 2024 adoption credit is capped at $16,810, is nonrefundable, and any excess carries forward up to five years.

questions.stem: Carla pays a daycare $9,000 to care for her two children under 13 so she can work. Her AGI is $50,000 and her tax before credits is sufficient. For the Child and Dependent Care Credit, what is the maximum amount of expenses she can use?
questions.rationale: The Child and Dependent Care Credit caps eligible expenses at $3,000 for one and $6,000 for two or more qualifying persons.

questions.stem: Which contribution is generally deductible as a charitable contribution if the taxpayer itemizes?
options: A political campaign contribution
The value of volunteer time donated
A donation to a qualified 501(c)(3) public charity
A gift directly to a needy individual
questions.rationale: Only contributions to qualified organizations are deductible; donated time, political gifts, and gifts to individuals are not.

questions.stem: Dev contributed appreciated stock held 3 years (FMV $8,000, basis $2,000) to a public charity in 2024. Assuming AGI limits are not exceeded, what is his charitable deduction?
questions.rationale: Long-term appreciated publicly traded stock donated to a public charity is generally deductible at fair market value.

questions.stem: Farah paid $3,000 of student loan interest in 2024. Her MAGI is $70,000 (single); the 2024 single phaseout begins at $80,000. What is her deduction?
options: $2,000 after phaseout
questions.rationale: Student loan interest is deductible up to $2,500 above the line; phaseout for singles begins at $80,000 MAGI for 2024.

questions.stem: Grace, single with no qualifying children, is age 28 and has earned income of $14,000 and AGI of $14,000 in 2024. She is not a dependent and not a full-time student. Is she potentially eligible for the Earned Income Credit?
options: No, the EIC requires a qualifying child
No, she earns too much regardless of children
Yes, childless workers age 25 to 64 may qualify if within income limits
Yes, but only if she is over age 65
questions.rationale: Childless workers between ages 25 and 64 who meet income limits may claim a reduced Earned Income Credit.

questions.stem: Ivy and Jon (MFJ) had combined Medicare wages of $300,000 in 2024. The Additional Medicare Tax threshold for MFJ is $250,000. How much of their wages is subject to the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax?
questions.rationale: The 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies to earned income exceeding the filing-status threshold ($250,000 for MFJ).

questions.stem: Kenji bought 2024 Marketplace health coverage and received advance premium tax credits. At year-end his actual income was higher than estimated, exceeding 400% of the federal poverty line. What is the consequence?
options: Advance credits are never repaid
He keeps all advance credits regardless of income
He automatically qualifies for the full PTC
He may have to repay excess advance premium tax credits, subject to repayment caps if under 400% FPL
questions.rationale: Advance premium tax credits are reconciled on Form 8962; excess credits may be repaid, with repayment caps only below 400% of the federal poverty line.

questions.stem: Lena, single, is an active participant in her employer's 401(k) and has MAGI of $90,000 in 2024. The active-participant traditional IRA deduction phaseout for singles is $77,000 to $87,000. How much of a $6,000 traditional IRA contribution is deductible?
questions.rationale: An active plan participant loses the traditional IRA deduction entirely once MAGI exceeds the top of the phaseout range.

questions.stem: Mei had a $9,000 net long-term capital loss and a $3,000 net short-term capital gain in 2024 (no other capital transactions). How much capital loss can she deduct against ordinary income, and what carries over?
options: $3,000 deduction, $6,000 carryover
$9,000 deduction, $0 carryover
$6,000 deduction, $0 carryover
$3,000 deduction, $3,000 carryover
questions.rationale: After netting, up to $3,000 of net capital loss offsets ordinary income annually, with the remainder carried forward.

questions.stem: Noah, single, has 2024 taxable income of $48,000, including a $5,000 net long-term capital gain. The 0% LTCG bracket for singles tops out at $47,025. Roughly how is the gain taxed?
options: Entirely at 0%
Entirely at 20%
Entirely at 15%
Part at 0% and part at 15%
questions.rationale: Long-term capital gains stack on ordinary income; gain spanning the 0% ceiling is taxed partly at 0% and partly at 15%.

questions.stem: Which of the following income items can trigger the alternative minimum tax (AMT) as a preference or adjustment for an individual?
options: Tax-exempt interest from certain private activity bonds
Qualified dividends
Wages reported on Form W-2
Standard deduction for AMT purposes is allowed in full
questions.rationale: Interest on certain private activity bonds is an AMT preference item, and the standard deduction is not allowed for AMT.

questions.stem: Olivia owes $1,500 of self-employment tax for 2024. How does this affect her income tax return beyond the tax itself?
options: She may deduct the full SE tax as an itemized deduction
She gets no related deduction
SE tax replaces her income tax
She may deduct one-half of the SE tax as an adjustment to income
questions.rationale: A taxpayer may deduct one-half of self-employment tax as an adjustment to income.

questions.stem: Pablo's 2023 total tax was $20,000 and his 2024 AGI was over $150,000. To avoid an underpayment penalty using the prior-year safe harbor, what percentage of his 2023 tax must his 2024 estimated payments/withholding generally equal?
questions.rationale: Higher-income taxpayers (prior-year AGI over $150,000) must pay 110% of the prior-year tax to use the prior-year safe harbor.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's regular tax liability before credits is $4,000, and they have a $5,000 nonrefundable credit. Ignoring carryovers, what is the immediate effect?
options: Tax becomes negative $1,000
Tax is reduced to $0 and they receive $1,000 as a refund
Tax is reduced to $0; the extra $1,000 cannot create a refund
The credit is fully refundable
questions.rationale: Nonrefundable credits reduce tax to zero at most; excess amounts do not create refunds.

questions.stem: Rosa, married filing jointly, has 2024 taxable income of $400,000 from a specified service trade or business (consulting). For the qualified business income (QBI) deduction, what is the effect of being above the MFJ phaseout ceiling?
options: She gets the full 20% QBI deduction
QBI applies only to C corporations
SSTB income always qualifies regardless of income
The QBI deduction for an SSTB is fully phased out at her income level
questions.rationale: The QBI deduction for a specified service trade or business is fully phased out above the applicable taxable-income threshold.

questions.stem: Sara, single, has 2024 taxable income of $60,000. She is figuring her tax. Which statement about marginal vs. effective rates is correct?
options: Only the income within each bracket is taxed at that bracket's rate
The effective rate equals the marginal rate
Her entire income is taxed at her top bracket rate
Brackets do not apply to single filers
questions.rationale: Under the progressive system, each bracket's rate applies only to income within that bracket, so the effective rate is below the marginal rate.

questions.stem: Theo received a state income tax refund of $900 in 2024 for tax year 2023. In 2023 he claimed the standard deduction. How much of the refund is taxable in 2024?
options: Depends on his 2024 bracket
questions.rationale: Under the tax benefit rule, a state tax refund is taxable only to the extent the prior deduction reduced tax; standard-deduction filers exclude it.

questions.stem: A client realizes in June 2024 that they failed to report $5,000 of freelance income on their already-filed 2023 return. What should the practitioner advise?
options: Wait for the IRS to find it
Ignore it since the return is filed
Report it on the 2024 return instead
File Form 1040-X to amend the 2023 return and pay any additional tax
questions.rationale: Discovered omissions should be corrected by filing Form 1040-X for the affected year and paying any additional tax promptly.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's joint refund was applied entirely to the other spouse's past-due child support. The first spouse wants their share of the refund. Which form should they file?
options: Form 8379, Injured Spouse Allocation
Form 911, Taxpayer Advocate request
Form 1040-X, Amended Return
Form 8857, Innocent Spouse Relief
questions.rationale: Form 8379, Injured Spouse Allocation, lets a non-liable spouse claim their portion of a joint refund seized for the other spouse's separate debt.

questions.stem: A spouse signed a joint return but did not know the other spouse omitted significant income, and it would be unfair to hold them liable. Which relief is most appropriate?
options: An installment agreement
An offer in compromise
Injured spouse relief
Innocent spouse relief under §6015
questions.rationale: Innocent spouse relief under §6015 can relieve a spouse from joint liability for an understatement they did not know about when it would be inequitable to hold them liable.

questions.stem: How long should taxpayers generally keep records supporting income and deductions on a filed return, in the typical case?
options: At least 3 years from the date filed (the general assessment period)
Indefinitely for all records
1 year
6 months
questions.rationale: Records should generally be kept at least three years, matching the standard assessment statute of limitations.

questions.stem: A client wants to reduce next year's tax. Which is a legitimate planning strategy a practitioner may suggest?
options: Underreport tip income
Claim dependents who do not qualify
Backdate documents to an earlier year
Maximize deductible retirement plan contributions before year-end
questions.rationale: Legitimate planning includes maximizing deductible retirement contributions; misreporting income or dependents is illegal.

questions.stem: A taxpayer cannot pay the full balance due by the filing deadline. What should the practitioner advise to minimize penalties?
options: Do not file until they can pay in full
File the return on time and request an installment agreement
Request an extension, which extends time to pay
File a fraudulent return showing no tax
questions.rationale: Filing on time avoids the larger failure-to-file penalty; payment can be arranged through an installment agreement.

questions.stem: A taxpayer faces a substantial balance they likely cannot ever fully pay and wants to settle for less based on doubt as to collectibility. Which option fits?
options: Injured spouse allocation
Offer in compromise
Innocent spouse relief
Currently not collectible status only
questions.rationale: An offer in compromise lets a taxpayer settle a tax debt for less than the full amount, including on doubt-as-to-collectibility grounds.

questions.stem: A client asks whether they can deduct commuting costs from home to their regular office. What is the correct advice?
options: Yes, if they use their own car
Yes, all commuting is deductible
No, ordinary commuting from home to a regular workplace is a nondeductible personal expense
Only the mileage over 20 miles is deductible
questions.rationale: Commuting between home and a regular workplace is a personal, nondeductible expense.

questions.stem: A minister's salary and housing allowance are subject to which tax for Social Security/Medicare purposes, absent an approved exemption?
options: FICA withholding as an employee
Self-employment tax (SECA) on ministerial earnings including the housing allowance
Only Medicare tax
No Social Security tax at all
questions.rationale: Ministers pay self-employment tax (SECA) on ministerial earnings, and the housing allowance is included in the SE tax base.

questions.stem: A taxpayer can elect to include otherwise-excludable combat pay in earned income for one specific purpose. What is the typical reason to make this election?
options: To avoid self-employment tax
To potentially increase the Earned Income Credit or additional child tax credit
To increase the standard deduction
To make the pay deductible
questions.rationale: Electing to include nontaxable combat pay as earned income can increase refundable credits like the EIC and additional child tax credit.

questions.stem: A taxpayer reports rental of a vacation home used personally 30 days and rented 100 days in 2024. Because personal use exceeds the greater of 14 days or 10% of rental days, what is the key limitation?
options: Losses are fully deductible against wages
Rental deductions are limited to rental income (no rental loss allowed)
No expenses are deductible
The home is treated as fully personal
questions.rationale: When personal use of a dwelling exceeds the threshold, rental deductions are capped at rental income and no loss is allowed.

questions.stem: A taxpayer actively participates in a rental real estate activity and has a $30,000 loss in 2024. Their MAGI is $110,000. How much of the special $25,000 allowance is available?
questions.rationale: The $25,000 active-participation rental loss allowance phases out 50% for MAGI between $100,000 and $150,000.

questions.stem: A self-employed individual had a $4,000 net casualty loss to personal-use property in a federally declared disaster area in 2024. How may this be claimed?
options: Not deductible at all
As an itemized deduction after the $100-per-event floor and 10%-of-AGI reduction
Fully deductible with no limits
As a business expense on Schedule C
questions.rationale: Personal casualty losses from federally declared disasters are itemized deductions reduced by $100 per event and 10% of AGI.

questions.stem: A taxpayer engaged in an activity not for profit (a hobby) earned $3,000 in 2024 and had $4,000 of related expenses. How are the income and expenses treated for 2024?
options: Report $3,000 income; hobby expenses are generally not deductible for individuals
Report $3,000 income; deduct $4,000 fully against it
Neither income nor expense is reported
Net to a $1,000 loss on Schedule C
questions.rationale: Hobby income is taxable, but under current law the related expenses are generally not deductible for individuals.

questions.stem: A self-employed sole proprietor reports business income and expenses on which schedule?
options: Schedule B
Schedule C
Schedule A
Schedule E
questions.rationale: A sole proprietor reports business profit or loss on Schedule C.

questions.stem: Beatriz received a $7,000 distribution from a Roth IRA in 2024. She is 60 and opened the Roth 8 years ago. How is the distribution taxed?
options: Fully taxable as ordinary income
Subject to a 10% penalty
Tax-free as a qualified distribution
Only the earnings are taxable
questions.rationale: A Roth IRA distribution is qualified and tax-free if made after age 59 1/2 and the 5-year holding period is met.

questions.stem: Carlos, age 50, took a $10,000 early distribution from his traditional IRA in 2024 to pay $10,000 of qualified higher education expenses for his daughter. The funds are otherwise taxable. What is the penalty consequence?
options: 10% penalty on the full $10,000
No 10% additional tax due to the higher education exception
The distribution is entirely tax-free
Penalty applies only to half
questions.rationale: Early IRA distributions used for qualified higher education expenses avoid the 10% penalty but remain subject to income tax.

questions.stem: Which credit is available to lower-income taxpayers who make eligible contributions to a retirement account, subject to AGI limits?
options: The Premium Tax Credit
The Adoption Credit
The Saver's Credit (Retirement Savings Contributions Credit)
The Foreign Tax Credit
questions.rationale: The Saver's Credit gives eligible lower-income taxpayers a credit for contributions to retirement accounts.

questions.stem: Diego, single, contributed $2,000 to his IRA in 2024 and has AGI of $20,000. The Saver's Credit rate for his AGI band is 50%. What is his Saver's Credit, given the maximum contribution counted is $2,000?
questions.rationale: The Saver's Credit equals the applicable percentage (here 50%) of up to $2,000 of eligible contributions.

questions.stem: Which tax is computed on Schedule SE for a self-employed individual?
options: Additional Medicare tax only
Alternative minimum tax
Net investment income tax
Self-employment tax (Social Security and Medicare)
questions.rationale: Schedule SE computes self-employment tax (the Social Security and Medicare portions) on net self-employment earnings.

questions.stem: Which of the following individuals can be claimed as a qualifying relative dependent, assuming all other tests are met and 2024 gross income limit is $5,050?
options: A sibling who filed a joint return claiming a refund of all withholding plus a credit
A cousin who lived with the taxpayer all year and earned $4,000
A friend who earned $9,000
A parent who earned $6,000
questions.rationale: A qualifying relative must have gross income under the annual limit ($5,050 for 2024) and meet the other dependency tests.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: Elaine's employer paid $60,000 of group-term life insurance coverage on her behalf in 2024. How much of the cost is generally taxable to her?
options: The cost (per IRS table) of coverage exceeding $50,000
Half of the premium
Nothing, since employer-paid insurance is always tax-free
The full cost of all coverage
questions.rationale: Employer-provided group-term life insurance is tax-free up to $50,000; the IRS table cost of coverage above that is taxable.

questions.stem: Felix sold §1244 small business stock at a $60,000 loss in 2024. He is single. How is the loss generally treated?
options: Entirely as an ordinary loss with no limit
Nondeductible because it is a personal loss
Entirely as a capital loss limited to $3,000 per year
Up to $50,000 as an ordinary loss, with the remainder as a capital loss
questions.rationale: Losses on §1244 small business stock are ordinary up to $50,000 ($100,000 MFJ) annually, with any excess treated as capital loss.

questions.stem: Gina paid $1,200 of qualified mortgage insurance premiums and $9,000 of home mortgage interest on acquisition debt of $300,000 in 2024. Which is generally deductible as an itemized deduction for 2024?
options: Only the mortgage insurance premiums
Neither item
The $9,000 mortgage interest on acquisition debt
Both items in full
questions.rationale: Home mortgage interest on acquisition debt is deductible; the mortgage insurance premium deduction expired after 2021.

questions.stem: Henry, single, age 67, is figuring his standard deduction for 2024. The base single standard deduction is $14,600 and the additional amount for being 65 or older is $1,950. What is his standard deduction?
questions.rationale: Taxpayers 65 or older get an additional standard deduction; for a single filer in 2024 that is $14,600 + $1,950 = $16,550.

questions.stem: Isabel must make 2024 estimated tax payments. Her 2024 expected tax is $12,000 and withholding is $3,000. Using the 90%-of-current-year safe harbor, what minimum total must be covered by withholding plus estimates to avoid penalty (assume prior-year safe harbor is higher)?
questions.rationale: One safe harbor is paying at least 90% of the current-year tax through withholding and estimates.

questions.stem: Jorge cashed Series EE U.S. savings bonds and used the proceeds for his daughter's qualified college tuition in 2024. His MAGI is within limits. How might the bond interest be treated?
options: Always fully taxable
Taxable at a flat 10%
Tax-deferred indefinitely
Potentially excludable under the education savings bond exclusion
questions.rationale: Series EE/I bond interest may be excludable when used for qualified higher education, subject to MAGI limits.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a Form 1099-K reporting $15,000 of payments for selling handmade goods online as a business in 2024. How should this be reported?
options: Ignored because 1099-K amounts are informational
As capital gains on Schedule D
As wages on line 1
As business gross receipts on Schedule C
questions.rationale: Form 1099-K business proceeds are reported as gross receipts on Schedule C, not ignored.

questions.stem: Kim contributed $300 cash to a qualified charity in 2024 but takes the standard deduction. How much of the contribution can she deduct?
options: $300 above the line
$300 as an itemized deduction
$0, because the above-the-line charitable deduction was not available for 2024
questions.rationale: The temporary above-the-line charitable deduction for non-itemizers expired after 2021, so standard-deduction filers get no charitable deduction for 2024.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally TAXABLE income?
options: Tips received from customers
Gifts received from a relative
Workers' compensation for a job injury
A qualified scholarship used for tuition
questions.rationale: Tips are taxable income; qualified scholarships, workers' comp, and gifts received are generally not.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's qualifying child meets all tests for two people (the mother and the grandmother) who lived in the same household. If both could claim the child and they cannot agree, who has the right under the tie-breaker rules?
options: The grandmother automatically
They must split the benefits
Whoever files first
The parent (the mother)
questions.rationale: The tie-breaker rules give a parent priority over a non-parent when more than one person could claim the same qualifying child.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: Which item is added back in computing alternative minimum taxable income (AMTI) for many individuals?
options: Charitable contributions
State and local taxes deducted on Schedule A
Home mortgage interest on acquisition debt
Medical expenses above 10% of AGI
questions.rationale: State and local taxes deducted on Schedule A are a common AMT add-back.

questions.stem: Laila has three qualifying children and earned income of $25,000 in 2024 with no investment income issues. She owes $0 income tax before credits. Which credit can still produce a refund for her?
options: The Earned Income Credit and the refundable Additional Child Tax Credit
The Lifetime Learning Credit
The Foreign Tax Credit
The nonrefundable portion of the Child Tax Credit only
questions.rationale: Refundable credits like the EIC and the Additional Child Tax Credit can produce refunds even when income tax is already zero.

questions.stem: Marco received $4,000 in dividends in 2024, all reported as qualified dividends. How are qualified dividends generally taxed?
options: At a flat 28% rate
As ordinary income at marginal rates
At the lower long-term capital gains rates
Always tax-free
questions.rationale: Qualified dividends are taxed at the preferential long-term capital gains rates.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has passive losses of $12,000 from a limited partnership in 2024 but only $4,000 of passive income from another activity. They do not materially participate in either. What happens to the excess loss?
options: Fully deductible against portfolio income
Permanently disallowed
$4,000 offsets passive income; the remaining $8,000 is suspended and carried forward
Fully deductible against wages
questions.rationale: Passive activity losses offset passive income only; the excess is suspended and carried forward to future years.

questions.stem: Nadia, single with MAGI of $250,000, has a qualifying child age 4. The Child Tax Credit phaseout begins at $200,000 for single filers and reduces $50 per $1,000 of excess. By how much is her $2,000 CTC reduced?
options: $2,000 (fully eliminated)
questions.rationale: The CTC phases out $50 per $1,000 of MAGI over the threshold; a $50,000 excess yields a $2,500 reduction, eliminating the credit.

questions.stem: Long-term capital gain results from the sale of a capital asset held for more than what period?
options: 18 months
1 year
6 months
2 years
questions.rationale: A capital asset must be held more than one year to qualify for long-term capital gain treatment.

questions.stem: Omar received a $2,000 state income tax refund and $300 of interest from a corporate bond in 2024, and a $1,000 gift from his aunt. Which amounts are potentially taxable?
options: All three
The corporate bond interest, and the state refund only if it provided a prior tax benefit
Only the gift
Only the state refund
questions.rationale: Corporate bond interest is taxable; a state refund is taxable only under the tax benefit rule; gifts received are not taxable.

questions.stem: A U.S. citizen living abroad must report worldwide income. To avoid double taxation on foreign-taxed income not excluded under the FEIE, what may they claim?
options: A reduced filing requirement
The Foreign Tax Credit or a deduction for foreign taxes paid
An automatic exemption from U.S. tax
A second standard deduction
questions.rationale: Foreign taxes on income that is taxed by both countries can be relieved via the Foreign Tax Credit or a deduction.

questions.stem: Petra paid for daycare so she could work, but her earned income was only $2,500 while her spouse (filing jointly) earned $60,000. Their dependent care expenses were $5,000. For the Child and Dependent Care Credit, what limits the expenses they can use?
options: $6,000 because they have one child
The full $5,000 with no earned-income limit
Their combined earned income
The lower-earning spouse's earned income of $2,500
questions.rationale: For married couples, dependent care expenses used for the credit cannot exceed the earned income of the lower-earning spouse.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who is legally married on December 31, 2024, but separated (no decree of divorce or separate maintenance) is considered what for the full 2024 year?
options: Married
Head of household automatically
Unmarried
Single
questions.rationale: Marital status is determined on the last day of the year; a couple without a final decree is treated as married.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes a refundable tax credit?
options: It can only reduce tax to zero
It can reduce tax below zero and generate a refund
It must be carried forward if unused
It applies only to business taxpayers
questions.rationale: A refundable credit can reduce tax below zero and result in a refund of the excess amount.

questions.stem: Rhea sold a rental property in 2024. Total depreciation taken was $40,000, and she had a $100,000 gain. How is the unrecaptured §1250 portion generally taxed?
options: Entirely at 0%
At ordinary rates up to 37%
At a maximum 25% rate for the depreciation portion
At a flat 15% for the whole gain
questions.rationale: Unrecaptured §1250 gain from real property depreciation is taxed at a maximum rate of 25%.

questions.stem: Sofia paid $2,000 of qualified expenses for an energy-efficient home improvement (e.g., exterior doors and insulation) in 2024. What credit may apply?
options: The Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit
The Child Tax Credit
The Earned Income Credit
The Saver's Credit
questions.rationale: Qualifying energy-efficient home improvements may yield the Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit, subject to annual caps.

questions.stem: A practitioner notices a client's prior-year return (prepared elsewhere) contains a clear error that overstated a deduction. What is the appropriate action?
options: Report the prior preparer to the police
Say nothing because they did not prepare it
Refuse to prepare the current-year return
Advise the client of the error and the potential consequences of not correcting it
questions.rationale: Circular 230 requires a practitioner to advise a client of any noticed error or omission and its potential consequences.

questions.stem: Alimony under a divorce agreement executed in 2024 is treated how for federal income tax?
options: Neither deductible by the payer nor taxable to the recipient
Deductible by the payer and taxable to the recipient
Taxable to the recipient only
Deductible by the payer only
questions.rationale: For divorce agreements executed after 2018, alimony is neither deductible by the payer nor includible by the recipient.

questions.stem: A dependent child, age 17, has $2,000 of wages and $400 of interest income in 2024. What is the child's standard deduction (assuming the dependent standard deduction rules)?
questions.rationale: A dependent's 2024 standard deduction is the greater of $1,300 or earned income plus $450, capped at the regular standard deduction.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: How is a nonqualified distribution of earnings from a Coverdell ESA generally treated?
options: The earnings portion is taxable and subject to a 10% additional tax
Treated as a gift
Fully tax-free if the beneficiary is under 18
Tax-free in all cases
questions.rationale: Nonqualified Coverdell ESA distributions tax the earnings portion and generally add a 10% additional tax.

questions.stem: A clergy member who is conscientiously opposed to public insurance can apply to be exempt from self-employment tax on ministerial earnings using which form?
options: Form 2555
Form 4868
Form 8332
Form 4361
questions.rationale: Ministers seeking exemption from self-employment tax on ministerial earnings file Form 4361.

questions.stem: Tara is married filing jointly with one child in college. She paid $4,000 of tuition and wants to maximize education benefits but cannot use the same expenses twice. Which is true?
options: She must use the tuition for a deduction, not a credit
She may claim either the AOTC or the LLC for that student, but not both on the same expenses
Both credits are refundable
She may claim both the AOTC and LLC on the same $4,000
questions.rationale: The AOTC and LLC cannot both be claimed for the same student's same expenses; the taxpayer chooses one.

questions.stem: Victor's employer reimbursed $500 of qualified parking under an accountable transportation fringe benefit plan in 2024, within the monthly exclusion limit. How is it treated?
options: Taxable only if cash
Excludable from income up to the monthly limit
Deductible by Victor
Taxable wages
questions.rationale: Qualified transportation fringe benefits like parking are excludable from employee income up to the monthly limit.

questions.stem: Which statement about the standard deduction vs. itemizing is correct?
options: A taxpayer must always itemize
Itemizing is required if AGI exceeds $100,000
Married filing separately filers always use the standard deduction
A taxpayer should generally use whichever method yields the larger deduction
questions.rationale: Taxpayers generally choose the larger of the standard deduction or itemized deductions, subject to applicable rules.

questions.stem: Wendy received a $25,000 distribution from a qualified retirement plan in 2024 and rolled $25,000 into an IRA within 60 days, but $5,000 was withheld for taxes and she only deposited $20,000. To avoid tax on the full amount, what was required?
options: Only $20,000 can ever be rolled over
Nothing; the rollover is automatically complete
She must replace the $5,000 withheld with other funds to roll over the full $25,000
The withheld $5,000 is always tax-free
questions.rationale: Amounts withheld from a distribution must be replaced with other funds to complete a full rollover; otherwise the unreplaced portion is taxable.

questions.stem: Yusuf, age 70, is still working and has earned income in 2024. Can he contribute to a traditional IRA?
options: Only if he has no employer plan
Only to a Roth, never a traditional IRA
Yes, there is no age limit for traditional IRA contributions if he has earned income
No, contributions are barred after age 70 1/2
questions.rationale: The SECURE Act removed the age limit for traditional IRA contributions; earned income is the key requirement.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to e-file but must provide identity verification. Which number is used to verify identity for e-filing by matching a prior-year figure?
options: The routing number on a check
The employer identification number
The prior-year adjusted gross income (AGI) or a self-select PIN
The taxpayer's bank account number
questions.rationale: E-file identity verification typically uses the prior-year AGI or a self-select PIN.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer operates a farm and reports income and expenses on Schedule F. They had a net farm loss in 2024. Which special averaging provision may be available to farmers?
options: A flat 10% farm tax rate
Income averaging using Schedule J
Tax-free treatment of all farm income
Mandatory five-year carryback
questions.rationale: Farmers may elect to average farm income over the prior three years using Schedule J.

questions.stem: Zara forgave a $6,000 personal loan she had made to a friend who never repaid it. Can she claim a nonbusiness bad debt deduction?
options: Yes, as a business expense
Yes, as a short-term capital loss if the debt is totally worthless and was a bona fide loan
No, personal loans are never deductible
Yes, as an ordinary deduction
questions.rationale: A totally worthless bona fide nonbusiness debt is deductible as a short-term capital loss.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has a net operating loss (NOL) arising in 2024. Under current rules, how may the NOL generally be used?
options: Carried forward indefinitely, limited to 80% of taxable income in the carryforward year
Carried back 2 years and forward 20 years
Carried back 5 years only
Used only in the year incurred
questions.rationale: Post-2017 NOLs generally carry forward indefinitely and are limited to 80% of taxable income in the year used.

questions.stem: Aria received a $1,200 distribution of her own after-tax contributions (basis) from a nonqualified annuity in 2024 under the exclusion ratio. How is the basis portion treated?
options: Fully taxable
The return-of-basis portion is not taxable
Taxable only if she is under 59 1/2
Subject to a 20% penalty
questions.rationale: The exclusion ratio treats the return-of-basis portion of annuity payments as nontaxable.

questions.stem: A client received an IRS CP2000 notice proposing additional tax because of unreported 1099 income that was in fact correct. What is the best advice?
options: Respond by the deadline, agreeing and arranging payment or explaining any disagreement
File a brand-new original return
Immediately file an offer in compromise
Ignore the notice
questions.rationale: A CP2000 should be answered by the deadline, either agreeing and paying or explaining a documented disagreement.

questions.stem: Ben, single, has MAGI of $145,000 in 2024 and wants to contribute to a Roth IRA. The single Roth phaseout range is $146,000 to $161,000. What can he do?
options: Nothing; he is over the limit
Contribute the full amount because his MAGI is below the phaseout start
Contribute only half
Convert to a traditional IRA only
questions.rationale: A full Roth IRA contribution is allowed when MAGI is below the start of the phaseout range ($146,000 single for 2024).

questions.stem: Which type of income is reported on Form 1099-INT?
options: Nonemployee compensation
Dividends
Interest income
Wages
questions.rationale: Form 1099-INT reports interest income paid to a taxpayer.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's tax is being computed and they have both a $1,000 refundable credit and a $2,000 nonrefundable credit. Their tax before credits is $1,500. After applying credits in the proper order, what is the result?
options: A $2,500 refund
A $1,500 balance due
Tax reduced to $0 with a $1,000 refund from the refundable credit
No refund possible
questions.rationale: Nonrefundable credits reduce tax to zero first; refundable credits can then generate a refund.

questions.stem: A taxpayer materially participates in a real estate business and qualifies as a real estate professional. What is the effect on rental losses?
options: Rental income becomes tax-free
Losses are doubled
All rental losses are still passive
Rental losses may be treated as nonpassive and deductible against other income
questions.rationale: A real estate professional who materially participates can treat rental real estate losses as nonpassive.

questions.stem: Cora paid $600 in 2024 to a licensed daycare for her disabled spouse who is physically incapable of self-care so she could work. Does this qualify for the Child and Dependent Care Credit?
options: Only if the spouse is under 13
No, spouses never qualify
No, only children qualify
Yes, a spouse incapable of self-care is a qualifying person for the credit
questions.rationale: A spouse who is incapable of self-care qualifies for the Child and Dependent Care Credit.

questions.stem: Derek's home was destroyed by a hurricane (federally declared disaster) in 2024. His insurance reimbursement exceeded his adjusted basis, creating a $30,000 gain. What option may he have?
options: The gain is exempt because it is a casualty
He must report it as ordinary income
He may defer the gain by reinvesting in similar property within the replacement period under §1033
The gain is always immediately taxable
questions.rationale: Section 1033 allows deferral of gain from an involuntary conversion when proceeds are reinvested in qualifying replacement property in time.

questions.stem: Which filing status generally provides the most favorable standard deduction and brackets for a married couple?
options: Married filing separately
Married filing jointly
Single
Head of household
questions.rationale: Married filing jointly usually offers the most favorable standard deduction and tax brackets for couples.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A self-employed taxpayer with net SE earnings computes SE tax. What portion of net self-employment income is the SE tax base (the adjustment factor)?
options: 100% of net SE income
92.35% of net SE income
50% of net SE income
15.3% of net SE income
questions.rationale: Self-employment tax is computed on 92.35% of net self-employment earnings.

questions.stem: Which credit may help offset foreign income taxes paid on income also taxed by the U.S.?
options: The Saver's Credit
The American Opportunity Credit
The Foreign Tax Credit
The Child Tax Credit
questions.rationale: The Foreign Tax Credit offsets U.S. tax for foreign income taxes paid on the same income.

questions.stem: Emma, an Uber driver, received a 1099-NEC for $18,000 in 2024 and has $4,000 of related vehicle and phone expenses. How is her net profit taxed beyond income tax?
options: Subject only to NIIT
No additional tax
Exempt as gig income
Subject to self-employment tax on net earnings
questions.rationale: A gig worker's net self-employment profit is subject to self-employment tax in addition to income tax.

questions.stem: A taxpayer claims head of household but the qualifying person is the taxpayer's mother, who does not live with the taxpayer. Can the taxpayer still qualify?
options: No, parents never qualify a taxpayer for head of household
No, the qualifying person must always live with the taxpayer
Only if the parent lives in the same state
Yes, a dependent parent need not live with the taxpayer if the taxpayer pays over half the cost of the parent's home
questions.rationale: A dependent parent need not live with the taxpayer for head of household if the taxpayer pays over half the cost of the parent's home.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: Greg, married filing jointly, has two children in college and $10,000 of combined qualified expenses. He can claim the AOTC for each eligible student. What is the maximum combined AOTC (assuming no phaseout and each qualifies fully)?
options: $10,000 total
$4,000 total
$5,000 total ($2,500 per student)
$2,500 total
questions.rationale: The AOTC is up to $2,500 per eligible student, so two qualifying students can yield up to $5,000.

questions.stem: A surviving spouse with a dependent child may use qualifying surviving spouse status for how many years after the year of the spouse's death (assuming requirements are met)?
options: Three years
Two years
One year
Indefinitely
questions.rationale: Qualifying surviving spouse status applies for the two years after the year of the spouse's death, given a dependent child and other requirements.

questions.stem: Lena received $3,000 of jury duty pay in 2024 but had to turn $2,800 of it over to her employer (who continued her salary). How is this handled?
options: Only $200 is reported as income
The $3,000 is income, but the $2,800 paid to the employer is an above-the-line deduction
Nothing is reported
The $2,800 is a charitable deduction
questions.rationale: Jury duty pay is taxable income, but amounts turned over to an employer are deductible as an adjustment to income.

questions.stem: Maya, single, contributed $4,000 to a traditional IRA in 2024 and is not covered by an employer plan. Her MAGI is $200,000. How much is deductible?
questions.rationale: A taxpayer not covered by an employer retirement plan can fully deduct traditional IRA contributions regardless of income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer underpaid their 2024 estimated taxes. The underpayment penalty is generally calculated as what?
options: A flat 25% penalty
Interest-based, computed at the federal short-term rate plus 3% on the underpayment for the period it was underpaid
A criminal fine
10% of total tax
questions.rationale: The estimated tax underpayment penalty is essentially interest on the shortfall at the IRS underpayment rate for the underpaid period.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally NONtaxable to the recipient?
options: A qualified gift from a friend
Lottery winnings
Bonus income
Severance pay
questions.rationale: Gifts received are not taxable to the recipient, unlike lottery winnings, severance, or bonuses.

questions.stem: Nina has self-only HDHP coverage from July through December 2024 (6 months) and uses the full-year contribution under the last-month rule. What testing-period requirement must she meet?
options: She must contribute again next year
None; the last-month rule has no strings
She must be over age 55
She must remain HSA-eligible through the entire following year (the testing period) or face income inclusion and a 10% additional tax
questions.rationale: The HSA last-month rule lets a mid-year-eligible person contribute the full annual amount but requires remaining eligible through the following year's testing period.

questions.stem: Oscar received a $1,000 prize for winning a local photography contest in 2024. How is it treated?
options: Taxable as other income
Taxable only if over $5,000
Nontaxable as a gift
Nontaxable because it is a hobby
questions.rationale: Prizes and awards are generally taxable as other income.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a requirement to claim the Earned Income Credit?
options: Must have investment income above a threshold
Must have a valid Social Security number and earned income within limits
Must be over age 65
Must own a home
questions.rationale: The EIC requires earned income within limits and a valid Social Security number, among other rules.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a large bonus that pushed part of their income into a higher bracket. Which statement is accurate?
options: They lose all deductions
Only the portion of income within the higher bracket is taxed at that higher rate
Bonuses are tax-free
Their entire income is now taxed at the higher rate
questions.rationale: In a progressive system, only income within the higher bracket is taxed at the higher rate.

questions.stem: Quill, single, has a modified AGI of $90,000 and paid $2,500 of student loan interest in 2024. The single phaseout range is $80,000 to $95,000. Approximately how much is deductible?
options: About $833
questions.rationale: Student loan interest phases out ratably over the $15,000 single range; at $90,000 MAGI about one-third of the $2,500 remains.

questions.stem: Rosa received $5,000 in unemployment compensation in 2024. How is it treated for federal income tax?
options: Fully taxable as ordinary income
Only half is taxable
Fully nontaxable
Taxable only if over $10,200
questions.rationale: Unemployment compensation is fully taxable for 2024; the temporary 2020 exclusion no longer applies.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who is a statutory employee receives a W-2 with the 'statutory employee' box checked. How do they report income and expenses?
options: On Form 1040 line 1 with no expense deduction
On Schedule C, where they can deduct business expenses, but the income is not subject to SE tax
On Schedule E
On Schedule F only
questions.rationale: Statutory employees report their W-2 income on Schedule C to deduct business expenses, but are not subject to self-employment tax.

questions.stem: Sven, age 40, took a $15,000 distribution from his 401(k) after leaving his employer in 2024 and did not roll it over. He used it for general living expenses. What are the tax consequences?
options: Taxable at capital gains rates
Subject only to a 10% penalty
Tax-free because it was his money
Taxable as ordinary income plus a 10% early-distribution penalty
questions.rationale: A pre-59 1/2 401(k) distribution not rolled over is ordinary income plus a 10% early-distribution penalty absent an exception.

questions.stem: A client wants to claim a deduction that lacks substantiation and is likely not allowable. Under Circular 230, what is the practitioner's duty?
options: Decline to take an unsupported position lacking a reasonable basis and advise the client accordingly
Claim it to satisfy the client
Refer the client to a different IRS office
Claim it but disclose nothing
questions.rationale: Under Circular 230, a practitioner should not take a position lacking a reasonable basis and must advise the client appropriately.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's qualified dividends and long-term capital gains total $10,000 and their taxable income places them entirely in the 0% capital gains bracket. What is the tax on these items?
questions.rationale: Long-term capital gains and qualified dividends are taxed at 0% when the taxpayer is within the 0% bracket.

questions.stem: Tina supports her disabled adult son, age 30, who lives with her and earned $3,000 in 2024 (below the gross income limit). Can she claim him as a dependent?
options: Only as a qualifying relative with no credit
Yes, a permanently and totally disabled child can be a qualifying child regardless of age
No, adult children never qualify
No, he is too old
questions.rationale: A permanently and totally disabled child meets the qualifying-child age test regardless of age.

questions.stem: Ulises sold collectibles (e.g., rare coins) held 3 years at a gain in 2024. What is the maximum federal rate on this long-term collectibles gain?
questions.rationale: Long-term gains on collectibles are taxed at a maximum rate of 28%.

questions.stem: Which test is NOT one of the tests for a qualifying child?
options: Age test
Relationship test
Gross income test
Residency test
questions.rationale: The qualifying child tests are relationship, age, residency, support, and joint return; the gross income test applies to qualifying relatives.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: Vince, single, age 50, contributes to a traditional IRA in 2024. What is his maximum contribution including any catch-up?
questions.rationale: For 2024, the IRA contribution limit is $7,000 plus a $1,000 catch-up at age 50+, totaling $8,000.

questions.stem: A married couple filing separately wants to claim different deduction methods. Which rule applies?
options: If one spouse itemizes, the other generally must itemize too (cannot take the standard deduction)
Both must take the standard deduction
Each may freely choose
Both must itemize regardless
questions.rationale: For MFS, if one spouse itemizes, the other generally must itemize as well.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received income from foreign financial accounts and the aggregate value exceeded $10,000 at any time in 2024. What additional reporting may be required?
options: FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR) reporting the foreign accounts
Only a note on Schedule B
None
Form 1099 from the foreign bank
questions.rationale: U.S. persons with foreign financial accounts over $10,000 in aggregate must file the FBAR (FinCEN Form 114).

questions.stem: Which document reports an employee's annual wages and withholding?
options: Form W-2
Form 1098
Form 1099-NEC
Form 1095-A
questions.rationale: Form W-2 reports an employee's wages and tax withholding for the year.

questions.stem: Wendy is eligible for both the standard deduction and itemized deductions of $12,000. The 2024 single standard deduction is $14,600. Which should she generally take?
options: Itemized deductions
Whichever she prefers regardless of amount
The standard deduction
Half of each
questions.rationale: A taxpayer takes the larger of the standard or itemized deductions; here the $14,600 standard deduction exceeds $12,000 itemized.

questions.stem: A taxpayer realizes a $4,000 gain on §1256 contracts (regulated futures) held at year-end 2024. How are these marked-to-market gains generally taxed?
options: 100% long-term
As ordinary income only
100% short-term
60% long-term and 40% short-term (the 60/40 rule)
questions.rationale: Section 1256 contracts are taxed 60% long-term and 40% short-term under the mark-to-market 60/40 rule.

questions.stem: A client asks whether they can deduct the cost of clothing they wear to their office job. What is the correct advice?
options: No, ordinary business attire suitable for everyday wear is not deductible
Only suits over $500 are deductible
Yes, all work clothing is deductible
Yes, if they only wear it to work
questions.rationale: Ordinary business attire suitable for everyday wear is a nondeductible personal expense.

questions.stem: Xena received a $2,000 distribution from a 529 plan; all of it covered qualified tuition. How is the distribution taxed?
options: Entirely tax-free as a qualified distribution
Earnings portion is taxable
Subject to a 10% penalty
Taxable as ordinary income
questions.rationale: 529 distributions used for qualified education expenses are entirely tax-free.

questions.stem: Yael has $40,000 of investment income and $10,000 of investment interest expense in 2024. She wants to deduct the investment interest. What generally limits the deduction?
options: It is limited to 10% of AGI
It is never deductible
It is unlimited
It is limited to net investment income
questions.rationale: The investment interest expense deduction is limited to net investment income; the excess carries forward.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to determine if they can be claimed as a dependent by someone else, which would affect their own standard deduction. If they can be claimed, what is true about their personal situation?
options: Their standard deduction may be limited under the dependent rules
They automatically owe more tax
They get the full standard deduction
They cannot file a return
questions.rationale: Individuals who can be claimed as dependents are subject to the limited dependent standard deduction.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: Priya moved from Texas to California on July 1, 2024, establishing California residency. For her 2024 California return she is generally treated as a part-year resident. How is her wage income earned while still living in Texas (January–June) treated for California tax purposes?
options: All wages are fully taxable by California because she ended the year as a resident
