California fully exempts all of her 2024 income because Texas has no income tax
Wages earned before she became a California resident are generally not taxable by California, though California may use them to compute the tax rate on California-source income
Only half of her total annual wages are taxable by California regardless of when earned
questions.rationale: Part-year residents are taxed on all income while a resident and on state-source income while a nonresident; pre-move out-of-state wages are generally not taxed by the new state.

questions.stem: A married couple are domiciled in a community property state. The husband earns $90,000 in wages; the wife earns $30,000. They file separate federal returns (MFS) and no special election applies. Under general community property rules, how much wage income must each spouse report?
options: Each reports $45,000, splitting only the husband's wages
Each spouse reports $60,000, representing one-half of total community wages
Husband reports $120,000 and the wife reports $0 because he is the higher earner
Husband reports $90,000 and wife reports $30,000, matching their actual earnings
questions.rationale: In community property states, wages earned during marriage are community income and are split equally between spouses on MFS returns.

questions.stem: Under the IRS rules for spouses living apart all year in a community property state, when may a spouse report only his or her own actual earnings rather than half of community income?
options: Whenever the spouses simply choose to file separately
Never; community property splitting is mandatory in all circumstances

When the spouses lived apart the entire year, did not file jointly, and one or more conditions for relief from community property treatment under IRC §66 are met, such as no transfer of earned income between them
Only if one spouse earned less than the standard deduction
questions.rationale: IRC §66 lets spouses who lived apart all year, did not file jointly, and met the conditions report their own earned income instead of split community income.

questions.stem: Devon, unmarried, provides a home for his girlfriend's 6-year-old son, who is not related to Devon and lived with him all year. Devon provides all support, and the child is not the qualifying child of anyone else. Which filing status can Devon use based on this child?
options: Qualifying Surviving Spouse
Head of Household, because the child is a qualifying child for Head of Household purposes
Married Filing Jointly with his girlfriend
Single, because the child is not related to Devon and therefore cannot make him eligible for Head of Household even though the child may be a qualifying relative dependent
questions.rationale: An unrelated dependent (qualifying relative) does not qualify a taxpayer for Head of Household; only specified relatives do.

questions.stem: For 2024, what is the gross income test threshold a person must stay under to be claimed as a qualifying relative (subject to inflation adjustment)?
options: The qualifying relative's gross income must be less than the standard deduction
The qualifying relative's gross income must be less than the exemption amount of $5,050 for 2024
The qualifying relative's gross income must be less than $10,000
There is no income limit for a qualifying relative
questions.rationale: A qualifying relative's gross income must be less than the exemption amount, which is $5,050 for 2024.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is a 'dual-status' alien in 2024, having become a U.S. resident partway through the year. Which statement about her filing is correct?
options: A dual-status taxpayer must file as Head of Household
A dual-status taxpayer may always claim the full standard deduction

A dual-status taxpayer generally cannot claim the standard deduction (with a limited exception for certain spouses electing to be treated as residents) and files reporting worldwide income only for the resident portion plus U.S.-source income for the nonresident portion
A dual-status taxpayer reports worldwide income for the entire year regardless of residency period
questions.rationale: Dual-status aliens generally cannot use the standard deduction and report worldwide income only for the resident portion of the year.

questions.stem: Maria's husband died in March 2023. She has a dependent child living with her and has not remarried. For tax year 2024, which filing status is most advantageous and available to her?
options: Single only
Qualifying Surviving Spouse for 2024
Married Filing Jointly for 2024
Head of Household only
questions.rationale: Qualifying Surviving Spouse is available for the two years after the year of a spouse's death if the taxpayer maintains a home for a dependent child and has not remarried.

questions.stem: A nonresident alien married to a U.S. citizen makes a §6013(g) election to be treated as a U.S. resident for the full year so the couple can file MFJ. What is a key consequence of this election?
options: Only U.S.-source income of the electing spouse becomes taxable
The election makes the couple ineligible for the standard deduction
Both spouses' worldwide income becomes subject to U.S. tax for the year, though foreign tax credit or the foreign earned income exclusion may apply
The election can be made and revoked freely every year without restriction
questions.rationale: A §6013(g) election treats the nonresident spouse as a full-year U.S. resident, subjecting worldwide income to U.S. tax, mitigated by FTC/FEIE.

questions.stem: Two unmarried parents live together all year with their child, who is a qualifying child of both. They cannot agree on who claims the child. Under the tiebreaker rules, who is entitled to claim the child?
options: They must split the dependency exemption equally
The parent with whom the child lived the longer period during the year, and if equal, the parent with the higher adjusted gross income
The parent who provided the most financial support
Neither parent may claim the child if they cannot agree
questions.rationale: The parent-vs-parent tiebreaker awards the child to the parent of longer residence; if equal, the higher-AGI parent claims the child.

questions.stem: Which of the following individuals can NEVER be claimed as a dependent regardless of meeting other tests?
options: A married person who files a joint return with their spouse (except solely to claim a refund of withholding with no tax liability)
A 25-year-old full-time student child with low income
A qualifying relative who is a U.S. citizen
A parent who does not live with the taxpayer
questions.rationale: The joint return test disqualifies a married dependent who files jointly, except when the joint return is filed solely to claim a refund with no tax liability.

questions.stem: An individual is present in the United States 120 days in 2024, 120 days in 2023, and 120 days in 2022. Applying the substantial presence test weighting (current year days + 1/3 prior year + 1/6 second prior year), does she meet the 183-day threshold for 2024?
options: Yes, because the weighted total is 120 + 40 + 20 = 180, which rounds up to 183
No, because the weighted total is 120 + 40 + 20 = 180, which is less than 183
No, because she failed the 31-day current-year minimum
Yes, because she was present more than 31 days in 2024 and the weighted total is exactly 183
questions.rationale: Substantial presence weights current-year days fully, prior year by 1/3, and second prior year by 1/6; 120/120/120 yields 180, below 183.

questions.stem: A taxpayer abandons her green card and meets the long-term resident definition. Under the expatriation rules, which threshold can trigger 'covered expatriate' status (resulting in potential mark-to-market exit tax)?
options: Simply leaving the United States for more than 30 days
Earning more than $50,000 in the year of expatriation
Having any foreign bank account
Meeting a net worth test of $2 million or more, a specified average annual net income tax test, or failing to certify five years of tax compliance
questions.rationale: Covered expatriate status is triggered by the $2 million net worth test, the income tax liability test, or failing the 5-year compliance certification.

questions.stem: Alex pays $2,000 per month in alimony under a divorce decree executed in 2017 that has never been modified. How is this alimony treated on the 2024 returns of the parties?
options: The payer cannot deduct it and the recipient does not include it, under the post-2018 rules
The payer deducts it as an above-the-line adjustment and the recipient includes it in gross income, because the agreement predates 2019 and was not modified to adopt the new rules
Both parties ignore alimony entirely for federal tax purposes
The payer must capitalize the payments and the recipient treats them as a gift
questions.rationale: Alimony under pre-2019 instruments (not modified to adopt the new rules) is deductible by the payer and taxable to the recipient.

questions.stem: A divorce instrument executed in 2015 is modified in 2024, and the modification expressly states that the post-2018 alimony rules now apply. What is the effect on 2024 alimony payments under that instrument?
options: The modification has no effect on tax treatment under any circumstances
The recipient may elect to include the payments to claim a credit
The payments remain deductible/includible because the instrument originated before 2019
Because the modification expressly adopts the new rules, the payments are neither deductible by the payer nor includible by the recipient
questions.rationale: A post-2018 modification that expressly adopts the new rules makes alimony nondeductible and nontaxable.

questions.stem: Which threshold triggers the Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% on wages for a married couple filing jointly in 2024, and who is liable to withhold it?
options: $125,000 for MFJ; the employee never owes any reconciliation
$250,000 combined wages for MFJ; however, the employer withholds the extra 0.9% on any individual employee's wages over $200,000 regardless of filing status, with reconciliation on the return
$200,000 combined; the employer withholds based on combined wages
There is no threshold; the tax applies to all wages
questions.rationale: Additional Medicare Tax (0.9%) applies above $250,000 MFJ; employers withhold on individual wages over $200,000, with reconciliation on Form 8959.

questions.stem: A single retiree receives $24,000 in Social Security benefits and has $30,000 of other income, including $5,000 of tax-exempt municipal bond interest. When computing the taxable portion of Social Security benefits, how is the tax-exempt interest treated?
options: It is taxed directly at ordinary rates
It makes the entire Social Security benefit nontaxable
It is ignored entirely for all purposes
It is added back when computing 'modified AGI' (provisional income) used in the Social Security benefits worksheet, potentially increasing the taxable portion of benefits
questions.rationale: Tax-exempt interest is added back to provisional income in the Social Security worksheet, which can raise the taxable portion of benefits.

questions.stem: Which of the following items is included in net investment income for NIIT purposes?
options: Net rental income, interest, dividends, and net capital gains from property held for investment
Distributions from a qualified retirement plan
Wages and self-employment income
Tax-exempt municipal bond interest
questions.rationale: NII includes interest, dividends, capital gains, and rental/passive income; it excludes wages, SE income, retirement distributions, and tax-exempt interest.

questions.stem: A cash-basis individual receives a $10,000 distribution from a nonqualified deferred compensation arrangement and also has $4,000 of unemployment compensation in 2024. Which statement about the taxability of these items is correct?
options: Both the nonqualified deferred compensation distribution and the unemployment compensation are includible in gross income
Both the deferred compensation and unemployment compensation are tax-free
Only the unemployment compensation is taxable; deferred comp is always exempt
Only the deferred compensation is taxable; unemployment is exempt under federal law
questions.rationale: Both nonqualified deferred compensation distributions and unemployment compensation are includible in federal gross income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer cancels a $5,000 personal credit card debt in 2024 and is solvent both before and after. How is the canceled debt treated?
options: It is generally includible in gross income as cancellation of debt income because no exclusion (such as insolvency or bankruptcy) applies
It is excluded because personal debt cancellation is never taxable
It reduces the taxpayer's basis in personal assets
It is taxed as a capital gain
questions.rationale: Canceled debt is ordinary COD income unless a statutory exclusion (e.g., insolvency or bankruptcy) applies.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who was insolvent by $8,000 immediately before a $12,000 debt cancellation excludes COD income to the extent of insolvency. How much COD income must be recognized?
options: $12,000, the full canceled amount
$0, because insolvency fully shields canceled debt
$8,000, the insolvency amount
$4,000, the amount of canceled debt that exceeds the $8,000 insolvency
questions.rationale: The insolvency exclusion is limited to the amount of insolvency; canceled debt above that amount is taxable COD income.

questions.stem: Jury duty pay of $300 is received by an employee who turned the pay over to her employer because the employer continued her salary during jury service. What is the correct tax treatment?
options: The $300 is not reported anywhere
The $300 jury pay is included in gross income, and the amount turned over to the employer is deducted as an above-the-line adjustment
The $300 is excluded because it was given to the employer
The $300 is reported as a capital gain
questions.rationale: Jury duty pay is taxable income; if remitted to the employer who continued the salary, the taxpayer deducts it above the line.

questions.stem: A taxpayer receives a state income tax refund of $1,200 in 2024 from her 2023 return. In 2023 she itemized but her total state and local taxes were capped at the $10,000 SALT limit and she would have exceeded $10,000 even without the refunded amount. Under the tax benefit rule, how much of the refund is taxable in 2024?
options: $0, because the refunded tax provided no tax benefit in 2023 given the $10,000 SALT cap already limited her deduction
The full $1,200 is taxable because she itemized
Half the refund, $600, is taxable
$10,000 is taxable
questions.rationale: Under the tax benefit rule, a state tax refund is taxable only to the extent the deducted tax produced a tax benefit; the SALT cap can eliminate that benefit.

questions.stem: A self-employed taxpayer pays $9,600 in health insurance premiums for herself in 2024 and has $40,000 of net self-employment profit. She was not eligible for any employer-subsidized plan. How is the premium treated?
options: It is deductible only as an itemized medical expense subject to the 7.5% AGI floor
It is deductible as an above-the-line self-employed health insurance deduction, limited to her net earnings from self-employment
It is fully nondeductible because she is self-employed
It must be deducted on Schedule C as a business expense
questions.rationale: Self-employed health insurance premiums are deductible above the line, limited to net self-employment earnings, when no subsidized employer coverage is available.

questions.stem: For 2024, an active participant in an employer retirement plan who is single has MAGI of $82,000. The traditional IRA deduction phaseout for an active participant who is single is $77,000–$87,000. He contributes $7,000. What is his deductible amount (rounded to the nearest $10)?
options: $7,000, fully deductible
$0, no deduction allowed
$5,000 flat regardless of phaseout
$3,500, the partially phased-out amount based on being halfway through the $10,000 phaseout range
questions.rationale: An active participant's IRA deduction phases out ratably across the range; $82,000 is halfway through $77,000–$87,000, allowing roughly half the contribution as a deduction.

questions.stem: A married couple file jointly. The wife is an active participant in a 401(k); the husband is not covered by any employer plan. For the husband's traditional IRA deduction, which phaseout range applies for 2024?
options: His deduction phases out over the spousal range of $230,000–$240,000 MAGI (the range for a noncovered spouse married to a covered spouse)
He has no phaseout regardless of income
He cannot deduct any IRA contribution because his spouse is covered
His deduction phases out over the active-participant range of $123,000–$143,000
questions.rationale: A noncovered spouse married to a covered spouse uses the higher $230,000–$240,000 (2024) deduction phaseout range.

questions.stem: Which describes a proper 'backdoor Roth IRA' for a high earner whose income exceeds the Roth contribution limits?
options: Making a nondeductible contribution to a traditional IRA and then converting it to a Roth IRA, with tax due only on any pre-conversion earnings and subject to the pro-rata rule for other pretax IRA balances
Contributing to a SEP IRA and calling it a Roth
Contributing directly to a Roth IRA despite the income limit
Rolling a 401(k) directly into a Roth with no tax ever
questions.rationale: A backdoor Roth is a nondeductible traditional IRA contribution converted to Roth; the pro-rata rule applies when other pretax IRA balances exist.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has three traditional IRAs totaling $90,000, of which $9,000 represents nondeductible (after-tax) basis. She converts $10,000 to a Roth IRA. Under the pro-rata rule, what portion of the $10,000 conversion is nontaxable?
options: $9,000, the full basis amount
$0, all conversions are fully taxable
$10,000, because she designates it as the after-tax money
$1,000, because 10% of total IRA value ($9,000 / $90,000) is after-tax basis and that percentage applies to the conversion
questions.rationale: The pro-rata rule treats each distribution/conversion as part basis and part pretax based on the after-tax fraction of all traditional IRAs combined.

questions.stem: A taxpayer pays $2,500 of student loan interest in 2024 but has MAGI of $95,000 (single), within the phaseout range. Which statement is correct about the student loan interest deduction?
options: The full $2,500 is always deductible regardless of income
Student loan interest is an itemized deduction subject to the 2% floor
The maximum deduction is $2,500, but it is phased out for higher-MAGI taxpayers and may be reduced or eliminated within the applicable range
Only interest paid in the first 60 months of repayment is deductible
questions.rationale: The student loan interest deduction is an above-the-line adjustment capped at $2,500 and phased out over a MAGI range.

questions.stem: A couple files jointly with two qualifying children under age 13 and incurs $9,000 of qualifying dependent care expenses so both can work. The employer also provided a $5,000 dependent care FSA, which they fully used and excluded from income. For the Child and Dependent Care Credit, what is the maximum amount of additional expenses they can use to compute the credit?
options: $0, because using an FSA bars the credit entirely
$6,000, the full two-child limit, ignoring the FSA
$9,000, the total expenses incurred
$1,000, because the $6,000 expense limit for two or more dependents is reduced by the $5,000 excluded FSA benefit
questions.rationale: The dependent care credit expense limit ($6,000 for two+) is reduced by employer-provided dependent care benefits excluded from income.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the 2024 Saver's Credit (Retirement Savings Contributions Credit)?
options: It provides a flat $1,000 credit to anyone who contributes to an IRA
It applies only to Roth contributions, not traditional
It is a refundable credit available to all taxpayers regardless of income

It is a nonrefundable credit of up to 50%, 20%, or 10% of eligible retirement contributions (up to $2,000 per person), available to lower-income taxpayers who meet AGI limits and are not full-time students or dependents
questions.rationale: The Saver's Credit is a nonrefundable, income-limited credit at 50/20/10% rates on up to $2,000 of contributions per person.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's 2024 American Opportunity Tax Credit is fully claimed at the maximum $2,500. What portion, if any, is refundable, and is there a restriction tied to the kiddie tax?
options: Up to 40% ($1,000) is refundable, but the refundable portion is generally not available to a taxpayer subject to the kiddie tax rules
None of it is refundable
The entire $2,500 is refundable with no restrictions
Up to 100% is refundable for students under age 18
questions.rationale: Up to 40% ($1,000) of the AOTC is refundable, but the refundable portion is denied to taxpayers subject to the kiddie tax.

questions.stem: The Lifetime Learning Credit differs from the American Opportunity Tax Credit in which key respect?
options: The Lifetime Learning Credit can only be claimed for graduate school
The Lifetime Learning Credit is nonrefundable, has no four-year limit, and is computed as 20% of up to $10,000 of qualified expenses per return (not per student)
The Lifetime Learning Credit requires at least half-time enrollment
The Lifetime Learning Credit is partially refundable while the AOTC is not
questions.rationale: The LLC is nonrefundable, has no year limit, allows any course load, and equals 20% of up to $10,000 of expenses per return.

questions.stem: A taxpayer makes a $600 cash contribution to a qualified public charity and a $400 contribution to a private nonoperating foundation, both in 2024. The cash-to-public-charity AGI limit is 60% and the foundation limit is 30%. If AGI is $50,000 and these are the only gifts, are both fully deductible this year?
options: No, because total charitable gifts cannot exceed $1,000
Yes, because both gifts are far below their respective AGI percentage limits ($30,000 and $15,000)
No, because contributions to private foundations are never deductible
Only the public charity gift is deductible
questions.rationale: Cash gifts to public charities (60% limit) and to private foundations (30% limit) are deductible up to those AGI percentages; small gifts are fully deductible.

questions.stem: Beginning in 2024, what is the floor for deducting unreimbursed medical expenses as an itemized deduction?
options: There is no floor
10% of AGI
2% of AGI
7.5% of AGI
questions.rationale: Unreimbursed medical expenses are deductible only to the extent they exceed 7.5% of AGI.

questions.stem: On March 10, 2024, a taxpayer sells 100 shares of stock at a $1,500 loss. On March 25, 2024, she buys 100 shares of the same stock. Under the wash sale rules of §1091, what is the result?
options: The $1,500 loss is disallowed and added to the basis of the newly purchased shares; the holding period of the old shares tacks on
The $1,500 loss is fully deductible because she sold before repurchasing
Half the loss is deductible and half is disallowed
The loss is deductible but the new shares get a stepped-up basis
questions.rationale: A wash sale disallows the loss and adds it to the basis of the replacement shares, with the old holding period tacked on.

questions.stem: A taxpayer receives a gift of stock with a donor's basis of $20,000 and a fair market value of $15,000 on the date of the gift. She later sells it for $13,000. What is her recognized gain or loss?
options: A $7,000 gain
A $2,000 loss using the $15,000 FMV (the lower basis for determining loss)
No gain or loss because the sale price falls between the two basis figures
A $7,000 loss using the donor's $20,000 basis
questions.rationale: Gifted property with FMV below the donor's basis uses a dual basis: donor's basis for gain, FMV for loss; here a $2,000 loss results.

questions.stem: Using the same gift facts (donor basis $20,000, FMV $15,000 at gift), if the donee instead sells the stock for $17,000, what is the recognized gain or loss?
options: A $17,000 gain because there is no basis in gifted property
A $3,000 loss using the donor's $20,000 basis
A $2,000 gain using the $15,000 FMV
Neither gain nor loss, because the $17,000 sale price falls between the $15,000 FMV and the $20,000 donor's basis
questions.rationale: Under the dual-basis gift rule, a sale price between the FMV (loss basis) and the donor's basis (gain basis) yields no recognized gain or loss.

questions.stem: A taxpayer inherits real estate from a decedent who died in 2024 when the property's FMV was $400,000; the decedent's adjusted basis was $120,000. The estate did not elect the alternate valuation date. What is the heir's basis and holding period?
options: $120,000 basis with the decedent's holding period
$400,000 basis (stepped up to date-of-death FMV) and automatically long-term holding period
$260,000 basis, the average of the two figures
$400,000 basis but short-term holding period until held one year
questions.rationale: Inherited property takes a date-of-death FMV basis (step-up) and is automatically long-term.

questions.stem: A married decedent in a community property state dies in 2024. Community property worth $500,000 with a basis of $100,000 passes so the surviving spouse owns the whole property. What basis does the surviving spouse have in the entire property?
options: $300,000, stepping up only the decedent's half
$500,000, because both halves of community property receive a step-up to FMV at the death of one spouse
$250,000, half the FMV
$100,000, the original community basis with no step-up
questions.rationale: Community property generally receives a full (double) basis step-up to FMV at the first spouse's death, unlike separate-property joint tenancy.

questions.stem: An individual sells a parcel of investment land for $200,000, with a basis of $80,000, taking back a note payable $40,000 per year for five years (no interest stated separately for this question). Under the installment method, what gross profit percentage applies to each payment?
options: 40%, the basis recovery percentage
100%, the entire payment is gain
20%, one-fifth per year
60%, because gross profit ($120,000) divided by contract price ($200,000) equals 60%
questions.rationale: Under the installment method, each principal payment is multiplied by the gross profit percentage (gross profit / contract price) to determine recognized gain.

questions.stem: Which type of property is INELIGIBLE for installment sale reporting?
options: A vacation home held for personal use and investment appreciation
Inventory or property regularly sold in the ordinary course of a dealer's business
Shares of a closely held corporation sold to a third party
Investment land sold to an unrelated buyer
questions.rationale: Dealer dispositions and sales of inventory cannot use the installment method; capital and §1231 assets generally can.

questions.stem: An individual exchanges investment real property (basis $150,000, FMV $300,000) for like-kind real property worth $260,000 plus $40,000 cash boot in a qualifying §1031 exchange. How much gain is recognized?
options: $150,000, the full realized gain
$40,000, the amount of cash boot received, since recognized gain is the lesser of realized gain ($150,000) or boot ($40,000)
$0, because §1031 defers all gain
$110,000, the difference between FMV and basis less boot
questions.rationale: In a §1031 exchange, gain is recognized to the extent of boot received, limited to the realized gain.

questions.stem: After 2017, which of the following can still qualify for §1031 like-kind exchange treatment for an individual?
options: A swap of cryptocurrency for cryptocurrency
An exchange of collectible artwork for other artwork
An exchange of real property held for investment or productive use in a trade or business for other like-kind real property
A trade of business vehicles
questions.rationale: After 2017, §1031 applies only to exchanges of real property held for business or investment use.

questions.stem: An individual realizes a $30,000 net long-term capital loss and has no capital gains in 2024. What is the maximum capital loss that can offset ordinary income this year, and what happens to the rest?
options: No capital loss may offset ordinary income
$3,000 offsets ordinary income this year and the remaining $27,000 carries forward indefinitely, retaining its long-term character
$1,500 offsets ordinary income and the rest is lost
The full $30,000 offsets ordinary income this year
questions.rationale: Individuals can offset up to $3,000 of net capital loss against ordinary income yearly; excess carries forward indefinitely with its character preserved.

questions.stem: A taxpayer sells §1202 qualified small business stock (QSBS) held more than five years, acquired in 2021, with a realized gain of $1,000,000. Assuming all requirements are met and the acquisition date supports a 100% exclusion, how is the gain treated?
options: Up to 100% of the gain may be excluded from gross income (subject to the per-issuer cap of the greater of $10 million or 10x basis)
Only 50% of the gain can ever be excluded
The gain is fully taxable but at the 0% capital gains rate
The entire gain is taxed as ordinary income
questions.rationale: Qualified small business stock acquired after 9/27/2010 and held 5+ years can be 100% excluded, capped at the greater of $10M or 10x basis per issuer.

questions.stem: An individual sells their main home, in which they lived and owned for the last 4 years, for a $300,000 gain. They are single and have not used the exclusion in the past two years. How much gain is excludable under §121?
options: $250,000, the single-filer maximum exclusion, leaving $50,000 taxable
The full $300,000 because it is a primary residence
$0; gain on a personal residence is never excludable
$500,000, the joint exclusion
questions.rationale: Section 121 excludes up to $250,000 (single) of gain on a principal residence meeting the 2-of-5-year tests; excess is taxable.

questions.stem: A taxpayer turned 73 in 2024 and has a traditional IRA. He fails to take his $20,000 required minimum distribution (RMD) for 2024. Under current law (after SECURE 2.0), what is the excise tax penalty on the shortfall, and can it be reduced?
options: 25% of the shortfall, reduced to 10% if the failure is corrected within the applicable correction window
There is no penalty for missing an RMD
10% flat with no reduction
50% of the shortfall with no possibility of reduction
questions.rationale: Under SECURE 2.0, the missed-RMD excise tax is 25%, reduced to 10% if corrected within the correction window.

questions.stem: Under SECURE 2.0, what is the age at which required minimum distributions must generally begin for an individual who reaches that age in 2024?
questions.rationale: The RMD beginning age is 73 for those reaching it in 2024 and increases to 75 in 2033.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old taxpayer directs $25,000 from her traditional IRA directly to a qualified charity as a qualified charitable distribution (QCD) in 2024. What are the tax consequences?
options: Up to the annual QCD limit (inflation-adjusted, $105,000 for 2024) is excluded from gross income and can count toward her RMD, but no separate charitable deduction is allowed
The full $25,000 is included in income and then deductible as a charitable contribution
QCDs are only allowed from Roth IRAs
The distribution is fully taxable with no offsetting benefit
questions.rationale: A QCD (up to $105,000 in 2024) is excluded from income, counts toward the RMD, and yields no separate charitable deduction.

questions.stem: For 2024, the kiddie tax applies to a child's net unearned income above a threshold. A 16-year-old dependent has $4,000 of interest and dividends and no earned income. The first $1,300 is offset by the standard deduction and the next $1,300 is taxed at the child's rate. How is the remaining unearned income taxed?
options: At the child's own marginal rate
At the parents' marginal tax rate (the kiddie tax), applying to unearned income above $2,600 for 2024
At a flat 10% rate
It is exempt from tax entirely
questions.rationale: For 2024 the kiddie tax taxes a child's net unearned income above $2,600 at the parents' marginal rate.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a common AMT preference or adjustment item that can increase alternative minimum taxable income for an individual?
options: Qualified dividends
Wages reported on a W-2
Mortgage interest on acquisition debt for a primary residence
The bargain element on exercise of an incentive stock option (ISO) that is not sold in the same year
questions.rationale: The ISO bargain element on exercise (without same-year sale) is a classic AMT adjustment item.

questions.stem: An employee exercises an incentive stock option (ISO) in 2024 and holds the shares. The exercise price was $10/share and FMV at exercise was $30/share for 1,000 shares. For regular tax, no income is recognized at exercise. What is the AMT consequence in 2024?
options: No AMT effect at exercise
Ordinary income of $20,000 for both regular tax and AMT
A $30,000 AMT adjustment based on full FMV
A $20,000 AMT adjustment (the $20/share bargain element times 1,000 shares) increases AMTI in the year of exercise
questions.rationale: Exercising an ISO and holding the shares adds the bargain element to AMTI in the exercise year, creating AMT basis.

questions.stem: An employee exercises a nonqualified stock option (NQSO) in 2024 with a bargain element of $15,000. How is this treated for regular income tax at the time of exercise?
options: Only AMT applies, not regular tax
No income until the shares are sold
The $15,000 is a long-term capital gain at exercise
The $15,000 bargain element is ordinary compensation income at exercise, subject to income and payroll tax withholding
questions.rationale: NQSO exercise produces ordinary compensation income equal to the bargain element, with payroll and income tax withholding.

questions.stem: An employee participates in a qualifying §423 Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP) with a 15% discount. She holds the shares for the required period (more than two years from grant and one year from purchase), making it a qualifying disposition. Upon sale, how is the discount taxed?
options: Ordinary income is recognized equal to the lesser of the actual gain or the discount measured at grant, with the remainder of any gain taxed as long-term capital gain
No income is ever recognized on ESPP shares
The whole gain is ordinary income
The entire gain is long-term capital gain
questions.rationale: A qualifying ESPP disposition recognizes ordinary income up to the lesser of actual gain or the grant-date discount, with the rest as long-term capital gain.

questions.stem: To avoid an underpayment penalty using the prior-year safe harbor, a high-income individual (prior-year AGI over $150,000) must generally pay through withholding and estimated payments at least what percentage of the prior year's tax?
options: 80% of the prior year's tax
110% of the prior year's tax
100% of the prior year's tax
90% of the prior year's tax
questions.rationale: For prior-year AGI over $150,000, the prior-year safe harbor is 110% of the prior year's tax (or 90% of the current year).

questions.stem: An individual with highly seasonal income earns most of her income late in the year. Which method allows her to compute required estimated tax installments based on income actually earned in each period, potentially reducing early-period penalties?
options: The prior-year safe harbor only
The cash-flow averaging method
The annualized income installment method (Form 2210, Schedule AI), which bases each installment on year-to-date income
The flat four-equal-installment method only
questions.rationale: The annualized income installment method (Schedule AI of Form 2210) bases installments on income earned through each period, helping seasonal earners.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old takes a $10,000 early distribution from a traditional IRA in 2024 that is fully taxable, and no exception applies. Besides ordinary income tax, what additional tax generally applies?
options: A 25% additional tax
No additional tax
A 10% additional tax on early distributions
A 20% additional tax
questions.rationale: An early (pre-59 1/2) taxable IRA distribution with no exception incurs a 10% additional tax plus ordinary income tax.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an exception to the 10% early distribution penalty for an IRA but NOT for a 401(k) plan in the same way?
options: Distributions made as part of a series of substantially equal periodic payments
Distributions up to $10,000 for a first-time home purchase
Distributions after death
Distributions due to total and permanent disability
questions.rationale: The $10,000 first-time homebuyer exception to the 10% penalty applies to IRAs but not to 401(k) plan distributions.

questions.stem: A SIMPLE IRA participant takes a distribution within the first two years of participation, before age 59 1/2, with no exception. What additional tax rate applies?
questions.rationale: Early distributions from a SIMPLE IRA within the first two years of participation carry a 25% additional tax instead of 10%.

questions.stem: An individual is a limited partner in a partnership and receives a Schedule K-1 showing a $20,000 ordinary loss. Her outside basis at the start of the year is $12,000, and there were no distributions or additional contributions. How much of the loss can she deduct on her 1040 this year (ignoring at-risk and passive limits)?
options: $20,000, the full reported loss
$12,000, limited to her outside basis, with the remaining $8,000 suspended and carried forward
$8,000, the excess over basis
$0, because limited partners cannot deduct losses
questions.rationale: Pass-through losses are deductible only up to the partner's outside basis; the excess is suspended and carried forward until basis is restored.

questions.stem: An S corporation shareholder has stock basis of $5,000 and a loan basis (direct loan to the corporation) of $7,000. The K-1 shows a $10,000 ordinary loss. After applying the loss, what are the shareholder's stock and debt basis?
options: Stock basis $0 and debt basis $2,000, because the loss first reduces stock basis to zero, then reduces debt basis
Stock basis $5,000 and debt basis $0
Stock basis $0 and debt basis $7,000
Both reduced to negative amounts
questions.rationale: S corporation losses reduce stock basis to zero first, then loan (debt) basis; neither can drop below zero.

questions.stem: Unlike a partner, an S corporation shareholder generally may NOT include which of the following in basis for purposes of deducting losses?
options: Direct loans the shareholder makes to the corporation
The shareholder's share of the corporation's third-party (entity-level) debt for which the shareholder is not personally lending
Additional purchases of the corporation's stock
Capital contributions of cash
questions.rationale: S corporation shareholders get basis only from contributions and bona fide direct loans, not from the entity's third-party debt (unlike partners).

questions.stem: Under the passive activity rules of §469, a taxpayer wants to group several business activities so they are treated as a single activity for passive loss purposes. Which standard governs whether activities may be grouped?
options: Activities may be grouped only if they constitute an 'appropriate economic unit,' considering factors such as similarities in business type, common control, common ownership, geographic location, and interdependence, with consistency required across years
Activities may be grouped at will every year with no consistency requirement
Grouping is never permitted for individuals
Only activities in the same state may be grouped
questions.rationale: Section 469 grouping is allowed when activities form an 'appropriate economic unit,' judged by factors like business type, control, ownership, location, and interdependence, applied consistently.

questions.stem: An individual actively participates in a rental real estate activity and has a $30,000 loss. Her MAGI is $90,000. Under the special allowance for active rental participation, how much of the loss can she generally deduct against nonpassive income?
options: $30,000, the full loss
$25,000, the maximum special allowance, since her MAGI is below the $100,000 phaseout start
$0, because rental losses are always passive
$12,500, the MFS allowance
questions.rationale: The §469 active-participation special allowance lets up to $25,000 of rental loss offset other income, phasing out between $100,000 and $150,000 MAGI.

questions.stem: The $25,000 active-participation rental loss allowance phases out by 50 cents per dollar of MAGI above $100,000. At what MAGI is the allowance fully eliminated, and what happens to disallowed losses?
options: $150,000; disallowed passive losses are suspended and carried forward to offset future passive income or are freed upon disposition of the activity
$200,000; losses are deductible the next year automatically
$125,000; disallowed losses are permanently lost
$100,000; the allowance never phases in
questions.rationale: The $25,000 special allowance phases out fully at $150,000 MAGI; disallowed passive losses suspend and carry forward, freeing up on disposition.

questions.stem: A U.S. citizen lives and works abroad and qualifies under the bona fide residence or physical presence test. For 2024, what is the approximate maximum Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE)?
options: $126,500 (the 2024 inflation-adjusted maximum)
There is no maximum
questions.rationale: The 2024 maximum Foreign Earned Income Exclusion is $126,500.

questions.stem: Which form does an individual generally use to claim the Foreign Tax Credit, and is the credit refundable?
options: Schedule C; the credit is refundable
Form 1116; the foreign tax credit is generally nonrefundable but unused amounts may be carried back one year and forward ten years
Form 8862; the credit cannot be carried over
Form 2555; the credit is fully refundable
questions.rationale: The Foreign Tax Credit is claimed on Form 1116; it is nonrefundable with a 1-year carryback and 10-year carryforward.

questions.stem: An individual receives a Schedule K-1 from a partnership reporting $5,000 of guaranteed payments for services and a $3,000 distributive share of ordinary business income. How are these treated for self-employment tax purposes for a general partner?
options: Only the guaranteed payment is subject to self-employment tax
Both the $5,000 guaranteed payment for services and the $3,000 distributive share of trade-or-business income are generally subject to self-employment tax for a general partner
Neither is subject to self-employment tax
Only the distributive share is subject to self-employment tax
questions.rationale: A general partner's guaranteed payments for services and distributive share of trade-or-business income are both subject to self-employment tax.

questions.stem: An individual receives $1,200 in qualified REIT dividends reported on a K-1/1099. For the qualified business income (QBI) deduction, how are qualified REIT dividends treated?
options: They qualify for the 20% QBI deduction (as qualified REIT dividends) without regard to the W-2 wage or UBIA limitations
They are deductible at 50%
They are ineligible for any QBI deduction
They qualify only if the taxpayer materially participates in the REIT
questions.rationale: Qualified REIT dividends qualify for the 20% QBI deduction without the W-2 wage or UBIA limitations.

questions.stem: A passive activity is fully disposed of in a taxable transaction to an unrelated party. What happens to the activity's suspended passive losses?
options: They are freed and become fully deductible in the year of the complete disposition, first against passive income, then against other income
They are added to the basis of the property sold
They are permanently disallowed
They remain suspended indefinitely
questions.rationale: A complete taxable disposition of a passive activity frees suspended losses, which become fully deductible that year.

questions.stem: A taxpayer materially participates in a business if she meets any one of several tests. Which of the following is one of the material participation tests under the §469 regulations?
options: Owning at least 5% of the activity regardless of hours
Participating for any amount of time, even one hour
Participating in the activity for more than 500 hours during the tax year
Holding the investment for more than one year
questions.rationale: One material participation test is more than 500 hours of participation in the activity during the year.

questions.stem: An employee believes too little federal income tax is being withheld and wants to increase withholding. Which action correctly accomplishes this on the current Form W-4?
options: File Form 1099 with the employer
Request the employer to stop withholding Social Security tax
Enter an additional withholding amount per pay period in the extra-withholding line of Form W-4
Claim more allowances
questions.rationale: The current Form W-4 lets an employee request an extra dollar amount of federal income tax withholding per pay period.

questions.stem: A nonresident alien sells U.S. real property. Under FIRPTA, what general withholding requirement applies to the buyer?
options: The seller withholds tax on the buyer
No withholding is ever required on real estate sales
The buyer withholds 30% of the gain only
The buyer generally must withhold 15% of the amount realized on the disposition of a U.S. real property interest by a foreign person, subject to certain exceptions
questions.rationale: FIRPTA generally requires the buyer to withhold 15% of the amount realized on a foreign person's disposition of U.S. real property, with limited exceptions.

questions.stem: A taxpayer maintains a household and provides more than half the cost of keeping it up for his dependent mother, who lives in her own separate apartment (a nursing home would also qualify). Can he claim Head of Household based on his mother?
options: Yes, but only if the mother is under age 65
Yes, because a dependent parent is a special case for Head of Household who need not live with the taxpayer, provided the taxpayer pays more than half the cost of the parent's main home
No, because parents can never be a qualifying person for Head of Household
No, because the qualifying person must live with the taxpayer in all cases
questions.rationale: A dependent parent is the one qualifying person who need not live with the taxpayer for Head of Household, if the taxpayer pays over half the cost of the parent's home.

questions.stem: An employee receives a $5,000 signing bonus and $2,000 in tips that were not reported to the employer. How are these treated on her individual return?
options: Neither is taxable
Both the signing bonus and the tips are taxable wages; unreported tips must be reported by the employee and may require additional Social Security and Medicare tax via Form 4137
Tips are taxable but bonuses are gifts
Only the bonus is taxable; unreported tips are exempt
questions.rationale: Signing bonuses and tips are taxable wages; tips not reported to the employer are reported by the employee, with FICA computed on Form 4137.

questions.stem: An individual contributes $4,000 to a Health Savings Account (HSA) for self-only coverage in 2024, where the self-only limit is $4,150. The contribution was made personally (not through payroll). How is it treated?
options: It is a nondeductible personal expense
It is deductible as an above-the-line adjustment to income, within the annual HSA limit, even if the taxpayer does not itemize
It is deductible only as an itemized medical expense
It is fully taxable
questions.rationale: Out-of-pocket HSA contributions within the annual limit are deductible above the line, available even to non-itemizers.

questions.stem: An investor sells stock at a gain and the stock was held for exactly 12 months (one year) and a day. How is the gain characterized?
options: Long-term, because the stock was held more than one year
Short-term, because one year is the cutoff
Ordinary income because stock gains are never capital
Tax-free because it was held long enough
questions.rationale: Long-term capital gain requires holding the asset more than one year; exactly a year and a day qualifies.

questions.stem: A taxpayer contributes the maximum to a traditional IRA and is age 52 in 2024. What is the maximum contribution including any catch-up?
options: $6,500 total
$8,000, consisting of the $7,000 base plus a $1,000 catch-up for those age 50 and older
$10,000 with a $3,000 catch-up
$7,000 with no catch-up
questions.rationale: For 2024, the IRA contribution limit is $7,000 plus a $1,000 catch-up for those 50 and older, totaling $8,000.

questions.stem: A general partner's Schedule K-1 reports a $4,000 §179 expense deduction passed through. What limitation must the individual partner consider at the partner level?
options: No limitation applies at the partner level
The §179 deduction is subject to the partner's own taxable income limitation and the overall §179 dollar cap, applied at the partner level in addition to the partnership level
The deduction is automatically doubled at the partner level
The partner must capitalize it instead
questions.rationale: Pass-through §179 deductions are limited at both the entity and the partner level, including the dollar cap and the taxable income limitation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is required for a taxpayer to file as Head of Household?
options: The taxpayer must be unmarried (or considered unmarried), pay more than half the cost of keeping up a home, and have a qualifying person live with them more than half the year (with the dependent-parent exception)
The taxpayer must earn less than $50,000
The taxpayer must be married at year-end
The taxpayer must have a spouse who lived in the home all year
questions.rationale: Head of Household requires being unmarried/considered unmarried, paying over half the home cost, and a qualifying person (parents may live elsewhere).

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally NOT included in gross income?
options: Bartering income
Gambling winnings
Prizes and awards
Qualified scholarship amounts used for tuition and required fees by a degree candidate
questions.rationale: Qualified scholarships used for tuition and required fees are excluded; gambling winnings, prizes, and bartering income are taxable.

questions.stem: Which of the following remains deductible as an above-the-line adjustment to income for 2024?
options: One-half of self-employment tax
Unreimbursed employee business expenses
Tax preparation fees for an individual return
Investment advisory fees
questions.rationale: One-half of self-employment tax is still an above-the-line deduction; most 2%-floor miscellaneous itemized deductions are suspended.

questions.stem: A taxpayer donates appreciated long-term publicly traded stock (held 3 years, basis $2,000, FMV $10,000) to a public charity. What is the general charitable deduction amount and any AGI limit?
options: $10,000, the fair market value, subject to a 30% of AGI limit for appreciated capital gain property given to a public charity
$0, because donating stock is not deductible
$2,000, limited to basis
$10,000 with no AGI limit at all
questions.rationale: Long-term appreciated stock donated to a public charity is generally deductible at FMV, subject to the 30% of AGI limit.

questions.stem: A taxpayer rolls a distribution from a 401(k) to a traditional IRA but receives the check personally (an indirect rollover). To avoid taxation, within how many days must the funds be deposited into the IRA?
options: 90 days
180 days
60 days
30 days
questions.rationale: An indirect rollover must be redeposited within 60 days to avoid taxation (and possible penalty).

questions.stem: A U.S. citizen child is the qualifying child of a parent, but the parent's AGI is lower than the AGI of the child's grandparent, who also lived with the child all year and with whom the child is a qualifying child. Under the tiebreaker rules when a parent can claim the child but does not, who may claim the child?
options: Only the parent, never anyone else
The grandparent may always claim the child regardless of AGI
A non-parent (such as the grandparent) may claim the child only if that person's AGI is higher than the AGI of any parent who could claim the child
No one may claim the child
questions.rationale: A non-parent can claim a child who is also a parent's qualifying child only if the non-parent's AGI exceeds that of any parent who could claim the child.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has a net qualified disaster loss to personal-use property in a federally declared disaster area in 2024. How is the casualty loss deduction generally computed for such a loss?
options: The loss is deductible only as a business expense
Personal casualty losses are never deductible after 2017
The full loss is always deductible with no reductions
A casualty loss in a federally declared disaster area is deductible, reduced by $100 per casualty and by 10% of AGI, subject to the rules in effect for the year
questions.rationale: Personal casualty losses are deductible only in federally declared disasters, after the $100-per-event floor and 10%-of-AGI reduction (with special rules for some qualified disasters).

questions.stem: A taxpayer sells §1244 small business stock at a $90,000 loss. The stock was originally issued to her and met all §1244 requirements. As a single filer, how is the loss treated?
options: The entire $90,000 is an ordinary loss
Up to $50,000 of the loss is treated as an ordinary loss (deductible against ordinary income), with the remaining $40,000 a capital loss
Entirely as a capital loss limited to $3,000 per year against ordinary income
The loss is nondeductible
questions.rationale: Section 1244 allows up to $50,000 ($100,000 MFJ) of qualifying small business stock loss as ordinary; the rest is a capital loss.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has AMT in 2024 caused by the exercise of an ISO in a prior year, generating a minimum tax credit. What does the minimum tax credit allow in future years?
options: A credit against regular tax in future years to the extent regular tax exceeds tentative minimum tax, recovering AMT paid on timing (deferral) items like ISO exercises
A deduction for the AMT paid
A permanent exemption from AMT
A refund of all AMT paid immediately
questions.rationale: The minimum tax credit offsets future regular tax above tentative minimum tax, recovering AMT paid on deferral items like ISO exercises.

questions.stem: An individual partner's at-risk amount in an activity is $8,000, although her outside basis is $15,000. The K-1 shows a $12,000 loss that is otherwise allowed under the basis rules. How much loss is deductible after applying the at-risk limitation (ignoring passive rules)?
options: $12,000, the full loss
$8,000, limited to her at-risk amount, with the remaining $4,000 suspended under the at-risk rules
$15,000, her outside basis
$0, because at-risk rules disallow all losses
questions.rationale: The at-risk rules limit a loss to the amount the taxpayer has at risk; the excess is suspended until the at-risk amount increases.

questions.stem: A married couple disagree, and one spouse wants to file MFS while the other files MFJ. What is the rule?
options: The higher earner decides the filing status for both
Either spouse can unilaterally file MFJ binding both
A joint return requires the consent and signature of both spouses; if one spouse insists on filing separately, the other generally cannot file MFJ
They must file Head of Household
questions.rationale: A joint return requires both spouses' consent and signatures; one spouse cannot compel a joint filing.

questions.stem: A retiree receives a distribution from a traditional IRA that includes nondeductible (basis) contributions made over the years, tracked on Form 8606. How is each distribution taxed?
options: Each distribution is partly taxable and partly a nontaxable return of basis, based on the ratio of nondeductible contributions to the total IRA value
The entire distribution is fully taxable regardless of basis
The entire distribution is tax-free because some basis exists
The first dollars out are always the after-tax basis, tax-free
questions.rationale: Traditional IRA distributions with nondeductible basis are prorated between taxable earnings and nontaxable basis on Form 8606.

questions.stem: A taxpayer holds 200 shares purchased at different times and sells 50 shares. To use the specific identification method instead of FIFO, what must the taxpayer generally do?
options: Nothing; FIFO is the only method allowed
Average the cost of all shares
Sell only the oldest shares
Adequately identify the specific shares being sold (e.g., by lot) to the broker at or before the sale and receive confirmation
questions.rationale: Specific identification requires adequately identifying the shares to the broker at/before sale; otherwise FIFO applies (averaging is only for mutual funds).

questions.stem: What is the additional standard deduction feature available to a taxpayer who is age 65 or older or blind?
options: A doubling of the standard deduction
A tax credit of $1,000 per condition
No additional amount is available
An additional standard deduction amount is added for each condition (age 65+ and/or blindness), increasing the total standard deduction
questions.rationale: Taxpayers 65 or older and/or blind receive an additional standard deduction amount for each condition.

questions.stem: A taxpayer receives a Schedule K-1 from a partnership reporting a distribution of cash exceeding her outside basis. What is the consequence?
options: The excess reduces the partnership's basis only
The excess distribution is tax-free
Cash distributions in excess of the partner's outside basis are generally taxable as capital gain
The distribution is treated as ordinary income in all cases
questions.rationale: Cash distributions exceeding a partner's outside basis generally result in capital gain to the extent of the excess.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $3,000 advance commission in December 2024 that she must repay if certain sales are reversed. Under the claim of right doctrine, how is the $3,000 treated in 2024?
options: It is included in 2024 income because she received it under a claim of right without restriction on its use, even though she might later have to repay it
It is excluded as a loan
It is deferred until the repayment contingency is resolved
It is taxed only when the sales are finalized
questions.rationale: Under the claim of right doctrine, amounts received without restriction are taxed when received, with a possible §1341 credit if later repaid.

questions.stem: A taxpayer pays $12,000 of mortgage interest on $900,000 of home acquisition debt incurred in 2024 to buy a primary residence. What limitation applies to the deductibility of the interest?
options: All interest on any amount of acquisition debt is deductible
Home mortgage interest is deductible on acquisition debt up to $750,000 (for debt incurred after December 15, 2017), so interest on the portion above the limit is not deductible
No home mortgage interest is deductible after 2017
Only interest on $1 million of debt is deductible for post-2017 debt
questions.rationale: Acquisition-debt mortgage interest is deductible up to $750,000 of debt incurred after December 15, 2017 (interest on the excess is nondeductible).

questions.stem: A taxpayer made excess contributions of $2,000 to a Roth IRA and did not withdraw them by the deadline. What excise tax applies to the excess for each year it remains?
options: No penalty
6% per year on the excess amount until corrected
10% per year
25% one time
questions.rationale: Excess IRA contributions incur a 6% excise tax for each year they remain uncorrected in the account.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is 'considered unmarried' for Head of Household purposes even though still legally married. Which condition supports this treatment?
options: The couple filed a joint return last year
The taxpayer earns more than the spouse

The taxpayer's spouse did not live in the home during the last six months of the year, and the taxpayer paid more than half the cost of a home that was the main home of a qualifying child for more than half the year
The spouses simply choose to live in separate bedrooms
questions.rationale: A married taxpayer is 'considered unmarried' (eligible for HOH) if the spouse was absent the last six months, the taxpayer paid over half the home cost, and a qualifying child lived there over half the year.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is a real estate professional under §469(c)(7). What is the tax significance of qualifying as a real estate professional?
options: All rental income becomes tax-free
The taxpayer cannot deduct any rental expenses
The taxpayer must treat all rentals as passive
Rental real estate activities in which the taxpayer materially participates are not automatically treated as passive, so losses can offset nonpassive income
questions.rationale: A real estate professional who materially participates in rentals avoids automatic passive treatment, allowing rental losses to offset nonpassive income.

questions.stem: An individual wins a $7,500 prize on a game show. Which statement is correct?
options: Game show winnings are exempt up to $10,000
The fair market value of the prize is includible in gross income as 'other income,' reported on Form 1040
The prize is tax-free because it is not earned income
Only cash prizes are taxable, not merchandise prizes
questions.rationale: Prizes and awards, including game show winnings (cash or the FMV of merchandise), are taxable as other income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer makes a $40,000 cash gift to a public charity but has AGI of only $50,000, with the 60% limit applying. What is the current-year deduction and the treatment of any excess?
options: None of the gift is deductible because it exceeds AGI limits
Only $25,000 is deductible and the rest is lost
The full $40,000 is deductible this year with no carryover
$30,000 (60% of $50,000 AGI) is deductible this year, and the remaining $10,000 carries forward for up to five years
questions.rationale: Cash gifts to public charities are limited to 60% of AGI per year; the excess carries forward up to five years.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has a §1231 net gain of $10,000 in 2024 but had $4,000 of unrecaptured §1231 losses in the prior five years. How does the lookback rule affect the character of the current gain?
options: $4,000 of the current §1231 gain is recharacterized as ordinary income (to the extent of unrecaptured net §1231 losses in the prior five years), with the remaining $6,000 as long-term capital gain
The entire $10,000 is long-term capital gain
The lookback rule does not affect individuals
The entire $10,000 is ordinary income
questions.rationale: The §1231 five-year lookback recharacterizes current net §1231 gain as ordinary income to the extent of nonrecaptured prior net §1231 losses.

questions.stem: Which of the following retirement distributions is generally NOT subject to required minimum distributions during the original owner's lifetime?
options: Traditional IRA
401(k) plan
SEP IRA
Roth IRA owned by the original account holder
questions.rationale: Roth IRAs are not subject to RMDs during the original owner's lifetime, unlike traditional IRAs, SEP IRAs, and 401(k)s.

questions.stem: A taxpayer receives Schedule K-1 income from a publicly traded partnership (PTP). How are passive losses from a PTP generally treated?
options: They can offset wages and portfolio income freely
They can offset any passive income from other activities
They are never deductible
Passive losses from a PTP can generally only offset passive income from the same PTP, not from other passive activities
questions.rationale: PTP passive losses can only offset income from the same PTP; they cannot offset other passive, portfolio, or active income.

questions.stem: Which of the following individuals is treated as a U.S. resident for income tax purposes regardless of the substantial presence test?
options: A diplomat on assignment
A foreign student on an F visa in the first year
A lawful permanent resident (green card holder) at any time during the year
A tourist visiting for two weeks
questions.rationale: Green card holders are U.S. residents for tax purposes regardless of the substantial presence test.

questions.stem: A taxpayer pays $5,000 of state income taxes, $4,000 of property taxes, and $2,000 of state sales tax (electing income tax) in 2024. What is the maximum SALT deduction allowed?
options: $11,000, the full amount
$10,000, the SALT deduction cap for the combined state and local taxes
Unlimited
questions.rationale: The SALT itemized deduction is capped at $10,000 ($5,000 MFS) for combined state/local income (or sales) and property taxes.

questions.stem: A taxpayer gifts appreciated stock to a friend. What is the friend's holding period in the gifted stock for capital gain purposes (assuming a later sale at a gain)?
options: It starts fresh on the date of the gift
It is always treated as long-term regardless of the donor's holding period
It is always treated as short-term
The donor's holding period tacks on, so the recipient includes the donor's holding period (using the carryover basis for gain)
questions.rationale: For gifted property sold at a gain (carryover basis), the donor's holding period tacks on to the donee's.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old taxpayer wants to make a one-time qualified charitable distribution to fund a charitable gift annuity. Under SECURE 2.0, what is generally true?
options: A one-time QCD of up to an inflation-adjusted limit ($53,000 for 2024) may be made to a qualifying charitable gift annuity or certain charitable trusts
QCDs to gift annuities are unlimited
Only taxpayers under 59 1/2 may make such QCDs
QCDs cannot fund any split-interest entity
questions.rationale: SECURE 2.0 permits a one-time QCD (inflation-adjusted to $53,000 in 2024) to fund a charitable gift annuity or certain charitable trusts.

questions.stem: A self-employed individual has net Schedule C profit of $50,000. Approximately what portion of net earnings is subject to self-employment tax (after the deduction for the employer-equivalent portion)?
options: 92.35% of net profit, because net earnings are reduced to account for the employer-equivalent half of SE tax
None of it
questions.rationale: Self-employment tax is computed on 92.35% of net Schedule C profit.

questions.stem: A taxpayer receives a Form 1099-K reporting $15,000 of payments for goods sold through an online marketplace. The items were personal property sold at a loss. How is this reported?
options: It is ignored because a 1099-K is informational only
The full $15,000 is taxable income
The amounts are reported, but because the personal-use items were sold at a loss, no taxable gain results (and the personal loss is nondeductible)
The loss is deductible against wages
questions.rationale: Personal items sold at a loss via a 1099-K produce no taxable gain, and the loss is nondeductible, but the amounts should be reconciled on the return.

questions.stem: Which credit is specifically aimed at low-to-moderate-income working taxpayers and is refundable?
options: Child and Dependent Care Credit
Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)
Lifetime Learning Credit
Foreign Tax Credit
questions.rationale: The EITC is a refundable credit designed for low-to-moderate-income working taxpayers.

questions.stem: A taxpayer sells depreciable real property used in a business (§1250 property) at a gain. To the extent of straight-line depreciation taken, the gain attributable to depreciation is taxed at what maximum rate for an individual?
options: 37% ordinary rate
25% (the unrecaptured §1250 gain rate)
20% standard long-term rate
questions.rationale: Unrecaptured §1250 gain (from straight-line depreciation on real property) is taxed at a maximum 25% rate for individuals.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who is age 55 and covered by a high-deductible health plan can make an additional catch-up contribution to an HSA. What is the HSA catch-up amount for those age 55 and older?
questions.rationale: The HSA catch-up contribution for those 55 and older is $1,000.

questions.stem: An individual is a passive investor in two separate activities: Activity A has $10,000 of passive income and Activity B has $15,000 of passive loss. What is the net effect on the taxpayer's return for the year (ignoring prior suspended losses)?
options: Neither item is reported
The full $15,000 loss is deductible against ordinary income
$10,000 of the passive loss offsets the $10,000 of passive income, leaving a $5,000 suspended passive loss carried forward
The $15,000 loss offsets wages and the $10,000 income is exempt
questions.rationale: Passive losses offset passive income; the unused passive loss is suspended and carried forward.

questions.stem: A child is born on December 15, 2024, and lives the rest of the year with the parents. For the dependency residency test, how is this short period treated?
options: The child must live at least six months to qualify
The child fails the residency test because of the short time
A child born during the year is treated as having lived with the taxpayer for the entire year (for the portion of the year the child was alive), satisfying the residency test
The child can only be claimed in the following year
questions.rationale: A child born during the year is treated as living with the taxpayer for the entire year, satisfying the residency test.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has $200,000 of qualified business income from a specified service trade or business (SSTB) and taxable income above the upper threshold for the QBI deduction. What is the result for the QBI deduction on the SSTB income?
options: The full 20% QBI deduction is allowed
A 50% deduction is allowed
The deduction is unlimited for SSTBs
No QBI deduction is allowed on SSTB income once taxable income exceeds the upper phaseout threshold
questions.rationale: Above the upper taxable income threshold, SSTB income is fully excluded from the QBI deduction.

questions.stem: An individual abandons worthless securities. When a security becomes wholly worthless during the year, how is the loss treated for timing purposes?
options: The loss is an ordinary loss in all cases
The loss can never be claimed
The security is treated as sold on the last day of the tax year in which it became wholly worthless, generating a capital loss
The loss is deductible only when the security is sold
questions.rationale: A wholly worthless security is treated as sold on the last day of the year it became worthless, yielding a capital loss.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who reaches age 73 in 2024 takes the first RMD. What is the deadline for taking that first-year RMD, and what is the trade-off of deferring it?
options: It must be taken within 30 days of turning 73
There is no deadline for the first RMD
It must be taken by December 31, 2024 with no deferral option
The first RMD may be delayed until April 1, 2025 (the required beginning date), but deferring means two RMDs are taken in 2025, potentially increasing 2025 income
questions.rationale: The first RMD can be deferred to April 1 of the following year, but that causes two RMDs in that year, potentially raising income.

questions.stem: An individual receives a Schedule K-1 from an S corporation. Which item, if any, is generally subject to self-employment tax for the shareholder?
options: All distributions received
The shareholder's pro-rata share of ordinary business income
Only dividend income
None of the pass-through income; S corporation shareholders are not subject to SE tax on their distributive share (though reasonable wages paid to them are subject to payroll tax)
questions.rationale: S corporation pass-through income is not subject to SE tax; instead, reasonable wages to shareholder-employees are subject to payroll tax.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received Series EE U.S. savings bond interest. Under the education savings bond exclusion, the interest may be excludable if used for qualified higher education expenses. Which condition can disqualify the exclusion?
options: Using the bonds for the taxpayer's own education
Holding the bonds more than five years
Cashing the bonds in the same year as the expenses
The taxpayer's modified AGI exceeding the applicable phaseout threshold, or the bonds being registered in the name of a child rather than the taxpayer (or spouse)
questions.rationale: The education savings bond interest exclusion phases out at higher MAGI and requires the bonds to be in the taxpayer's (or spouse's) name, not the child's.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a capital asset in the hands of an individual?
options: Inventory held for sale to customers
Depreciable property used in a trade or business
Accounts receivable from the taxpayer's business
Stock held for investment
questions.rationale: Investment stock is a capital asset; inventory, receivables, and depreciable business property are not.

questions.stem: A taxpayer takes a hardship distribution from a 401(k) before age 59 1/2. Which statement is correct?
options: Hardship distributions are generally subject to income tax and, unless an exception applies, the 10% early withdrawal penalty
Hardship distributions are exempt from the 10% early withdrawal penalty
Hardship distributions can always be repaid like a loan
Hardship distributions are always tax-free
questions.rationale: 401(k) hardship distributions are taxable and generally subject to the 10% early-distribution penalty unless a separate exception applies.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's qualifying child is a 20-year-old full-time student who earned $8,000 from a part-time job and provided $7,000 toward her own support; the parents provided $9,000. Does the child meet the support test to be a qualifying child?
options: No, because the child earned income
Yes, because for a qualifying child the test is that the child did not provide more than half of his or her own support, and here the child provided less than half
No, because the child must provide more than half of her own support
Yes, but only if the child is under 19
questions.rationale: For a qualifying child, the test is that the child did not provide more than half of his or her own support; full-time students qualify up to age 24.

questions.stem: A landlord (individual, not a real estate dealer) collects $18,000 in rent and receives a $1,500 security deposit she must return at lease end. How are these amounts treated in the year received?
options: Only the security deposit is taxable
Both the rent and deposit are taxable income
Neither amount is taxable
The $18,000 rent is taxable income, but the $1,500 refundable security deposit is not income when received (unless retained)
questions.rationale: Rent is taxable when received, but a refundable security deposit is not income unless the landlord retains it.

questions.stem: A taxpayer pays $3,000 in qualified adoption expenses in 2024 and finalizes a domestic adoption. Which statement about the adoption credit is correct?
options: There is no adoption credit
The adoption credit is refundable
The adoption credit is nonrefundable but unused amounts may be carried forward for up to five years, subject to a per-child maximum and income phaseout
The credit is unlimited and fully refundable
questions.rationale: The adoption credit is nonrefundable with a 5-year carryforward, a per-child maximum, and an income phaseout.

questions.stem: A taxpayer converts a personal residence to a rental property when its FMV ($250,000) is below the original cost basis ($300,000). For computing depreciation and a later loss, what basis is used?
options: Always the original $300,000 cost basis
For depreciation and determining a loss on a later sale, the basis is the lower of cost or FMV at the date of conversion ($250,000)
Zero basis
The average of cost and FMV
questions.rationale: When converting personal-use property to rental, basis for depreciation and loss is the lower of adjusted cost or FMV at the conversion date.

questions.stem: A self-employed individual wants to set up a retirement plan with high contribution limits for 2024. Which plan generally allows the largest combined employee deferral plus employer contribution for a sole proprietor with modest income?
options: A traditional IRA
A Roth IRA only
A SIMPLE IRA only
A solo 401(k), which permits both an employee elective deferral and an employer profit-sharing contribution
questions.rationale: A solo 401(k) combines an employee deferral and employer contribution, often allowing the largest total for a sole proprietor.

questions.stem: An individual has $50,000 of qualified business income, taxable income of $120,000 (below the threshold), and is single. Which limitation does NOT apply at this income level for the QBI deduction?
options: The 20% of QBI computation
The W-2 wage and unadjusted basis (UBIA) limitations, which only apply above the income thresholds
The overall taxable income limit
The requirement that QBI be from a U.S. trade or business
questions.rationale: Below the taxable income thresholds, the W-2 wage/UBIA limits and SSTB restriction do not apply to the QBI deduction.

questions.stem: An individual who is a U.S. citizen must generally report which income on the U.S. tax return?
options: Worldwide income, including foreign-source income, subject to available exclusions and credits
Only investment income
Only income reported on a W-2
Only income earned within the United States
questions.rationale: U.S. citizens must report worldwide income, mitigated by exclusions and foreign tax credits.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has a Premium Tax Credit (PTC) reconciliation: advance PTC of $6,000 was paid to the insurer, but the actual PTC based on year-end income is only $4,500. What is the consequence (assuming no repayment limitation applies)?
options: There is no reconciliation required
The taxpayer receives an additional $1,500 refund
The taxpayer must repay the $1,500 excess advance PTC, subject to any applicable repayment limitation based on income
The insurer absorbs the difference
questions.rationale: Excess advance Premium Tax Credit must be repaid on Form 8962, subject to income-based repayment limitations.

questions.stem: An individual sells a personal-use automobile for less than its original cost. How is the loss treated?
options: It is a deductible capital loss
It is deductible as a casualty loss
It is an ordinary loss
It is a nondeductible personal loss because losses on personal-use property are not deductible
questions.rationale: Losses on the sale of personal-use property, such as a personal automobile, are nondeductible.

questions.stem: Contributions to a Roth IRA can be withdrawn at any time without tax or penalty up to what amount?
options: Only the earnings
Nothing can be withdrawn before age 59 1/2
The amount of the taxpayer's own contributions (basis), because contributions come out first and are always tax- and penalty-free
Only after five years
