OID is taxed only when the bond is sold or matures
OID on the corporate bond is generally included in income annually as it accrues, even before cash is received
Treasury bill discount is exempt from all federal tax
questions.rationale: Corporate OID is taxed annually as it accrues. Treasury obligation interest is federally taxable but exempt from state and local income tax.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $1,500 qualified dividend and a $400 capital gain distribution from a mutual fund, plus $200 of nondividend (return of capital) distribution. The taxpayer's stock basis is $5,000. What is the immediate tax treatment of the $200 nondividend distribution?
options: Taxed as a capital gain distribution
Taxed as a qualified dividend
Not taxed currently; it reduces the stock basis to $4,800
Taxed as ordinary income
questions.rationale: A nondividend distribution is a return of capital that reduces the shareholder's basis and is not taxed until basis is exhausted, after which further distributions are capital gain.

questions.stem: A retiree received Social Security benefits of $24,000 and has other income (pension and interest) of $40,000, filing single. Approximately what portion of the Social Security may be taxable?
options: Up to 85%
Up to 50%
Always 100%
questions.rationale: Up to 85% of Social Security benefits become taxable once provisional income exceeds the upper threshold; benefits are never more than 85% taxable.

questions.stem: A single taxpayer paid $9,000 of state income tax, $4,500 of real estate tax, and $1,200 of personal property tax in 2024. What is her allowable itemized deduction for state and local taxes?
questions.rationale: The state and local tax (SALT) itemized deduction is capped at $10,000 ($5,000 MFS), so taxpayers paying more than that are limited to the cap.

questions.stem: A taxpayer used a $50,000 home equity loan to pay off credit cards (not to buy, build, or improve the home). For 2024, how is the interest on this home equity loan treated?
options: Not deductible as home mortgage interest because the proceeds were not used to buy, build, or improve the home
Deductible as a business expense
Deductible as investment interest
Fully deductible as home mortgage interest
questions.rationale: Under current law, home equity loan interest is deductible only if the proceeds are used to buy, build, or substantially improve the residence that secures the loan.

questions.stem: A taxpayer with AGI of $100,000 donated publicly traded stock held three years (FMV $40,000, basis $10,000) to a public charity. He makes no special election. What is his maximum charitable deduction for this gift in 2024?
options: $40,000, but limited to 30% of AGI, so $30,000 this year with the excess carried forward
$60,000, which is 60% of AGI
$10,000, the basis
questions.rationale: Gifts of long-term appreciated capital gain property to public charities are deductible at fair market value but limited to 30% of AGI, with a five-year carryover for the excess.

questions.stem: A taxpayer with AGI of $80,000 made cash contributions of $55,000 to a qualified public charity in 2024. How much can he deduct this year, and what happens to the rest?
options: $80,000, full AGI
$55,000, all deductible this year
$48,000 (60% of AGI) deductible now; $7,000 carries forward up to five years
$24,000 (30% of AGI) deductible now; rest carries forward
questions.rationale: Cash contributions to public charities are deductible up to 60% of AGI, with any excess carried forward for up to five years.

questions.stem: A taxpayer donated a used car to a qualified charity. The charity sold the car for $2,800. The taxpayer estimates its FMV at $4,000. With no exceptions, what is the deduction?
options: $0, because vehicles are not deductible
$1,200, the difference
$2,800, the gross proceeds from the charity's sale
$4,000, the estimated FMV
questions.rationale: When a donated vehicle is sold by the charity, the deduction is generally limited to the gross proceeds of that sale, as reported on Form 1098-C.

questions.stem: A taxpayer with AGI of $90,000 incurred $14,000 of unreimbursed qualified medical expenses in 2024. What amount may she deduct as a medical itemized deduction?
questions.rationale: Medical expenses are deductible to the extent they exceed 7.5% of AGI. With AGI $90,000, the floor is $6,750, so $14,000 - $6,750 = $7,250 is deductible.

questions.stem: A taxpayer suffered a personal casualty loss when a tornado (a federally declared disaster) destroyed property. After insurance, the unreimbursed loss was $20,000 and her AGI is $60,000. What is the deductible casualty loss?
options: $0, because personal casualty losses are never deductible
questions.rationale: For 2018-2025, personal casualty losses are deductible only if attributable to a federally declared disaster, reduced by $100 per event and 10% of AGI.

questions.stem: For 2024, which of the following is still allowed as a miscellaneous itemized deduction not subject to the 2%-of-AGI floor?
options: Unreimbursed employee business expenses
Gambling losses up to gambling winnings
Investment advisory fees
Tax preparation fees for a personal return
questions.rationale: Most 2%-floor miscellaneous deductions are suspended for 2018-2025, but gambling losses up to winnings remain a valid itemized deduction not subject to the 2% floor.

questions.stem: A volunteer drove 1,000 miles in 2024 doing charitable work and spent $60 on parking and tolls for that work. Using the standard charitable mileage rate of 14 cents per mile, what is her charitable transportation deduction?
questions.rationale: Charitable use of a car is deductible at 14 cents per mile, and actual parking fees and tolls are deductible in addition to mileage.

questions.stem: A single taxpayer is age 67 and not blind in 2024. Compared with a younger taxpayer, what is true about her standard deduction?
options: She must itemize because she is over 65
She gets no increase for age
She receives an additional standard deduction amount for being 65 or older
Her standard deduction is reduced for being over 65
questions.rationale: Taxpayers who are 65 or older (or blind) are entitled to an additional standard deduction amount added to the basic standard deduction.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who is claimed as a dependent on her parents' return earned $400 in wages and received $1,500 in interest income in 2024. How is her standard deduction generally determined?
options: Her total income amount
The full single standard deduction
Zero, because dependents get no standard deduction
The greater of $1,300 or earned income plus $450 (limited to the regular standard deduction)
questions.rationale: A dependent's standard deduction equals the greater of a fixed minimum ($1,300 for 2024) or earned income plus $450, capped at the regular standard deduction.

questions.stem: A self-employed taxpayer with $80,000 of net SE income paid $9,000 in health insurance premiums for himself and his family and had a net profit before the deduction. Neither he nor his spouse was eligible for employer-subsidized coverage. How is the $9,000 premium treated?
options: Deductible only as an itemized medical expense subject to the 7.5% floor
Deductible as an above-the-line self-employed health insurance deduction, limited to net SE earnings
Not deductible at all
Deductible only on Schedule C reducing SE tax
questions.rationale: Self-employed individuals can deduct health insurance premiums above the line (Schedule 1), limited to net self-employment income, if not eligible for employer-subsidized coverage; it does not reduce SE tax.

questions.stem: A K-12 teacher spent $400 on classroom supplies in 2024. What is the maximum educator expense deduction she may claim above the line?
options: $0, only itemized
questions.rationale: Eligible K-12 educators may deduct up to $300 (2024) of unreimbursed classroom expenses above the line; amounts above the cap are not deductible.

questions.stem: A self-employed consultant with qualified business income of $120,000 and taxable income (before QBI deduction) of $150,000, filing single, is below the QBI phase-in threshold. What is her tentative QBI deduction before the taxable-income limit?
questions.rationale: For taxpayers below the threshold, the QBI deduction is 20% of qualified business income, limited overall to 20% of taxable income minus net capital gain.

questions.stem: A married-filing-jointly taxpayer with taxable income above the upper QBI threshold operates a specified service trade or business (a law firm). What is the effect on his QBI deduction?
options: He receives the full 20% deduction regardless of income
His QBI deduction for the SSTB is fully phased out (disallowed)
He may deduct 20% of W-2 wages only
SSTBs always get a 50% deduction
questions.rationale: Specified service trades or businesses lose the QBI deduction entirely once the owner's taxable income exceeds the upper phase-out threshold.

questions.stem: Which type of income is NOT qualified business income (QBI) eligible for the QBI deduction?
options: Net rental income from a qualifying rental real estate enterprise
Reasonable compensation paid to an S corporation shareholder-employee
Net profit from a sole proprietorship retail store
Ordinary income from a partnership engaged in manufacturing
questions.rationale: QBI excludes wages, including reasonable compensation paid to an S corporation shareholder-employee and guaranteed payments to partners.

questions.stem: A taxpayer had a $40,000 net operating loss generated in 2024 from his sole proprietorship. Under current rules for NOLs arising after 2020, how may he use this NOL?
options: Carry back 5 years only
Carry forward indefinitely, limited to 80% of taxable income in the year used
Carry back 2 years and carry forward 20 years
Deduct it all in 2024 against wages with no limit
questions.rationale: Post-2020 individual NOLs generally have no carryback and an indefinite carryforward, with the deduction limited to 80% of taxable income in the year used.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has wages of $50,000 and a Schedule C loss of $70,000 in 2024 with no other income. Which statement about a potential net operating loss is correct?
options: An NOL can include personal nonbusiness deductions in full
Personal exemptions and the standard deduction are added back when computing the NOL, so the NOL is generally less than the raw negative taxable income
Wages are not counted in the NOL computation
The entire $70,000 loss creates an NOL automatically
questions.rationale: An NOL is computed by adjusting taxable income to remove nonbusiness deductions exceeding nonbusiness income and other items, so it is generally less than the raw negative taxable income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is figuring the qualified business income deduction and is above the phase-in threshold for a non-SSTB. Which limitation may reduce the 20% QBI amount?
options: The greater of 50% of W-2 wages, or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of unadjusted basis of qualified property
Always a flat 25% reduction
The medical expense floor
Only the 20%-of-taxable-income overall limit
questions.rationale: Above the income threshold, the QBI deduction for a qualified (non-SSTB) business is limited by the W-2 wage and unadjusted basis of property tests.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received qualified REIT dividends of $5,000 and had no other business income in 2024. Are these eligible for any QBI-related deduction?
options: No, REIT dividends never qualify
Yes, qualified REIT dividends are eligible for a 20% deduction regardless of the W-2 wage limits
Only if the taxpayer is below the threshold
Only if held in a retirement account
questions.rationale: Qualified REIT dividends and qualified publicly traded partnership income qualify for a 20% deduction without the W-2 wage or qualified property limitations.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's only income is a Schedule C net profit of $30,000. He pays $4,239 in self-employment tax. When computing taxable income and QBI, which is correct?
options: QBI is reduced by the deductible portion of self-employment tax (one-half of SE tax) attributable to the business
QBI equals taxable income
SE tax is added to QBI
QBI is $30,000 with no reduction
questions.rationale: Qualified business income is net of the deductions attributable to the business, including the deductible portion of self-employment tax, self-employed health insurance, and SE retirement plan contributions.

questions.stem: A landlord wants her residential rental activity to qualify as a trade or business for the QBI deduction using the rental real estate safe harbor. Which requirement applies?
options: The landlord must be a licensed real estate professional
At least 250 hours of rental services must be performed for the enterprise during the year
The property must generate a profit
The property must be a personal residence
questions.rationale: The IRS rental real estate safe harbor for QBI generally requires 250 or more hours of rental services per year, separate books and records, and contemporaneous logs.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has a QBI deduction limited by the 20%-of-taxable-income overall cap. In computing that cap, which item reduces the taxable income base?
options: Self-employment tax is added back
Wages are subtracted
Net capital gain (including qualified dividends) is subtracted from taxable income
The standard deduction is added back
questions.rationale: The QBI deduction cannot exceed 20% of taxable income reduced by net capital gain, where net capital gain includes qualified dividends.

questions.stem: Which business is a 'specified service trade or business' (SSTB) for QBI purposes?
options: An architecture firm
A retail clothing store
A health care practice (physician)
A manufacturing company
questions.rationale: SSTBs include health, law, accounting, consulting, and similar fields where the principal asset is the reputation or skill of employees, but architecture and engineering are excluded.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has two businesses: Business A with QBI of $60,000 and Business B with a QBI loss of $20,000. He is below the threshold. What is his combined QBI deduction (ignoring the overall taxable income limit)?
options: $8,000 (20% of net $40,000 after netting the loss)
questions.rationale: Qualified business losses reduce qualified business income from other businesses; the 20% deduction applies to the net positive QBI.

questions.stem: A taxpayer had negative total QBI of $15,000 in 2024 (all businesses combined produced a net QBI loss). What happens to the negative QBI?
options: It is added to next year's income
It is lost permanently
It is deductible as a $15,000 QBI loss
It carries over as a negative QBI amount that reduces next year's QBI deduction
questions.rationale: A negative overall QBI amount carries forward and is treated as a loss from a separate business in the next year, reducing that year's QBI deduction.

questions.stem: A taxpayer enrolled in a Marketplace plan and received advance premium tax credit of $6,000 based on estimated income. At year end his actual household income made him eligible for only $4,000 of premium tax credit. He is not below the repayment-limitation threshold. What is the reconciliation result?
options: No reconciliation is needed
He receives an additional $2,000 credit
He repays the full $6,000
He must repay the $2,000 excess advance credit (subject to repayment caps)
questions.rationale: Form 8962 reconciles advance premium tax credit to the actual allowed credit; excess advance payments are repaid (subject to repayment limits based on income), and a shortfall increases the refund.

questions.stem: A married couple both worked for different employers in 2024 and together had Social Security tax withheld exceeding the maximum on the wage base from each spouse's combined jobs. One spouse's total Social Security withholding exceeded the annual maximum because he had two jobs. How is the excess recovered?
options: It is claimed as a refundable credit for excess Social Security tax on the spouse's return
It is lost; only the employer can recover it
It must be carried forward
It reduces next year's wages
questions.rationale: Excess Social Security tax withheld due to having more than one employer is claimed as a credit on the individual return. (Excess from a single employer must be recovered from that employer.)

questions.stem: A single taxpayer has one job and her employer withheld more Social Security tax than the annual maximum on the wage base. How does she recover the excess?
options: Claim the excess SS credit on her Form 1040
Ask the employer to adjust and refund the over-withholding
Carry it forward to next year
She cannot recover it
questions.rationale: The excess Social Security tax credit on the return is only for over-withholding caused by multiple employers; a single employer's error must be corrected by that employer.

questions.stem: A taxpayer with two qualifying children and earned income of $20,000 is computing the child and dependent care credit. She paid $9,000 of qualifying care expenses for both children. What is the maximum amount of expenses she may use to figure the credit?
questions.rationale: For the child and dependent care credit, qualifying expenses are limited to $3,000 for one qualifying person and $6,000 for two or more, further limited by earned income.

questions.stem: For the child and dependent care credit, a taxpayer and spouse must both have earned income unless one spouse is in a special category. Which counts as deemed earned income for this credit?
options: A spouse who is a full-time student or incapable of self-care has deemed monthly earned income
Alimony received under a 2020 decree
Unemployment compensation
Investment income
questions.rationale: For the dependent care credit, a spouse who is a full-time student or incapable of self-care is treated as having a deemed amount of earned income each month, allowing the credit despite no actual earnings.

questions.stem: A taxpayer (single, AGI $45,000) claims the American Opportunity Tax Credit for her first-year college expenses. She paid $4,500 of qualified tuition and fees. What is her AOTC, and how much of it is potentially refundable?
options: $2,500 maximum credit, up to 40% ($1,000) refundable
$2,000 credit, nonrefundable
$2,500 credit, fully nonrefundable
$4,500 credit, fully refundable
questions.rationale: The American Opportunity Tax Credit is up to $2,500 per eligible student (100% of the first $2,000 plus 25% of the next $2,000), with up to 40% ($1,000) refundable.

questions.stem: A taxpayer claims the Lifetime Learning Credit. Which statement is correct about this credit for 2024?
options: It is 40% refundable
It requires at least half-time enrollment
It is limited to the first four years of college
It equals 20% of up to $10,000 of qualified expenses, max $2,000 per return, nonrefundable
questions.rationale: The Lifetime Learning Credit is 20% of up to $10,000 in qualified expenses (max $2,000 per return), nonrefundable, with no enrollment-level or year limit.

questions.stem: A low-income taxpayer made a $2,000 contribution to her traditional IRA in 2024 and qualifies for the Saver's Credit (Retirement Savings Contributions Credit). What is true about this credit?
options: It is unlimited
It only applies to Roth IRAs
It is a nonrefundable credit of 10%, 20%, or 50% of up to $2,000 of contributions depending on AGI
It is fully refundable
questions.rationale: The Saver's Credit is a nonrefundable credit of 10%, 20%, or 50% of up to $2,000 of retirement contributions ($4,000 MFJ), with the rate decreasing as AGI rises.

questions.stem: A taxpayer with investment income of $12,000 (interest and dividends) wants to claim the Earned Investment Tax Credit (EITC). For 2024 the investment income limit is $11,600. What is the effect?
options: She still qualifies if earned income is low enough
She is disqualified from the EITC because her investment income exceeds the limit
Investment income does not affect the EITC
Only half the investment income counts
questions.rationale: The EITC is disallowed if a taxpayer's investment income exceeds the annual limit ($11,600 for 2024), regardless of earned income level.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old taxpayer with no qualifying children, who is not a dependent of anyone and lived in the U.S. more than half the year, wants the EITC for 2024. What is the minimum age generally required to claim the EITC with no qualifying children?
options: Any age if income is low
questions.rationale: To claim the EITC without a qualifying child for 2024, the taxpayer generally must be at least age 25 but under 65 and meet residency and dependency rules.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's child turned 17 on December 30, 2024. The child otherwise qualifies as a dependent. What credit is available for that child for 2024?
options: The earned income credit only
The $500 credit for other dependents, because the child was not under 17 at year end
No credit at all
The full $2,000 child tax credit
questions.rationale: A child must be under age 17 at the end of the year for the child tax credit. A 17-year-old dependent may instead qualify for the $500 credit for other dependents.

questions.stem: A married couple filing jointly has a tax liability before credits of $1,200 and qualifies for a $4,000 child tax credit (two children). What is the maximum additional (refundable) child tax credit they may receive for 2024, assuming they have sufficient earned income?
options: Up to $1,700 per child of the unused credit, subject to the earned income formula
$2,800 unlimited
questions.rationale: The refundable additional child tax credit is limited to $1,700 per qualifying child for 2024 and is computed as 15% of earned income exceeding $2,500, up to the unused credit.

questions.stem: A taxpayer installed qualifying residential solar electric panels on her main home in 2024, paying $20,000. What is her Residential Clean Energy Credit?
options: $6,000 (30% of cost), nonrefundable with carryforward
$5,000 (a flat cap)
$2,000 maximum
questions.rationale: The Residential Clean Energy Credit equals 30% of qualifying clean energy property costs (such as solar panels), is nonrefundable, and any excess carries forward.

questions.stem: A self-employed taxpayer estimates 2024 tax of $12,000 and his prior-year (2023) tax was $9,000 with AGI under $150,000. To avoid an underpayment penalty using the safe harbor, what is the minimum he must pay in timely estimated payments and withholding?
options: $12,000 (100% of current year)
The lesser of 90% of current-year tax ($10,800) or 100% of prior-year tax ($9,000)
questions.rationale: The estimated tax safe harbor is met by paying the lesser of 90% of the current year's tax or 100% of the prior year's tax (110% if prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000).

questions.stem: A taxpayer's income is highly uneven, with most earned late in the year. To minimize estimated-tax penalties, which method may reduce or eliminate the penalty for earlier quarters?
options: The annualized income installment method
The flat 25%-per-quarter method
Filing an extension
Paying everything by April 15 of the prior year
questions.rationale: The annualized income installment method allows taxpayers whose income is received unevenly to compute required estimated payments based on income actually earned in each period, reducing penalties.

questions.stem: A taxpayer (single) has modified AGI of $260,000 and net investment income of $30,000 in 2024. The net investment income tax (NIIT) of 3.8% applies to which amount?
options: $30,000, all net investment income
The lesser of net investment income ($30,000) or MAGI over the $200,000 threshold ($60,000), i.e., $30,000
questions.rationale: The 3.8% net investment income tax applies to the lesser of net investment income or the amount by which MAGI exceeds the threshold ($200,000 single, $250,000 MFJ).

questions.stem: A U.S. citizen has signature authority over a foreign bank account that held a maximum balance of $15,000 during 2024. What is her FBAR (FinCEN Form 114) obligation?
options: FBAR is only for accounts she owns, not signature authority
FBAR is filed with the income tax return
She must file an FBAR because the aggregate foreign account value exceeded $10,000 at any time
No reporting because the balance is under $50,000
questions.rationale: A U.S. person must file an FBAR if the aggregate value of foreign financial accounts exceeds $10,000 at any point in the year, including accounts where they only have signature authority. It is filed electronically with FinCEN.

questions.stem: A taxpayer recharacterized a $6,000 contribution from a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA (or vice versa) in 2024 before the due date. What is the effect of a proper recharacterization?
options: It is treated as a taxable distribution
It triggers a 10% penalty
It is a prohibited transaction
The contribution (plus earnings) is treated as if originally made to the second IRA, with no tax on the transfer
questions.rationale: A recharacterization (allowed for contributions, not for Roth conversions after 2017) treats the contribution and earnings as originally made to the receiving IRA, with no current tax or penalty.

questions.stem: A retiree age 75 has three traditional IRAs and one 401(k) from a former employer. He must take required minimum distributions. How may he satisfy the RMDs?
options: Aggregate the IRA RMDs and take the total from any one or more IRAs, but take the 401(k) RMD separately from the 401(k)
Take all RMDs from the 401(k) only
Take one combined RMD from any single account
No aggregation is ever allowed
questions.rationale: Traditional IRA RMDs can be aggregated and withdrawn from any one or more IRAs, but employer plan RMDs (e.g., 401(k)) must each be taken from that specific plan.

questions.stem: A taxpayer failed to take a required minimum distribution of $4,000 from his IRA in 2024. What is the excise tax penalty on the missed RMD under current law (before any timely correction reduction)?
options: 25% of the shortfall (reducible to 10% if timely corrected)
10% flat
50% of the shortfall
No penalty
questions.rationale: Under SECURE 2.0, the excise tax on a missed RMD is 25% of the shortfall, reduced to 10% if the failure is corrected within the correction window.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants protection against tax-related identity theft by using an Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN). Which statement is correct about the IP PIN for 2024 filing?
options: It is a six-digit number that is generally valid for one calendar year and must be entered on the return
Only victims of identity theft may obtain one
It replaces the Social Security number
It is a permanent number that never changes
questions.rationale: The IRS Identity Protection PIN is a six-digit number, generally valid for one calendar year, entered on the return to prevent fraudulent filings; any eligible taxpayer can opt in.

questions.stem: A taxpayer contributed $7,000 to a traditional IRA for 2024 but later realizes the total exceeds the allowed limit because of low compensation. If the excess is not withdrawn, what is the consequence?
options: A 10% early withdrawal penalty
No consequence
The IRA is disqualified entirely
A 6% excise tax applies to the excess contribution each year it remains
questions.rationale: Excess IRA contributions are subject to a 6% excise tax for each year they remain in the account unless timely withdrawn (with earnings) by the due date.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old taxpayer took a $10,000 early distribution from his traditional IRA to pay for qualified first-time home purchase expenses. How much of the distribution avoids the 10% early withdrawal penalty under the first-time homebuyer exception?
options: $10,000, the full distribution
$0, no exception exists
Up to $10,000 lifetime is exempt from the 10% penalty (but still taxable)
$10,000 of income tax is waived too
questions.rationale: The first-time homebuyer exception waives the 10% early distribution penalty on up to $10,000 lifetime from an IRA, but the distribution is still subject to ordinary income tax.

questions.stem: A taxpayer made a $7,000 nondeductible contribution to a traditional IRA that already held $63,000 of pre-tax money, then converted $10,000 to a Roth in 2024. Under the pro-rata rule, what portion of the conversion is taxable?
options: $3,000, fully tax-free
$9,000, because only 10% is basis ($7,000 / $70,000)
$10,000, fully taxable
$0, because the conversion came from the nondeductible contribution
questions.rationale: The pro-rata rule treats all traditional IRAs as one; the nontaxable portion of a conversion equals the basis ratio (here 10%), so $9,000 of the $10,000 is taxable.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a direct rollover of $50,000 from a 401(k) to a traditional IRA via a trustee-to-trustee transfer in 2024. What is the tax treatment?
options: Subject to the 10% early withdrawal penalty
Nontaxable; a direct trustee-to-trustee rollover is not a taxable distribution
Fully taxable in 2024
Subject to 20% mandatory withholding
questions.rationale: A direct trustee-to-trustee rollover from a 401(k) to a traditional IRA is nontaxable, avoids the 20% mandatory withholding, and is not subject to the early distribution penalty.

questions.stem: A taxpayer took a distribution from her IRA and intended a 60-day rollover, but she had already done one IRA-to-IRA rollover within the prior 12 months. What is the consequence of this second 60-day rollover?
options: The second rollover is disallowed; the distribution is taxable (and possibly penalized) because only one IRA-to-IRA 60-day rollover is allowed per 12 months
She may do unlimited rollovers if under 59 1/2
Both rollovers become taxable
It is allowed without limit
questions.rationale: A taxpayer may make only one IRA-to-IRA 60-day rollover in any 12-month period; an additional one is treated as a taxable (and possibly penalized) distribution. Direct trustee transfers are unlimited.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old made a $20,000 qualified charitable distribution (QCD) directly from his IRA to a public charity in 2024. How is it treated?
options: Subject to the 10% penalty
Treated as a Roth conversion
Included in income and deductible as a charitable contribution
Excluded from gross income (up to the annual limit) and can count toward the RMD
questions.rationale: A qualified charitable distribution from an IRA (for taxpayers 70 1/2 or older) is excluded from gross income, counts toward the RMD, and is limited to $105,000 for 2024.

questions.stem: At what age must a taxpayer who turned 73 in 2024 generally begin taking required minimum distributions from a traditional IRA?
questions.rationale: SECURE 2.0 raised the required beginning age for RMDs to 73 (for individuals reaching 72 after 2022); it rises to 75 in 2033.

questions.stem: A nonspouse beneficiary inherited a traditional IRA in 2024 from a person who died after the required beginning date. Under the SECURE Act 10-year rule for a non-eligible designated beneficiary, what is required?
options: The account must generally be fully distributed by the end of the 10th year, with annual RMDs in years 1-9 when the owner died after the RBD
No distributions are ever required
Distribute everything within 5 years
Take RMDs over the beneficiary's life expectancy
questions.rationale: Under the SECURE Act, a non-eligible designated beneficiary must fully distribute an inherited IRA within 10 years, with annual RMDs in years 1-9 if the owner died after the required beginning date.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to contribute to a Roth IRA for 2024 but his modified AGI is above the upper Roth phase-out limit. What planning technique allows indirect Roth funding?
options: A SEP rollover only
A direct excess Roth contribution
A spousal deduction
A 'backdoor Roth': a nondeductible traditional IRA contribution followed by a conversion to Roth
questions.rationale: High earners barred from direct Roth contributions can use a backdoor Roth: contribute (nondeductibly) to a traditional IRA, then convert to a Roth, because conversions have no income limit (pro-rata rule applies).

questions.stem: A taxpayer reports virtual currency activity. In 2024, he received cryptocurrency as payment for services worth $1,500 at the time of receipt. How must he answer the digital asset question and report this?
options: Answer 'No' and report nothing
Report it only as a capital gain
Answer 'Yes' to the digital asset question and report $1,500 of ordinary income
It is tax-free until sold
questions.rationale: Cryptocurrency received as payment for services is ordinary income equal to its fair market value when received, and the taxpayer must answer 'Yes' to the Form 1040 digital asset question.

questions.stem: A taxpayer made a $7,000 contribution to a SEP-IRA as a self-employed individual and also wants to make a personal traditional IRA contribution for 2024. Which statement is correct?
options: SEP contributions count against the personal IRA limit
SEP and traditional IRA limits are combined into one
A SEP-IRA contribution does not reduce the separate personal traditional IRA contribution limit, but active-participant rules may limit deductibility
SEP-IRA holders cannot contribute to a traditional IRA
questions.rationale: A SEP-IRA contribution does not count toward the personal IRA limit, but SEP coverage makes the taxpayer an active participant, potentially phasing out the deductibility of a traditional IRA contribution.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's adult son, age 30, lived with her all year, earned $3,000, and she provided over half his support. He is not disabled. Can she claim him, and under which category?
options: Qualifying child, because he lives with her
Neither, because he is over 24
Qualifying child, because he earned under $4,700
Qualifying relative, because his gross income is under the limit and she provided over half his support
questions.rationale: An adult child who is too old to be a qualifying child can still be claimed as a qualifying relative if the gross income test is met and the taxpayer provides over half his support.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received jury duty pay of $300 but had to remit $250 of it to her employer, who continued paying her salary while she served. How is this handled?
options: Report $300 income; no offset
Report $300 of jury pay as income and deduct the $250 remitted to the employer as an above-the-line adjustment
Report only $50
Report nothing because the employer paid her salary
questions.rationale: Jury duty pay is taxable income, but if the taxpayer surrenders it to an employer who continued her salary, she can take an above-the-line deduction for the amount turned over.

questions.stem: An employee exercised a nonqualified stock option (NQSO) in 2024: she paid a $10 strike price for stock worth $35 at exercise. She bought 100 shares. What ordinary income does she recognize at exercise?
options: $0 until she sells the stock
$3,500, the full value
$2,500, the bargain element (100 x ($35 - $10))
$1,000, the exercise cost
questions.rationale: Exercising a nonqualified stock option produces ordinary income equal to the bargain element (FMV minus exercise price) at exercise; that amount is added to basis for later sale.

questions.stem: A taxpayer made a $400 cash contribution to a qualified charity and received a coffee mug worth $15 in return. What is the deductible amount?
options: $385, the contribution reduced by the value of the benefit received
questions.rationale: For a quid pro quo contribution, only the excess of the payment over the fair market value of goods or services received is deductible.

questions.stem: A taxpayer made a single cash donation of $300 to a church but has no bank record or written acknowledgment. What is the deductibility result if she itemizes?
options: Not deductible without a bank record or written communication from the charity
Fully deductible without any record
Deductible up to $250 without records
Deductible only if over $500
questions.rationale: All cash contributions require a bank record or written charity acknowledgment, and gifts of $250 or more need a contemporaneous written acknowledgment; without it the deduction is disallowed.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has excess business losses for 2024 as a noncorporate taxpayer. Under the excess business loss limitation, what happens to a business loss exceeding the annual threshold?
options: It is permanently lost
The disallowed excess business loss is carried forward as a net operating loss to the next year
It offsets only passive income
It is fully deductible against wages
questions.rationale: The excess business loss limitation caps how much business loss noncorporate taxpayers can use against nonbusiness income; the disallowed portion carries forward as a net operating loss.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is subject to the alternative minimum tax (AMT). Which item is a common AMT preference or adjustment that increases AMT income?
options: Qualified dividends
The standard deduction and state/local taxes deducted for regular tax
Mortgage interest on acquisition debt
Charitable contributions
questions.rationale: Common AMT adjustments include adding back the standard deduction and state and local taxes, which are deductible for regular tax but not for AMT.

questions.stem: Divorced parents have one child. The custodial parent (mother) earns $30,000; the noncustodial father has Form 8332 and claims the child as a dependent. The child lived with the mother 300 nights. Who may claim head of household and the EIC?
options: The mother, because head of household and EIC stay with the custodial parent regardless of Form 8332
The father, since he has the dependency
Both parents may split them
Neither parent
questions.rationale: Even when the custodial parent releases the dependency via Form 8332, head of household filing status and the EIC tied to that child remain with the custodial parent.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $5,000 distribution from a 529 qualified tuition plan; $4,000 was used for qualified higher education expenses and $1,000 was not. The earnings portion of the nonqualified $1,000 is $300. What is the tax treatment of that $300?
options: Treated as a gift
Tax-free but penalized 6%
Taxable as income and generally subject to a 10% additional tax
Fully tax-free
questions.rationale: The earnings portion of a nonqualified 529 distribution is included in income and generally subject to a 10% additional tax; the contribution (basis) portion is tax-free.

questions.stem: A taxpayer prepaid in December 2024 her January 2025 mortgage payment, which included $1,800 of interest accruing in January 2025. May she deduct the prepaid interest in 2024?
options: Yes, half is deductible
No, prepaid interest generally must be deducted in the period to which it relates
Only if she is on the accrual method
Yes, all prepaid interest is deductible when paid
questions.rationale: Prepaid interest generally must be capitalized and deducted over the period to which it relates; paying January's interest in December does not make it a current-year deduction.

questions.stem: A taxpayer materially participates in his S corporation. He has $40,000 of stock basis and the S corporation passes through a $55,000 ordinary loss. How much loss can he deduct in 2024 (no debt basis)?
options: $40,000, limited to his basis; the $15,000 excess is suspended and carried forward
questions.rationale: S corporation losses are limited to the shareholder's stock plus debt basis; losses exceeding basis are suspended and carried forward until the shareholder has sufficient basis.

questions.stem: A taxpayer owed $3,000 in tax and filed his return on time but did not pay until three months later. Which penalty primarily applies to the unpaid balance?
options: Failure-to-pay penalty of 0.5% per month on the unpaid tax
A flat 20% accuracy penalty
Failure-to-file penalty of 5% per month
No penalty because he filed on time
questions.rationale: Filing on time but paying late incurs the failure-to-pay penalty of 0.5% per month on the unpaid balance, plus interest, but not the failure-to-file penalty.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files his return 60+ days late and owes tax. What is the minimum failure-to-file penalty concept for a return more than 60 days late (2024)?
options: There is no minimum penalty
Only interest applies
A minimum penalty applies equal to the lesser of a set dollar amount or 100% of the tax due
Always exactly $50
questions.rationale: When a return is more than 60 days late, the minimum failure-to-file penalty is the smaller of a set (inflation-adjusted) dollar amount or 100% of the tax required to be shown on the return.

questions.stem: A taxpayer realizes he omitted $5,000 of interest income on his already-filed 2023 return. What form does he use to correct it, and what is the general time limit to claim a refund if the correction created an overpayment?
options: Form 4868; one year
Form 1040-ES; no limit
Form 8888; six years
Form 1040-X; generally within three years of filing or two years of paying, whichever is later
questions.rationale: Amended returns are filed on Form 1040-X; a refund claim must generally be filed within three years of filing the original return or two years of paying the tax, whichever is later.

questions.stem: A taxpayer reasonably relied in good faith on the written advice of a competent tax professional and a substantial understatement penalty is proposed. Which defense may apply?
options: The statute of limitations defense
No defense exists once a penalty is proposed
The reasonable cause and good faith defense, which can abate the accuracy-related penalty
Automatic abatement for all first-time errors
questions.rationale: The accuracy-related penalty may be avoided where the taxpayer shows reasonable cause and acted in good faith, such as good-faith reliance on competent professional advice.

questions.stem: A married couple's child is a resident of Canada living there all year with relatives; the parents are U.S. citizens and support the child. Can a child who is not a U.S. citizen or resident be claimed as a dependent?
options: Never, if the child lives abroad
Generally only if the dependent is a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, or a resident of the U.S., Canada, or Mexico
Yes, any child anywhere can be claimed
Only if the child has an SSN
questions.rationale: The dependent citizen/resident test requires the person to be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, or resident of the U.S., Canada, or Mexico; a child residing in Canada meets that test.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received $1,200 of foreign dividends from a mutual fund and $90 of foreign tax was withheld and reported on the 1099-DIV. What is generally the simplest way to obtain a benefit for the foreign tax without filing Form 1116?
options: Exclude the dividends from income
Claim the foreign tax as a credit without Form 1116, since the amount is within the de minimis limit for passive foreign tax
Deduct the dividends
No benefit is available
questions.rationale: Small amounts of foreign tax on passive income (under $300 single/$600 MFJ) reported on a 1099 may be claimed as a foreign tax credit directly without the detailed Form 1116.

questions.stem: A taxpayer made federal estimated payments of $8,000 and had $4,000 withheld from wages. His total 2024 tax is $13,000, and he meets no safe harbor. For penalty timing, how is withholding generally treated compared to estimated payments?
options: Both are credited only when actually paid
Estimated payments are spread evenly; withholding is credited when received
Withholding is generally treated as paid evenly throughout the year, while estimated payments are credited when made
Neither matters for penalty timing
questions.rationale: For estimated tax penalty purposes, withholding is generally deemed paid evenly throughout the year regardless of when withheld, while estimated payments are credited only when actually paid.

questions.stem: A taxpayer disagrees with a proposed IRS examination change and wants to dispute it before paying. Which option preserves the right to dispute without first paying the tax?
options: Request a private letter ruling
File a petition with the U.S. Tax Court after receiving a statutory notice of deficiency
File a Form 1040-X
Pay the tax and sue for refund only
questions.rationale: The U.S. Tax Court is the forum that allows a taxpayer to contest a deficiency without first paying, by timely petitioning after a statutory notice of deficiency.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants direct deposit of her refund split among three accounts. Which form is used to allocate a refund among multiple accounts?
options: Form 8862
Form 8332
Form 8949
Form 8888
questions.rationale: Form 8888, Allocation of Refund, lets a taxpayer direct-deposit a refund into multiple accounts or purchase U.S. savings bonds.

questions.stem: A taxpayer married on December 31, 2024. For the entire year before that she was single and maintained a home for her child. What filing status options does she have for 2024?
options: Single or head of household, because she was single most of the year
Married filing jointly or married filing separately, because marital status is determined on the last day of the year
Qualifying surviving spouse
Head of household only
questions.rationale: Marital status is determined on the last day of the tax year; marrying on December 31 makes the taxpayer married for the entire year, so the choices are MFJ or MFS.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received $2,000 in punitive damages and $10,000 for physical injury in a personal injury lawsuit. How much is taxable?
options: $2,000, the punitive damages
$10,000, the physical injury portion
questions.rationale: Compensatory damages for physical injury or sickness are excluded from income, but punitive damages are taxable even if received in a personal physical injury case.

questions.stem: An employee received $60,000 of group-term life insurance coverage paid by her employer. The cost of the first $50,000 is excludable. The IRS Table I cost of the excess $10,000 of coverage for the year is $48. How is this handled?
options: All coverage is tax-free
Only $50,000 of coverage is taxable
The $48 cost of coverage over $50,000 is included in taxable wages
The full premium is taxable
questions.rationale: Employer-provided group-term life insurance is excludable up to $50,000; the Table I cost of coverage above $50,000 is taxable wages to the employee.

questions.stem: A taxpayer made a $40,000 charitable contribution carryover from 2023 (cash to public charity) and a $20,000 cash gift in 2024. Her 2024 AGI is $50,000. How are current-year gifts and carryovers ordered?
options: Current-year contributions are deducted first, then carryovers, all subject to the 60% AGI limit
Carryovers are used before current-year gifts
Carryovers expire if not used in one year
Both are deducted in full regardless of AGI
questions.rationale: Current-year charitable contributions are deducted first up to the AGI limit, and prior-year carryovers are then used to the extent of remaining limit, with unused amounts carried forward up to five years.

questions.stem: A sole proprietor uses part of her home regularly and exclusively as her principal place of business. She wants to use the simplified home office deduction. What is the simplified method rate and cap for 2024?
options: $5 per square foot up to 300 square feet (max $1,500)
$10 per square foot, no cap
Actual expenses only
2% of AGI
questions.rationale: The simplified home office deduction is $5 per square foot of qualifying space, capped at 300 square feet, for a maximum deduction of $1,500.

questions.stem: A taxpayer claimed the EITC two years ago and it was disallowed due to reckless disregard of the rules. What must he do to claim the EITC again?
options: Nothing; he can just claim it
Wait ten years
He is permanently barred
File Form 8862 to claim the EITC after disallowance
questions.rationale: After an EITC disallowance (other than a math error), the taxpayer must attach Form 8862 to claim the credit in a later year; reckless disregard also triggers a two-year ban.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who is a U.S. citizen living and working abroad wants to exclude foreign earned income for 2024. Which test can qualify him for the foreign earned income exclusion?
options: Filing an FBAR
Paying foreign tax
Meeting either the bona fide residence test or the physical presence test (330 full days in a 12-month period)
Owning foreign property
questions.rationale: To claim the foreign earned income exclusion, a taxpayer must have a tax home abroad and satisfy either the bona fide residence test or the physical presence test (330 full days in 12 months).

questions.stem: A taxpayer's domestic partner (not a spouse) lived with him all year, had gross income of $3,000, and he provided all her support. Their relationship does not violate local law. May he claim her as a dependent?
options: No, only relatives can be claimed
Yes, as a qualifying relative (member of household) if all tests are met and the relationship does not violate local law
Yes, as a qualifying child
No, partners can never be dependents
questions.rationale: An unrelated individual can be a qualifying relative if they live with the taxpayer the entire year as a household member, meet the gross income and support tests, and the relationship does not violate local law.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received $400 of interest on municipal bonds issued by his home state and $600 of interest on U.S. Treasury notes. For federal income tax, what is taxable?
options: $400, the municipal interest
$600, the Treasury interest
questions.rationale: Interest on state and local municipal bonds is generally exempt from federal income tax, while U.S. Treasury interest is federally taxable (but state-tax-exempt).

questions.stem: A taxpayer donated appreciated artwork she created herself (FMV $8,000, her cost of materials $500) to a museum. What is her charitable deduction for this self-created property?
options: $8,000, the FMV
$500, her basis (cost of materials), because it is ordinary-income property to the creator
$4,250, the average
questions.rationale: For ordinary-income property such as artwork created by the donor, the charitable deduction is limited to the donor's basis (cost), not the fair market value.

questions.stem: A partner received a guaranteed payment of $40,000 from a partnership for services. How is this treated on the partner's return?
options: Tax-free return of capital
A capital gain
Ordinary income to the partner and generally subject to self-employment tax; it is not QBI
A nontaxable draw
questions.rationale: Guaranteed payments for services are ordinary income to the partner, generally subject to self-employment tax, and do not qualify as QBI for the QBI deduction.

questions.stem: A taxpayer can pay a balance due in installments but cannot pay immediately. Which IRS arrangement allows monthly payments of a tax debt?
options: An audit reconsideration
An installment agreement
Offer in compromise only
A private letter ruling
questions.rationale: An IRS installment agreement allows a taxpayer to pay a tax liability in monthly installments; interest and penalties continue to accrue until paid.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to designate someone to discuss only the processing of his current-year return with the IRS. Which option grants this limited authority on the return itself?
options: No authorization is possible
Form 8821 for all years
Form 2848 power of attorney
The Third Party Designee (checkbox) on the Form 1040
questions.rationale: The Third Party Designee box on the Form 1040 lets a taxpayer authorize a named individual to discuss the processing of that year's return with the IRS, a limited authority that expires after about one year.

questions.stem: A taxpayer surrendered a life insurance policy and received $40,000. He had paid total premiums of $30,000 over the years. How much, if any, is taxable?
options: $10,000, the excess of proceeds over total premiums paid
questions.rationale: When a life insurance policy is surrendered, the amount received over the policyholder's investment in the contract (premiums paid) is taxable as ordinary income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer pays $3,000 of investment interest expense and has $2,000 of net investment income for 2024. How much investment interest may she deduct, and what happens to the rest?
options: $3,000, all deductible
$1,000 deductible
$2,000 deductible (limited to net investment income); $1,000 carries forward
questions.rationale: Investment interest expense is deductible (as an itemized deduction) only up to net investment income, with any excess carried forward indefinitely.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has a passive activity that generated suspended losses of $18,000 over the years. In 2024 he sells his entire interest in the passive activity to an unrelated party in a fully taxable transaction. What happens to the suspended losses?
options: They become capital losses only
They are lost
They are fully released and become deductible in the year of the complete taxable disposition
They remain suspended
questions.rationale: Suspended passive activity losses are released and become fully deductible when the taxpayer disposes of the entire interest in the activity in a fully taxable transaction to an unrelated party.

questions.stem: A taxpayer claimed a $2,000 child tax credit but the IRS determined the child did not qualify, finding the claim due to reckless disregard. Besides repaying the credit, what additional consequence may apply?
options: Immediate criminal prosecution
A two-year ban on claiming the child tax credit
Loss of all future credits permanently
No additional consequence
questions.rationale: Improperly claiming the child tax credit due to reckless or intentional disregard of rules triggers a two-year ban (10 years for fraud) and requires Form 8862 to reclaim it later.

questions.stem: A taxpayer named a spousal beneficiary on her traditional IRA. After her death in 2024, the surviving spouse wants the most flexibility. Which option is uniquely available to a spouse beneficiary?
options: Only a five-year payout
Treat the inherited IRA as his own by rolling it over or electing to be the owner
No options
Only the 10-year rule
questions.rationale: A surviving spouse beneficiary uniquely may treat the inherited IRA as their own, allowing continued contributions and RMDs based on their own age, unlike nonspouse beneficiaries.

questions.stem: A married couple chooses married filing separately. Which of the following is generally a consequence of MFS?
options: Certain benefits (like the EITC and some education credits) are generally disallowed, and if one spouse itemizes the other must too
They can each use head of household
They get a larger standard deduction
They can each claim the EITC
questions.rationale: Married filing separately limits many tax benefits (EITC, certain education and dependent care credits) and requires both spouses to itemize if either does.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $1,000 state income tax refund, having itemized last year and deducted state income taxes. However, last year he was subject to the AMT and received no tax benefit from the state tax deduction. How much of the refund is taxable?
options: $0, because he received no tax benefit from the deduction
Half is taxable
questions.rationale: A state tax refund is taxable only to the extent the deduction produced a tax benefit; if AMT eliminated the benefit of the state tax deduction, the refund is not taxable.

questions.stem: A taxpayer prepaid two years of property taxes in December 2024 (the current-year bill plus next year's, which had not yet been assessed). What is deductible for 2024?
options: Both years' property tax
Half of the total
Only the currently assessed/billed property tax; prepaid taxes not yet assessed are not deductible
None
questions.rationale: Real estate taxes are deductible when assessed and paid; prepaying taxes that have not been assessed does not produce a current deduction, and the $10,000 SALT cap also applies.

questions.stem: A taxpayer operates a sole proprietorship and has net Schedule C profit of $50,000. What is the rate used to compute the deductible portion (employer-equivalent) of self-employment tax?
options: The full SE tax is deductible
One-half of the self-employment tax is deductible above the line
None of it is deductible
The full SE tax reduces SE income directly
questions.rationale: Self-employed individuals may deduct one-half of their self-employment tax as an adjustment to income (above the line), reflecting the employer-equivalent portion.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has regular tax of $9,000 and a tentative minimum tax of $11,500 for 2024. What is the alternative minimum tax owed, and how is it reported?
options: $0, because regular tax is lower
$2,500 AMT, the excess of tentative minimum tax over regular tax, added on Form 6251
$11,500 total tax
questions.rationale: The alternative minimum tax is the amount by which the tentative minimum tax exceeds the regular tax; it is computed on Form 6251 and added to the regular tax liability.

questions.stem: A taxpayer realizes he qualifies for first-time penalty abatement (FTA) for a late-payment penalty. What is a key requirement for FTA?
options: FTA applies only to corporations
He must be over age 65
He must pay double the penalty
He must have a clean compliance history with no penalties in the prior three years and be current on filing/payment
questions.rationale: First-time penalty abatement requires a clean compliance history (no significant penalties in the prior three years) and being current with filing and payment obligations.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's only dependent is her qualifying child who lived with her exactly six months (183 nights) and with the child's father the other 182 nights. The parents are divorced and there is no Form 8332. Who is the custodial parent for tax purposes?
options: The mother, because the child lived with her the greater number of nights
The father, because they split time
Neither, because time is roughly equal
They alternate by IRS assignment
questions.rationale: For divorced or separated parents, the custodial parent is the one with whom the child lived the greater number of nights during the year, and that parent has the dependency unless released by Form 8332.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $1,500 distribution from a Health Savings Account (HSA) and used $1,200 for qualified medical expenses and $300 for a non-medical purpose. He is age 50. How is the $300 treated?
options: Tax-free
Included in income and subject to a 20% additional tax
Subject only to a 10% penalty
Tax-free but reduces future contributions
questions.rationale: HSA distributions not used for qualified medical expenses are included in income and, for those under 65, subject to a 20% additional tax.

questions.stem: A married couple filing jointly paid $9,000 of mortgage interest and $11,000 of SALT, and made $4,000 of cash charitable gifts in 2024. Their total itemized deductions are $24,000 but the 2024 standard deduction for MFJ is $29,200. What should they generally do?
options: Split: itemize some and use standard for the rest
Itemize, because they have deductions
They must itemize because they have a mortgage
Take the standard deduction, since it exceeds their itemized total
questions.rationale: Taxpayers should claim the greater of the standard deduction or total itemized deductions; here the $29,200 standard deduction beats $24,000 of itemized deductions (after the SALT cap).

questions.stem: A taxpayer contributed appreciated inventory from his sole proprietorship to charity. For ordinary-income property like inventory, the charitable deduction is generally limited to what amount?
options: Twice the basis
The lower of fair market value or the taxpayer's basis (cost) in the inventory
Zero
Fair market value
questions.rationale: Contributions of ordinary-income property such as business inventory are generally deductible only up to the property's basis (cost), not fair market value.

questions.stem: A taxpayer qualifies for the premium tax credit and her actual income ended up LOWER than estimated, so her allowed PTC exceeds the advance payments received. What is the reconciliation result on Form 8962?
options: She must repay the difference
No effect
She loses the credit
She receives the additional premium tax credit, increasing her refund or reducing tax
questions.rationale: If the allowed premium tax credit exceeds advance payments, the taxpayer claims the net premium tax credit, which increases the refund or reduces tax owed.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to know how long the IRS generally has to assess additional tax if he filed a complete, non-fraudulent return understating income by 30%. What is the statute of limitations?
options: Six years, because gross income was understated by more than 25%
Ten years
Three years from filing
No limit
questions.rationale: The normal three-year assessment statute extends to six years when a taxpayer omits more than 25% of gross income; it is unlimited only for fraud or failure to file.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to file as qualifying surviving spouse for 2024. Her husband died in 2022. Which condition must she meet?
options: She must maintain a household that is the main home of her dependent child for the year
She must have remarried
She must have filed separately in the year of death
She must be over 65
questions.rationale: To file as a qualifying surviving spouse for the two years after the spouse's death, the taxpayer must not have remarried and must maintain a household that is the main home of a dependent child.

questions.stem: A cash-basis taxpayer was awarded a constructive receipt situation: her employer issued a paycheck on December 30, 2024, and made it available, but she chose not to cash it until January 2025. In which year is it income?
options: Split between both years
Neither, until deposited
2025, when cashed
2024, under the constructive receipt doctrine
questions.rationale: Under constructive receipt, income is taxed when it is credited or made available without substantial limitation, even if the taxpayer chooses not to take possession until later.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $2,400 in points to obtain a mortgage to buy her main home in 2024. The points are within customary local amounts and meet the tests for current deduction. How are the points treated?
options: Added to basis only
Not deductible
Generally fully deductible in 2024 as home mortgage interest because they were paid to buy the main home
Amortized over the loan term only
questions.rationale: Points paid to buy or build a main home are generally deductible in full in the year paid if they meet the IRS requirements; points on a refinance are usually amortized over the loan term.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $2,500 of qualified tuition and qualifies for both the AOTC and the Lifetime Learning Credit for the same student in the same year. What is the rule?
options: He may claim both if income is low
He may claim both for the same student
He may claim only one education credit per student per year
Education credits are unlimited
questions.rationale: A taxpayer cannot claim both the American Opportunity Tax Credit and the Lifetime Learning Credit for the same student in the same year; only one applies per student.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received an IRS notice (CP2000) proposing additional tax based on unreported 1099 income he actually did report under a different name. What is the appropriate first response?
options: File a Tax Court petition right away
Respond by the deadline, explaining and documenting why the income was reported, agreeing or disagreeing as appropriate
Immediately pay the proposed amount
Ignore it
questions.rationale: A CP2000 is an automated underreporter notice proposing changes; the taxpayer should respond by the deadline with documentation showing the correct treatment, rather than ignoring or prematurely litigating it.

questions.stem: A taxpayer cashed Series I savings bonds and qualifies for the education interest exclusion but used only part of the proceeds for tuition. If qualified expenses are less than total bond proceeds, how is the excludable interest determined?
options: The exclusion is prorated based on the ratio of qualified expenses to total proceeds
No interest is excluded
All interest is excluded
Only the principal is excluded
questions.rationale: If only part of the bond proceeds is used for qualified education expenses, the interest exclusion is prorated based on the ratio of qualified expenses to total redemption proceeds.

questions.stem: A taxpayer drove 1,200 miles for qualifying medical care in 2024. Using the 2024 medical mileage rate of 21 cents per mile, what is the deductible medical transportation cost (before applying the AGI floor)?
questions.rationale: Medical-related driving is deductible at 21 cents per mile for 2024; 1,200 miles equals $252, included with other medical expenses subject to the 7.5% AGI floor.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is an S corporation shareholder and received a Schedule K-1 reporting $5,000 of separately stated tax-exempt interest. What effect does this have on the shareholder's stock basis?
options: It increases the shareholder's stock basis even though it is tax-exempt
It decreases basis
It is added to taxable income
No effect because it is tax-exempt
questions.rationale: S corporation tax-exempt income increases a shareholder's stock basis (and nondeductible expenses decrease it), even though tax-exempt income is not taxed.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is married filing jointly and both spouses are 67. For 2024 they want the additional standard deduction. How many additional standard deduction amounts can they claim if neither is blind?
options: One
Zero
Two (one for each spouse who is 65 or older)
Four
questions.rationale: Each spouse who is 65 or older receives an additional standard deduction amount; an additional amount also applies for blindness, so a couple can claim up to four extra amounts if both are 65+ and blind.

questions.stem: A taxpayer reaching 73 in 2024 took only part of his RMD in 2024 because he was hospitalized. He corrects the shortfall promptly in early 2025 and files Form 5329 with a reasonable-cause statement. What relief may apply?
options: The RMD requirement is canceled
Automatic doubling of the penalty
The IRS may waive the excise tax for reasonable cause if the shortfall is corrected and Form 5329 with an explanation is filed
No relief is ever available
questions.rationale: The excise tax on a missed RMD may be waived for reasonable cause when the shortfall is corrected and the taxpayer files Form 5329 with a statement explaining the reasonable error and remediation.

questions.stem: A taxpayer settled a lawsuit and received $20,000 for emotional distress that did NOT originate from a physical injury, plus $5,000 reimbursement for related medical care she previously deducted. How are these treated?
options: Both are tax-free because they relate to distress
Both are tax-free
The $20,000 emotional distress award is taxable, and the $5,000 medical reimbursement is taxable to the extent of the prior deduction benefit
Only the $5,000 is tax-free
questions.rationale: Damages for emotional distress not arising from a physical injury are taxable, and reimbursed medical expenses are taxable to the extent of any prior deduction benefit under the tax benefit rule.

questions.stem: A taxpayer donated $600 of cash and also gave $200 of used clothing in good condition to a qualified charity in 2024. She itemizes. What documentation is required for the noncash clothing gift under $250?
options: A receipt from the charity showing its name, date, and a description of the items
A Form 8283 with appraisal
An independent appraisal
No record is needed
questions.rationale: Noncash charitable gifts under $250 require a receipt from the charity describing the items; Form 8283 is needed when total noncash gifts exceed $500, and appraisals generally when over $5,000.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is a partner with an outside basis of $25,000. The partnership distributes $30,000 cash to her in a current distribution. What is the tax consequence?
options: No gain; basis goes negative
She recognizes $5,000 of gain to the extent the cash exceeds her basis; basis becomes zero
She recognizes $30,000 of gain
The distribution is fully taxable as ordinary income
questions.rationale: A current cash distribution is tax-free up to the partner's outside basis; any cash received in excess of basis is recognized as gain (generally capital), and basis cannot go below zero.

questions.stem: A taxpayer claims the child and dependent care credit. The applicable credit percentage for 2024 ranges from 20% to 35% based on AGI. For a higher-income taxpayer (AGI over $43,000), what is the minimum credit rate?
questions.rationale: For 2024, the child and dependent care credit rate is 35% for the lowest incomes, decreasing to a minimum of 20% for AGI over $43,000.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a balance-due notice and believes he qualifies to settle for less than the full amount because he cannot full-pay even over time. Which IRS program may apply?
options: Innocent spouse relief
An offer in compromise based on doubt as to collectibility
A Third Party Designee
Form 8332
questions.rationale: An offer in compromise based on doubt as to collectibility lets a taxpayer settle a tax liability for less than the full amount when full payment (even over time) is not feasible.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is unsure whether a $4,700 gross income test applies to her qualifying child. Which statement correctly distinguishes the income tests?
options: A qualifying child has no gross income limit, but a qualifying relative is subject to the gross income test
Only qualifying children have a gross income limit
Neither has any income test
Both qualifying children and qualifying relatives have a gross income limit
questions.rationale: A qualifying child is not subject to a gross income limit (only a self-support test), while a qualifying relative must have gross income below the annual threshold.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received unemployment compensation of $9,000 in 2024 and had $900 of federal income tax voluntarily withheld from it. How is the unemployment compensation treated?
options: Fully taxable as ordinary income; the $900 withholding is a credit toward tax
Only half is taxable
Tax-free in 2024
Taxable only if over $10,200
questions.rationale: Unemployment compensation is fully taxable income for 2024; voluntary withholding from it is treated as a tax payment credited on the return.

questions.stem: A taxpayer with AGI of $200,000 made a $130,000 cash gift to a public charity in 2024. How much is deductible this year and what happens to the excess?
options: $120,000 (60% of AGI) this year; $10,000 carries forward up to five years
$60,000 this year
$130,000, but only as a carryover
$130,000, all this year
questions.rationale: Cash contributions to public charities are deductible up to 60% of AGI; the excess carries forward for up to five years.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a Schedule K-1 from a partnership showing a $3,000 ordinary loss, but he does not materially participate and has no passive income. How is the loss treated for 2024?
options: Deductible as a capital loss
Suspended as a passive loss, deductible only against passive income or upon disposition
Fully deductible against wages
Half deductible
questions.rationale: Losses from passive activities (no material participation) are suspended and can only offset passive income or be released upon a complete disposition of the activity.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who had no tax liability last year and expects none this year wants to stop federal income tax withholding. What is required to claim exempt status on Form W-4?
options: Nothing; it is automatic
She must meet both conditions (no liability last year and expecting none this year) and certify exempt on Form W-4, which she must renew annually
She must be under age 18
She must be self-employed
questions.rationale: An employee may claim exempt from withholding only if they had no tax liability last year and expect none this year; the exemption must be re-certified on Form W-4 annually.

questions.stem: A married couple filed a joint return, and the IRS later assessed additional tax due solely to the husband's unreported business income that the wife did not know about and had no reason to know. Which relief might the wife pursue?
options: Form 8888
An installment agreement
A Third Party Designee
Innocent spouse relief
questions.rationale: Innocent spouse relief can relieve a joint filer of responsibility for tax, interest, and penalties from an understatement caused by the other spouse that the requesting spouse did not know and had no reason to know about.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $3,000 distribution from a Roth IRA. She is 62 and opened the Roth eight years ago. How is the distribution taxed?
options: Fully taxable
Subject to a 10% penalty
Taxable to the extent of earnings
Tax-free, because it is a qualified distribution (over 59 1/2 and the 5-year rule met)
questions.rationale: A qualified Roth IRA distribution (5-year holding period met and owner over 59 1/2) is entirely tax-free, including earnings, with no penalty.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $5,000 of mortgage insurance premiums (PMI) in 2024 on a home loan. How are these treated for 2024?
options: Fully deductible as mortgage interest
The deduction for mortgage insurance premiums has expired and is not available for 2024
Deductible above the line
Deductible as a medical expense
questions.rationale: The itemized deduction for qualified mortgage insurance premiums expired after 2021 and is not available for the 2024 tax year.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's home office qualifies and she uses the regular (actual expense) method. The home office is 10% of the home's square footage. Which expense is allocated using that percentage?
options: Mortgage principal payments
Indirect expenses like utilities, insurance, and depreciation are allocated by the business-use percentage
Only direct expenses of the office
Personal grocery costs
questions.rationale: Under the regular home office method, indirect expenses such as utilities, insurance, and depreciation are deductible in proportion to the business-use percentage of the home.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to grant her enrolled agent the authority to represent her before the IRS for a specific tax year and matter. Which form is used?
options: Form 4868
Form 8888
Form 8821
Form 2848 (Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative)
questions.rationale: Form 2848, Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative, authorizes an eligible representative such as an enrolled agent to act for and represent the taxpayer before the IRS.

questions.stem: A taxpayer maintained a household for her 25-year-old brother who is permanently and totally disabled and earned $6,000 in a sheltered workshop. Can she claim him as a qualifying child, and can the sheltered-workshop income disqualify him?
options: No, his earnings exceed the limit
Yes, but only as a qualifying relative
No, he is over 24
Yes, a permanently and totally disabled person has no age limit as a qualifying child, and certain sheltered-workshop income is disregarded
questions.rationale: A permanently and totally disabled person can be a qualifying child regardless of age, and income earned at a sheltered workshop is disregarded for related income tests.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received $5,000 in tips during 2024 but reported only $3,000 to her employer. How must the unreported $2,000 be handled?
options: Tips under a threshold are exempt
It is tax-free
Only reported tips are taxable
All $5,000 of tips is taxable; the unreported $2,000 must be reported as income (and may owe Social Security/Medicare via Form 4137)
questions.rationale: All tips are taxable income; tips not reported to the employer must still be reported on the return, with Social Security and Medicare tax computed on Form 4137.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to deduct gambling losses. He had $8,000 of winnings and $9,500 of documented losses and itemizes. What is the maximum loss deduction?
options: $8,000, limited to gambling winnings
questions.rationale: Gambling losses are deductible as an itemized deduction only to the extent of gambling winnings; excess losses are never deductible.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is a real estate professional who materially participates in his rental activities, spending more than 750 hours and more than half his personal services in real property trades. What is the effect on his rental losses?
options: They remain passive and suspended
They become capital losses
His rental real estate activities are treated as nonpassive, so losses can offset other income
They are limited to $25,000
questions.rationale: A real estate professional (over 750 hours and more than half of personal services in real property trades) who materially participates can treat rental losses as nonpassive, fully offsetting other income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files his 2024 return and is due a refund but never files. How long does he generally have to file and still claim the refund?
options: Six years
One year from the due date
No time limit for refunds
Generally three years from the original due date of the return
questions.rationale: A taxpayer generally must file within three years of the return's original due date to claim a refund; otherwise the overpayment is lost to the Treasury.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has foreign financial accounts with an aggregate value of $250,000 and must consider Form 8938 (FATCA) in addition to the FBAR. Where is Form 8938 filed?
options: Attached to the income tax return with the IRS
It is never required
With the state tax authority
Separately with FinCEN
questions.rationale: Form 8938 (FATCA reporting of specified foreign financial assets) is attached to the federal income tax return when the applicable thresholds are exceeded; it is separate from the FBAR filed with FinCEN.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's employer reimbursed $3,000 of moving expenses in 2024 (not a member of the Armed Forces). How is the reimbursement treated?
options: Half taxable
Taxable wages, because the moving expense exclusion is suspended for non-military taxpayers
Deductible as an adjustment
Tax-free, as a qualified moving expense reimbursement
questions.rationale: Except for certain Armed Forces members, employer-paid moving expense reimbursements are taxable wages for 2018-2025, and the moving expense deduction is suspended.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $1,200 of state and local general sales tax and $3,000 of state income tax in 2024. She itemizes. Which can she deduct?
options: Neither
Both, totaling $4,200
Only sales tax
Either state income tax OR general sales tax (not both), so she would choose the larger $3,000
questions.rationale: As an itemized deduction, a taxpayer may elect to deduct either state and local income taxes or general sales taxes (whichever is larger), but not both, subject to the $10,000 SALT cap.
