questions.stem: A taxpayer reports income from a hobby that is incorrectly classified. If the activity is actually a business, what is the major tax advantage of business (versus hobby) treatment?
options: Business expenses are deductible (and a net loss may offset other income), while hobby expenses are not deductible
Business income is tax-free
Hobby income is tax-free
No advantage exists
questions.rationale: Business treatment allows deduction of ordinary and necessary expenses (and potentially a deductible loss), while hobby income is fully taxable but related expenses are not deductible for 2018-2025.

questions.stem: A single taxpayer's tax before credits is $400. She qualifies for a $1,000 nonrefundable Lifetime Learning Credit and a $1,200 refundable additional child tax credit. How do these credits interact with her $400 liability?
options: The nonrefundable LLC reduces tax to $0 (using $400); the remaining LLC is lost, and the $1,200 refundable ACTC is paid as a refund
Both credits fully refund
The LLC is paid as a refund
She gets a $2,200 refund of all credits
questions.rationale: Nonrefundable credits (like the Lifetime Learning Credit) only reduce tax to zero with no refund of excess, while refundable credits (like the additional child tax credit) can produce a refund beyond the tax liability.

questions.stem: A taxpayer must report a foreign gift. He received a $150,000 gift from a nonresident alien individual in 2024. What is his reporting obligation?
options: No reporting is required
He owes income tax on the gift
He must report the foreign gift on Form 3520 because it exceeds the threshold, though the gift itself is not taxable income
He reports it on Schedule B
questions.rationale: Large gifts from foreign persons (over $100,000 from a nonresident alien individual) must be reported on Form 3520, even though gifts are not taxable income to the recipient.

questions.stem: A taxpayer and her sister both want to claim their elderly father, whom neither alone supported over half but together they provided 70%. The sister provided 45% and the taxpayer 25%. Who may claim him?
options: Neither, because no one provided over half
Only the sister, automatically
Both simultaneously
Either the sister or the taxpayer (each provided over 10%) under a multiple support agreement, with the other signing Form 2120
questions.rationale: When no single person provides over half the support but the group provides over half, any member who provided more than 10% may claim the dependent if the others sign Form 2120 waivers.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $2,000 prize on a TV game show (cash) and $500 worth of merchandise as a separate award. How much is includible in income?
options: $500 only
$2,500, both the cash and the FMV of merchandise
$0, prizes are tax-free
$2,000 only
questions.rationale: Prizes and awards are taxable at fair market value, including noncash merchandise, so both the cash and the value of goods received are included in income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer with AGI $120,000 has total itemized deductions including $12,000 of mortgage interest, $10,000 of SALT (after the cap), and a $40,000 cash charitable gift. The cash gift is within the 60% AGI limit. What is her total itemized deduction (ignoring other items)?
questions.rationale: Itemized deductions sum the allowed components: $12,000 interest + $10,000 (capped SALT) + $40,000 charitable (within the 60% AGI limit) = $62,000.

questions.stem: A self-employed taxpayer wants to deduct business meals in 2024. What is the general deductible percentage for qualifying business meals in 2024?
questions.rationale: For 2024, qualifying business meals are generally 50% deductible; the temporary 100% deduction for restaurant meals applied only to 2021-2022.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is computing the additional child tax credit using earned income. The refundable amount is 15% of earned income over a threshold. What is that earned income threshold for 2024?
questions.rationale: The refundable additional child tax credit is generally 15% of earned income above $2,500, limited to $1,700 per qualifying child for 2024.

questions.stem: A taxpayer made an excess Roth IRA contribution of $2,000 for 2024 and timely withdrew the $2,000 plus $150 of attributable earnings before the due date. How are the earnings treated?
options: Tax-free
Only the $2,000 is taxable
The whole $2,150 is taxable
The $150 of earnings is taxable in the year of the contribution and may be subject to a 10% penalty if under 59 1/2
questions.rationale: A timely-corrected excess IRA contribution avoids the 6% excise tax, but the earnings withdrawn with it are taxable (and subject to the 10% early-distribution penalty if under 59 1/2).

questions.stem: A taxpayer's son is age 18, not a student, and lived with him all year. The son earned $5,000 and provided 60% of his own support. Can the father claim him as a qualifying child?
options: Yes, because he is under 19
Yes, because he lived with the father
No, because his income exceeds $4,700
No, because the son provided more than half his own support, failing the support test
questions.rationale: A qualifying child must not have provided more than half of their own support; the son's 60% self-support disqualifies him as a qualifying child.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $1,000 distribution from a Coverdell ESA, of which $800 was used for qualified education expenses and $200 was not. The earnings portion of the nonqualified $200 is $60. How is the $60 treated?
options: Tax-free
Treated as a contribution
Subject to a 6% excise tax
Taxable and generally subject to a 10% additional tax
questions.rationale: Earnings on the nonqualified portion of a Coverdell ESA distribution are taxable and generally subject to a 10% additional tax, like a 529 plan.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $4,000 of qualified tuition in 2024 and wants to choose between the tuition-and-fees deduction and an education credit. What is true for 2024?
options: Only the deduction is allowed
The tuition-and-fees deduction is available
Both can be claimed together
The tuition-and-fees deduction has expired; education benefits are claimed through credits (AOTC or LLC)
questions.rationale: The tuition and fees deduction expired after 2020; education tax benefits are now obtained through the American Opportunity or Lifetime Learning credits.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's sole proprietorship had a 2024 net profit of $100,000. He contributes to a SEP-IRA. The maximum SEP contribution for a self-employed person is generally 20% of net self-employment income (after the SE tax deduction). Roughly what is the key adjustment in the SEP calculation?
options: Reduce net earnings by one-half of SE tax, then apply the effective 20% rate for the owner
Use 25% of gross receipts
Use 50% of net profit
No adjustment is needed
questions.rationale: A self-employed SEP contribution is based on net earnings reduced by one-half of self-employment tax, using an effective 20% rate (because the 25% rate is applied to income net of the contribution).

questions.stem: A taxpayer's modified AGI puts her in the phase-out range for the child tax credit. The CTC phases out by what amount for each $1,000 (or part) of MAGI over the threshold?
questions.rationale: The child tax credit is reduced by $50 for each $1,000 (or part thereof) of modified AGI above the threshold ($400,000 MFJ; $200,000 others).

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to verify a refund status and protect against fraud. Which is a legitimate IRS practice the taxpayer should expect?
options: The IRS will call demanding immediate gift-card payment
The IRS texts threatening arrest
The IRS generally initiates contact by mail, not by demanding immediate payment by phone or gift card
The IRS emails requesting bank passwords
questions.rationale: The IRS generally first contacts taxpayers by mail and never demands immediate payment via gift cards or threatens arrest; unsolicited calls, emails, or texts demanding payment are scams.

questions.stem: Two unmarried individuals live together; one is the child's biological parent and the other is unrelated. The unrelated partner has higher AGI and supported the household. Only the parent meets the relationship test for a qualifying child; can the unrelated partner claim the child as a qualifying child?
options: No, an unrelated person cannot claim the child as a qualifying child because the relationship test is not met
They must split the claim
Yes, because he supported the household
Yes, because he has higher AGI
questions.rationale: An unrelated household member cannot claim a child as a qualifying child because the relationship test fails; the AGI tie-breaker only applies among people who actually qualify to claim the child.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's Social Security benefits were paid in 2024 but include a lump-sum payment attributable to a prior year. What option may reduce the tax on the lump-sum benefits?
options: Making a lump-sum election to figure the taxable portion using the prior year's income
Treating them as a gift
Excluding all benefits
Reporting them as wages
questions.rationale: The lump-sum election allows a taxpayer who receives Social Security benefits attributable to prior years to figure the taxable portion as if received in those earlier years, often reducing the tax.

questions.stem: A taxpayer made a noncash charitable contribution of stock valued at $6,000 to a public charity. What additional substantiation is required because the value exceeds $5,000?
options: Nothing beyond a receipt
A police report
Only Form 1098-C
Generally a qualified appraisal and Form 8283 Section B, though publicly traded securities are exempt from the appraisal requirement
questions.rationale: Noncash gifts over $5,000 generally require a qualified appraisal and completion of Form 8283 Section B; however, publicly traded securities are exempt from the appraisal requirement.

questions.stem: A taxpayer leases a vehicle used 100% for her self-employed business. Under the actual expense method for a leased vehicle, which adjustment may apply for an expensive vehicle?
options: Lease payments are never deductible
Only depreciation is allowed
No adjustments ever apply
An income inclusion amount may reduce the deductible lease expense for higher-value vehicles
questions.rationale: For leased business vehicles above a value threshold, the taxpayer must add back a lease inclusion amount that reduces the deductible portion of the lease payments.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received advance premium tax credit but failed to file a tax return to reconcile it. What is a likely consequence?
options: She is barred from Marketplace coverage permanently
No consequence
She may become ineligible for advance premium tax credit in future years until she files and reconciles
She owes double the credit automatically
questions.rationale: Failing to file and reconcile advance premium tax credit on Form 8962 can make a taxpayer ineligible for advance payments in future years until she files the required return.

questions.stem: A taxpayer reached 73 in 2024 and must take his first RMD. What is the latest date he may take that first (2024) RMD without penalty?
options: December 31, 2024
April 15, 2025
April 1, 2025 (the required beginning date)
December 31, 2025
questions.rationale: The first required minimum distribution may be deferred until April 1 of the year after reaching the RMD age (73), but doing so means two RMDs in that next year.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to verify a preparer's authorization to represent clients before the IRS. Which credential allows unlimited practice rights before the IRS?
options: A state-issued notary commission
A PTIN held by an unenrolled return preparer
An Annual Filing Season Program record of completion
An enrolled agent designation
questions.rationale: Enrolled agents, CPAs, and attorneys have unlimited practice rights before the IRS, while PTIN-only and AFSP preparers have limited or no representation rights.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: Before preparing a return, a practitioner should confirm a taxpayer's identity. Which document is acceptable to establish a taxpayer's identity and SSN?
options: A bank statement showing the account balance
A handwritten note stating the SSN
A photocopy of a utility bill only
A Social Security card together with a government-issued photo ID
questions.rationale: Sound preparer due diligence includes verifying identity with government photo ID and confirming the SSN with the Social Security card.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A 2024 return is being prepared for a married couple. The wife died in March 2024 and the husband has not remarried. There are no dependents. What is the correct filing status for the 2024 return?
options: Head of household
Single
Qualifying surviving spouse
Married filing jointly
questions.rationale: For the tax year in which a spouse dies, the surviving spouse may still file married filing jointly, provided they did not remarry before the end of the year.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer has a child with an ITIN rather than an SSN. The child otherwise meets all qualifying child tests. For 2024, which benefit is the parent denied solely because the child lacks an SSN?
options: The Child Tax Credit
The medical expense deduction for the child
The dependency claim for the child
Head of household filing status based on that child
questions.rationale: The Child Tax Credit specifically requires the child to have an SSN valid for employment; an ITIN child may still be a dependent and support head of household status and the credit for other dependents.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A practitioner discovers a client's prior-year return, prepared by someone else, contains an error that understated tax. What is the practitioner's correct obligation under Circular 230?
options: Advise the client of the error and the consequences of not correcting it
Immediately notify the IRS of the error
Refuse to prepare the current-year return
Amend the return without telling the client
questions.rationale: Circular 230 §10.21 requires a practitioner who learns of a client's error or omission to advise the client of it and the consequences under the law, but the decision to correct rests with the client.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer was a U.S. resident alien for part of 2024 and a nonresident for the remainder, meeting the dual-status rules. Which statement about the dual-status return is correct?
options: The taxpayer may claim the standard deduction for the full year
The taxpayer must use Form 1040-EZ
The taxpayer generally cannot claim the standard deduction
The taxpayer must file as married filing jointly
questions.rationale: Dual-status aliens generally cannot claim the standard deduction; they itemize allowable deductions for the resident portion and report only U.S.-source income for the nonresident portion.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A divorced taxpayer wants to claim head of household for 2024. The taxpayer's parent lives in a nursing home that the taxpayer pays over half the cost of, and the parent qualifies as the taxpayer's dependent. Does this support HOH status?
options: No, the parent must live in the taxpayer's home
No, a parent can never be a qualifying person for HOH
Yes, a dependent parent qualifies even if the parent does not live with the taxpayer
Yes, but only if the parent has no income
questions.rationale: A dependent parent is the unique HOH qualifying person who does not have to live with the taxpayer; paying over half the cost of the parent's home, including a nursing home, can satisfy the requirement.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer received an Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN) from the IRS. What is the consequence of omitting the IP PIN on an electronically filed 2024 return?
options: The e-filed return will be rejected
The return will be accepted with a penalty
The refund will be doubled
Nothing; the IP PIN is optional
questions.rationale: When the IRS issues an IP PIN, it must be entered on the return; omission causes e-file rejection and delays paper-return processing.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: For an individual using the cash method, when is income generally reported?
options: When it is earned, regardless of receipt
Only when deposited in a bank
When it is actually or constructively received
When the related expense is paid
questions.rationale: A cash-method individual recognizes income in the year it is actually or constructively received, even if not yet deposited.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer maintained a home for a foster child placed by an authorized agency for eight months of 2024. The child otherwise meets the qualifying child tests. May the foster child be a qualifying child?
options: Only if the child is legally adopted
Only if the child is under age 5
No, foster children never qualify
Yes, if placed by an authorized agency or court order and the residency test is met
questions.rationale: An authorized-placement foster child meets the relationship test and can be a qualifying child if the age, residency, support, and joint-return tests are satisfied.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer received $1,200 of interest from a corporate bond and $300 of interest from a U.S. Treasury note in 2024. How is the $300 of Treasury interest treated for state income tax purposes in most states?
options: Exempt from state income tax
Subject to backup withholding
Fully taxable by the state
Taxable only if over $500
questions.rationale: Interest on U.S. Treasury obligations is taxable for federal purposes but exempt from state and local income taxation.

questions.stem: In 2024 a taxpayer sold publicly traded stock for $9,000. The shares were acquired by gift; the donor's adjusted basis was $4,000 and the FMV on the date of the gift was $7,000. No gift tax was paid. What is the taxpayer's gain on the sale?
questions.rationale: For gifted property sold at a gain, the donee uses the donor's carryover adjusted basis; here $9,000 − $4,000 = $5,000 of gain.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received gifted stock with a donor's adjusted basis of $10,000 and a date-of-gift FMV of $6,000. The taxpayer later sells the stock for $7,000. What gain or loss is recognized?
options: $1,000 gain
$1,000 loss
$3,000 loss
No gain or loss
questions.rationale: For gifted property with FMV below donor basis, gains use donor basis and losses use FMV basis; a sale price between the two figures produces no recognized gain or loss.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's traditional IRA distribution of $12,000 in 2024 includes $3,000 of after-tax (nondeductible) contributions that were previously reported on Form 8606. The IRA's year-end value plus the distribution requires a pro-rata calculation; assume the nontaxable portion is $1,500. How much of the distribution is taxable?
questions.rationale: Distributions from a traditional IRA with basis are partly nontaxable under the pro-rata rule; the taxable amount is the distribution less the recovered basis, here $12,000 − $1,500 = $10,500.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a Form 1099-C reporting $8,000 of cancelled credit card debt in 2024. Immediately before the cancellation, the taxpayer's total liabilities were $40,000 and total assets were $35,000. How much of the cancelled debt may be excluded under the insolvency exclusion?
questions.rationale: Cancelled debt is excludable only to the extent of insolvency immediately before the cancellation; with $5,000 of insolvency, $5,000 is excluded and the remaining $3,000 is taxable income.

questions.stem: Which of the following amounts received by an individual is generally excluded from gross income?
options: Jury duty pay
Unemployment compensation
Gambling winnings
Qualified scholarship used for tuition
questions.rationale: A qualified scholarship used for tuition, fees, books, and required supplies by a degree candidate is excluded from gross income; amounts for room and board are taxable.

questions.stem: A taxpayer sold a rental property in 2024 for a $50,000 gain. Of that gain, $18,000 is attributable to depreciation previously taken on the building. How is the depreciation-related portion characterized?
options: Ordinary income taxed at marginal rates
Section 1250 unrecaptured gain taxed at a maximum 25% rate
Section 1245 ordinary recapture
Tax-free as return of capital
questions.rationale: Gain attributable to straight-line depreciation on real property is unrecaptured Section 1250 gain, taxed at a maximum 25% rate rather than ordinary or 1245 treatment.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received Series EE U.S. savings bond interest of $4,000 at redemption in 2024 and paid $4,500 of qualified higher education expenses for a dependent. The taxpayer's MAGI is below the phaseout. Assuming the bonds qualify, how much of the interest may be excluded?
questions.rationale: Under the education savings bond exclusion, interest is fully excludable when qualified higher education expenses equal or exceed the bond proceeds (principal plus interest), subject to MAGI limits.

questions.stem: An individual operating a sole proprietorship received a $600 award of merchandise from a supplier in 2024 for top sales volume. How is this treated?
options: Treated as a tax-free gift
Included in gross income at fair market value
Excluded as a de minimis fringe
Reportable only if cash
questions.rationale: Awards received in connection with a trade or business are includible in gross income at their fair market value, whether paid in cash or merchandise.

questions.stem: A taxpayer exchanged investment real estate (basis $200,000, FMV $300,000) for like-kind investment real estate worth $260,000 plus $40,000 cash in a qualifying Section 1031 exchange in 2024. How much gain is recognized?
questions.rationale: In a like-kind exchange, recognized gain equals the lesser of realized gain or boot received; with $40,000 cash boot and $100,000 realized gain, $40,000 is recognized.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a state income tax refund of $700 in 2024 from the 2023 return. The taxpayer claimed the standard deduction on the 2023 return. How much of the refund is taxable in 2024?
questions.rationale: A state tax refund is taxable only to the extent it produced a tax benefit; a taxpayer who took the standard deduction received no benefit, so the refund is not taxable.

questions.stem: A cash-method taxpayer received a check for services on December 30, 2024, but did not deposit it until January 3, 2025. When is the income reported?
options: 2025, when deposited
Split between both years
Neither year, if under $600
2024, when received
questions.rationale: A cash-method taxpayer reports income when a check is received and available, regardless of when it is deposited; receipt in December 2024 makes it 2024 income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer holds 100 shares of XYZ purchased at $50 each. XYZ declares a nontaxable 2-for-1 stock split, giving the taxpayer 200 shares. What is the per-share basis after the split?
questions.rationale: A nontaxable stock split does not change total basis; the original $5,000 basis is reallocated across the new 200 shares, producing a $25 per-share basis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is deductible as an above-the-line adjustment to income for 2024?
options: State income taxes
Educator expenses up to $300
Mortgage interest
Charitable contributions
questions.rationale: The educator expense deduction allows eligible K-12 teachers to deduct up to $300 of unreimbursed classroom supplies as an adjustment to income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer made cash charitable contributions of $40,000 to a public charity in 2024 and has AGI of $60,000. What is the maximum cash contribution deductible this year, with any excess carried forward?
questions.rationale: Cash contributions to public charities are deductible up to 60% of AGI; with $60,000 AGI the limit is $36,000, and the $4,000 excess carries forward up to five years.

questions.stem: A taxpayer donated appreciated publicly traded stock held three years (basis $5,000, FMV $20,000) to a public charity in 2024. AGI is $50,000. Assuming no special election, what is the deduction limit for this gift and the deductible amount this year?
options: The deduction is limited to 30% of AGI, capping the current deduction at $15,000
The deduction is limited to basis of $5,000
The deduction is limited to 60% of AGI, allowing the full $20,000
The full $20,000 is deductible because stock is cash-equivalent
questions.rationale: Long-term appreciated capital gain property given to a public charity is deductible at fair market value but subject to a 30%-of-AGI limit; with $50,000 AGI, the current deduction is capped at $15,000 and the remaining $5,000 carries forward.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $14,000 of qualified mortgage interest, $6,000 of state and local taxes, and $2,000 of charitable cash contributions in 2024, filing single. Should the taxpayer itemize or take the standard deduction?
options: Itemize, because total itemized deductions of $22,000 exceed the standard deduction
Take the standard deduction, because it is larger
Neither is allowed in the same year
Either; they are equal
questions.rationale: When total itemized deductions ($22,000) exceed the standard deduction ($14,600 single for 2024), itemizing produces the larger deduction.

questions.stem: A taxpayer incurred $20,000 of unreimbursed medical expenses in 2024 with AGI of $120,000. How much of the medical expense is deductible as an itemized deduction?
questions.rationale: Medical expenses are deductible only to the extent they exceed 7.5% of AGI; with $120,000 AGI the floor is $9,000, leaving $11,000 deductible.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $11,000 of state income tax and $4,500 of real estate property tax in 2024. What is the maximum deduction for state and local taxes (SALT) on Schedule A?
questions.rationale: The combined deduction for state and local income, sales, and property taxes is limited to $10,000 ($5,000 for married filing separately) for 2024.

questions.stem: For 2024, a couple filing jointly paid $5,000 of qualified child care expenses for two children so both spouses could work. The applicable credit percentage is 20%. What is their Child and Dependent Care Credit, given the $6,000 expense limit for two or more qualifying persons?
questions.rationale: The dependent care credit equals the applicable percentage times the lesser of qualified expenses paid or the limit ($6,000 for two or more); 20% of $5,000 is $1,000.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $5,000 of qualified tuition for a freshman in 2024 and claims the American Opportunity Tax Credit. What is the maximum AOTC, and how much is potentially refundable?
options: $1,500 maximum, none refundable
$2,500 maximum, with up to $1,000 refundable
$2,000 maximum, fully nonrefundable
$2,500 maximum, fully refundable
questions.rationale: The American Opportunity Tax Credit is worth up to $2,500 per eligible student (100% of the first $2,000 and 25% of the next $2,000), and up to 40% ($1,000) is refundable.

questions.stem: A taxpayer contributed $3,000 to a traditional IRA in 2024 and is an active participant in an employer plan with MAGI above the phaseout range for joint filers. What is the deductible IRA amount?
questions.rationale: For an active plan participant whose MAGI exceeds the applicable phaseout ceiling, the traditional IRA deduction is fully phased out, although nondeductible contributions remain allowed.

questions.stem: Student loan interest paid in 2024 is deductible up to what maximum as an adjustment to income, subject to MAGI limits?
questions.rationale: The student loan interest deduction allows up to $2,500 of qualified interest as an above-the-line deduction, phased out at higher MAGI levels.

questions.stem: A married couple filing jointly has two qualifying children with SSNs and a 2024 tax liability before credits of $1,200. Their earned income is $30,000 and they otherwise qualify for the Child Tax Credit. Considering the additional (refundable) portion, what is the most they can receive related to the CTC?
options: $1,600, limited to one child
$3,200, including the refundable portion
$4,000, the full $2,000 per child
$1,200, limited to tax liability
questions.rationale: The Child Tax Credit is $2,000 per qualifying child; the nonrefundable part offsets tax liability and the Additional Child Tax Credit is refundable up to $1,700 per child for 2024, so the family can receive more than its tax liability.

questions.stem: For 2024, which form is generally used to calculate self-employment tax?
options: Schedule SE
Schedule A
Form 2106
Schedule D
questions.rationale: Self-employment tax is computed on Schedule SE, which determines Social Security and Medicare tax on net self-employment earnings.

questions.stem: A self-employed taxpayer had net profit of $80,000 in 2024. The self-employment tax base is 92.35% of net earnings. What is the approximate self-employment tax (combined 15.3% on the SE base, ignoring any wage base cap issues)?
questions.rationale: Self-employment tax applies 15.3% to 92.35% of net earnings; $80,000 × 0.9235 × 0.153 ≈ $11,304.

questions.stem: A taxpayer may deduct what portion of self-employment tax as an adjustment to income?
options: The full amount
None
One-half of the SE tax
One-quarter of the SE tax
questions.rationale: Taxpayers may deduct one-half of their self-employment tax as an adjustment to income, mirroring the employer share of payroll taxes.

questions.stem: A single taxpayer has wages of $180,000 and net self-employment earnings of $60,000 in 2024. The Social Security wage base is $168,600. For the OASDI (Social Security) portion of SE tax, how much of the SE earnings is subject to the 12.4% Social Security rate?
questions.rationale: Wages count first against the Social Security wage base; since $180,000 of wages exceeds $168,600, no SE earnings are subject to the 12.4% Social Security tax, though the 2.9% Medicare portion still applies.

questions.stem: For 2024, the Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% applies to wages and self-employment income above which threshold for a single filer?
questions.rationale: The Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% applies to earned income exceeding $200,000 (single), $250,000 (MFJ), or $125,000 (MFS).

questions.stem: The Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) is imposed at what rate on the lesser of net investment income or the excess of MAGI over the threshold?
questions.rationale: The Net Investment Income Tax is 3.8% on the lesser of net investment income or MAGI exceeding the applicable threshold ($200,000 single, $250,000 MFJ).

questions.stem: A single taxpayer has MAGI of $230,000, including $40,000 of net investment income, in 2024. The NIIT threshold for single filers is $200,000. What is the Net Investment Income Tax?
questions.rationale: NIIT equals 3.8% of the lesser of net investment income or the excess of MAGI over the threshold; here the $30,000 excess is smaller, so 3.8% × $30,000 = $1,140.

questions.stem: A taxpayer subject to the Alternative Minimum Tax must add back which of the following as a preference or adjustment item?
options: Qualified dividends
Charitable contributions
Mortgage interest on acquisition debt
State and local taxes deducted on Schedule A
questions.rationale: For AMT, the SALT itemized deduction is disallowed and added back, while charitable contributions and acquisition-debt mortgage interest remain deductible.

questions.stem: In 2024 a child under age 19 has unearned income of $4,000. Under the kiddie tax, the portion of the child's net unearned income exceeding a threshold is taxed at what rate structure?
options: A flat 10%
The parents' marginal tax rate
Tax-free
The child's rate entirely
questions.rationale: Under the kiddie tax, a child's net unearned income above the annual threshold is taxed at the parents' marginal rate to prevent income shifting.

questions.stem: What is the long-term capital gains tax rate applied to a single taxpayer in 2024 whose taxable income, including the gain, is well within the 0% bracket threshold?
questions.rationale: Net long-term capital gains are taxed at 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on taxable income; taxpayers under the 0% threshold pay no tax on those gains.

questions.stem: A taxpayer made estimated tax payments and withholding totaling $9,000 for 2024. Total 2024 tax is $12,000, and prior-year (2023) tax was $10,000 with AGI under $150,000. Is the taxpayer subject to an underpayment penalty under the safe harbor?
options: No, because payments equal or exceed 100% of prior-year tax
Yes, because estimated payments were too low
Yes, because tax owed exceeds payments by $3,000
No, because payments are at least 90% of current-year tax
questions.rationale: To avoid an underpayment penalty, payments must reach the lesser of 90% of current-year tax or 100% of prior-year tax (110% if AGI over $150,000); $9,000 fails both safe harbors here.

questions.stem: Qualified dividends are taxed at which rates for 2024?
options: Ordinary income rates
A flat 28%
Always 0%
The same preferential rates as net long-term capital gains
questions.rationale: Qualified dividends are taxed at the same preferential 0%, 15%, or 20% rates as net long-term capital gains.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $5,000 distribution from a traditional IRA at age 55 in 2024 with no exception applying. What additional tax applies on top of regular income tax?
options: 10% early distribution penalty
No additional tax
questions.rationale: Distributions from a traditional IRA before age 59½ are subject to a 10% additional tax unless an exception applies.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to reduce 2024 taxable income before year-end through retirement savings. Which action is generally still permitted after December 31, 2024, but before the filing deadline?
options: Making a 2024 Roth 401(k) contribution
Making a 2024 traditional IRA contribution
Recharacterizing wages
Increasing 401(k) elective deferrals for 2024
questions.rationale: Unlike 401(k) deferrals, which must be made by December 31, traditional IRA contributions for a tax year may be made up to the unextended filing deadline.

questions.stem: A taxpayer expects to be in a higher tax bracket next year. Which year-end strategy generally makes sense for 2024?
options: Take the standard deduction regardless
Accelerate income into 2024 and defer deductions into 2025
Convert all assets to municipal bonds
Defer income into 2025 and accelerate deductions into 2024
questions.rationale: When a higher bracket is expected next year, accelerating income into the current lower-bracket year and deferring deductions to the higher-bracket year generally minimizes total tax.

questions.stem: A client wants to gift assets to reduce a future taxable estate. For 2024, what is the annual gift tax exclusion per donee?
questions.rationale: For 2024, an individual may gift up to $18,000 per donee without using the lifetime exemption or filing a gift tax return.

questions.stem: A married couple wants to maximize tax-free gifts to their three grandchildren in 2024 using gift splitting. What is the maximum they can give all three grandchildren combined without using lifetime exemption?
questions.rationale: With gift splitting, a married couple can give $36,000 per donee ($18,000 each) annually; for three grandchildren the combined tax-free total is $108,000.

questions.stem: A self-employed client with a profitable business wants to maximize 2024 retirement contributions but did not establish a plan during the year. Which plan can generally still be established after year-end and funded for 2024?
options: A SIMPLE IRA
A traditional defined benefit funded only by deferrals
A 401(k) with employee deferrals only
A SEP-IRA
questions.rationale: A SEP-IRA may be both established and funded for the prior year up to the due date of the return including extensions, making it useful for after-year-end planning.

questions.stem: Which account allows tax-free growth and tax-free qualified distributions for retirement, with contributions made after-tax?
options: Roth IRA
Traditional IRA
Health Savings Account
529 plan
questions.rationale: A Roth IRA is funded with after-tax dollars; qualified distributions, including earnings, are tax-free in retirement.

questions.stem: A client age 73 in 2024 must take required minimum distributions. What penalty (excise tax) applies to the amount of an RMD not taken, after recent law changes?
options: No penalty
25% of the shortfall, reducible to 10% if timely corrected
50% of the shortfall
10% of the shortfall
questions.rationale: Under SECURE 2.0, the excise tax for a missed RMD is 25% of the shortfall, reduced to 10% if the taxpayer corrects it within the applicable correction period.

questions.stem: A client realized a $10,000 long-term capital gain and is considering selling another holding at a $7,000 loss before year-end. What is the tax effect of harvesting the loss in 2024?
options: Net capital gain is reduced to $3,000
The loss is disallowed against the gain
Losses cannot offset long-term gains
The loss creates a $7,000 deduction in addition to the gain
questions.rationale: Tax-loss harvesting allows capital losses to offset capital gains; a $7,000 loss against a $10,000 gain leaves $3,000 of net capital gain.

questions.stem: A taxpayer over age 70½ wants to satisfy charitable goals tax-efficiently from an IRA. Which strategy excludes the distribution from income while satisfying RMDs?
options: A qualified charitable distribution (QCD)
A Roth conversion
A backdoor Roth
A nondeductible IRA contribution
questions.rationale: A qualified charitable distribution allows taxpayers 70½ or older to direct IRA funds to charity, excluding the amount from income while it counts toward the RMD.

questions.stem: A client wants to convert a $50,000 traditional IRA to a Roth IRA in 2024. The IRA contains $10,000 of nondeductible basis, and the client has no other IRAs. How much of the conversion is taxable?
questions.rationale: On a Roth conversion, nondeductible basis is recovered tax-free; converting $50,000 with $10,000 of basis produces $40,000 of taxable income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer expects a large refund each year. From a planning perspective, what does a consistently large refund indicate?
options: Eligibility for more credits
Underpayment penalties are likely
Over-withholding, effectively an interest-free loan to the government
Optimal tax planning
questions.rationale: A persistently large refund indicates over-withholding; adjusting Form W-4 can increase take-home pay during the year instead of lending money interest-free to the government.

questions.stem: A U.S. citizen living and working abroad may exclude foreign earned income up to what maximum for 2024 under the foreign earned income exclusion?
questions.rationale: The maximum foreign earned income exclusion for 2024 is $126,500 per qualifying individual.

questions.stem: A nonresident alien received $5,000 of U.S.-source dividends not effectively connected with a U.S. trade or business in 2024, with no treaty benefit. What is the default U.S. tax treatment?
options: 30% flat withholding on the gross amount
Taxed at graduated rates on a net basis
Taxed at long-term capital gains rates
Exempt from U.S. tax
questions.rationale: U.S.-source FDAP income, such as dividends, paid to a nonresident alien is generally subject to a flat 30% withholding tax on the gross amount unless reduced by treaty.

questions.stem: An individual died in 2024. Who is responsible for filing the decedent's final Form 1040?
options: The personal representative or executor of the estate
The IRS automatically
No final return is required
The decedent's employer
questions.rationale: The decedent's final Form 1040 is filed by the personal representative or executor, covering income from January 1 through the date of death.

questions.stem: Income earned by a decedent but not received before death, such as a final paycheck paid afterward, is characterized as what?
options: Tax-free to all parties
Income in respect of a decedent (IRD)
A capital contribution
A gift to the estate
questions.rationale: Income in respect of a decedent is income earned but not received before death; it is taxable to the estate or beneficiary that receives it, retaining its original character.

questions.stem: An estate has gross income of $5,000 in its first tax year and distributes all income to the sole beneficiary. How is the income generally taxed?
options: Taxed twice
Passed through to the beneficiary via the distribution deduction and taxed to the beneficiary
Tax-free at both levels
Entirely at the estate level
questions.rationale: An estate is a pass-through to the extent of distributions; it deducts distributed DNI and the beneficiary reports that income, avoiding double taxation.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has a child with $14,000 of wages from a part-time job and $200 of interest income in 2024. Must the child file a return, and can the child still be a dependent?
options: The child must file because earned income exceeds the filing threshold, and can still be a dependent
No return needed; cannot be a dependent
The child cannot be a dependent because of the wages
No filing is ever required for minors
questions.rationale: A dependent with earned income above the filing threshold must file, yet a qualifying child can still be claimed as a dependent regardless of the amount earned, provided the support test is met.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received Social Security benefits in 2024. What is the maximum portion of benefits that can be subject to federal income tax?
questions.rationale: Depending on the taxpayer's combined income, up to 85% of Social Security benefits may be included in taxable income.

questions.stem: A nonresident alien married to a U.S. citizen wants to be taxed as a U.S. resident to file jointly. What is generally required?
options: Renouncing foreign citizenship
A signed election to treat the nonresident spouse as a U.S. resident for the entire year
Nothing; it is automatic
Living in the U.S. for 330 days
questions.rationale: A U.S. citizen and a nonresident alien spouse may elect to treat the nonresident as a U.S. resident for the full year, allowing a joint return but subjecting worldwide income to U.S. tax.

questions.stem: A self-employed minister received a housing allowance of $24,000 designated by the church in 2024, and the fair rental value of the home plus utilities was $20,000. The minister's actual housing expenses were $22,000. How much of the allowance is excludable from income tax?
questions.rationale: A minister's housing allowance exclusion is limited to the least of the amount designated, actual housing expenses, or the fair rental value of the home plus utilities; here the $20,000 fair rental value is the smallest.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's spouse has been missing for several years with no death certificate. The taxpayer maintains a home for a dependent child. For the current year, which filing status is generally appropriate?
options: Single
Qualifying surviving spouse
Head of household automatically
Married filing separately or, if abandoned-spouse rules are met, head of household
questions.rationale: Without proof of a spouse's death, the taxpayer remains married and generally files MFS, unless the abandoned-spouse rules permit head of household.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: What is the filing deadline for a 2024 individual federal income tax return absent an extension or special circumstances?
options: October 15, 2025
April 15, 2025
March 15, 2025
questions.rationale: The unextended due date for 2024 individual returns is generally April 15, 2025.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer received $2,000 in alimony in 2024 under a divorce decree executed in 2017 and never modified. How is the alimony treated by the recipient?
options: Treated as child support
Excluded from income
Included in gross income
Treated as a gift
questions.rationale: For divorce or separation agreements executed before 2019 (and not modified to follow post-2018 rules), alimony remains deductible by the payer and taxable to the recipient.

questions.stem: How are life insurance proceeds paid to a beneficiary by reason of the insured's death generally treated?
options: Fully taxable as ordinary income
Generally excluded from gross income
Taxable as capital gain
Taxable only above $50,000
questions.rationale: Life insurance proceeds paid to a beneficiary because of the insured's death are generally excluded from gross income, though any interest paid on delayed proceeds is taxable.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $3,000 of investment interest expense and had $2,000 of net investment income in 2024. How much investment interest is deductible this year?
questions.rationale: Investment interest expense is deductible only to the extent of net investment income; the $1,000 excess carries forward to future years.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has a casualty loss of $30,000 to a personal-use home in a federally declared disaster area in 2024, with $5,000 of insurance reimbursement. AGI is $80,000. After applying the $100 floor and the 10% AGI limit, what is the deductible loss?
questions.rationale: A personal casualty loss in a federally declared disaster is reduced by reimbursements, then the $100 floor, then 10% of AGI: $25,000 − $100 − $8,000 = $16,900.

questions.stem: What is the maximum amount of net capital loss an individual can deduct against ordinary income in a single year?
options: Unlimited
questions.rationale: Individuals may deduct up to $3,000 of net capital loss against ordinary income each year ($1,500 if MFS), carrying the excess forward indefinitely.

questions.stem: A client with fluctuating income wants to smooth the tax impact of a large 2024 Roth conversion. Which approach is generally most effective?
options: Wait until after age 73 to convert
Never convert because conversions are always taxable
Spread conversions over several lower-income years
Convert the entire amount in one high-income year
questions.rationale: Spreading Roth conversions across lower-income years helps keep the converted amounts in lower tax brackets, reducing the overall tax cost.

questions.stem: A taxpayer claims the foreign tax credit for income taxes paid to another country. Which form is used to compute the credit for an individual?
options: Form 2555
Form 8938
Form 1116
Form 8949
questions.rationale: Individuals generally compute the foreign tax credit on Form 1116, which may reduce U.S. tax on foreign-source income to avoid double taxation.

questions.stem: An individual cannot use both the foreign earned income exclusion and the foreign tax credit on what?
options: Different categories of income
Any foreign income at all
The same dollars of excluded income
Wages from any source
questions.rationale: A taxpayer cannot claim a foreign tax credit on income excluded under the foreign earned income exclusion, but may claim the credit on foreign income that was not excluded.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wishes to claim a parent as a qualifying relative dependent in 2024. The parent's gross income was $4,500. What is the gross income limit issue?
options: The limit is $10,000
The parent fails because gross income exceeds the limit
The limit is $5,050 for 2024, so the parent may qualify
The parent qualifies because there is no gross income limit for parents
questions.rationale: A qualifying relative's gross income must be below the annual limit, which is $5,050 for 2024; a parent with $4,500 of gross income satisfies this test.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer sold a principal residence in 2024 owned and used as a main home for the last 4 years, realizing a $300,000 gain. The taxpayer is single. How much gain is excludable under Section 121?
questions.rationale: Under Section 121, a single taxpayer who owned and used the home as a principal residence for at least 2 of the last 5 years may exclude up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 MFJ).

questions.stem: For 2024, the additional standard deduction for a single taxpayer who is age 65 or older is approximately how much above the regular standard deduction?
questions.rationale: For 2024, an unmarried taxpayer who is 65 or older (or blind) receives an additional standard deduction of $1,950 per qualifying condition.

questions.stem: A client wants to fund a grandchild's college and also remove assets from the taxable estate. Which 529 plan strategy uniquely accelerates gifting?
options: Contributing unlimited amounts tax-free
Naming the estate as beneficiary
Contributing $18,000 only
Electing to treat a lump-sum contribution as made over 5 years (superfunding up to $90,000)
questions.rationale: A unique 529 feature lets a donor elect to spread a lump-sum contribution over five years for gift tax purposes, allowing up to $90,000 (5 × $18,000) per beneficiary in 2024 without using lifetime exemption.

questions.stem: A bona fide resident of Puerto Rico for the entire 2024 tax year earned income solely from Puerto Rico sources. How is that income generally treated for U.S. federal tax?
options: Generally excluded from U.S. gross income
Reported but tax-free worldwide
Fully taxable on a U.S. return
Taxed at a flat 30%
questions.rationale: A bona fide resident of Puerto Rico for the entire year generally excludes Puerto Rico-source income from U.S. gross income, though U.S.-source income remains taxable.

questions.stem: Divorced parents have a child who lived with the mother 210 nights and the father 155 nights in 2024. The custodial parent signed Form 8332 releasing the dependency claim to the father. Who may claim head of household based on this child?
options: The father, because he has the release
The mother, because she is the custodial parent
Either parent
Neither parent
questions.rationale: Form 8332 transfers the dependency exemption and Child Tax Credit to the noncustodial parent, but head of household status, the EITC, and the dependent care credit remain with the custodial parent.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $1,000 qualified dividend and $400 of nonqualified (ordinary) dividends in 2024. How are these reported and taxed?
options: Qualified at LTCG rates; nonqualified at ordinary rates
Both at long-term capital gains rates
Both tax-free
Both at ordinary rates
questions.rationale: Qualified dividends are taxed at preferential capital gains rates; ordinary (nonqualified) dividends are taxed at the taxpayer's ordinary income rates.

questions.stem: Gambling losses are deductible only to what extent for a taxpayer who itemizes?
options: Up to gambling winnings reported
Only if a professional gambler
Up to $3,000
Without limit
questions.rationale: Gambling losses are deductible as an itemized deduction, but only up to the amount of gambling winnings reported as income.

questions.stem: Collectibles, such as art or coins, held long-term are subject to a maximum capital gains rate of what for 2024?
questions.rationale: Net long-term capital gains from collectibles are taxed at a maximum rate of 28%.

questions.stem: A client wants to maximize tax-free medical savings. For 2024, what is a key requirement to contribute to a Health Savings Account?
options: Having a flexible spending account
Enrollment in any health plan
Coverage under a qualifying high-deductible health plan (HDHP) with no disqualifying coverage
Being over age 65
questions.rationale: To contribute to an HSA, an individual must be covered by a qualifying high-deductible health plan, have no disqualifying coverage, and not be enrolled in Medicare.

questions.stem: A grantor trust's income in 2024 is taxed to whom?
options: The grantor who retained control
The trust as a separate taxpayer
No one until distributed
The beneficiaries only
questions.rationale: In a grantor trust, the grantor who retains certain powers or interests is treated as the owner, so the trust's income is reported on the grantor's individual return.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a Form W-2 and a Form 1099-NEC for $3,000 of side work in 2024. How is the 1099-NEC income generally reported?
options: On Schedule C as self-employment income
As other income not subject to SE tax
As additional wages on the W-2 line
It need not be reported under $5,000
questions.rationale: Nonemployee compensation reported on Form 1099-NEC is generally self-employment income, reported on Schedule C and subject to self-employment tax.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer found $500 cash on the street in 2024 and kept it. How is this treated for federal income tax?
options: Nontaxable windfall
A nontaxable gift
Taxable as other income (treasure trove)
Taxable only if over $5,000
questions.rationale: Found property, or treasure trove, is includible in gross income at its fair market value in the year the taxpayer takes undisputed possession.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's home office is used regularly and exclusively for a qualifying business and occupies 250 square feet. Using the simplified method for 2024 ($5 per square foot, max 300 sq ft), what is the home office deduction?
questions.rationale: Under the simplified home office method, the deduction is $5 per square foot up to 300 square feet; 250 sq ft × $5 = $1,250.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's only income in 2024 was $50,000 of wages, and they had $7,000 withheld. They have no credits beyond withholding. If total tax is $4,200, what is the result?
options: No refund or balance
A $4,200 refund
A $2,800 balance due
A $2,800 refund
questions.rationale: When withholding ($7,000) exceeds the total tax ($4,200), the difference is refunded; here the refund is $2,800.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to defer recognizing a capital gain on appreciated stock while diversifying. Which approach defers the gain?
options: Selling the stock immediately
Holding the stock rather than selling
Gifting to a related party at a loss
Selling and rebuying within 30 days
questions.rationale: Gain is not recognized until a sale or disposition; continuing to hold the appreciated stock defers the tax, though it does not by itself diversify the position.

questions.stem: An estate must file Form 1041 for a tax year if it has gross income of at least what amount for 2024?
questions.rationale: A decedent's estate must file Form 1041 if it has gross income of $600 or more for the tax year (or a beneficiary who is a nonresident alien).

questions.stem: What is a PTIN, which a paid return preparer must obtain?
options: A Partnership Tax Information Notice
A Personal Tax Identification Number for taxpayers
A Preparer Tax Identification Number required to prepare returns for compensation
A Payment Transfer Identification Number
questions.rationale: A Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN) is required for any individual who prepares or assists in preparing federal tax returns for compensation.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer inherited stock from a decedent who died in 2024. The decedent's basis was $20,000 and the FMV at the date of death was $50,000. The taxpayer sells it for $52,000 shortly after. What is the gain and its character?
options: $2,000 short-term gain
$32,000 long-term gain
$32,000 short-term gain
$2,000 long-term gain
questions.rationale: Inherited property generally receives a stepped-up basis to date-of-death FMV and is automatically treated as long-term; selling for $52,000 yields a $2,000 long-term gain.

questions.stem: A taxpayer made qualified contributions to a Roth IRA in 2024. Are Roth IRA contributions deductible?
options: Only if the taxpayer is over 50
Yes, fully deductible
Yes, up to 50%
No, Roth contributions are never deductible
questions.rationale: Roth IRA contributions are made with after-tax dollars and are not deductible; the trade-off is tax-free qualified distributions in retirement.

questions.stem: What schedule reports capital gains and losses that flow from Form 8949 for an individual?
options: Schedule C
Schedule SE
Schedule E
Schedule D
questions.rationale: Capital gains and losses are summarized on Schedule D, with transaction detail reported on Form 8949.

questions.stem: A client expects significant medical expenses next year. Which timing strategy could increase the medical deduction's value?
options: Pay medical bills with a credit card to delay deduction
Always take the standard deduction
Spread expenses evenly across years
Bunch elective medical expenses into one year to exceed the 7.5% AGI floor
questions.rationale: Because medical expenses are deductible only above 7.5% of AGI, bunching elective procedures into one year can push total expenses over the floor and maximize the deduction.

questions.stem: A nonresident alien student on an F-1 visa is generally treated how for the substantial presence test during the first several calendar years in the U.S.?
options: As an exempt individual whose days do not count toward substantial presence
Days are always counted
Subject to FBAR only
Automatically a resident
questions.rationale: An F-1 student is generally treated as an exempt individual for the first five calendar years, so days present do not count toward the substantial presence test, keeping them a nonresident alien.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to e-file but the return was rejected for a dependent SSN already claimed on another return. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Report the other filer to the police
File a paper return claiming the dependent if entitled, and let the IRS resolve the duplicate claim
Change the dependent's SSN
Drop the dependent permanently
questions.rationale: When an e-filed return is rejected because a dependent's SSN was already used, an entitled taxpayer should file a correct paper return; the IRS will then resolve the conflicting claims.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $600 cash rebate from a manufacturer after purchasing a car for personal use in 2024. How is the rebate treated?
options: Taxable income
A nontaxable reduction in the purchase price
Capital gain
A taxable gift
questions.rationale: A rebate from a seller or manufacturer is generally treated as a reduction in the purchase price of the item, not as taxable income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has self-employment income and contributes to a solo 401(k) in 2024. For the employee elective deferral portion, what is the 2024 limit for someone under age 50?
questions.rationale: For 2024, the elective deferral limit for a 401(k), including a solo 401(k), is $23,000 for participants under age 50.

questions.stem: A taxpayer exercised an incentive stock option (ISO) in 2024, with a bargain element of $40,000, and held the shares past year-end. What is the immediate tax consequence?
options: No tax consequence at all
Capital gain of $40,000
Ordinary income of $40,000
No regular tax, but the $40,000 bargain element is an AMT preference item
questions.rationale: Exercising an ISO and holding the stock produces no regular taxable income at exercise, but the bargain element is a preference item that can trigger the alternative minimum tax.

questions.stem: To avoid the wash sale rule when harvesting a loss, a taxpayer should avoid repurchasing substantially identical securities within what window?
options: 90 days before the sale
10 days before or after the sale
30 days before or after the sale
60 days after the sale
questions.rationale: The wash sale rule disallows a loss if substantially identical securities are purchased within 30 days before or after the sale; the disallowed loss is added to the new shares' basis.

questions.stem: A taxpayer claims a dependent who is a resident of Canada. Can a resident of Canada qualify as a dependent?
options: Yes, residents of Canada or Mexico can qualify if other tests are met
No, dependents must be U.S. citizens
Only U.S. residents qualify
Only if the dependent has a green card
questions.rationale: The dependency citizen-or-resident test is satisfied by a U.S. citizen, national, or resident, or a resident of Canada or Mexico, if the other dependency tests are met.

questions.stem: A taxpayer used the wrong filing status on an already-filed 2024 return and needs to correct it. Which form is used to amend an individual return?
options: Form 1040
Form 4868
Form 1045
Form 1040-X
questions.rationale: An individual corrects a previously filed return by filing Form 1040-X, the Amended U.S. Individual Income Tax Return.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $1,000 distribution from a Roth IRA that is a qualified distribution. How is it taxed?
options: Tax-free
Subject to 10% penalty
Taxable only on earnings
Fully taxable
questions.rationale: A qualified Roth IRA distribution, taken after age 59½ and after the five-year period, is entirely tax-free, including earnings.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $1,500 of real estate taxes on a personal residence and $2,000 of homeowner's association dues in 2024. What is deductible as an itemized SALT item (assuming under the cap)?
questions.rationale: Real estate taxes on a personal residence are deductible (within the SALT cap), but homeowner's association dues are nondeductible personal expenses.

questions.stem: For 2024, the standard mileage rate for business use of an automobile is what?
options: 70 cents per mile
65.5 cents per mile
67 cents per mile
58.5 cents per mile
questions.rationale: The IRS business standard mileage rate for 2024 is 67 cents per mile.

questions.stem: A high-income client wants to contribute to a Roth IRA but exceeds the income limits. Which strategy is commonly used?
options: A backdoor Roth: nondeductible traditional IRA contribution followed by conversion
Contribute to a spouse's 401(k)
Direct Roth contribution despite the limit
Withdraw all retirement funds
questions.rationale: The backdoor Roth strategy lets high earners contribute to a nondeductible traditional IRA and then convert it to a Roth, though the pro-rata rule applies if other pre-tax IRA balances exist.

questions.stem: A taxpayer abroad qualifies for an automatic extension to file. What is the automatic extended due date for U.S. citizens living and working abroad?
options: June 15
December 15
October 15
April 15
questions.rationale: U.S. citizens and residents living and working abroad receive an automatic two-month extension to June 15 to file, though interest still accrues from April 15.

questions.stem: Under the qualifying child relationship test, which of the following individuals does NOT qualify?
options: A stepchild
A cousin
A grandchild
A younger sibling
questions.rationale: The qualifying child relationship test includes the taxpayer's children, siblings, and their descendants; a cousin does not qualify as a qualifying child.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A landlord received $1,200 in advance rent in December 2024 for January 2025 occupancy. When is it taxable to a cash-method landlord?
options: January 2025
December 2024, when received
Spread across both months
Not taxable until earned
questions.rationale: Advance rent is included in income in the year received, regardless of the period it covers or the accounting method.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally a deductible itemized charitable contribution?
options: Cash donated to a qualified church
Political campaign contributions
The value of volunteer time
Dues to a country club
questions.rationale: Cash gifts to qualified charitable organizations, including churches, are deductible; the value of volunteer time, political contributions, and club dues are not.

questions.stem: A client wants to reduce taxable income through pre-tax retirement savings via an employer. Which contribution reduces current taxable wages?
options: Employer stock purchases
Traditional (pre-tax) 401(k) elective deferrals
After-tax non-Roth contributions
Roth 401(k) contributions
questions.rationale: Pre-tax (traditional) 401(k) elective deferrals reduce current taxable wages, deferring tax until distribution; Roth deferrals do not reduce current wages.

questions.stem: A dependent cannot generally file a return claiming what for themselves?
options: Withholding refund
Their own wages
Standard deduction
A personal exemption or being claimed as their own dependent essentially through certain credits
questions.rationale: A person who can be claimed as a dependent on another return cannot claim certain tax benefits for themselves, though they still report income and may receive refunds of withholding.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer sold business equipment (Section 1245 property) for $12,000. Original cost was $20,000 and accumulated depreciation was $15,000, giving an adjusted basis of $5,000. What is the character of the $7,000 gain?
options: $7,000 ordinary income (depreciation recapture)
$5,000 capital gain
$7,000 long-term capital gain
Tax-free
questions.rationale: Under Section 1245, gain on depreciable personal property is ordinary income to the extent of depreciation taken; since the $7,000 gain is below the $15,000 depreciation, all of it is ordinary recapture.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $2,400 in mortgage insurance premiums (PMI) in 2024. How is this generally treated for 2024?
options: Deductible without limit
Not deductible, because the PMI deduction has expired
Fully deductible as mortgage interest
Deductible as a business expense
questions.rationale: The itemized deduction for qualified mortgage insurance premiums expired and is not available for the 2024 tax year.

questions.stem: What is the employee share of the Social Security (OASDI) tax rate on wages in 2024?
questions.rationale: The employee share of Social Security (OASDI) tax is 6.2% on wages up to the annual wage base, plus 1.45% for Medicare.

questions.stem: A client wants to make a deductible charitable gift but keep flexibility about which charities receive funds. Which vehicle provides an immediate deduction with later grant-making?
options: A direct gift only
A charitable gift annuity to themselves
A donor-advised fund
A private foundation requiring annual filings
questions.rationale: A donor-advised fund allows an immediate charitable deduction in the year of contribution while letting the donor recommend grants to charities over time.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received distributions from an inherited traditional IRA in 2024 as a non-eligible designated beneficiary (e.g., an adult child) subject to the 10-year rule. Which statement is correct?
options: The account must be emptied immediately
The account generally must be fully distributed by the end of the 10th year after the owner's death
The beneficiary may stretch over their life expectancy
No distributions are ever required
questions.rationale: Under the SECURE Act 10-year rule, most non-eligible designated beneficiaries must fully distribute an inherited traditional IRA by December 31 of the tenth year after the account owner's death.

questions.stem: A married couple is deciding between MFJ and MFS for 2024. Which is generally a disadvantage of filing MFS?
options: Lower tax rates than MFJ
Loss of certain credits such as the EITC and education credits
Access to a higher standard deduction
Unlimited capital loss deduction
questions.rationale: Married filing separately typically disqualifies taxpayers from credits like the EITC, education credits, and the dependent care credit, and reduces several limits, making it often less favorable than MFJ.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer received $3,000 in dividends reinvested automatically through a dividend reinvestment plan (DRIP) in 2024. Are reinvested dividends taxable?
options: Only the portion over $1,500
No, because no cash was received
Yes, reinvested dividends are taxable in the year credited
Only when the shares are sold
questions.rationale: Dividends reinvested through a DRIP are taxable in the year credited just like cash dividends, and the reinvested amounts add to the basis of the newly purchased shares.

questions.stem: A taxpayer contributed $7,000 to a traditional IRA for 2024 but is age 52. What is the maximum 2024 contribution including catch-up?
questions.rationale: For 2024, the IRA contribution limit is $7,000, plus a $1,000 catch-up contribution for taxpayers age 50 or older, for a total of $8,000.

questions.stem: A taxpayer owes $2,000 of additional tax with the 2024 return filed on time but cannot pay in full. Which option minimizes additional charges while paying over time?
options: Ignore the balance
Request an IRS installment agreement
Claim the tax is uncollectible without filing
File late to delay
questions.rationale: Filing on time and requesting an installment agreement lets a taxpayer pay over time; the failure-to-pay penalty rate is reduced while an approved agreement is in effect.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants tax-advantaged savings specifically for a child's qualified K-12 and college expenses. Which account is designed for education?
options: Roth 401(k)
SEP-IRA
529 qualified tuition program
Health Savings Account
questions.rationale: A 529 qualified tuition program offers tax-free growth and distributions for qualified education expenses, including limited K-12 tuition and higher education costs.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is a partner in a partnership and receives a Schedule K-1 showing self-employment earnings. Where is the partner's share of SE income generally subject to SE tax?
options: Exempt as passive income
Not subject to SE tax
Subject only to capital gains tax
Subject to self-employment tax on Schedule SE
questions.rationale: A general partner's distributive share of partnership trade or business income is self-employment income subject to SE tax, computed on Schedule SE.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files a 2024 return but later realizes additional income should have been reported. The original return was filed on April 1, 2025. By when must an amended return generally be filed to claim a refund if the amendment instead produced an overpayment?
options: Within 6 years
Generally within 3 years from the original due date or 2 years from when tax was paid, whichever is later
No deadline applies
Within 1 year of filing
questions.rationale: To claim a refund, an amended return must generally be filed within 3 years from the original return's filing (or due date) or 2 years from the date the tax was paid, whichever is later.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $200 cash prize from a local raffle in 2024. How is it treated?
options: Capital gain
Taxable only if over $600
Taxable as other income
Nontaxable gift
questions.rationale: Prizes and awards, including raffle and contest winnings, are taxable income regardless of whether a Form 1099 is issued.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to claim the Lifetime Learning Credit in 2024. What is the maximum credit amount?
questions.rationale: The Lifetime Learning Credit is 20% of up to $10,000 of qualified education expenses, for a maximum of $2,000 per tax return, and is nonrefundable.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's regular tax is $18,000 and tentative minimum tax (TMT) under the AMT system is $20,000 for 2024. What additional amount is owed as AMT?
questions.rationale: The alternative minimum tax owed is the amount by which the tentative minimum tax exceeds the regular tax; $20,000 − $18,000 = $2,000.

questions.stem: A client received a large bonus in December 2024 pushing them into a higher bracket. Which deduction-timing move could lower 2024 tax?
options: Delay all deductions
Defer charitable contributions to 2025
Prepay deductible state estimated taxes or make charitable gifts before year-end (subject to limits)
Take only the standard deduction
questions.rationale: In a high-income year, accelerating deductible payments such as charitable contributions or eligible state taxes (within applicable limits) increases their tax benefit at the higher marginal rate.

questions.stem: A nonresident alien is engaged in a U.S. trade or business in 2024. How is the income effectively connected with that business taxed?
options: Only by the foreign country
Flat 30% gross-basis withholding
Graduated U.S. tax rates on a net basis
Tax-free
questions.rationale: Income effectively connected with a U.S. trade or business is taxed to a nonresident alien at the regular graduated rates on a net basis, with allowable deductions.

questions.stem: A taxpayer requests an automatic extension of time to file the 2024 return. Which form is used, and what does it extend?
options: Form 4868; extends the time to file but not the time to pay
Form 2848; grants power of attorney
Form 9465; sets up payments
Form 1040-X; extends the refund period
questions.rationale: Form 4868 provides an automatic six-month extension to file the individual return, but it does not extend the time to pay; tax remains due by the original deadline to avoid penalties and interest.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: For 2024, contributions to a traditional IRA are subject to what maximum dollar limit for a taxpayer under 50?
questions.rationale: The 2024 traditional and Roth IRA contribution limit is $7,000 for taxpayers under age 50.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a $5,000 distribution from a 529 plan in 2024, of which $4,000 covered qualified education expenses and $1,000 did not. The earnings portion of the nonqualified part is $400. How is that $400 generally treated?
options: Tax-free but with a 10% penalty
Taxable income plus a 10% additional tax
Tax-free
A capital gain
questions.rationale: Earnings on the nonqualified portion of a 529 distribution are taxable and generally subject to a 10% additional tax, while amounts used for qualified expenses remain tax-free.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has wages subject to withholding plus significant investment income with no withholding. To avoid an underpayment penalty, the taxpayer should consider what?
options: Filing for an extension
Reducing wages
Making quarterly estimated tax payments
Nothing; withholding always covers it
questions.rationale: When significant income is not subject to withholding, quarterly estimated tax payments help the taxpayer meet a safe harbor and avoid the underpayment penalty.

questions.stem: A client age 60 wants to access retirement funds before 59½-type penalties would have applied, but is now over 59½. Which statement about distributions after 59½ is correct?
options: A 10% early-distribution penalty still applies
All distributions are tax-free after 59½
RMDs begin at 59½
Distributions from a traditional IRA after 59½ avoid the 10% penalty but remain subject to income tax
questions.rationale: Once a taxpayer reaches 59½, the 10% early distribution penalty no longer applies, but distributions from a traditional IRA are still taxed as ordinary income.

questions.stem: Who is generally required to file a U.S. income tax return reporting worldwide income?
options: U.S. citizens and resident aliens, regardless of where they live
Nonresident aliens only
Only U.S. residents physically in the U.S.
Only those earning over $1 million
questions.rationale: U.S. citizens and resident aliens must report worldwide income on a U.S. return regardless of where they reside, subject to exclusions and credits to mitigate double taxation.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's correct identifying number on a return for a U.S. citizen with employment authorization is generally what?
options: A Social Security number
An EIN
A PTIN
An ITIN
questions.rationale: A U.S. citizen uses a Social Security number as the taxpayer identification number; ITINs are for individuals not eligible for an SSN.
questions.source: Part 1 – Preliminary Work and Taxpayer Data

questions.stem: A taxpayer surrendered a life insurance policy in 2024, receiving $30,000. Total premiums paid (investment in the contract) were $22,000. How much is taxable?
questions.rationale: On surrender of a life insurance policy, the amount received exceeding the investment in the contract (total premiums paid) is taxable as ordinary income; $30,000 − $22,000 = $8,000.

questions.stem: For 2024, the maximum Earned Income Tax Credit generally requires the taxpayer to have what?
options: Self-employment income only
Only investment income
No income at all
Earned income within applicable limits and qualifying criteria
questions.rationale: The Earned Income Tax Credit requires earned income (from wages or self-employment) within the applicable limits, a valid SSN, and investment income below the annual threshold.

questions.stem: What is the top marginal ordinary federal income tax rate for individuals in 2024?
questions.rationale: The highest marginal individual income tax rate for 2024 is 37%.

questions.stem: Nadia's son, age 22, was a full-time student for five months of the year, lived with her all year, and paid for 30% of his own support. He is unmarried and Nadia is 49. Is he her qualifying child for the dependency exemption rules?
options: No; any child who works must provide less than 10% of their own support
Yes; he meets the relationship, age (under 24 and a full-time student), residency, and support tests
No; a qualifying child must be under 19 at the end of the year with no exceptions
No; a child age 19 or older can never be a qualifying child
questions.rationale: Qualifying child: relationship, age, residency (more than half the year), support (child provides no more than half own support), and joint return tests.

questions.stem: A child lived with her mother for seven months and with her grandmother for five months. Her mother and grandmother are both eligible to claim her, and the mother does not file jointly with anyone. Who is entitled to claim the child as a qualifying child?
options: Whichever of them files first, since the IRS processes returns in order
The mother, since a parent takes priority over a non-parent
The grandmother, since her AGI is higher than the mother's
Neither of them; the child is a qualifying relative of both
questions.rationale: Tiebreaker: parent over non-parent; if both are parents, the one the child lived with longer; if equal, the higher AGI.

questions.stem: Delroy is single and paid all the costs of a home where his father lived the entire year. His father, a U.S. citizen with $3,000 of gross income, lives in a separate house Delroy pays for. Can Delroy file as head of household?
options: Yes, but only if his father is under age 65 at year end
No; head of household status always requires a qualifying child
No; a parent must live with the taxpayer to count as a qualifying person
