She recognizes no gain and her basis is reduced to $3,000
She recognizes $6,000 of gain and her basis becomes $9,000
She recognizes a $3,000 loss and her basis becomes zero
questions.rationale: A current cash distribution is tax-free to the extent it does not exceed the partner's outside basis; it simply reduces that basis dollar for dollar.

questions.stem: An S corporation generally must use which tax year unless it can establish a business purpose for a different one or makes a permitted election?
options: Any 52-53 week year chosen by the shareholders
A short year of less than 12 months
A calendar year
A fiscal year ending June 30
questions.rationale: S corporations are generally required to adopt a calendar tax year unless a business purpose is established or a §444 election is made.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of shareholders an S corporation is permitted to have?
options: There is no limit on the number of shareholders
75 shareholders
35 shareholders
100 shareholders
questions.rationale: An S corporation is limited to 100 shareholders, with members of a family eligible to be treated as a single shareholder.

questions.stem: Quartz Corp, an S corporation, was formerly a C corporation and has accumulated earnings and profits (E&P) from those C years. It also has substantial passive investment income. Which adverse consequence can result from this combination?
options: The S election is automatically void as of the date of incorporation
The corporation may owe a corporate-level tax on excess net passive income and risk termination of S status if it persists for three consecutive years
The corporation must immediately convert back to a partnership
Shareholders lose the ability to deduct any losses
questions.rationale: An S corporation that has accumulated C corporation E&P and excessive passive investment income may face the passive income tax and termination of its S election after three consecutive years.

questions.stem: Which form is used by an employer to report federal income tax withheld, plus Social Security and Medicare taxes, on a quarterly basis?
options: Form 1099-NEC
Form 941
Form W-2
Form 940
questions.rationale: Employers report withheld income tax and FICA taxes quarterly on Form 941; Form 940 covers FUTA annually.

questions.stem: A business pays an unincorporated independent contractor $2,500 for services during the calendar year. Which information return is the business generally required to issue to report this payment?
options: Form 1098
Form 941
Form 1099-NEC
Form W-2
questions.rationale: Nonemployee compensation of $600 or more paid to a service provider is reported on Form 1099-NEC.

questions.stem: For 2024, what is the maximum amount of qualifying property a business can elect to expense under Section 179, before the dollar-for-dollar phase-out and taxable income limitation apply?
questions.rationale: For tax year 2024 the Section 179 maximum deduction is $1,220,000, reduced dollar-for-dollar once qualifying purchases exceed the investment threshold.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct statement about the Section 179 deduction?
options: The Section 179 deduction is limited to the taxpayer's aggregate taxable income from the active conduct of any trade or business
Section 179 applies only to real property such as buildings
The Section 179 deduction can create or increase a business net operating loss
Land qualifies as Section 179 property
questions.rationale: Section 179 expensing is capped at business taxable income; any disallowed amount carries forward, and the deduction cannot itself create a loss.

questions.stem: A self-employed consultant has net earnings from self-employment of $80,000 for 2024. Approximately what percentage rate applies for computing self-employment tax on net earnings (before the income adjustments), combining Social Security and Medicare?
questions.rationale: Self-employment tax is 15.3% total—12.4% Social Security (up to the wage base) plus 2.9% Medicare—applied to net earnings from self-employment.

questions.stem: When computing self-employment tax, a self-employed individual multiplies net profit by what factor to arrive at net earnings from self-employment subject to the tax?
questions.rationale: Net earnings from self-employment equal net profit multiplied by 92.35%, reflecting the deduction for the employer-equivalent portion of SE tax.

questions.stem: A self-employed taxpayer who owes self-employment tax may deduct what portion of that tax as an adjustment to gross income (an above-the-line deduction)?
options: Only the Medicare portion
None of it
One-half of the self-employment tax
The full amount of the self-employment tax
questions.rationale: Taxpayers may deduct one-half of their self-employment tax as an above-the-line adjustment, approximating the employer's share that an employee would not pay.

questions.stem: Under the general rules, a C corporation with average annual gross receipts of $40 million over the prior three years is required to use which overall method of accounting?
options: The cash method, because it is simpler
The accrual method, because it exceeds the gross receipts threshold for using the cash method
The installment method
Either method, with no restriction
questions.rationale: C corporations whose average annual gross receipts exceed the small-business threshold (about $30 million for 2024) generally must use the accrual method of accounting.

questions.stem: Under the accrual method of accounting, when does a business generally recognize income from the sale of goods?
options: At the end of the calendar year regardless of the sale date
Only when cash is actually received
When all events have occurred that fix the right to receive the income and the amount can be determined with reasonable accuracy
When the customer's check clears the bank
questions.rationale: Accrual-method income is recognized under the all-events test: when the right to income is fixed and the amount can be determined with reasonable accuracy, regardless of payment.

questions.stem: Beacon Inc., a C corporation, has gross income of $500,000 and deductible expenses of $620,000 for 2024, producing a net operating loss. Under the rules generally applicable to NOLs arising in 2024, how may Beacon use this NOL?
options: Carry it back two years and then forward 20 years
Carry it forward indefinitely, with the deduction generally limited to 80% of taxable income in the carryforward year
Carry it back five years with no limitation
Deduct it only in the year it arises or lose it entirely
questions.rationale: For NOLs arising after 2017, there is generally no carryback, the carryforward is indefinite, and the deduction is limited to 80% of taxable income in each carryforward year.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally a deductible ordinary and necessary business expense for a sole proprietor reporting on Schedule C?
options: The personal portion of a family vacation
The cost of commuting from home to the regular place of business
Wages paid to employees for services rendered to the business
A fine paid to a government agency for violating a law
questions.rationale: Ordinary and necessary business expenses such as employee wages are deductible, while commuting, fines, and personal costs are not.

questions.stem: For 2024, what percentage of the cost of business meals (food and beverages provided by a restaurant) is generally deductible?
questions.rationale: The temporary 100% deduction for restaurant meals ended after 2022, so for 2024 most business meals are subject to the standard 50% limitation.

questions.stem: Which form must an employer furnish to each employee by January 31 to report annual wages and the taxes withheld from those wages?
options: Form 940
Form W-4
Form 1099-MISC
Form W-2
questions.rationale: Employers must furnish Form W-2 to employees by January 31, reporting annual wages and the income and FICA taxes withheld.

questions.stem: What is the standard mileage rate that a business may use to deduct the cost of operating a vehicle for business purposes in 2024?
options: 58.5 cents per mile
67 cents per mile
65.5 cents per mile
70 cents per mile
questions.rationale: For 2024, the IRS business standard mileage rate is 67 cents per mile.

questions.stem: A business buys $50,000 of qualifying new equipment in 2024 and places it in service. The taxpayer wants to maximize current-year cost recovery using bonus depreciation (and elects no Section 179). What percentage of the cost may generally be deducted as bonus depreciation for property placed in service in 2024?
questions.rationale: Bonus depreciation is phasing down: 80% for 2023, 60% for 2024, and 40% for 2025 for most qualified property.

questions.stem: An employer is subject to the Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA). On which form and on what schedule is FUTA tax reported?
options: Form 940, filed annually
Form 941, filed quarterly
Form W-3, filed annually
Form 944, filed quarterly
questions.rationale: Federal unemployment tax is reported on Form 940, which is filed annually.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes an employee from an independent contractor for federal employment tax purposes?
options: Classification depends solely on whether the worker has a business license
A worker is always an independent contractor if paid by the hour
An employee is anyone the business calls a contractor in a written agreement
The key factor is the degree of behavioral and financial control the business has over the worker and the type of relationship
questions.rationale: Worker classification turns on the common-law factors of behavioral control, financial control, and the relationship of the parties—not on labels alone.

questions.stem: Under the uniform capitalization (UNICAP) rules of §263A, which of the following must generally be capitalized rather than currently deducted?
options: Selling and distribution expenses for goods already produced
Direct and certain indirect costs allocable to property the taxpayer produces or acquires for resale
Federal income taxes paid by the business
Interest on a personal residence mortgage
questions.rationale: Section 263A requires capitalizing direct and certain indirect costs allocable to inventory produced or held for resale, subject to a small-business gross receipts exception.

questions.stem: Cost of goods sold (COGS) reduces gross receipts to arrive at gross profit for a business that sells inventory. Which of the following is generally included in COGS?
options: The cost of merchandise purchased for resale and direct labor to produce goods
Office rent for administrative staff
The owner's draw
Advertising expense for the year
questions.rationale: Cost of goods sold consists of inventory and direct production costs such as merchandise, materials, and direct labor, not general operating expenses.

questions.stem: A small employer's accumulated payroll tax liability is low enough that the IRS notifies it to file an annual employment tax return instead of quarterly returns. Which form does such an employer file?
options: Form 944
Form 943
Form 940
Form 941
questions.rationale: Very small employers notified by the IRS file Form 944 annually instead of Form 941 quarterly to report withheld income tax and FICA.

questions.stem: A sole proprietor pays $1,200 for business liability insurance for the coming year. On Schedule C, how is this cost generally treated?
options: It must be capitalized and depreciated over 7 years
It is deductible only if the business shows a profit
It is a deductible ordinary and necessary business expense
It is a nondeductible personal expense
questions.rationale: Insurance premiums that are ordinary and necessary to the operation of a trade or business are deductible as a current business expense on Schedule C.

questions.stem: An S corporation provides each shareholder a document reporting their pro rata share of income, deductions, and credits. Which schedule serves this purpose?
options: Schedule C
Form 1099-DIV
Form W-2
Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S)
questions.rationale: Pass-through items from an S corporation are reported to each shareholder on Schedule K-1 of Form 1120-S.

questions.stem: A C corporation overpaid its estimated taxes and reports taxable income of $200,000 for 2024. At the flat corporate rate in effect for 2024, what is its regular income tax before credits?
questions.rationale: C corporations are taxed at a flat 21% rate, so $200,000 of taxable income produces $42,000 of tax before credits.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding a C corporation's dividends-received deduction (DRD) on dividends from a domestic corporation in which it owns less than 20%?
options: The corporation may deduct 100% of the dividends received
Dividends received by a corporation are fully taxable with no deduction
The deduction is available only to individual shareholders
The corporation may generally deduct 50% of the dividends received
questions.rationale: The dividends-received deduction generally allows a corporation to deduct 50% of dividends from a domestic corporation when ownership is below 20%, 65% for 20%-to-under-80% ownership, and 100% within an affiliated group.

questions.stem: Which form does a farmer who is a sole proprietor generally use to report income and expenses from farming?
options: Form 4835
Schedule F
Schedule E
Schedule C
questions.rationale: A sole proprietor engaged in farming reports income and expenses on Schedule F.

questions.stem: An estate generates more than $600 of gross income during its administration. Which income tax return must the fiduciary generally file for the estate?
options: Form 1040 for the deceased individual
Form 1065
Form 1041, U.S. Income Tax Return for Estates and Trusts
Form 706, United States Estate Tax Return
questions.rationale: An estate that earns $600 or more of gross income during administration must file Form 1041 to report that income; Form 706 is a separate transfer-tax return.

questions.stem: When an estate or trust distributes income to a beneficiary, which concept generally limits how much of that distribution is taxable to the beneficiary and deductible by the entity?
options: The alternative minimum tax
Distributable net income (DNI)
The accumulated earnings tax
The qualified business income deduction
questions.rationale: Distributable net income (DNI) caps the income distribution deduction for the estate or trust and the corresponding amount of income taxable to beneficiaries.

questions.stem: A tax-exempt organization recognized under §501(c)(3) operates an unrelated business that produces $3,000 of gross income from activities unrelated to its exempt purpose. Which return must it generally file to report this income?
options: Form 990-T to report and pay tax on unrelated business taxable income
No return, because exempt organizations never pay income tax
Form 990 only, with no tax due
Form 1120 as a regular C corporation
questions.rationale: An exempt organization with $1,000 or more of gross income from an unrelated trade or business must file Form 990-T and pay the unrelated business income tax.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a special tax rule available to qualifying farmers regarding estimated taxes?
options: Farmers may never use the cash method of accounting
A qualifying farmer who files and pays all tax by March 1 may avoid making estimated tax payments
Farmers must pay estimated taxes monthly
Farmers are completely exempt from paying any federal income tax
questions.rationale: Qualifying farmers can avoid estimated tax payments by filing their return and paying all tax due by March 1.

questions.stem: A complex trust earns $20,000 of taxable income but is permitted (and chooses) to accumulate the income rather than distribute it. Compared with individual taxpayers, what is notable about how trust income is taxed at higher levels?
options: Trusts reach the top marginal income tax bracket at a much lower income threshold than individuals
Trusts are taxed at a flat 10% rate on all income
Trusts are taxed only when the grantor dies
Trusts never pay income tax on accumulated income
questions.rationale: Trusts and estates use compressed brackets, reaching the top marginal rate at a much lower income level than individuals, which discourages accumulating income at the entity level.

questions.stem: Which return is generally used to report and pay the federal estate (transfer) tax for a decedent whose gross estate exceeds the applicable exclusion amount?
options: Form 1040
Form 709
Form 1041
Form 706
questions.rationale: The federal estate (transfer) tax is reported on Form 706 when the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts exceeds the exclusion amount.

questions.stem: A partnership reports its income on Form 1065 but, as a pass-through entity, generally does not pay income tax. How is the partnership's net income ultimately taxed?
options: It escapes all federal income tax
Each partner reports and pays tax on his or her distributive share via a Schedule K-1
It is taxed at the partnership level at 21%
Only the general partner pays tax on the entire amount
questions.rationale: Partnership income is taxed to the partners individually based on their distributive shares reported on Schedule K-1, not at the partnership level.

questions.stem: Which form is generally used by a tax-exempt charitable organization to file its annual information return with the IRS?
options: Form 941
Form 1065
Form 1120
Form 990 (or 990-EZ/990-N depending on size)
questions.rationale: Most tax-exempt organizations file the Form 990 series (990, 990-EZ, or 990-N) annually as their information return.

questions.stem: A farmer using the cash method sells crops in 2024 but received a $10,000 advance payment for the crops in late 2023. Under the cash method, in which year is the $10,000 generally included in income?
options: 2023, when the cash payment was actually received
2024, when the crops were delivered
It may be spread evenly over both years
Only when the buyer resells the crops
questions.rationale: Under the cash method, income is recognized in the year it is actually or constructively received, so a 2023 advance payment is 2023 income even though crops are delivered in 2024.

questions.stem: A grantor trust is one in which the grantor retains certain powers or interests. For federal income tax purposes, how is income of a grantor trust generally taxed?
options: The income is taxed only to the trust beneficiaries
The income is generally taxed directly to the grantor on the grantor's own return
The trust pays tax on all of its income at trust rates
The income is never taxed
questions.rationale: Because a grantor trust is treated as owned by the grantor, its income is generally reported and taxed directly on the grantor's individual return.

questions.stem: Three individuals form a corporation. Adam contributes property, Beth contributes property, and Carl contributes only services in exchange for stock. To meet the 80% control test of IRC §351, whose stock counts toward control immediately after the exchange?
options: All three, because each received stock
Only Adam and Beth, because stock received solely for services does not count toward the control group
Only Carl, because services are the most valuable contribution
None of them, because three transferors cannot qualify under §351
questions.rationale: Under §351, only persons transferring property are counted in the control group; one who receives stock solely for services is excluded and recognizes ordinary income.

questions.stem: Nina contributes land with an adjusted basis of $25,000 and a fair market value of $70,000 to a corporation in a qualifying §351 exchange. The corporation assumes a $30,000 mortgage on the land, and the assumption is not in excess of basis problems and has no tax-avoidance purpose. What is Nina's basis in the stock received?
questions.rationale: In a §351 exchange, the transferor's stock basis is the property's basis decreased by liabilities assumed by the corporation; when liabilities exceed basis under §357(c), the excess is recognized gain and stock basis cannot go below zero.

questions.stem: Paula contributes property with a basis of $15,000 and a fair market value of $40,000 to a corporation in a tax-free §351 exchange. What is the corporation's basis in the property received (ignoring any gain recognized by Paula)?
options: $15,000, a carryover (transferred) basis
$25,000, the built-in gain
$40,000, the fair market value
questions.rationale: Section 362 gives the corporation a transferred (carryover) basis in property received in a §351 exchange, increased by any gain recognized by the transferor.

questions.stem: Ramos LLC, taxed as a partnership, makes a liquidating distribution to partner Ed of $10,000 cash when his outside basis is $18,000. He receives no other property. What is the tax result to Ed?
options: He recognizes no gain or loss and reduces basis to $8,000
He recognizes $10,000 of ordinary income
He recognizes a $8,000 capital loss
He recognizes a $8,000 gain
questions.rationale: On a liquidating distribution consisting solely of money (and only money, unrealized receivables, or inventory), a partner recognizes loss to the extent outside basis exceeds the cash received.

questions.stem: A partnership pays partner Gloria a $50,000 guaranteed payment for services, determined without regard to partnership income. How is this guaranteed payment treated?
options: It is a tax-free return of capital to Gloria
It is taxed to all partners in proportion to their interests
It is deductible by the partnership (if otherwise an ordinary expense) and is ordinary income to Gloria
It is a nondeductible distribution that reduces only Gloria's capital account
questions.rationale: Guaranteed payments for services or capital, determined without regard to partnership income, are deductible by the partnership and are ordinary income to the receiving partner.

questions.stem: Hank contributes appreciated property (basis $20,000, fair market value $50,000) to a partnership. Two years later the partnership sells the property for $50,000. Under §704(c), how is the $30,000 of built-in gain generally allocated?
options: Entirely to Hank, the contributing partner, to account for the pre-contribution appreciation
Entirely to the partnership at the entity level
Equally among all partners according to their interests
It is not recognized because the property was contributed tax-free
questions.rationale: Section 704(c) prevents shifting of pre-contribution gain or loss by allocating built-in gain or loss on contributed property to the contributing partner.

questions.stem: A domestic eligible entity wishes to change its default federal tax classification (for example, to be taxed as a corporation). Which form does it file to make this entity classification election?
options: Form 1065
Form SS-4
Form 2553
Form 8832
questions.rationale: Under the check-the-box regulations, an eligible entity uses Form 8832 to elect its classification; an S election is then made separately on Form 2553.

questions.stem: When a new partner contributes only cash to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest, what is the general tax consequence at the time of contribution?
options: The partner recognizes ordinary income on the cash contributed
The partner recognizes gain equal to the value of the interest received
Neither the partner nor the partnership generally recognizes gain or loss on the contribution
The partnership recognizes income equal to the cash received
questions.rationale: Section 721 provides that no gain or loss is recognized on the contribution of property to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest.

questions.stem: An S corporation that was never a C corporation has accumulated adjustments account (AAA) of $40,000 and makes a $60,000 cash distribution to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis is $100,000. The corporation has no accumulated earnings and profits. How is the $60,000 distribution generally treated?
options: $40,000 tax-free and $20,000 taxable dividend
Fully taxable as a dividend
Fully taxable as capital gain
Tax-free return of basis (reducing stock basis to $40,000), because the corporation has no accumulated E&P
questions.rationale: For an S corporation with no accumulated E&P, distributions are tax-free to the extent of the shareholder's stock basis; the AAA ordering rules matter mainly when accumulated C-corporation E&P exists.

questions.stem: Beacon Corp elected S status effective January 1, 2024, having been a C corporation with appreciated assets. In 2024 it sells an asset that had a built-in gain on the conversion date. Which tax may apply at the corporate level?
options: The built-in gains (BIG) tax under §1374
The accumulated earnings tax
The personal holding company tax
No corporate-level tax ever applies to an S corporation
questions.rationale: When a C corporation converts to an S corporation, the built-in gains tax under §1374 can apply to gains that were built in at the conversion date if recognized within the recognition period.

questions.stem: Which of the following trusts is an eligible shareholder of an S corporation?
options: A qualified subchapter S trust (QSST) that has made the proper election
A foreign trust
A C corporation
A partnership acting as trustee
questions.rationale: Eligible S corporation shareholders include individuals, estates, certain trusts such as QSSTs and ESBTs, and certain exempt organizations; partnerships, corporations, and nonresident aliens are not eligible.

questions.stem: An S corporation election can be involuntarily terminated. Which of the following events would generally cause an automatic termination of S status?
options: The corporation declares no distributions for three years
The corporation earns a net operating loss for the year
The corporation transfers stock to a nonresident alien individual
The corporation hires more than 100 employees
questions.rationale: S status terminates automatically if the corporation ceases to meet the eligibility requirements—for example, when stock is held by an ineligible shareholder such as a nonresident alien.

questions.stem: Iris is a 50% partner whose outside basis is $5,000. Her share of partnership losses for the year is $8,000. How much of the loss may she deduct currently, and what happens to the rest?
options: She deducts $4,000, half of the loss
She deducts $5,000 currently; the remaining $3,000 is suspended and carried forward until she has basis
She deducts nothing because losses are never deductible by partners
She deducts the full $8,000 currently
questions.rationale: A partner may deduct distributive losses only up to outside basis; losses in excess of basis are suspended and carried forward until the partner has sufficient basis (also subject to at-risk and passive activity limits).

questions.stem: When does a partnership generally terminate for federal income tax purposes under current law?
options: When no part of any business, financial operation, or venture continues to be carried on by any of its partners in a partnership
When any one partner sells 25% of his or her interest
When the partnership earns a loss for two consecutive years
When the partnership changes its name
questions.rationale: Under current law a partnership terminates only when no part of any of its business continues to be carried on by any of its partners in a partnership (the prior 50%-sale technical termination rule was repealed).

questions.stem: Which characteristic is unique to a C corporation compared with an S corporation?
options: Limited liability for its owners
The requirement to file an annual federal return
Ability to have an unlimited number and any type of shareholders, including other corporations and foreign persons
The use of a tax identification number
questions.rationale: Unlike an S corporation, a C corporation has no restrictions on the number or type of shareholders, so it can have foreign, corporate, or partnership owners and more than 100 shareholders.

questions.stem: A single-member LLC owned by an individual has not made any entity classification election. For federal income tax purposes, how is it generally treated?
options: As a disregarded entity, with its activity reported on the owner's return
As a partnership filing Form 1065
As an S corporation
As a separate corporation that files Form 1120
questions.rationale: By default, a domestic single-member LLC is a disregarded entity; its income and expenses are reported directly by the single owner.

questions.stem: A partnership distributes property (not cash) with an inside basis of $12,000 to a partner in a current (nonliquidating) distribution. The partner's outside basis just before the distribution is $9,000. What basis does the partner take in the distributed property?
options: $9,000, limited to the partner's outside basis
$12,000, the partnership's inside basis
The property's fair market value
questions.rationale: In a current distribution, a partner takes a carryover basis in distributed property, but not more than the outside basis remaining after any cash distributed; here basis is capped at $9,000.

questions.stem: How does a partner's share of partnership recourse liabilities generally affect that partner's outside basis?
options: It decreases outside basis dollar for dollar
An increase in the partner's share of liabilities increases outside basis, treated as a deemed cash contribution
It has no effect on outside basis
It only affects the partnership's inside basis, never the partner's
questions.rationale: A partner's outside basis includes the partner's share of partnership liabilities; increases are treated as deemed contributions (raising basis) and decreases as deemed distributions (lowering basis).

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of pass-through taxation that applies to partnerships and S corporations but not to C corporations?
options: Owners can never use business losses on their personal returns
Business income and losses flow through to the owners and are taxed only once at the owner level
Earnings are taxed twice, once at the entity level and again to owners
The entity pays a flat 21% tax
questions.rationale: Pass-through entities such as partnerships and S corporations generally avoid the entity-level tax, so income is taxed once at the owner level and losses can pass through subject to limitations.

questions.stem: An S corporation shareholder's stock basis is adjusted for the year. In what order are the following generally applied to stock basis: (1) increases for income items, (2) decreases for distributions, and (3) decreases for losses and deductions?
options: Losses first, then income, then distributions
Income increases first, then distributions, then losses and deductions
Distributions first, then losses, then income
All three are applied simultaneously with no ordering
questions.rationale: S corporation stock basis is adjusted in order: increase for income items, decrease for distributions, then decrease for nondeductible expenses and losses/deductions.

questions.stem: Which item is a separately stated item that an S corporation passes through to shareholders rather than including in ordinary business income on the face of Form 1120-S?
options: Charitable contributions
Cost of goods sold
Rent paid for the business premises
Employee wages
questions.rationale: Items that may be subject to special treatment or limits at the owner level—such as charitable contributions, capital gains, and §179 expense—are separately stated on Schedule K-1 rather than buried in ordinary income.

questions.stem: What does the accumulated adjustments account (AAA) of an S corporation generally measure?
options: The fair market value of the corporation's assets
The cumulative undistributed net income of the S corporation that has been taxed to shareholders
The corporation's accumulated C corporation earnings and profits
The total wages paid to all employees
questions.rationale: The AAA is an account reflecting the S corporation's accumulated, previously taxed but undistributed income; it governs the tax treatment of distributions when the corporation also has accumulated C-corporation E&P.

questions.stem: After a corporation's S election is terminated, when may the corporation generally re-elect S status without IRS consent?
options: Never; a terminated S election can never be reinstated
Generally not until the fifth tax year after the year of termination, absent IRS consent
Immediately in the next tax year
After 10 years in all cases
questions.rationale: Following a termination or revocation, a corporation generally cannot re-elect S status until the fifth tax year after the termination year unless the IRS consents to an earlier re-election.

questions.stem: Olive contributes equipment to a partnership in exchange for a 30% interest. The equipment has a fair market value of $60,000 and is subject to a $20,000 liability that the partnership assumes. The other partners bear 70% of partnership liabilities. Generally, how is the net liability relief treated for Olive at contribution?
options: Olive is treated as receiving a deemed distribution for the portion of the liability shifted to other partners, which reduces her basis and can trigger gain only if it exceeds basis
The liability has no effect because §721 makes all contributions tax-free in every respect
The entire $20,000 is immediately taxable gain
Olive must recognize ordinary income of $20,000
questions.rationale: When a partnership assumes a contributing partner's liability, the portion shifted to other partners is a deemed cash distribution that reduces the contributor's basis and produces gain only to the extent it exceeds basis.

questions.stem: A taxpayer places nonresidential real property (a commercial building) in service in 2024. Under MACRS, over what recovery period is the building depreciated using the straight-line method?
options: 7 years
39 years
27.5 years
15 years
questions.rationale: Under MACRS, nonresidential real property uses a 39-year straight-line recovery period, while residential rental property uses 27.5 years.

questions.stem: Residential rental property placed in service in 2024 is depreciated under MACRS over which recovery period?
options: 27.5 years
39 years
10 years
20 years
questions.rationale: MACRS assigns residential rental property a 27.5-year straight-line recovery period.

questions.stem: Under MACRS, which convention generally applies to depreciable personal property (such as machinery) placed in service during the year, absent the mid-quarter convention?
options: The full-year convention
The mid-week convention
The mid-month convention
The half-year convention
questions.rationale: MACRS personal property generally uses the half-year convention unless more than 40% of property is placed in service in the last quarter, which triggers the mid-quarter convention.

questions.stem: A business places $1,000,000 of qualifying machinery in service during 2024, of which $700,000 was placed in service in the fourth quarter. The other $300,000 was placed in service earlier in the year. Which depreciation convention generally applies to this personal property?
options: The half-year convention
No convention applies
The mid-month convention
The mid-quarter convention, because more than 40% of the property was placed in service in the last quarter
questions.rationale: If more than 40% of the aggregate basis of personal property is placed in service in the final quarter, the mid-quarter convention applies to all personal property placed in service that year.

questions.stem: Listed property, such as a passenger automobile used in business, is subject to special rules. If business use of listed property does not exceed 50%, which depreciation method must generally be used?
options: 200% declining balance under regular MACRS
Section 179 immediate expensing
150% declining balance
The straight-line method under the alternative depreciation system (ADS)
questions.rationale: When qualified business use of listed property is 50% or less, the taxpayer must use straight-line depreciation under ADS and cannot claim §179 expensing or bonus depreciation.

questions.stem: Which of the following assets is NOT depreciable for federal income tax purposes?
options: A warehouse building
A delivery truck used in the business
Office computers
Land on which the business building sits
questions.rationale: Land is never depreciable because it has no determinable useful life; only improvements and other assets that wear out are depreciated.

questions.stem: A business sells equipment for $30,000. The equipment originally cost $50,000, and the business had claimed $35,000 of depreciation, leaving an adjusted basis of $15,000. How much of the $15,000 gain is recaptured as ordinary income under §1245?
options: $0; the entire gain is §1231 capital gain
$15,000, because the gain does not exceed the depreciation taken
questions.rationale: Under §1245, gain on the sale of depreciable personal property is recaptured as ordinary income to the extent of prior depreciation; here the entire $15,000 gain is ordinary recapture.

questions.stem: A taxpayer sells business real property at a gain. Part of the gain is attributable to depreciation previously deducted using straight-line on the building. For a noncorporate taxpayer, how is the unrecaptured §1250 portion of the gain generally taxed?
options: It is fully exempt from tax
At a maximum capital gains rate of 25% (unrecaptured §1250 gain)
As ordinary income at the taxpayer's regular rate
At a 0% rate in all cases
questions.rationale: For noncorporate taxpayers, the portion of real property gain attributable to prior straight-line depreciation is unrecaptured §1250 gain, taxed at a maximum 25% rate rather than ordinary rates.

questions.stem: How are net §1231 gains and losses generally characterized for a taxpayer who has a net §1231 gain for the year (ignoring the 5-year lookback recapture rule)?
options: Both net §1231 gains and losses are ordinary
A net §1231 gain is treated as ordinary income
A net §1231 gain is treated as long-term capital gain, while a net §1231 loss is treated as an ordinary loss
Both net §1231 gains and losses are capital
questions.rationale: Section 1231 provides the best of both worlds: net gains are long-term capital gains, while net losses are fully deductible ordinary losses (subject to the 5-year lookback recapture rule).

questions.stem: An investor exchanges business real property (adjusted basis $100,000, fair market value $250,000) for like-kind business real property worth $250,000 in a qualifying §1031 exchange, receiving no boot. What is the investor's recognized gain and basis in the new property?
options: Recognized gain $150,000; basis $250,000
Recognized gain $0; basis $250,000
Recognized gain $150,000; basis $100,000
Recognized gain $0; basis $100,000 (carryover)
questions.rationale: In a §1031 like-kind exchange of real property with no boot, gain is deferred (not recognized), and the replacement property takes the relinquished property's carryover basis.

questions.stem: After the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, like-kind exchange treatment under §1031 is limited to exchanges of which type of property?
options: Vehicles used in business
Machinery and equipment
Inventory held for sale
Real property held for productive use in a trade or business or for investment
questions.rationale: Since 2018, §1031 nonrecognition is limited to real property; exchanges of personal property such as equipment or vehicles no longer qualify.

questions.stem: In a §1031 exchange, a taxpayer must identify replacement property within how many days, and complete the exchange within how many days, of transferring the relinquished property?
options: 60 days to identify; 120 days to complete
30 days to identify; 90 days to complete
90 days to identify; 365 days to complete
45 days to identify; 180 days to complete
questions.rationale: A deferred §1031 exchange requires identifying replacement property within 45 days and receiving it within 180 days (or the return due date, if earlier) of the transfer of the relinquished property.

questions.stem: A business using the accrual method may generally deduct a year-end accrued bonus to a non-related-party employee in the current year if it is paid within how many days after year-end (under the 2.5-month rule)?
options: 6 months
2.5 months (generally 75 days)
30 days
12 months
questions.rationale: Under the 2.5-month rule, a fixed and determinable accrued bonus paid to an unrelated employee within 2.5 months after year-end is treated as paid in the accrual year and deductible then.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally TRUE about the cash method of accounting for a small business?
options: It may never be used by any business
Income is reported when actually or constructively received, and expenses are deducted when paid
Income is reported only when earned, regardless of receipt
Expenses are always deducted when incurred, regardless of payment
questions.rationale: The cash method recognizes income when actually or constructively received and deducts expenses when paid, in contrast to the accrual method's all-events test.

questions.stem: A small business with average annual gross receipts of $20 million (below the §448(c) threshold for 2024) wants to use the cash method and avoid maintaining inventories. Which statement is correct?
options: It must capitalize all inventory under §263A regardless of size
It is barred from the cash method because it sells goods

It generally qualifies as a small business taxpayer exempt from the required accrual method, UNICAP, and the inventory rules, and may treat inventory as non-incidental materials and supplies or follow its books
It must use the accrual method and full inventory accounting
questions.rationale: Under §448(c), taxpayers with average annual gross receipts below the inflation-adjusted threshold (about $30 million for 2024) may use the cash method, are exempt from §263A, and may use simplified inventory methods.

questions.stem: To change an overall method of accounting (for example, from cash to accrual), a taxpayer generally must obtain IRS consent by filing which form?
options: Form 8832
Form 2553
Form 4562
Form 3115, Application for Change in Accounting Method
questions.rationale: A taxpayer changing an accounting method generally must file Form 3115 to obtain the IRS's consent, whether under automatic or non-automatic procedures.

questions.stem: Employers generally must deposit federal payroll taxes (withheld income tax and FICA) on either a monthly or semiweekly schedule. What primarily determines which deposit schedule applies for a given calendar year?
options: The number of employees on the payroll
The total tax liability reported during a lookback period
The industry in which the business operates
Whether the business is incorporated
questions.rationale: An employer's monthly or semiweekly deposit schedule is determined by the total taxes reported in a lookback period; larger liabilities require more frequent deposits.

questions.stem: The trust fund recovery penalty can be assessed against a responsible person who willfully fails to collect, account for, and pay over withheld taxes. The penalty equals what amount?
options: 10% of the unpaid taxes
50% of the gross payroll
100% of the unpaid trust fund taxes (withheld income tax and the employee share of FICA)
The employer's share of FICA only
questions.rationale: The trust fund recovery penalty under §6672 is 100% of the withheld income tax and employee FICA that a responsible person willfully fails to pay over.

questions.stem: Which form transmits paper Forms W-2 to the Social Security Administration?
options: Form 1096
Form 940
Form W-4
Form W-3, Transmittal of Wage and Tax Statements
questions.rationale: Form W-3 transmits Forms W-2 to the SSA, while Form 1096 is the analogous transmittal for paper 1099-series information returns.

questions.stem: Which form transmits paper information returns such as Forms 1099-NEC to the IRS?
options: Form 941
Form 8809
Form W-3
Form 1096, Annual Summary and Transmittal of U.S. Information Returns
questions.rationale: Paper 1099-series information returns are transmitted to the IRS with Form 1096; W-2s are transmitted with Form W-3.

questions.stem: For 2024, the Social Security portion of FICA and self-employment tax applies only up to an annual wage base. Approximately what is the 2024 Social Security wage base?
questions.rationale: For 2024, Social Security tax (the 12.4% portion) applies only to the first $168,600 of wages or net self-employment earnings; the 2.9% Medicare portion has no wage cap.

questions.stem: The Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% applies to wages and self-employment income above a threshold. Who is responsible for the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax?
options: It is split equally between employer and employee with no thresholds
It applies only to corporations
It is imposed on the employee/individual; employers withhold it on wages over $200,000, and any balance is reconciled on the individual return
The employer pays the entire 0.9%
questions.rationale: The 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax is an employee/individual tax; employers withhold it once wages exceed $200,000, and the individual reconciles the actual liability (based on filing-status thresholds) on Form 8959.

questions.stem: Which credit rewards employers for a portion of wages paid to employees from certain targeted groups, such as qualified veterans or long-term unemployment recipients?
options: The Earned Income Credit
The Work Opportunity Tax Credit
The Child Tax Credit
The Foreign Tax Credit
questions.rationale: The Work Opportunity Tax Credit is a general business credit for employers who hire individuals from specified targeted groups, claimed on Form 5884.

questions.stem: Most business tax credits flow into and are combined under which mechanism, which is subject to its own limitation and carryback/carryforward rules?
options: The foreign tax credit
The alternative minimum tax credit
The general business credit (Form 3800)
The premium tax credit
questions.rationale: Components such as the WOTC, research credit, and disabled access credit combine into the general business credit on Form 3800, which carries back 1 year and forward 20 years if limited.

questions.stem: A C corporation must generally make estimated tax payments if it expects its tax to be $500 or more. By when are the four installments generally due for a calendar-year corporation?
options: The 15th day of the 4th, 6th, 9th, and 12th months of the tax year
Only once, on April 15
January, April, July, and October 15
The 15th day of the 3rd, 6th, 9th, and 12th months
questions.rationale: A calendar-year corporation owing $500 or more makes estimated payments on the 15th of April, June, September, and December.

questions.stem: A calendar-year S corporation timely files Form 7004 to extend its Form 1120-S. What is the extended due date for the 2024 return, and how long is the extension?
options: December 15, 2025; a 9-month extension
September 15, 2025; a 6-month extension from the March 15 due date
October 15, 2025; a 7-month extension
April 15, 2025; a 1-month extension
questions.rationale: An S corporation return is due March 15; Form 7004 grants a 6-month extension to September 15 for a calendar-year filer.

questions.stem: A noncorporate taxpayer has a net §1231 gain of $40,000 this year. In the prior five years, the taxpayer deducted $15,000 of net §1231 losses that have not yet been recaptured. Under the 5-year lookback rule, how is the current $40,000 §1231 gain characterized?
options: $15,000 is capital gain and $25,000 is ordinary income
$15,000 is recharacterized as ordinary income and $25,000 is long-term capital gain
All $40,000 is ordinary income
All $40,000 is long-term capital gain
questions.rationale: The §1231 5-year lookback rule recharacterizes net §1231 gain as ordinary income to the extent of nonrecaptured net §1231 losses deducted in the prior five years.

questions.stem: For 2024, a passenger automobile used in business is subject to depreciation caps (luxury auto limits). What is the general effect of these limits?
options: They eliminate any depreciation on business autos
They apply only to heavy trucks over 14,000 pounds
They cap the annual depreciation (including §179 and bonus) that may be claimed on a passenger automobile
They allow unlimited first-year expensing
questions.rationale: Section 280F imposes annual dollar caps on depreciation (including §179 and bonus) for passenger automobiles, spreading recovery over more years than for unconstrained property.

questions.stem: A self-employed individual reports net profit on Schedule C. On which schedule is the self-employment tax computed?
options: Schedule B
Schedule SE
Schedule D
Schedule A
questions.rationale: Net earnings from self-employment flow from Schedule C to Schedule SE, where the 15.3% self-employment tax is calculated.

questions.stem: A cash-method business prepays $12,000 on December 1, 2024, for a 12-month insurance policy covering December 2024 through November 2025. Under the 12-month rule for prepaid expenses, how is this generally treated?
options: It must be capitalized and amortized over the policy period
It may be fully deducted in 2024 because the benefit does not extend beyond 12 months and not beyond the end of the next tax year
It is never deductible
Only $1,000 is deductible in 2024
questions.rationale: The 12-month rule permits a current deduction for prepaid expenses where the benefit does not extend beyond the earlier of 12 months or the end of the next tax year.

questions.stem: Under the de minimis safe harbor election for tangible property, a taxpayer WITHOUT an applicable financial statement may generally deduct amounts paid for property up to what per-item or per-invoice threshold?
questions.rationale: The de minimis safe harbor allows immediate expensing of tangible property up to $2,500 per item/invoice without an applicable financial statement (or $5,000 with one).

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally NOT deductible as a business expense?
options: Professional fees paid to an accountant for business work
Interest paid on a business loan
Bribes or kickbacks that are illegal under federal or state law
Supplies consumed in the business
questions.rationale: The Code disallows deductions for illegal bribes, kickbacks, fines, and penalties, even if connected with a business.

questions.stem: The qualified business income (QBI) deduction under §199A generally allows eligible owners of pass-through businesses to deduct up to what percentage of qualified business income?
questions.rationale: The §199A deduction permits eligible taxpayers to deduct up to 20% of qualified business income from sole proprietorships, partnerships, and S corporations, subject to wage/property and taxable income limits.

questions.stem: Above the taxable income threshold, the §199A QBI deduction for a specified service trade or business (SSTB), such as a law or accounting firm, is subject to which rule?
options: SSTBs always receive the full 20% regardless of income
The deduction is phased out and ultimately disallowed for SSTB income once taxable income exceeds the upper threshold
The deduction is increased for SSTBs
SSTBs may deduct 40% instead of 20%
questions.rationale: Income from a specified service trade or business qualifies for the §199A deduction only below the threshold; above the phase-out range, the SSTB QBI deduction is entirely lost.

questions.stem: For 2024, what is the FUTA tax rate before the state unemployment credit, and on what amount of each employee's wages does it apply?
options: 2.9% on all wages
12.4% on the first $168,600
0.6% on all wages
6.0% on the first $7,000 of wages
questions.rationale: FUTA is imposed at 6.0% on the first $7,000 of each employee's annual wages, but a credit for state unemployment taxes generally reduces the effective rate to 0.6%.

questions.stem: An employer must obtain which form from a new employee to determine the correct amount of federal income tax to withhold from wages?
options: Form W-4
Form 1099-NEC
Form W-2
Form W-9
questions.rationale: Employees complete Form W-4 to give the employer the information needed to compute federal income tax withholding from their wages.

questions.stem: A business requests a taxpayer identification number from an independent contractor before paying for services. Which form does the contractor complete to provide this information?
options: Form SS-8
Form W-9, Request for Taxpayer Identification Number and Certification
Form W-4
Form 1099-NEC
questions.rationale: Payers collect a payee's taxpayer identification number on Form W-9 to support information reporting and avoid backup withholding.

questions.stem: A business fails to obtain a payee's correct taxpayer identification number for reportable payments. Under the backup withholding rules, what rate of tax must the payer generally withhold?
questions.rationale: When a payee fails to furnish a correct TIN (or in other specified situations), the payer must apply backup withholding at 24% to reportable payments.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes amortization for tax purposes?
options: The depreciation of land
The recovery of the cost of certain intangible assets ratably over a set period
The deduction of dividends paid
The immediate expensing of inventory
questions.rationale: Amortization spreads the cost of qualifying intangibles (for example, §197 intangibles over 15 years) ratably over a prescribed recovery period, analogous to depreciation for tangible assets.

questions.stem: A business acquires goodwill and other §197 intangibles when purchasing another company's assets. Over what period are §197 intangibles generally amortized?
options: 15 years
They are not amortizable
27.5 years
5 years
questions.rationale: Acquired goodwill and other §197 intangibles are amortized ratably over 15 years beginning in the month of acquisition.

questions.stem: Excess business losses of a noncorporate taxpayer are subject to a limitation under §461(l). What happens to a noncorporate taxpayer's business loss that exceeds the §461(l) threshold for the year?
options: The excess is disallowed for the current year and carried forward as a net operating loss
It is permanently disallowed
It is fully deductible against wages with no limit
It must be carried back five years
questions.rationale: Under §461(l), a noncorporate taxpayer's aggregate business losses exceeding the inflation-adjusted threshold are disallowed currently and carried forward as a net operating loss.

questions.stem: A corporation pays its sole shareholder-employee a salary that the IRS later determines is unreasonably high relative to services performed. How might the IRS recharacterize the excessive portion?
options: As additional deductible wages
As a charitable contribution
As a nondeductible constructive dividend to the shareholder
As a tax-free return of capital with no consequence
questions.rationale: Only reasonable compensation is deductible; the IRS may treat excessive salary to a shareholder-employee as a nondeductible constructive dividend.

questions.stem: A bad debt arises when a business cannot collect an amount previously included in income on the accrual method. How is such a business bad debt generally treated?
options: It must be amortized over 15 years
It is never deductible
It is deductible as an ordinary business deduction when it becomes worthless
It is deductible only as a short-term capital loss
questions.rationale: Business bad debts are deductible as ordinary losses when they become worthless, in contrast to nonbusiness bad debts, which are treated as short-term capital losses.

questions.stem: A cash-method, accrual-basis question: a business using the accrual method receives a $5,000 advance payment in 2024 for services to be performed in 2025. Under the deferral rules for advance payments, how may the business treat the income?
options: It is never taxable
It must always defer all advance payments until services are completed
It must be reported only when the customer is satisfied
It may elect to include the payment in income in 2024 (year of receipt) or defer the portion not earned to 2025 under the one-year deferral method
questions.rationale: Under §451(c), an accrual-method taxpayer may defer an advance payment for goods or services to the year after receipt at the latest, generally matching the financial statement deferral.

questions.stem: A simple trust is required to distribute all of its income currently and makes no charitable contributions. How is the income of a simple trust generally taxed?
options: It is exempt from tax
To the beneficiaries, who are taxed on the income required to be distributed (up to DNI), with the trust taking a distribution deduction
Entirely at the trust level
Only when the trust terminates
questions.rationale: A simple trust must distribute all income currently; beneficiaries report that income (limited to DNI), and the trust claims a corresponding distribution deduction.

questions.stem: What is the personal exemption amount allowed to a simple trust on Form 1041?
questions.rationale: On Form 1041, a simple trust is allowed a $300 exemption, a complex trust $100, and an estate $600.

questions.stem: What exemption amount is allowed to an estate on its fiduciary income tax return (Form 1041)?
questions.rationale: Estates receive a $600 exemption on Form 1041, while simple trusts get $300 and complex trusts $100.

questions.stem: An estate may elect a fiscal year for income tax purposes. By contrast, what tax year must a trust (other than a tax-exempt or charitable trust) generally use?
options: A 52-53 week year only
A calendar year
Any fiscal year it chooses
The same fiscal year as the decedent's final return
questions.rationale: Trusts generally must adopt a calendar tax year, while estates have the flexibility to elect a fiscal year ending at the close of any month.

questions.stem: On a decedent's final Form 1040, which income is generally reported for a cash-method taxpayer?
options: No income, because death cancels all tax obligations
Income actually or constructively received up to the date of death
Only income received by the estate after death
All income the decedent would have earned over their lifetime
questions.rationale: The decedent's final Form 1040 reports income received (for a cash-method taxpayer) up to the date of death; income received afterward is income in respect of a decedent reported by the estate or heir.

questions.stem: Income in respect of a decedent (IRD), such as a final paycheck or accrued but unpaid interest received after death, is generally taxed how?
options: It is always tax-free to the beneficiary
It is taxed only on Form 706, the estate tax return
It is taxed to the recipient (estate or heir) and retains the same character it would have had to the decedent
It is never taxed because it relates to a deceased person
questions.rationale: Income in respect of a decedent is included in the income of whoever receives it (estate or beneficiary) and retains its original character; it may also be subject to estate tax, with an offsetting income tax deduction.

questions.stem: Which form does a partnership farming operation use to report farm income, and which schedule do its partners receive?
options: Form 1065 with Schedule F attached, and partners receive Schedule K-1
Schedule F filed directly by each partner with no entity return
Form 1120 with Schedule C attached
Form 1041 with Schedule E
questions.rationale: A farming partnership reports its activity on Form 1065 (with farm income on Schedule F) and passes results to partners on Schedule K-1.

questions.stem: A qualifying farmer wants to use income averaging to smooth out a high-income year. Which schedule allows eligible farmers (and fishermen) to average current farm income over the prior three years?
options: Schedule D
Schedule J (Form 1040)
Schedule SE
Schedule F
questions.rationale: Farm income averaging is computed on Schedule J, allowing qualifying farmers and fishermen to spread elected farm income across the three prior tax years' brackets.

questions.stem: A §501(c)(3) public charity wants to maintain its tax-exempt status. Which activity could jeopardize its exemption?
options: Paying reasonable salaries to employees
Receiving donations from the public
Devoting a substantial part of its activities to lobbying or participating in a political campaign for public office
Investing in a diversified portfolio
questions.rationale: A §501(c)(3) organization may not intervene in political campaigns at all and may not devote a substantial part of its activities to lobbying without risking its exemption.

questions.stem: Which of the following activities of a tax-exempt organization would generally produce unrelated business taxable income (UBTI)?
options: Receiving charitable contributions
Receiving dividends and interest from investments
Collecting membership dues
Regularly operating a commercial business (such as a public restaurant) not substantially related to its exempt purpose
questions.rationale: UBTI arises from a trade or business that is regularly carried on and not substantially related to the organization's exempt purpose; passive investment income and contributions are generally excluded.

questions.stem: A landowner rents farmland to a tenant farmer and does not materially participate in the farming operation, receiving cash rent. Which form is generally used to report this rental activity?
options: Schedule F
Form 1120
Form 4835 or Schedule E, depending on the arrangement
Schedule C
questions.rationale: A landowner who does not materially participate reports farm rental income on Form 4835 (for share arrangements) or Schedule E (for cash rent), not Schedule F.

questions.stem: A personal holding company (PHC) is a closely held C corporation with a high proportion of passive income. What is the consequence of PHC status?
options: It automatically becomes an S corporation
It is exempt from all federal tax
It may owe an additional personal holding company tax on undistributed personal holding company income
It receives a larger dividends-received deduction
questions.rationale: The personal holding company tax is an additional tax on undistributed PHC income, designed to prevent closely held corporations from sheltering passive income.

questions.stem: Which form is used to report and pay the federal gift tax on lifetime transfers exceeding the annual exclusion?
options: Form 1041
Form 990
Form 706
Form 709, United States Gift (and Generation-Skipping Transfer) Tax Return
questions.rationale: Lifetime gifts above the annual exclusion are reported on Form 709, the gift tax return.

questions.stem: For 2024, what is the annual gift tax exclusion amount per donee?
questions.rationale: For 2024, a donor may give up to $18,000 per donee without using any lifetime exclusion or filing a gift tax return for those gifts.

questions.stem: An estate elects the alternate valuation date under §2032. Generally, when is the alternate valuation date, and what condition must be met to elect it?
options: The date the estate tax return is filed, regardless of effect
Three months after death, with no effect on tax
One year after death, with no conditions
Six months after death, and only if the election decreases both the value of the gross estate and the estate tax liability
questions.rationale: Under §2032, an estate may value assets six months after death only if doing so reduces both the value of the gross estate and the combined estate and GST tax liability.

questions.stem: Property acquired from a decedent generally receives what income tax basis in the hands of the heir?
options: The decedent's original cost basis (carryover basis)
The fair market value on the date the heir sells the property
A basis stepped up (or down) to fair market value on the date of death (or alternate valuation date)
Zero basis
questions.rationale: Under §1014, property acquired from a decedent takes a fair-market-value basis as of the date of death (or the alternate valuation date), commonly called a stepped-up basis.

questions.stem: An estate's Form 1041 reports a net operating loss or excess deductions in its final year. What generally happens to these unused amounts?
options: They must be carried back to the decedent's prior returns
They may be passed through to the beneficiaries succeeding to the estate's property on the final-year Schedule K-1
They are permanently lost
They convert to a credit for the estate
questions.rationale: On termination of an estate or trust, unused capital loss and NOL carryovers and excess deductions pass through to the beneficiaries succeeding to the property, reported on the final-year Schedule K-1.

questions.stem: A partnership with 50 partners is generally subject to the centralized partnership audit regime. Under this regime, who is primarily liable for any imputed underpayment resulting from an audit adjustment, absent an election out or push-out election?
options: The partnership itself, at the entity level in the adjustment year
The IRS absorbs the underpayment
Each partner individually, automatically
Only the managing partner
questions.rationale: Under the BBA centralized partnership audit regime, audit adjustments are generally assessed and collected at the partnership level unless the partnership validly elects out or pushes the adjustments out to its reviewed-year partners.

questions.stem: Which person generally represents a partnership before the IRS and binds it under the centralized partnership audit regime?
options: The IRS examiner
The partnership representative
The tax matters partner under the old TEFRA rules
Every partner equally
questions.rationale: The centralized partnership audit regime designates a partnership representative with sole authority to act on the partnership's behalf, replacing the former tax matters partner.

questions.stem: An S corporation must report distributions and provide shareholders the information needed for the qualified business income deduction. Which form does the S corporation file as its income tax return?
options: Form 1120-S
Form 1120
Form 1041
Form 1065
questions.rationale: An S corporation files Form 1120-S and reports each shareholder's share of income and §199A information on Schedule K-1.

questions.stem: An electing small business trust (ESBT) holds S corporation stock. How is the portion of the ESBT consisting of S corporation stock generally taxed?
options: It is taxed as a C corporation
It is exempt from tax
It is taxed entirely at the beneficiaries' rates with no entity tax
The S corporation portion is taxed at the highest trust income tax rate, separately from the rest of the trust
questions.rationale: An ESBT is divided into S and non-S portions; the S corporation portion is taxed at the highest trust rate at the trust level, which is why ESBTs are an eligible but tax-costly S corporation shareholder.

questions.stem: Which return does a fiduciary file to report the income of a bankruptcy estate of an individual debtor in a Chapter 7 or Chapter 11 case?
options: Form 990
Form 1065
Form 1041 with a Form 1040 attached as a statement for the bankruptcy estate
Form 1120-S
questions.rationale: An individual's Chapter 7 or 11 bankruptcy estate is a separate taxable entity that files Form 1041 as a transmittal, attaching a Form 1040 that computes the estate's income tax using individual rules.

questions.stem: A trust earns net investment income and has undistributed income above the applicable threshold. The trust may be subject to which additional tax that also applies to high-income individuals?
options: The self-employment tax
The accumulated earnings tax
The FUTA tax
The 3.8% net investment income tax
questions.rationale: Estates and trusts are subject to the 3.8% net investment income tax on the lesser of undistributed net investment income or the excess of AGI over the threshold at which the highest trust bracket begins.

questions.stem: A cooperative (such as a farmers' cooperative) may deduct patronage dividends it pays to its patrons. Which return does a taxable cooperative generally file?
options: Form 1120-C, U.S. Income Tax Return for Cooperative Associations
Form 1040
Form 990
Form 1065
questions.rationale: Cooperatives file Form 1120-C and reduce taxable income by qualified patronage dividends and certain other distributions to patrons, generally avoiding double taxation on patronage income.

questions.stem: When does the income tax obligation of an estate generally end?
options: It never ends
When the administration of the estate is complete and the estate is closed (terminated)
Exactly one year after the decedent's death in all cases
When the executor is appointed
questions.rationale: An estate is a temporary taxpayer that files Form 1041 during the period of administration and ceases to exist once administration is reasonably complete and the estate is closed.

questions.stem: A farmer experiences weather-related forced sales of livestock in excess of normal. Which special rule may allow the farmer to defer or postpone the gain?
options: The like-kind exchange rules for livestock of the same sex
There is no special rule for weather-related sales
The election to defer income from livestock sold due to drought, flood, or other weather conditions
The QBI deduction
questions.rationale: Farmers forced to sell more livestock than usual because of weather-related conditions may elect to defer the resulting gain, and certain breeding-stock sales due to weather may allow replacement deferral.

questions.stem: A partnership distributes property to a partner. Under IRC §704(c), built-in gain or loss on property contributed to a partnership must be allocated to:
options: The partner with the largest capital account
The contributing partner, to account for the difference between the property's basis and fair market value at contribution
The partnership at the entity level
All partners equally
questions.rationale: §704(c) prevents tax shifting by allocating pre-contribution built-in gain or loss to the partner who contributed the appreciated or depreciated property.

questions.stem: A partnership has a §754 election in effect. A new partner buys an existing partner's interest for $90,000 when that partner's share of inside basis is $60,000. What is the amount of the §743(b) positive basis adjustment for the incoming partner?
questions.rationale: A §743(b) adjustment under a §754 election equals outside basis minus the transferee's share of inside basis: $90,000 − $60,000 = $30,000.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a 'hot asset' under IRC §751 that can cause ordinary income on the sale of a partnership interest?
options: Marketable securities held for investment
Unrealized receivables and substantially appreciated inventory
Land held as a capital asset
Goodwill purchased from a third party
questions.rationale: Hot assets under §751 are unrealized receivables and inventory; gain attributable to them is ordinary, not capital.

questions.stem: A C corporation has a deficit in current earnings and profits (E&P) of $40,000 but accumulated E&P of $100,000. It distributes $70,000 to shareholders during the year. How much of the distribution is a taxable dividend?
questions.rationale: When current E&P is negative, it is netted against accumulated E&P; here $60,000 of positive E&P still supports treating the full $70,000 distribution as a dividend.

questions.stem: Section 1244 allows an individual to treat a loss on qualifying small business stock as an ordinary loss. What is the maximum ordinary loss a married couple filing jointly may claim under §1244 in a single tax year?
questions.rationale: §1244 permits an ordinary loss of up to $50,000 (single) or $100,000 (married filing jointly) per year; excess is a capital loss.

questions.stem: A taxpayer incurs $52,000 of start-up costs before beginning an active trade or business in 2024. How much may be deducted immediately, and how is the remainder treated?
options: $10,000 deductible immediately, remainder amortized over 60 months
None is deductible until the business is sold
The full $52,000 is deductible immediately
$5,000 reduced dollar-for-dollar by the excess over $50,000, with the remainder amortized over 180 months
questions.rationale: §195 allows a $5,000 immediate deduction, phased out dollar-for-dollar above $50,000; with $52,000 of costs, only $3,000 is deductible currently and the balance amortizes over 180 months.

questions.stem: Organizational expenditures of a corporation are deducted and amortized under which Code section?
questions.rationale: Corporate organizational expenditures are deducted and amortized under §248; partnerships use §709.

questions.stem: A partner has an outside basis of $20,000. The partnership allocates a $35,000 ordinary loss to the partner. Assuming the at-risk and passive loss rules do not further limit the loss, how much loss may the partner currently deduct?
questions.rationale: Partnership losses are deductible only to the extent of outside basis ($20,000); the $15,000 excess is carried forward until basis increases.

questions.stem: Under the §267 related-party rules, a loss on the sale of property between a taxpayer and a more-than-50%-owned corporation is:
options: Fully deductible by the seller
Deferred and deducted ratably over five years
Disallowed to the seller, but the buyer may reduce later gain by the disallowed loss
Converted to a capital loss regardless of asset type
questions.rationale: §267 disallows losses between related parties; the disallowed loss can later reduce gain when the buyer resells the property.

questions.stem: An S corporation makes a distribution to a shareholder. The corporation has a positive Accumulated Adjustments Account (AAA) and no accumulated E&P from prior C years. The distribution is treated as:
options: Always fully taxable as a dividend
A tax-free return of basis to the extent of stock basis, then capital gain
Ordinary compensation income
A taxable dividend to the extent of AAA
questions.rationale: An S corporation with no accumulated E&P distributes tax-free to the extent of basis, with any excess taxed as capital gain.

questions.stem: The accumulated earnings tax may apply when a C corporation retains earnings beyond reasonable business needs. What is the rate of the accumulated earnings tax?
questions.rationale: The accumulated earnings tax is a 20% penalty on improperly accumulated taxable income retained beyond reasonable business needs.

questions.stem: For 2024, what is the corporation's accumulated earnings credit (minimum accumulation) generally allowed before the accumulated earnings tax applies to a non-service C corporation?
questions.rationale: Most C corporations get a $250,000 accumulated earnings credit; certain personal service corporations get only $150,000.

questions.stem: A shareholder contributes appreciated property to a corporation in a §351 exchange but also receives $10,000 of cash boot. The shareholder's realized gain is $25,000. How much gain is recognized?
questions.rationale: In a §351 exchange, gain is recognized to the extent of boot received, limited to realized gain: the lesser of $25,000 and $10,000 is $10,000.

questions.stem: A partnership distributes only cash of $50,000 to a partner whose outside basis is $30,000. How is the excess treated?
options: $20,000 ordinary income
No gain because cash distributions are never taxable
$50,000 capital gain
$20,000 capital gain
questions.rationale: Cash distributions reduce basis first; any amount over outside basis ($50,000 − $30,000 = $20,000) is capital gain.

questions.stem: Which entity files Form 1065 and issues Schedule K-1 to its owners?
options: Sole proprietorship
C corporation
S corporation
Partnership
questions.rationale: Partnerships report on Form 1065 and pass income/deductions to partners via Schedule K-1.

questions.stem: To qualify as an S corporation, the entity may have no more than how many shareholders?
options: No limit
questions.rationale: An S corporation is limited to 100 shareholders, with certain family members treated as a single shareholder.

questions.stem: A partner contributes property with a fair market value of $80,000 and an adjusted basis of $50,000, subject to a $30,000 liability the partnership assumes. The partner has a 25% interest in partnership liabilities. What is the partner's deemed cash distribution from the liability relief that could reduce basis?
questions.rationale: Liability relief is a deemed cash distribution; the partner's deemed distribution is $30,000 assumed minus the 25% share retained ($7,500) = $22,500.

questions.stem: A business with average annual gross receipts under what threshold is generally exempt from the §163(j) business interest limitation (the small business exemption for 2024)?
options: $10 million
$30.5 million
$5 million
$30 million
questions.rationale: Small businesses meeting the §448(c) gross receipts test (about $30.5 million for 2024) are exempt from the §163(j) interest limitation.

questions.stem: Under the installment method (§453), gross profit is recognized as payments are received. The gross profit percentage is computed as:
options: Selling price divided by adjusted basis
Adjusted basis divided by gross profit
Contract price divided by gross profit
Gross profit divided by the contract price
questions.rationale: Under §453, gross profit percentage = gross profit ÷ contract price, applied to each principal payment to recognize gain over time.

questions.stem: A taxpayer sells business equipment for $100,000 under an installment sale. The equipment had $40,000 of §1245 depreciation recapture. How is the recapture treated under §453?
options: Spread over the installment payments
Treated as capital gain on each payment
Recognized entirely in the year of sale regardless of payments received
Not taxable until the final payment
questions.rationale: Depreciation recapture under §1245/§1250 is reported in full in the year of an installment sale; only gain exceeding recapture is deferred.

questions.stem: In a §1031 like-kind exchange (2024 rules), like-kind treatment is available only for:
options: Machinery and equipment
Inventory held for resale
Stocks and bonds
Real property held for productive use in a trade or business or for investment
questions.rationale: Since 2018, §1031 like-kind exchanges are limited to real property used in a trade or business or held for investment.

questions.stem: For 2024, the maximum §179 expensing deduction is $1,220,000, which begins to phase out dollar-for-dollar once total qualifying property placed in service exceeds:
questions.rationale: For 2024, §179 allows up to $1,220,000 expensing, phasing out once property placed in service exceeds $3,050,000.

questions.stem: Bonus depreciation under §168(k) for property placed in service in 2024 is allowed at what percentage?
questions.rationale: Bonus depreciation phases down 20 points per year; property placed in service in 2024 qualifies for 60% bonus depreciation.

questions.stem: Excess charitable contributions by a C corporation that exceed the 10% limit may be carried forward for how many years?
options: 10 years
5 years
3 years
Indefinitely
questions.rationale: Excess corporate charitable contributions carry forward up to five years.
