questions.rationale: Under Section 707(c), guaranteed payments for services or capital are determined without regard to partnership income, are deductible by the partnership if ordinary and necessary, and are ordinary income to the partner.

questions.stem: Which IRS form does a partnership use to report its income, deductions, and other items to the IRS?
options: Form 1120
Form 1120-S
Form 1065
Form 1041
questions.rationale: Partnerships file Form 1065 as an information return and issue Schedule K-1 to each partner reporting their distributive share.

questions.stem: The DRT Partnership has three equal partners. During the year it earned $90,000 of ordinary business income and made no distributions. How much ordinary business income must each partner report, and when is it taxed?
options: $30,000 each, but only taxed when distributed
$0, because no distributions were made
$30,000 each, taxed in the year earned regardless of distributions
$90,000 reported by the partnership and taxed at the entity level
questions.rationale: Partners are taxed on their distributive share of partnership income in the tax year it is earned, regardless of whether cash is actually distributed.

questions.stem: Nadia receives a liquidating distribution from a partnership consisting solely of cash of $18,000. Her outside basis immediately before the distribution was $24,000. What is the tax result to Nadia?
options: A $18,000 capital gain is recognized
A $6,000 capital loss is recognized
A $6,000 ordinary loss is recognized
No gain or loss; her remaining basis is $6,000
questions.rationale: Under Section 731, a partner recognizes a capital loss in a liquidating distribution only when nothing but cash (or cash, unrealized receivables, and inventory) is received and outside basis exceeds the amount received.

questions.stem: What event generally causes the technical termination concerns under prior law no longer to apply, meaning a partnership now continues for tax purposes as long as at least how many partners remain carrying on business?
options: At least three partners must remain
A majority of original partners must remain
At least two partners must remain carrying on partnership business
At least one partner remains, but business operations must cease
questions.rationale: A partnership terminates when no part of any business continues to be carried on by any of its partners, which effectively requires at least two partners to remain.

questions.stem: On a partner's Schedule K-1 (Form 1065), in which section are the partner's share of profit, loss, and capital percentages typically shown?
options: The accompanying Schedule K only
Part I (Information About the Partnership)
Part II (Information About the Partner)
Part III, line 1 (Ordinary business income)
questions.rationale: Schedule K-1 Part II reports partner-specific data, including the partner's profit, loss, and capital sharing percentages at the beginning and end of the year.

questions.stem: Owen contributed appreciated property to a partnership. Three years later the partnership sells that property at a gain. How is the precontribution (built-in) gain generally allocated?
options: It is not recognized because contributed property never triggers gain
Entirely to the non-contributing partners
Entirely to the contributing partner (Owen) to the extent of the built-in gain at contribution
Equally among all partners according to their general profit-sharing ratios
questions.rationale: Section 704(c) requires that built-in gain or loss existing at the time of contribution be allocated to the contributing partner to prevent shifting of tax consequences.

questions.stem: A partnership has a partner who is an individual using a calendar year and the partnership uses the calendar year. By default, when is the Form 1065 due (without extension) for the 2024 tax year?
options: April 15, 2025
October 15, 2025
March 15, 2025
September 15, 2025
questions.rationale: Partnership returns (Form 1065) are due the 15th day of the third month following the close of the tax year, which is March 15 for a calendar-year partnership.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally a separately stated item that passes through to partners on Schedule K-1 rather than being included in ordinary business income on page 1 of Form 1065?
options: Cost of goods sold
Repairs and maintenance expense
Net long-term capital gains
Salaries paid to non-partner employees
questions.rationale: Items whose tax treatment depends on the partner's situation, such as capital gains, charitable contributions, and Section 179, are separately stated on the K-1 to preserve their character.

questions.stem: A partner's distributive share of partnership losses is limited by which of the following ordering rules (applied first to last)?
options: Basis limit, then at-risk limit, then passive activity limit
Basis limit, then passive activity limit, then at-risk limit
At-risk limit, then basis limit, then passive activity limit
Passive activity limit, then basis limit, then at-risk limit
questions.rationale: Partnership loss deductibility is tested sequentially: basis limitation (Section 704(d)), then at-risk (Section 465), then passive activity loss rules (Section 469).

questions.stem: The QRS Partnership has a Section 754 election in effect. A new partner purchases an existing interest for $50,000 when the inside basis of the partnership's assets attributable to that interest is $35,000. What is the general effect of the Section 754 election?
options: The selling partner's gain is eliminated
The partnership recognizes $15,000 of gain
All partners receive a proportionate basis increase
A $15,000 step-up in inside basis is allocated to the purchasing partner under Section 743(b)
questions.rationale: A Section 754 election triggers a Section 743(b) basis adjustment on a transfer of interest, giving the incoming partner a special inside basis equal to the difference between purchase price and the share of inside basis.

questions.stem: Which entity is NOT eligible to be a partner in a partnership?
options: Another partnership
A corporation
An individual
None of the above; all of these may be partners
questions.rationale: There is no general restriction on the type of person that may be a partner; partnerships, corporations, trusts, estates, and individuals can all hold partnership interests.

questions.stem: A limited partner in a partnership receives a Schedule K-1 showing ordinary business income of $40,000 and a guaranteed payment of $12,000. Assuming the limited partner does not materially participate, which amount is generally subject to self-employment tax?
options: $12,000 (the guaranteed payment for services)
questions.rationale: Limited partners generally exclude their distributive share from self-employment income, but guaranteed payments received for services are subject to self-employment tax.

questions.stem: When a partnership makes a current distribution of cash that exceeds a partner's outside basis, what is the tax consequence?
options: The distribution is disallowed until basis is restored
The excess is a tax-free return of capital
The excess is recognized as ordinary income
The excess is recognized as capital gain
questions.rationale: Under Section 731, a partner recognizes capital gain to the extent money distributed exceeds the partner's adjusted basis in the partnership interest.

questions.stem: A partnership with how many or fewer partners, all of whom are eligible (such as individuals and C corporations), may generally elect out of the centralized partnership audit regime?
options: 50 or fewer
No limit applies
100 or fewer
10 or fewer
questions.rationale: Partnerships with 100 or fewer partners, all of whom are eligible (individuals, C corporations, S corporations, estates of deceased partners, or foreign entities treated as C corporations), may elect out of the centralized audit regime.

questions.stem: Greta and Hal are equal partners. The partnership borrows $100,000 of recourse debt. How does this borrowing generally affect each partner's outside basis?
options: Each partner's basis increases by $50,000
Only the managing partner's basis increases
No effect; debt does not change basis
Each partner's basis decreases by $50,000
questions.rationale: Under Section 752, an increase in a partner's share of partnership liabilities is treated as a deemed cash contribution that increases the partner's outside basis.

questions.stem: Which of the following shareholders would disqualify a corporation from making an S election if it owned stock?
options: A nonresident alien individual
An estate of a deceased shareholder
A resident alien individual
A single-member LLC owned by a U.S. citizen and disregarded
questions.rationale: S corporation shareholders must be eligible persons; nonresident aliens are not permitted and their ownership disqualifies the S election.

questions.stem: Lena is a 100% shareholder of an S corporation. At the start of the year her stock basis is $20,000 and she has a $5,000 loan basis (direct loan to the corporation). The S corporation passes through an ordinary loss of $30,000. How much loss may Lena deduct currently, and how is the remainder treated?
options: $30,000 deductible; nothing suspended
$5,000 deductible; $25,000 suspended
$25,000 deductible; $5,000 suspended
$20,000 deductible; $10,000 suspended
questions.rationale: S corporation losses are deductible only up to the shareholder's combined stock and debt basis; stock basis is reduced first, then debt basis, and disallowed losses carry forward.

questions.stem: An S corporation makes a cash distribution to a shareholder. The corporation has always been an S corporation and has no accumulated earnings and profits. The shareholder's stock basis exceeds the distribution. How is the distribution taxed?
options: Fully taxable as a dividend
Taxable as ordinary income
Tax-free return of capital that reduces stock basis
Taxable as capital gain
questions.rationale: Distributions from an S corporation with no accumulated E&P are tax-free to the extent of stock basis, reducing that basis, and create capital gain only when they exceed basis.

questions.stem: Which form is used to make the S corporation election?
options: Form 1120-S
Form 8832
Form 2553
Form 8869
questions.rationale: A corporation elects S status by timely filing Form 2553 with the consent of all shareholders.

questions.stem: To be effective for the entire 2024 tax year, a calendar-year corporation must generally file Form 2553 no later than which date?
options: April 15, 2024
January 1, 2025
December 31, 2023
March 15, 2024
questions.rationale: Form 2553 must be filed by the 15th day of the third month of the tax year (or any time in the preceding year) to be effective for that entire year.

questions.stem: An S corporation that was formerly a C corporation sells an asset during its recognition period. The asset had a built-in gain of $40,000 at the time of the S election. The corporation has taxable income of $50,000. What tax may apply at the entity level?
options: No entity-level tax because S corporations never pay tax
The accumulated earnings tax
The built-in gains tax on the recognized built-in gain
The personal holding company tax
questions.rationale: Under Section 1374, an S corporation that was formerly a C corporation may be subject to a corporate-level built-in gains tax when it disposes of appreciated assets within the recognition period.

questions.stem: The IRS may recharacterize distributions to an S corporation shareholder-employee as wages if the shareholder takes which of the following?
options: No distributions at all
Only guaranteed payments
Unreasonably low or no compensation while taking distributions for services performed
Reasonable compensation and large distributions
questions.rationale: Shareholder-employees of an S corporation must receive reasonable compensation for services; the IRS can recharacterize distributions as wages to collect employment taxes when compensation is unreasonably low.

questions.stem: Which of the following items increases an S corporation shareholder's stock basis?
options: Tax-exempt income passed through
Separately stated deductions
Nondeductible expenses
Distributions received
questions.rationale: Stock basis increases for income items, including tax-exempt income, and decreases for distributions, deductions, losses, and nondeductible expenses.

questions.stem: An S corporation election terminates automatically if the corporation has passive investment income exceeding 25% of gross receipts for how many consecutive years while having accumulated C corporation E&P?
options: 3 consecutive years
1 year
2 consecutive years
5 consecutive years
questions.rationale: Under Section 1362(d)(3), an S corporation with accumulated C corporation E&P loses its S status if passive investment income exceeds 25% of gross receipts for three consecutive tax years.

questions.stem: An S corporation with accumulated E&P from C corporation years makes a $60,000 distribution. The accumulated adjustments account (AAA) is $25,000, accumulated E&P is $15,000, and the shareholder's remaining stock basis after the AAA portion is $40,000. Ignoring other adjustments, how is the $60,000 distribution generally characterized in order?
options: $25,000 tax-free (AAA), $15,000 dividend, $20,000 return of basis
$25,000 dividend, $35,000 tax-free
$60,000 tax-free return of capital
$60,000 dividend
questions.rationale: For an S corporation with accumulated E&P, distributions are sourced first from AAA (tax-free to the extent of basis), then from accumulated E&P (taxable dividend), then from remaining basis as a return of capital.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding the allocation of an S corporation's income to shareholders?
options: Income is taxed only at the corporate level
Income may be specially allocated by agreement, like a partnership
Income is allocated on a per-share, per-day basis
Income is allocated only to shareholders who receive distributions
questions.rationale: S corporations must allocate income and loss on a per-share, per-day basis; special allocations available to partnerships are not permitted because there is only one class of stock.

questions.stem: An S corporation may have how many classes of stock?
options: One class of stock (differences solely in voting rights are allowed)
Unlimited classes of stock
Two classes of stock
No stock; only membership interests
questions.rationale: An S corporation may have only one class of stock, meaning all shares confer identical rights to distribution and liquidation proceeds, though voting differences are permitted.

questions.stem: How is an S corporation shareholder's basis adjusted for purposes of determining the deductibility of losses, regarding the ordering of decreases?
options: Losses reduce basis before distributions
Nondeductible expenses reduce basis before distributions
Distributions reduce basis after losses
Distributions reduce basis before nondeductible expenses and losses
questions.rationale: The general ordering is: increase basis for income items, then decrease for distributions, then for nondeductible noncapital expenses, then for deductible losses and deductions.

questions.stem: Marcus loaned his S corporation $10,000 directly and the corporation passed through losses that reduced his debt basis to $2,000. In a later year the corporation repays him the full $10,000 of principal. What is the tax consequence to Marcus on the repayment of the reduced-basis debt?
options: Income is recognized on the repayment to the extent it exceeds his debt basis
The repayment increases his stock basis
No income; loan repayments are always tax-free
A capital loss of $8,000
questions.rationale: When a shareholder loan's basis has been reduced by pass-through losses, repayment of principal in excess of the reduced debt basis produces income (capital or ordinary depending on the note).

questions.stem: Which entity-level item is reported on Form 1120-S and may create a tax for the S corporation itself?
options: Personal exemption
Standard deduction
Qualified business income deduction
Excess net passive income tax
questions.rationale: S corporations generally do not pay income tax, but certain entity-level taxes such as the excess net passive income tax and built-in gains tax can apply.

questions.stem: An S corporation shareholder has suspended losses due to insufficient basis. The shareholder then sells all of his stock. What happens to the suspended losses limited by basis?
options: They carry over to the buyer of the stock
They convert to a capital loss carryover for the seller
They become deductible by the corporation
They are generally lost (do not transfer) when the shareholder disposes of the stock
questions.rationale: Losses suspended solely due to lack of stock and debt basis are generally lost upon full disposition of S corporation stock because there is no provision to free them, unlike passive losses under Section 469.

questions.stem: The accumulated adjustments account (AAA) of an S corporation is generally NOT increased by which of the following?
options: Tax-exempt income
Net capital gains
Ordinary business income
Separately stated income items
questions.rationale: The AAA is adjusted similarly to stock basis but excludes tax-exempt income and related expenses, which are instead recorded in the other adjustments account.

questions.stem: What is the federal income tax filing form for a C corporation?
options: Form 1120
Form 990
Form 1120-S
Form 1065
questions.rationale: C corporations report income and pay tax using Form 1120, the U.S. Corporation Income Tax Return.

questions.stem: For tax years beginning after 2017, the federal corporate income tax rate on a C corporation's taxable income is:
options: A flat 35%
A flat 15%
A flat 21%
A graduated rate up to 35%
questions.rationale: C corporations are taxed at a flat federal rate of 21% on taxable income for years beginning after December 31, 2017.

questions.stem: Apex Corporation (a C corporation) owns 25% of the stock of Beta Corporation and receives a $100,000 dividend from Beta. What is Apex's dividends-received deduction (DRD), assuming the taxable income limitation does not apply?
questions.rationale: The DRD is 50% for under 20% ownership, 65% for 20% to under 80% ownership, and 100% for 80% or more (affiliated group) ownership.

questions.stem: A C corporation distributes cash to its shareholders. The distribution is a taxable dividend to the shareholders to the extent of what?
options: The corporation's current and accumulated earnings and profits (E&P)
The corporation's paid-in capital
The shareholder's stock basis
The corporation's retained cash balance
questions.rationale: Corporate distributions are dividends to the extent of current and accumulated E&P; amounts beyond E&P reduce stock basis and then produce capital gain.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the double taxation associated with C corporations?
options: Income is taxed twice at the corporate level
Income is taxed once at the corporate level and again to shareholders when distributed as dividends
Income is never taxed at the corporate level
Income is taxed twice to shareholders
questions.rationale: Double taxation refers to C corporation earnings being taxed at the entity level and then again at the shareholder level when distributed as dividends.

questions.stem: Zenith Corporation has a net capital loss of $15,000 for the current year. How may a C corporation use a net capital loss?
options: Carry it forward 20 years only
Carry it back 3 years and forward 5 years, deductible only against capital gains
Deduct it fully in the current year against ordinary income
Deduct it against ordinary income up to $3,000 per year
questions.rationale: Corporations may deduct capital losses only against capital gains; an unused net capital loss carries back 3 years and forward 5 years.

questions.stem: Under Section 351, a transfer of property to a corporation solely in exchange for stock is generally tax-free if the transferors, immediately after the exchange, control what percentage of the corporation?
options: At least 80% of voting power and 80% of each class of nonvoting stock
More than 50% of all stock
100% of the stock
At least 50% of the voting stock
questions.rationale: Section 351 defers gain on property transferred to a corporation for stock when the transferors control (80% test) the corporation immediately after the exchange.

questions.stem: Which of the following corporate-level taxes is designed to discourage corporations from retaining earnings beyond reasonable business needs to avoid shareholder-level tax?
options: Excise tax
Self-employment tax
Accumulated earnings tax
Built-in gains tax
questions.rationale: The accumulated earnings tax is a penalty tax on C corporations that accumulate earnings beyond the reasonable needs of the business to avoid shareholder-level dividend tax.

questions.stem: A C corporation makes a charitable contribution. The contribution deduction is generally limited to what percentage of taxable income (computed with certain modifications)?
questions.rationale: A corporation's charitable contribution deduction is generally limited to 10% of taxable income, with excess contributions carried forward up to five years.

questions.stem: Helix Corporation distributes appreciated land (FMV $90,000, basis $40,000) to a shareholder as a property dividend. What is the corporate-level tax consequence to Helix?
options: No gain is recognized because distributions are not sales
Helix recognizes $50,000 of gain as if it sold the land at FMV
The shareholder's basis carries over with no corporate effect
Helix recognizes a $40,000 loss
questions.rationale: Under Section 311(b), a corporation distributing appreciated property recognizes gain as if it had sold the property at fair market value; losses on distributed property generally are not recognized.

questions.stem: A C corporation's estimated tax payments are generally required if it expects to owe how much or more in tax for the year?
options: $500 or more
$5,000 or more
$1,000 or more
$10,000 or more
questions.rationale: A corporation generally must pay estimated income tax in installments if it expects its total tax for the year to be $500 or more.

questions.stem: Orion Corporation, a personal service corporation, has taxable income. Which statement about its tax rate is correct for years after 2017?
options: It is taxed at graduated individual rates
It is taxed at the same flat 21% rate as other C corporations
It is taxed at a special flat 35% rate
It is exempt from corporate tax
questions.rationale: With the move to a flat 21% corporate rate, the former special flat 35% rate applicable to personal service corporations no longer applies.

questions.stem: Which of the following is included in the computation of a corporation's earnings and profits (E&P) even though it is excluded from taxable income?
options: Charitable contributions in excess of the limit
Federal income tax paid
Tax-exempt municipal bond interest
Section 179 deduction
questions.rationale: E&P measures a corporation's economic ability to pay dividends, so items like tax-exempt interest are added back even though they are excluded from taxable income.

questions.stem: In a complete liquidation of a C corporation, a shareholder generally recognizes gain or loss measured by which of the following?
options: The corporation's E&P at liquidation
The difference between the FMV of property received and the shareholder's stock basis
The original paid-in capital
Zero, because liquidations are always tax-free
questions.rationale: Under Section 331, amounts received by a shareholder in a complete liquidation are treated as full payment in exchange for stock, producing capital gain or loss.

questions.stem: A C corporation has gross receipts averaging $40 million over the prior three years and pays $2 million of business interest expense and has $1 million of business interest income. Under Section 163(j), what is its business interest deduction limit (assume adjusted taxable income of $3 million and that it is not exempt)?
options: $1,900,000 (business interest income plus 30% of adjusted taxable income)
questions.rationale: Section 163(j) limits business interest deductions to business interest income plus 30% of adjusted taxable income (plus floor plan financing interest); excess interest carries forward.

questions.stem: The small business exemption from the Section 163(j) business interest limitation generally applies to taxpayers whose average annual gross receipts for the prior three years do not exceed (indexed) approximately:
options: $10 million
$50 million
$5 million
$30 million (indexed; $30 million for 2024)
questions.rationale: Businesses meeting the gross receipts test (average annual gross receipts not exceeding the indexed threshold, $30 million for 2024) are generally exempt from the Section 163(j) interest limitation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a requirement for a corporate reorganization to qualify for tax-free treatment under Section 368?
options: There must be a valid business purpose and continuity of interest
All assets must be sold for cash
The corporation must be newly formed
The transaction must increase the number of shareholders
questions.rationale: Tax-free reorganizations under Section 368 require continuity of interest, continuity of business enterprise, and a valid business purpose, in addition to meeting a statutory reorganization type.

questions.stem: A business places qualifying equipment in service in 2024 and elects Section 179 expensing. The Section 179 deduction begins to phase out (dollar-for-dollar) once the total cost of qualifying property placed in service exceeds an indexed threshold. This means the benefit targets:
options: Tax-exempt organizations
Large corporations with unlimited purchases
Only real estate investors
Smaller businesses, because the deduction phases out as purchases grow large
questions.rationale: The Section 179 deduction is reduced dollar-for-dollar when qualifying property placed in service exceeds the investment limitation, effectively limiting the benefit to smaller businesses.

questions.stem: A taxpayer buys new qualifying business equipment for $200,000 and places it in service in 2024. Bonus depreciation for property placed in service in 2024 is what percentage?
questions.rationale: Bonus depreciation phases down 20 points per year: 80% in 2023, 60% in 2024, 40% in 2025, and 20% in 2026.

questions.stem: Under MACRS, the recovery period for most office furniture and fixtures (7-year property) is determined using which depreciation system by default?
options: The General Depreciation System (GDS) using 200% declining balance
The Alternative Depreciation System (ADS) straight-line
Straight-line over 39 years
Units-of-production
questions.rationale: Most 5- and 7-year MACRS property uses the General Depreciation System with the 200% declining balance method, switching to straight-line to maximize the deduction.

questions.stem: A business buys a passenger automobile used 100% for business in 2024. Its annual depreciation deduction is limited by which rule?
options: No limits apply to business vehicles
The half-year convention only
The luxury automobile depreciation (Section 280F) limits
The mid-month convention
questions.rationale: Section 280F imposes annual dollar limits on depreciation (including bonus) for passenger automobiles, regardless of the vehicle's cost.

questions.stem: A taxpayer places several assets in service during the year, with 75% of the total basis placed in service in the fourth quarter. Which depreciation convention generally applies to the personal property?
options: Mid-month convention
Full-year convention
Mid-quarter convention
Half-year convention
questions.rationale: If more than 40% of the aggregate basis of personal property is placed in service in the last three months, the mid-quarter convention must be used for all such property placed in service that year.

questions.stem: Nonresidential real property placed in service after 1993 is depreciated under MACRS GDS using which method and recovery period?
options: 200% declining balance over 27.5 years
150% declining balance over 15 years
Straight-line over 27.5 years
Straight-line over 39 years
questions.rationale: Nonresidential real property uses the straight-line method over a 39-year recovery period with the mid-month convention.

questions.stem: Which IRS form is used to claim depreciation and amortization, including the Section 179 deduction?
options: Form 4562
Form 3115
Form 8824
Form 4797
questions.rationale: Form 4562, Depreciation and Amortization, is used to report depreciation, amortization, and the Section 179 expense deduction.

questions.stem: A small business with average annual gross receipts of $20 million wishes to use the cash method of accounting. Under current rules, is it generally permitted to do so even if it has inventory?
options: Yes, because it meets the gross receipts test (under the indexed $30 million threshold for 2024)
Only if it is a sole proprietorship
No, any business with inventory must use the accrual method
Only if it elects S corporation status
questions.rationale: Businesses meeting the gross receipts test may use the cash method and are exempt from certain inventory and UNICAP requirements, treating inventory as nonincidental materials and supplies or per their books.

questions.stem: A taxpayer using the accrual method ships goods to a customer in December 2024 and bills them; payment is received in February 2025. Under the all-events test, when is the income generally recognized?
options: December 2024 when the right to income is fixed and the amount is determinable
Whenever the taxpayer chooses
February 2025 when cash is received
Split evenly between the two years
questions.rationale: Under the accrual method's all-events test, income is recognized when the right to receive it becomes fixed and the amount is reasonably determinable, generally upon delivery, not when payment is received.

questions.stem: A business wishes to change from an impermissible accounting method to a permissible one. Which form is generally required to request the change?
options: Form 3115
Form 8716
Form 1128
Form 2553
questions.rationale: A taxpayer requests a change in accounting method by filing Form 3115, with the resulting Section 481(a) adjustment spread over the appropriate period.

questions.stem: Which inventory valuation method assumes the first units purchased are the first units sold?
options: Weighted average
LIFO
FIFO
Specific identification
questions.rationale: FIFO assumes that the first goods acquired are the first goods sold, leaving the most recently purchased items in ending inventory.

questions.stem: A taxpayer that adopts the LIFO method for tax purposes is generally subject to which conformity requirement?
options: It must use FIFO for book purposes
It may freely use any method for book purposes
It must also use LIFO for financial statements or credit purposes (the LIFO conformity rule)
It must obtain annual IRS approval
questions.rationale: Under the LIFO conformity rule, a taxpayer that uses LIFO for tax purposes must also use LIFO in its primary financial statements presented to creditors and owners.

questions.stem: Compute cost of goods sold: beginning inventory $30,000, purchases $120,000, freight-in $5,000, and ending inventory $25,000. What is COGS?
questions.rationale: Cost of goods sold equals beginning inventory plus net purchases (including freight-in) minus ending inventory.

questions.stem: A cash-basis business pays $24,000 on July 1, 2024, for a 24-month insurance policy. Under the 12-month rule for prepaid expenses, how much may it generally deduct in 2024?
options: $24,000 in full because cash basis allows full deduction
$6,000 (the portion attributable to 2024)
Nothing until the policy expires
questions.rationale: The 12-month rule allows current deduction of a prepaid expense only if the benefit does not extend beyond the earlier of 12 months or the end of the next tax year; a 24-month policy must be capitalized and amortized.

questions.stem: Which of the following business expenses is generally 50% deductible (subject to limitation) rather than fully deductible?
options: Utilities
Employee wages
Business meals (that are not otherwise 100%)
Office rent
questions.rationale: Business meals are generally subject to a 50% deduction limit; the temporary 100% deduction for restaurant meals applied only in 2021 and 2022.

questions.stem: Under current law, business entertainment expenses (such as taking a client to a sporting event) are generally:
options: Deductible only if over $75
50% deductible
Nondeductible
100% deductible
questions.rationale: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act generally eliminated the deduction for business entertainment expenses, while certain meals remain 50% deductible.

questions.stem: A business incurs $52,000 of startup costs before opening. How are startup costs generally treated for tax purposes?
options: Deducted over 60 months in all cases
Up to $5,000 deductible in the first year (reduced dollar-for-dollar over $50,000), remainder amortized over 180 months
Capitalized with no deduction ever
Fully deductible in the first year
questions.rationale: Under Section 195, a business may deduct up to $5,000 of startup costs (phased out dollar-for-dollar above $50,000) and amortize the remainder over 180 months beginning when the business starts.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a nondeductible business expense?
options: Depreciation on business equipment
Fines and penalties paid to a government for violating a law
Interest on a business loan
Advertising costs
questions.rationale: Under Section 162(f), fines and penalties paid to a government for violating the law are generally not deductible.

questions.stem: To be deductible under Section 162, a business expense must be:
options: Ordinary and necessary
Lavish and extravagant
Capital in nature
Personal to the owner
questions.rationale: Section 162 permits a deduction for ordinary and necessary expenses paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business.

questions.stem: A self-employed individual operates a business from a home office used regularly and exclusively for business. Which method allows a deduction of $5 per square foot up to 300 square feet?
options: The de minimis safe harbor
The simplified method
The standard mileage method
The actual expense method
questions.rationale: The simplified home office method allows a deduction of $5 per square foot of qualifying space, up to a maximum of 300 square feet ($1,500).

questions.stem: For 2024, the Social Security (OASDI) portion of FICA applies to wages up to the wage base limit, while the Medicare portion applies to:
options: Only the first $7,000 of wages
The same wage base limit as Social Security
All wages with no wage base limit
Only wages over $200,000
questions.rationale: The Social Security portion of FICA stops at the annual wage base, but the Medicare portion applies to all wages, with an additional 0.9% Medicare tax on wages above threshold amounts.

questions.stem: An employer misclassifies a worker as an independent contractor when the worker is actually an employee. What is a likely consequence?
options: The worker becomes exempt from all tax
Liability for unpaid employment taxes, plus possible penalties
The IRS automatically reclassifies the business as a corporation
No consequence if the worker agreed to the classification
questions.rationale: Improperly classifying an employee as an independent contractor can result in employer liability for back employment taxes and penalties, though relief may be available under Section 530.

questions.stem: A sole proprietor has net self-employment earnings of $100,000 in 2024. Approximately what amount of those earnings is subject to the SE tax computation after the 92.35% adjustment?
questions.rationale: Self-employment tax is computed on net earnings multiplied by 92.35% to account for the deduction equivalent to the employer's share of FICA.

questions.stem: A self-employed taxpayer may deduct what portion of the self-employment tax in computing adjusted gross income?
options: One-half (the employer-equivalent portion) of the SE tax
None of the SE tax
Only the Medicare portion
100% of the SE tax
questions.rationale: Self-employed taxpayers deduct one-half of their self-employment tax as an above-the-line adjustment, reflecting the employer-equivalent share.

questions.stem: Net earnings from self-employment of at least what amount generally trigger the requirement to pay self-employment tax?
questions.rationale: A taxpayer must pay self-employment tax and file Schedule SE if net earnings from self-employment are $400 or more.

questions.stem: Which schedule does a sole proprietor use to report business income and expenses on the Form 1040?
options: Schedule C
Schedule E
Schedule A
Schedule F
questions.rationale: A sole proprietor reports the income and expenses of a nonfarm business on Schedule C of Form 1040.

questions.stem: A business sells real property (a building) used in its trade for a gain. Part of the gain is attributable to straight-line depreciation. For a C corporation, Section 291 generally requires what additional treatment?
options: 20% of the additional depreciation that would be recaptured under Section 1245 is treated as ordinary income
The gain is entirely capital
The entire gain is ordinary income
No special treatment applies to corporations
questions.rationale: Section 291 requires a C corporation to recharacterize as ordinary income 20% of the amount that would have been recaptured if the property were Section 1245 property, in excess of actual Section 1250 recapture.

questions.stem: In a Section 1031 like-kind exchange (post-2017), which type of property qualifies for nonrecognition treatment?
options: Machinery and equipment
Real property held for productive use in a business or for investment
Stocks and bonds
Inventory held for sale
questions.rationale: Section 1031 now applies only to exchanges of real property held for business or investment; personal property exchanges no longer qualify after 2017.

questions.stem: In a like-kind exchange, a taxpayer trades real property (adjusted basis $40,000) and receives like-kind real property worth $70,000 plus $10,000 cash (boot). The realized gain is $40,000. How much gain is recognized?
options: $10,000 (limited to the boot received)
questions.rationale: In a like-kind exchange, recognized gain equals the lesser of realized gain or the fair market value of boot received; the balance of gain is deferred.

questions.stem: Under the installment method, a taxpayer who sells property and receives payments over several years generally reports gain:
options: All in the year of sale
Only in the final year
As payments are received, based on the gross profit percentage
Not at all until fully paid
questions.rationale: The installment method allows a seller to recognize gain proportionately as payments are received, applying the gross profit percentage to each payment.

questions.stem: Depreciation recapture income on the sale of property must generally be reported how when the installment method is used?
options: Spread over all installment payments
Never reported
Deferred until the last payment
Fully recognized in the year of sale, regardless of payments received
questions.rationale: Ordinary income from depreciation recapture is reported entirely in the year of the installment sale, even though the remaining gain may be deferred.

questions.stem: Which form is used to report sales of business property, including Section 1231 transactions and depreciation recapture?
options: Form 6252
Schedule D
Form 4797
Form 8949
questions.rationale: Form 4797 is used to report the sale or exchange of business property, including Section 1231 gains and losses and Section 1245/1250 recapture.

questions.stem: A taxpayer abandons worthless business equipment that has an adjusted basis of $8,000. There is no sale or salvage. What is the tax treatment?
options: No loss because there is no sale
A $8,000 capital loss
An $8,000 ordinary loss (abandonment loss)
An $8,000 nondeductible loss
questions.rationale: Abandonment of business property without a sale or exchange generally produces an ordinary loss equal to the property's adjusted basis.

questions.stem: A business has a loss from a casualty to property used in the business that is completely destroyed. The loss is generally measured by:
options: The decline in fair market value only
The adjusted basis of the property (less any insurance reimbursement)
The original purchase price
The replacement cost
questions.rationale: For business property that is completely destroyed, the casualty loss equals the adjusted basis less salvage and insurance reimbursement, even if that exceeds the FMV decline.

questions.stem: Goodwill acquired in the purchase of a business is a Section 197 intangible amortized over what period?
options: 10 years
5 years
15 years
39 years
questions.rationale: Acquired goodwill and other Section 197 intangibles are amortized on a straight-line basis over 15 years (180 months).

questions.stem: An estate or trust files which income tax return?
options: Form 1040
Form 706
Form 1065
Form 1041
questions.rationale: Estates and trusts report their income, deductions, and distributions on Form 1041, the fiduciary income tax return.

questions.stem: A complex trust has distributable net income (DNI) of $30,000 and distributes $20,000 to its beneficiary during the year. How much of the income is generally taxed to the beneficiary versus the trust?
options: $20,000 is taxed to the beneficiary; the remaining $10,000 of DNI is taxed to the trust
The full $30,000 is taxed to the beneficiary
The full $30,000 is taxed to the trust
Nothing is taxed because trusts are exempt
questions.rationale: DNI determines the maximum distribution deduction and the amount taxable to beneficiaries; income distributed (up to DNI) is taxed to beneficiaries and retained income is taxed to the trust.

questions.stem: A tax-exempt organization described in Section 501(c)(3) generally files which annual information return (if not eligible for the postcard)?
options: Form 990
Form 1065
Form 1120
Form 1041
questions.rationale: Tax-exempt organizations generally file Form 990 (or 990-EZ, or 990-N for the smallest) to report their activities and finances to the IRS.

questions.stem: A 501(c)(3) charity operates a commercial parking lot unrelated to its exempt purpose, generating $15,000 of net income. How is this income generally treated?
options: Entirely tax-exempt because the organization is a charity
Subject to the accumulated earnings tax
Subject to the unrelated business income tax (UBIT), reported on Form 990-T
Subject to self-employment tax
questions.rationale: Unrelated business taxable income, from a trade or business regularly carried on that is not substantially related to the exempt purpose, is taxed under UBIT and reported on Form 990-T.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally excluded from unrelated business taxable income (UBTI) for an exempt organization?
options: Dividends, interest, and certain passive investment income
Net income from a debt-financed rental venture
Income from a regularly operated restaurant unrelated to the mission
Advertising income in the organization's magazine
questions.rationale: Passive income such as dividends, interest, and royalties is generally excluded from UBTI unless it is debt-financed; active unrelated business and advertising income are taxable.

questions.stem: An exempt organization that fails to file a required annual return (Form 990 series) for how many consecutive years automatically loses its tax-exempt status?
options: 1 year
2 consecutive years
3 consecutive years
5 consecutive years
questions.rationale: Under Section 6033(j), an organization that fails to file a required Form 990-series return for three consecutive years automatically loses its tax-exempt status.

questions.stem: A qualified farmer who receives at least two-thirds of gross income from farming may avoid the estimated tax penalty by paying the required estimated tax and filing by which special deadline (for a calendar-year individual)?
options: File quarterly like other taxpayers
File and pay any balance by January 15
File and pay any balance by March 1
File and pay any balance by April 15
questions.rationale: Farmers and fishermen who derive at least two-thirds of gross income from farming or fishing can avoid estimated tax penalties by filing and paying in full by March 1.

questions.stem: A cash-basis farmer raises and sells livestock. The income from the sale of raised livestock held primarily for sale is generally reported as:
options: Capital gain on Schedule D
Ordinary income on Schedule F
Section 1231 gain on Form 4797
Tax-exempt income
questions.rationale: Livestock raised and held primarily for sale produce ordinary income reported on Schedule F, whereas livestock held for breeding or dairy purposes may qualify for Section 1231 treatment.

questions.stem: Which credit rewards a business for increasing its research and experimental expenditures?
options: The Foreign Tax Credit
The Research and Development (R&D) credit
The Disabled Access Credit
The Work Opportunity Credit
questions.rationale: The research credit under Section 41 incentivizes increases in qualified research expenses and can be claimed on Form 6765.

questions.stem: The Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC) is available to employers that hire individuals from which of the following?
options: Only family members
Targeted groups facing significant barriers to employment
Only highly compensated executives
Any new employee
questions.rationale: The Work Opportunity Tax Credit provides employers an incentive to hire individuals from specified targeted groups who have consistently faced barriers to employment.

questions.stem: A business has a general business credit that exceeds its tax liability limitation for the current year. The unused portion is generally:
options: Lost permanently
Carried forward 5 years only
Refunded in cash
Carried back 1 year and forward 20 years
questions.rationale: Unused general business credits may be carried back one year and carried forward up to 20 years, subject to the annual tax liability limitation.

questions.stem: A small employer that provides health insurance to employees may claim the Small Employer Health Insurance Credit if it has fewer than how many full-time equivalent employees (with average wages under a threshold)?
questions.rationale: The Small Employer Health Insurance Credit is available to employers with fewer than 25 full-time equivalent employees, average annual wages below the indexed limit, that pay a uniform percentage of premiums through the SHOP Marketplace.

questions.stem: A taxpayer with taxable income above the threshold operates a specified service trade or business (SSTB), such as a law firm. Above the upper income limit, the QBI deduction for the SSTB is:
options: Unaffected by income level
Fully allowed at 20%
Completely phased out (disallowed)
Increased to 30%
questions.rationale: For specified service trades or businesses, the QBI deduction phases out and is fully disallowed once taxable income exceeds the upper limit of the phase-out range.

questions.stem: When a partnership distributes property (other than money) in a current distribution, the partner's basis in the distributed property is generally:
options: A carryover of the partnership's basis, limited to the partner's remaining outside basis
The partner's original cost
Always zero
Always equal to fair market value
questions.rationale: In a current distribution, noncash property takes a carryover basis from the partnership, limited to the partner's remaining outside basis under Section 732.

questions.stem: A partner's capital account on a Schedule K-1 maintained on the tax basis reflects:
options: The partner's contributions plus share of income, less distributions and share of losses
The partnership's total assets
The fair market value of the interest
The partner's outside basis including liabilities
questions.rationale: A tax-basis capital account tracks contributions and allocated income less distributions and allocated losses, and generally differs from outside basis because it excludes the partner's share of liabilities.

questions.stem: An S corporation shareholder who does not materially participate in the S corporation's rental activity generally treats the passed-through rental loss as:
options: A capital loss
Fully deductible ordinary loss
Deductible without limitation against wages
A passive activity loss subject to the passive loss limitation rules
questions.rationale: Rental activities are generally passive; a shareholder who does not materially participate may deduct the passed-through loss only against passive income, with the excess suspended.

questions.stem: An S corporation distributes appreciated property (FMV $50,000, basis $30,000) to a shareholder. What is the effect at the S corporation level?
options: The corporation recognizes $20,000 of gain that passes through to shareholders
No gain is recognized
The shareholder recognizes the corporation's gain only
The basis simply carries over with no recognition
questions.rationale: Like a C corporation under Section 311(b), an S corporation distributing appreciated property recognizes gain, but that gain passes through to shareholders, increasing their stock basis.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the tax treatment when a new partner contributes services (rather than property) in exchange for a capital interest in the partnership?
options: The service partner generally recognizes ordinary compensation income equal to the FMV of the capital interest received
The partnership recognizes the gain
The contribution is always tax-free under Section 721
No income is recognized by the service partner
questions.rationale: Section 721 nonrecognition does not apply to services; a partner receiving a capital interest for services recognizes ordinary income equal to the value of the interest received.

questions.stem: A business that pays $750 in cash to an unincorporated service provider for repairs during the year must generally issue which information return?
options: Form 1099-INT
Form W-2
No return is required because the amount is under $1,000
Form 1099-NEC, because the payment is $600 or more
questions.rationale: A trade or business must file Form 1099-NEC for payments of $600 or more for services performed by a nonemployee who is not a corporation.

questions.stem: A C corporation has current E&P of $10,000 and accumulated E&P deficit of $40,000. It distributes $15,000 to its sole shareholder. How is the distribution characterized?
options: No dividend because accumulated E&P is negative
$15,000 return of capital
$10,000 dividend (from current E&P) and $5,000 return of capital/gain
$15,000 dividend
questions.rationale: Current E&P is tested first; a distribution is a dividend to the extent of current E&P even when accumulated E&P is negative, with the excess being a return of capital and then gain.

questions.stem: A corporation that wants to extend the time to file Form 1120 files which form?
options: Form 4868
Form 7004
Form 2350
Form 8809
questions.rationale: Businesses request an automatic filing extension for returns such as Form 1120, 1120-S, and 1065 using Form 7004.

questions.stem: An excess business loss limitation under Section 461(l) applies to which taxpayers?
options: Tax-exempt organizations
Foreign corporations only
Noncorporate taxpayers (such as individuals) with business losses exceeding the indexed threshold
C corporations
questions.rationale: Section 461(l) disallows current deduction of noncorporate taxpayers' aggregate business losses exceeding the indexed threshold; the excess becomes a net operating loss carryforward.

questions.stem: A C corporation generated an NOL of $200,000 in 2024 and has taxable income (before the NOL) of $150,000 in 2025. How much of the NOL may offset 2025 income?
questions.rationale: Post-2020 NOL carryforwards may offset only 80% of taxable income in the carryforward year, with the unused portion carried forward indefinitely.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a separately stated item that must appear on a partner's Schedule K-1 rather than in ordinary business income?
options: Cost of labor for production employees
Office supplies expense
Rent paid for the business premises
Section 179 expense deduction
questions.rationale: The Section 179 deduction is separately stated on the K-1 because its dollar and income limitations are applied at the partner level, not the partnership level.

questions.stem: An S corporation shareholder increases stock basis for a capital contribution of $5,000 and the corporation passes through $8,000 of income and a $2,000 distribution. If beginning basis was $10,000, what is ending stock basis?
questions.rationale: Stock basis increases for contributions and pass-through income and decreases for distributions; $10,000 + $5,000 + $8,000 - $2,000 = $21,000.

questions.stem: A business uses the standard mileage rate for a vehicle in its first year of business use. In a later year it may switch to actual expenses, but which depreciation method must it then use?
options: Section 179 expensing
200% declining balance
Straight-line over the remaining useful life
Accelerated MACRS
questions.rationale: Choosing the standard mileage rate in the first year is treated as an election out of MACRS; a later switch to actual expenses requires straight-line depreciation over the vehicle's remaining useful life.

questions.stem: Bad debts of an accrual-method business are generally deductible:
options: Never, because they reduce income
Using the reserve method
In the year the debt becomes wholly or partially worthless (specific charge-off method)
Only when the customer files bankruptcy
questions.rationale: Most businesses use the specific charge-off method, deducting a business bad debt in the year it becomes wholly or partially worthless, provided the amount was previously included in income.

questions.stem: The MNO Partnership distributes to a partner, in a liquidating distribution, only inventory with a partnership basis of $12,000. The partner's outside basis is $18,000. What is the partner's basis in the inventory, and is any loss recognized?
options: $18,000 basis; $6,000 ordinary loss recognized
$12,000 basis; $6,000 capital loss recognized
$18,000 basis; no loss recognized
$12,000 basis; no loss recognized
questions.rationale: When a liquidating distribution consists solely of money, unrealized receivables, and inventory, the partner takes a carryover basis in those assets and recognizes a capital loss for the excess of outside basis over the assets received.

questions.stem: A qualified subchapter S subsidiary (QSub) is:
options: A domestic corporation wholly owned by an S corporation for which a QSub election is made, treated as a disregarded entity
A C corporation subsidiary taxed separately
A foreign subsidiary of an S corporation
A partnership owned by an S corporation
questions.rationale: A QSub is a 100%-owned domestic corporate subsidiary of an S corporation for which a Form 8869 election is made; its assets, liabilities, and items are treated as those of the parent S corporation.

questions.stem: Which of the following entities is generally a disregarded entity for federal tax purposes by default?
options: A single-member LLC with an individual owner that makes no election
A C corporation
An S corporation
A multi-member LLC
questions.rationale: A single-member LLC defaults to disregarded entity status, so its income and expenses are reported directly on the owner's return (for example, Schedule C for an individual).

questions.stem: A C corporation incurs organizational expenditures of $3,000 in connection with creating the corporation. How may these be treated?
options: Deducted entirely in the year the corporation dissolves
Capitalized with no deduction allowed
Added to the basis of corporate stock
Up to $5,000 deducted in the first year (phased out over $50,000), remainder amortized over 180 months
questions.rationale: Under Section 248, a corporation may deduct up to $5,000 of organizational expenditures in the first year (reduced dollar-for-dollar above $50,000) and amortize the remainder over 180 months.

questions.stem: A partnership must generally adopt a required tax year. Absent a business purpose or Section 444 election, the required tax year is generally:
options: The fiscal year chosen by the managing partner
A 52-53 week year
A calendar year always
The tax year of the partners owning a majority interest (or the principal partners, or least aggregate deferral)
questions.rationale: A partnership's required tax year is generally the majority-interest partners' tax year; if none exists, the principal partners' year; otherwise the year of least aggregate deferral, unless a business purpose or Section 444 election applies.

questions.stem: An S corporation has one shareholder. The corporation pays the shareholder-employee a $20,000 salary and makes $150,000 of distributions, while the business clearly generated substantial value from the shareholder's services. What is the primary tax risk?
options: The S election will automatically terminate
The IRS may recharacterize part of the distributions as wages subject to FICA because the salary is unreasonably low
The salary is too high and will be disallowed
The distributions are taxed twice
questions.rationale: S corporations must pay shareholder-employees reasonable compensation; paying minimal salary while taking large distributions risks IRS reclassification of distributions as wages to collect payroll taxes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally NOT a deductible business expense?
options: Salaries to employees
Federal income taxes paid by a C corporation
Business insurance premiums
State and local business taxes
questions.rationale: Federal income tax is specifically nondeductible; ordinary and necessary expenses such as wages, state taxes, and insurance are deductible.

questions.stem: A business trades in an old machine (no longer eligible for like-kind treatment under current law) and buys a new one. How is the disposition of the old machine treated?
options: Tax-free like-kind exchange
Always a deductible loss
Deferred until the new machine is sold
A taxable sale of the old machine, potentially triggering gain or recapture
questions.rationale: Since the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act limited Section 1031 to real property, equipment trade-ins are taxable dispositions that can produce gain and depreciation recapture.

questions.stem: Which statement about a general partnership is correct?
options: A general partnership must file Form 1120
All general partners have limited liability
General partners cannot participate in management
General partners are jointly and severally liable for partnership debts
questions.rationale: In a general partnership, each general partner has unlimited personal liability and is jointly and severally responsible for partnership obligations.

questions.stem: A C corporation's tax year ends June 30, 2024. When is its Form 1120 generally due (without extension)?
options: September 15, 2024
October 15, 2024
October 15, 2024 for a June 30 fiscal-year corporation
September 15, 2024 for a June 30 fiscal-year corporation (15th day of the 3rd month)
questions.rationale: While most C corporations use the 15th day of the fourth month, corporations with a June 30 fiscal year end are subject to a special rule using the 15th day of the third month (September 15) through tax years before the rule sunsets.

questions.stem: An S corporation may deduct which of the following at the entity level (reducing ordinary business income on Form 1120-S)?
options: Investment interest expense
Section 179 expense
Charitable contributions
Wages paid to nonshareholder employees
questions.rationale: Ordinary operating expenses like employee wages reduce the S corporation's ordinary business income, while items such as charitable contributions and Section 179 are separately stated on the K-1.

questions.stem: A trust has $5,000 of tax-exempt interest and $15,000 of taxable interest, total DNI of $20,000, and distributes all income. What portion of the $20,000 distribution is generally taxable to the beneficiary?
options: $15,000 (the tax-exempt portion retains its character and remains tax-free to the beneficiary)
questions.rationale: Distributions carry out DNI proportionally, preserving the character of each income type; tax-exempt interest remains tax-exempt in the beneficiary's hands.

questions.stem: A partnership borrows $300,000 from a bank with full recourse to the general partner, Hana, who bears the entire economic risk of loss. The partnership also has $100,000 of nonrecourse debt with no partner bearing economic risk. The partnership has two equal partners: Hana (general) and Leo (limited). How is the $300,000 recourse liability allocated for outside basis purposes?
options: $150,000 to Hana and $150,000 to Leo, split equally
$300,000 to Hana, $0 to Leo
$300,000 to Leo, $0 to Hana
questions.rationale: Recourse liabilities are allocated under the constructive-liquidation analysis of Reg. 1.752-2 to the partner(s) bearing the economic risk of loss, not by the profit-sharing ratio.

questions.stem: A partnership has $90,000 of nonrecourse liabilities with no Section 704(c) minimum gain or built-in gain attached. The partners share profits 40% (Amir), 35% (Bree), and 25% (Carlos). Using the third tier of the nonrecourse liability allocation rules, how much of this liability is allocated to Bree?
questions.rationale: Under Reg. 1.752-3, after allocating minimum gain (tier 1) and Section 704(c) minimum gain (tier 2), remaining nonrecourse liabilities (tier 3) are generally allocated in accordance with the partners' shares of profits.

questions.stem: Dana contributes property with a fair market value of $100,000 and basis of $40,000 to a partnership; the property has a $60,000 built-in gain. The partnership uses the traditional method under Section 704(c) and later sells the property for $100,000. Tax gain is $60,000 but book gain is $0. How is the $60,000 tax gain allocated?
options: Allocated half to Dana and half to the other partners
Split equally among all partners by their interests
Entirely to Dana, the contributing partner
Entirely to the non-contributing partners
questions.rationale: Section 704(c) requires that built-in gain or loss on contributed property be allocated to the contributing partner to prevent shifting precontribution tax consequences to other partners.

questions.stem: A partnership using the traditional method with curative allocations under Section 704(c) finds the traditional method created a $5,000 ceiling-rule distortion in depreciation for a non-contributing partner. What does the curative allocation method permit the partnership to do?
options: Adjust the book value of the contributed property upward
Make an offsetting allocation of another item of actual tax income, gain, loss, or deduction to cure the distortion
Allocate a notional tax item that does not exist on the books
Reallocate the entire built-in gain back to the non-contributing partner
questions.rationale: The curative allocation method (Reg. 1.704-3(c)) corrects ceiling-rule distortions by allocating other actual tax items in a reasonable and consistent manner, unlike the remedial method which creates notional items.

questions.stem: Under the remedial allocation method of Section 704(c), how does a partnership cure a ceiling-rule limitation that the traditional method cannot fully address?
options: By electing out of Section 704(c) entirely
By revaluing the property to its original contributed basis
By creating offsetting notional (remedial) tax items that have no effect on book capital accounts
By distributing cash to the non-contributing partner equal to the distortion
questions.rationale: The remedial method (Reg. 1.704-3(d)) eliminates ceiling-rule distortions by creating offsetting remedial tax items, giving the non-contributing partner the correct allocation while charging the contributing partner an equal amount.

questions.stem: A partnership has a Section 754 election in effect. A partner sells her interest to an unrelated buyer for $200,000; the buyer's share of the inside basis of partnership assets is $120,000. Which Code section governs the resulting basis adjustment, and to whom does it apply?
options: Section 704(c), applying to the selling partner
Section 751(b), applying to the partnership as a whole
Section 743(b), applying only to the transferee buyer
Section 734(b), applying to all partners
questions.rationale: When a Section 754 election is in place, a transfer of an interest by sale or exchange triggers a Section 743(b) adjustment unique to the transferee, equal to outside basis minus the share of inside basis.

questions.stem: A partnership with a Section 754 election makes a current distribution of $50,000 cash to a partner whose outside basis is only $30,000, generating $20,000 of gain to that partner. Which basis adjustment applies and how does it affect the partnership's remaining assets?
options: No adjustment; distributions never trigger basis adjustments
Section 734(b); decreases the partnership's basis in remaining assets by $20,000
Section 734(b); increases the partnership's basis in its remaining capital-gain property by $20,000
Section 743(b); increases only the distributee's basis
questions.rationale: Section 734(b) increases the basis of partnership property by gain recognized by a distributee (or by a basis step-up of distributed property), when a Section 754 election is in effect.

questions.stem: Even without a Section 754 election, a partnership must make a basis adjustment in certain situations. Which event triggers a MANDATORY Section 743(b) adjustment?
options: A transfer of an interest when the partnership has a substantial built-in loss exceeding $250,000 immediately after the transfer
A current distribution of cash to any partner
The admission of a new partner by capital contribution
Any sale of a partnership interest
questions.rationale: Section 743(d) requires a mandatory downward basis adjustment on a transfer when the partnership has a substantial built-in loss (more than $250,000) immediately after the transfer, regardless of a Section 754 election.

questions.stem: A partnership distributes property (not cash) to a partner and the partner takes a basis in that property that is $40,000 lower than the partnership's inside basis was, due to limited outside basis. With a Section 754 election in effect, what is the Section 734(b) consequence to the partnership?
options: A $40,000 decrease to the basis of remaining partnership property
A $40,000 increase to the distributee partner's outside basis
No adjustment, because property distributions are excluded
A $40,000 increase to the basis of remaining partnership property
questions.rationale: Section 734(b) requires a downward adjustment to remaining partnership property when distributed property's basis to the distributee is reduced below the partnership's prior inside basis, preserving aggregate basis.

questions.stem: Under the centralized partnership audit regime (BBA), what is the default consequence when the IRS adjusts partnership items and assesses an imputed underpayment?
options: The adjustment is split equally among current partners regardless of ownership
The partnership itself pays the imputed underpayment in the adjustment (current) year at the highest applicable tax rate
The partnership is dissolved automatically
Each partner amends their individual return for the reviewed year
questions.rationale: The BBA centralized audit regime (effective for tax years beginning after 2017) defaults to entity-level payment of the imputed underpayment in the adjustment year, unless the partnership makes a push-out election or modification.

questions.stem: A partnership subject to the BBA audit regime wants to shift the economic burden of an audit adjustment to the partners who were partners during the reviewed year. Which mechanism allows this?
options: Designating a new partnership representative
Electing out of the BBA regime after the audit concludes
Making a push-out election under Section 6226 so reviewed-year partners take the adjustments into account
Filing an administrative adjustment request only
questions.rationale: The push-out election under Section 6226 transfers the imputed underpayment to the reviewed-year partners, who account for the adjustments on their returns, rather than the partnership paying at the entity level.

questions.stem: Which partnership may elect OUT of the BBA centralized audit regime for a tax year?
options: A partnership with 120 partners, all individuals
A partnership with a single-member LLC (disregarded entity) as a partner
A partnership that has another partnership as a partner
A partnership with 90 eligible partners that are individuals, C corporations, S corporations, and estates of deceased partners
questions.rationale: Under Section 6221(b), a partnership with 100 or fewer eligible partners (counting S corp shareholders) may elect out of BBA; partnerships, trusts, and disregarded entities as partners disqualify the election.

questions.stem: A general partner guarantees a partnership's otherwise-nonrecourse bank loan of $250,000, agreeing to pay the lender if the partnership defaults, with no right of reimbursement from the partnership. For Section 752 purposes, how is the guaranteed loan treated as to that partner?
options: It remains nonrecourse and is allocated by profit ratio
It is allocated half to the guarantor and half to the lender
It is excluded from all partners' bases
It becomes a recourse liability allocated to the guaranteeing partner because she now bears the economic risk of loss
questions.rationale: Under Reg. 1.752-2, a partner who bears economic risk of loss through a bona fide guarantee (without reimbursement) is allocated the liability as recourse, increasing that partner's outside basis.

questions.stem: Partner Quinn has an outside basis of $12,000. The partnership allocates her a $15,000 ordinary loss and makes a $3,000 cash distribution during the same year. In what order are these applied, and how much loss may she currently deduct?
options: Apply the loss first; she deducts $12,000 of loss
She deducts $15,000 because distributions do not affect loss limits
Apply the distribution first reducing basis to $9,000, then deduct $9,000 of loss; $6,000 loss is suspended
Apply both simultaneously; she deducts $15,000
questions.rationale: Under the ordering rules, a partner's basis is reduced first by distributions and then by losses; losses are limited to remaining basis under Section 704(d), with the excess carried forward.

questions.stem: A partnership makes a liquidating distribution to a retiring partner consisting solely of $80,000 cash; the partner's outside basis is $95,000. What is the tax result to the retiring partner?
options: $15,000 ordinary loss
$15,000 capital loss
$80,000 capital gain
No gain or loss; basis carries to a deemed asset
questions.rationale: Under Section 731(a)(2), a partner recognizes a capital loss on a liquidating distribution only when the distribution consists solely of money, unrealized receivables, and inventory, and total basis exceeds the amounts received.

questions.stem: A partnership distributes inventory (a hot asset under Section 751) disproportionately so that one partner receives more than her share of ordinary-income assets while another receives more capital assets. What does Section 751(b) require?
options: The partnership must dissolve
Only the partnership recognizes gain, not the partners
The disproportionate portion is treated as a taxable exchange between the partner and the partnership, producing ordinary income
The distribution is fully tax-free to all partners
questions.rationale: Section 751(b) prevents shifting of ordinary income by treating disproportionate distributions of unrealized receivables and substantially appreciated inventory as taxable exchanges to the extent of the disproportion.

questions.stem: What is a guaranteed payment to a partner for federal tax purposes?
options: A loan repayment to the partner
A payment for services or use of capital determined without regard to partnership income
A return of the partner's capital contribution
A distribution of partnership profits in proportion to capital
questions.rationale: Under Section 707(c), guaranteed payments are determined without regard to partnership income, are deductible by the partnership (if otherwise deductible), and are ordinary income to the receiving partner.

questions.stem: A partnership pays partner Rae a $60,000 guaranteed payment for services. The partnership has a net loss before the guaranteed payment of $10,000. How does Rae report the guaranteed payment, and what happens to the loss?
options: Rae reports $60,000 as capital gain
Rae reports nothing because the partnership had a loss
Rae reports $50,000 net; the loss is netted against the payment
Rae reports the full $60,000 guaranteed payment as ordinary income; her distributive share of the resulting loss is determined separately
questions.rationale: Guaranteed payments are reported in full as ordinary income by the recipient and deducted by the partnership in computing partnership income or loss; the resulting distributive share is a distinct item.

questions.stem: A two-member partnership has one partner buy out the other's entire interest for cash, leaving a single owner. For federal tax purposes, what happens to the partnership?
options: It must file a final return only if it elects to dissolve
It terminates because a partnership requires at least two partners, and the remaining owner is treated as acquiring the partnership's assets
It automatically becomes a C corporation
It continues as a partnership with one member
questions.rationale: A partnership terminates when it no longer has at least two partners (Section 708); the continuing owner is treated as acquiring the other partner's share of partnership assets, and the entity becomes a sole proprietorship or disregarded entity.

questions.stem: In a Section 708(b) technical analysis, a partnership sells substantially all its assets and distributes the proceeds to its partners in liquidation. Which Code provision determines whether the partnership is considered terminated?
options: Termination occurs when the partnership ceases to carry on any business, financial operation, or venture through its partners
Termination occurs only if a Section 754 election is filed
Termination occurs only when 50% or more of interests are sold within 12 months
Termination requires unanimous partner consent filed with the IRS
questions.rationale: After repeal of the technical-termination rule, a partnership terminates under Section 708(b)(1) only when no part of any business, financial operation, or venture is carried on by any partners in a partnership.

questions.stem: A new partnership wants to deduct as much of its $8,000 of organizational expenses as possible in its first year. Assuming it does not exceed the phase-out threshold, how much may it currently deduct and how is the remainder treated?
options: Deduct $0 and amortize the full $8,000 over 60 months
Deduct all $8,000 immediately
Deduct $5,000 in the first year and amortize the remaining $3,000 over 180 months
Deduct $5,000 and expense the remainder in year two
questions.rationale: Under Section 709, a partnership may deduct up to $5,000 of organizational costs in the first year (subject to a $50,000 phase-out) and amortize the balance over 180 months.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a SEPARATELY STATED item that a partnership must report to partners rather than including in ordinary business income on Form 1065 page 1?
options: Employee wages paid to non-partners
Cost of goods sold
Section 1231 gains and losses
Rent paid for the business premises
questions.rationale: Items whose tax character or limitation differs at the partner level, such as Section 1231 gains/losses, capital gains, charitable contributions, and Section 179, must be separately stated under Section 702.

questions.stem: A cash-basis partnership has a partner who renders services and receives a profits interest (no capital interest) in exchange. Under Rev. Proc. 93-27, when is the receipt of a pure profits interest generally NOT a taxable event?
options: Whenever any partnership interest is received
Only if the partner contributes cash equal to the interest
Never; all interests received for services are taxable
When the profits interest does not relate to a substantially certain and predictable stream of income, is held at least two years, and the partnership is not a publicly traded partnership
questions.rationale: Rev. Proc. 93-27 treats the receipt of a profits interest for services as a nontaxable event, subject to listed exceptions, because the interest has no liquidation value at grant.

questions.stem: A partner sells appreciated property to a partnership in which she owns, directly and indirectly, more than 50% of the capital interests, realizing a $20,000 loss. What is the tax treatment of that loss under the related-party rules of Section 707(b)?
options: Deductible only to the extent of partnership ordinary income
Deferred until the partnership sells the property
Disallowed because the sale is between a partner and a more-than-50%-owned partnership
Fully deductible as a capital loss
questions.rationale: Section 707(b)(1) disallows losses on sales between a partnership and a more-than-50% owner; the disallowed loss may reduce the buyer's later gain but is not deductible by the seller.

questions.stem: A partnership has gross receipts of $40 million for 2024 and is not a tax shelter. Which limitation does it AVOID due to the small-business gross receipts test under Section 448(c)?
options: The Section 199A QBI deduction
The basis limitation under Section 704(d)
The self-employment tax on general partners
The Section 163(j) business interest expense limitation
questions.rationale: The Section 448(c) average annual gross receipts threshold for 2024 is $30 million; entities at or below it (and not tax shelters) are exempt from Section 163(j), Section 263A, and may use the cash method. A $40 million partnership exceeds the threshold and is subject to 163(j).

questions.stem: A general partner's distributive share of partnership ordinary trade or business income is generally subject to what additional tax that a limited partner's share usually is not?
options: Accumulated earnings tax
Alternative minimum tax only
Net investment income tax only
Self-employment tax
questions.rationale: Under Section 1402, a general partner's distributive share of ordinary trade or business income (plus guaranteed payments for services) is self-employment income; limited partners generally exclude their distributive share except guaranteed payments.
