questions.stem: A partner contributes property to a partnership and, within two years, the partnership distributes cash to that same partner in a transaction that, in substance, is a sale. How is this treated under the disguised sale rules of Section 707(a)(2)(B)?
options: Treated as a guaranteed payment
Always tax-free as a contribution and a separate distribution
Treated as a loan from the partnership
Treated as a sale of the property by the partner to the partnership to the extent of the cash received
questions.rationale: Section 707(a)(2)(B) and its regulations recharacterize linked contributions and distributions as sales; transfers within two years are presumed to be a sale absent contrary facts.

questions.stem: A partnership has a partner who is also an estate of a deceased individual. For purposes of electing OUT of the BBA centralized audit regime, how is the estate treated?
options: As a disregarded entity
As two partners for counting purposes
As an eligible partner (estate of a deceased partner), so it does not bar the election
As an ineligible partner, barring the election
questions.rationale: Eligible partners for the BBA election out include individuals, C corporations, S corporations, foreign entities treated as C corporations, and estates of deceased partners; trusts and partnerships are ineligible.

questions.stem: What is the due date for a calendar-year partnership to file Form 1065, absent an extension?
options: April 15
The 15th day of the fourth month after year-end
March 15
May 15
questions.rationale: Partnerships file Form 1065 by the 15th day of the third month after year-end (March 15 for calendar-year filers), with a six-month extension available to September 15.

questions.stem: A partnership wants to revalue its capital accounts to fair market value (a book-up) upon admitting a new partner. Under the Section 704(b) regulations, what becomes necessary after such a revaluation for built-in gains/losses created at the revaluation?
options: All partners must recognize gain immediately
The partnership must terminate and reform
Nothing; revaluations have no tax consequences
Reverse Section 704(c) principles must be applied to allocate the book-tax disparity created by the revaluation
questions.rationale: A book-up under Reg. 1.704-1(b)(2)(iv)(f) creates a book-tax difference that must be allocated under reverse Section 704(c) principles to the partners who held interests before the revaluation.

questions.stem: A partner's share of partnership liabilities decreases by $10,000 during the year due to debt repayment. With no other changes, what is the immediate effect on the partner's outside basis?
options: Treated as a guaranteed payment
Treated as a deemed cash distribution that decreases outside basis by $10,000
Increases outside basis by $10,000
No effect on outside basis
questions.rationale: Section 752(b) treats a decrease in a partner's share of liabilities as a deemed cash distribution, reducing outside basis and potentially triggering gain under Section 731 if it exceeds basis.

questions.stem: A limited partnership has qualified nonrecourse financing on real estate of $200,000 secured by the property and borrowed from a commercial lender unrelated to the partners. For at-risk purposes under Section 465, how is this financing treated for the partners?
options: At-risk under the qualified nonrecourse financing exception for real property held by the activity
Disregarded entirely for at-risk purposes
Not at-risk because it is nonrecourse
At-risk only for general partners
questions.rationale: Section 465(b)(6) provides that qualified nonrecourse financing (secured by real property, from a qualified person, on commercial terms) is treated as at-risk, an exception to the general rule excluding nonrecourse debt.

questions.stem: A partnership reports a partner's capital account using the tax basis method on Schedule K-1, as required. Which of the following correctly increases that tax basis capital account?
options: A cash distribution to the partner
A capital contribution of cash by the partner
The partner's share of tax-exempt income is excluded entirely
The partner's share of nonrecourse liabilities
questions.rationale: The tax basis capital account is increased by contributions and the partner's share of income (including tax-exempt income) and decreased by distributions and losses; partnership liabilities are excluded from the capital account though they affect outside basis.

questions.stem: Which form does a partnership use to report each partner's distributive share of income, deductions, and credits?
options: Form 1099-MISC
Schedule C (Form 1040)
Form W-2
Schedule K-1 (Form 1065)
questions.rationale: Partnerships report each partner's share of income, deductions, credits, and other items on Schedule K-1 (Form 1065), which the partner uses to prepare their own return.

questions.stem: A partnership must determine its required tax year. Three partners hold equal one-third interests; two are calendar-year individuals and one is a C corporation with a June 30 fiscal year. Under the majority-interest and principal-partner rules, what is the partnership's required tax year?
options: December 31, the year of the majority interest
June 30, the corporate partner's year
A 52-53 week year ending nearest June 30
The least aggregate deferral year only
questions.rationale: Under Section 706(b), a partnership generally must use the tax year of partners owning more than 50% of interests (majority interest); only if none exists do the principal-partner and least-aggregate-deferral rules apply.

questions.stem: A partner receives a liquidating distribution of inventory with an inside basis of $30,000 when her outside basis is $50,000. No other property is distributed. What basis does she take in the inventory, and what happens to the remaining basis?
options: $30,000 basis in inventory; the $20,000 is added to her other assets
$0 basis; she recognizes $50,000 of gain
$30,000 basis in inventory (carryover, limited); the remaining $20,000 of outside basis is a capital loss
$50,000 basis in inventory; no further adjustment
questions.rationale: In a liquidating distribution of only money, unrealized receivables, and inventory, the partner takes carryover basis in those assets and recognizes a capital loss for any remaining unrecovered outside basis under Section 731(a)(2).

questions.stem: A partnership representative under the BBA regime makes a decision binding all partners. Which statement about the partnership representative is correct?
options: Each partner must individually consent to every IRS action
The partnership representative has the sole authority to act on behalf of the partnership in an IRS proceeding, and the partnership and all partners are bound
The partnership representative must be a partner
Only the IRS can designate the partnership representative
questions.rationale: Under Section 6223, the partnership representative has sole authority to act for the partnership in BBA proceedings, binding the partnership and all partners; the representative need not be a partner but must have a substantial U.S. presence.

questions.stem: A partnership distributes cash of $5,000 to a partner whose outside basis is $40,000 in a current distribution. What is the tax consequence to the partner?
options: $5,000 capital gain
No gain recognized; outside basis is reduced to $35,000
$5,000 of ordinary income
$5,000 is a guaranteed payment
questions.rationale: Under Section 731(a)(1), a partner recognizes gain on a current distribution only to the extent money distributed exceeds outside basis; otherwise the distribution merely reduces basis.

questions.stem: A partnership has both recourse and nonrecourse debt. A limited partner with no deficit restoration obligation is allocated nonrecourse deductions. To be respected, these allocations must satisfy which requirement?
options: No requirement; nonrecourse deductions are freely allocable
The at-risk rules only
The substantial economic effect test only
The alternate test for economic effect plus a minimum gain chargeback provision
questions.rationale: Because nonrecourse deductions lack economic effect, Reg. 1.704-2 provides a safe harbor requiring proper capital account maintenance, a minimum gain chargeback, and consistent allocation of nonrecourse deductions and distributions.

questions.stem: A partner contributes depreciable property with a built-in gain. The partnership uses the traditional method. Due to the ceiling rule, the non-contributing partner receives less tax depreciation than book depreciation. What is the fundamental cause of this ceiling-rule limitation?
options: The partnership lacks a Section 754 election
The contributing partner refuses to take depreciation
Book depreciation is always less than tax depreciation
Total tax depreciation cannot exceed the partnership's actual tax basis in the property, limiting allocations to non-contributing partners
questions.rationale: The ceiling rule (Reg. 1.704-3(b)) prevents allocating more tax depreciation than the partnership actually has; curative or remedial methods are needed to overcome the resulting book-tax distortion.

questions.stem: A partnership makes an administrative adjustment request (AAR) under the BBA regime to correct a previously filed return. How is the resulting adjustment generally taken into account?
options: By restating all prior K-1s and refiling Form 1065
By a refund automatically issued to the partnership
By the partnership computing an imputed underpayment in the year the AAR is filed, or pushing the adjustment out to reviewed-year partners
By having each partner amend prior returns
questions.rationale: Under Section 6227, a partnership corrects errors through an AAR; favorable and unfavorable adjustments are taken into account in the AAR year via an imputed underpayment or push-out statements to partners.

questions.stem: A partnership's ordinary business loss flows to a partner whose share is a passive activity. Even if the partner has sufficient outside basis and at-risk amount, the loss may still be limited by which rule?
options: The constructive receipt doctrine
The hobby loss rules
The passive activity loss rules of Section 469
The wash sale rule
questions.rationale: Partnership losses pass through three hurdles: basis (704(d)), at-risk (465), and passive activity (469); a passive loss is allowed only to the extent of passive income, with the remainder suspended.

questions.stem: Two partners contribute property to form a partnership in a transaction qualifying under Section 721. One partner contributes property subject to a liability that exceeds her basis in the property. What can result?
options: A guaranteed payment to the other partner
Gain recognition to the extent net liability relief exceeds her outside basis
An automatic Section 754 election
Always tax-free regardless of liabilities
questions.rationale: Although Section 721 generally provides nonrecognition, relief of liabilities in excess of basis is treated as a deemed cash distribution that can trigger gain under Sections 752(b) and 731(a).

questions.stem: A partnership distributes two properties in a liquidating distribution to a partner with $60,000 outside basis: Property A (inside basis $20,000) and Property B (inside basis $50,000), both capital assets. How is the partner's $60,000 basis allocated between the properties?
options: $10,000 to A and $50,000 to B by FMV
$30,000 to each property equally
$60,000 to Property B and $0 to A
$20,000 to A and $40,000 to B, by relative inside bases reduced for the basis shortfall
questions.rationale: Under Section 732(c), in a liquidating distribution the partner's outside basis is allocated first to unrealized receivables and inventory, then to other property up to inside basis, with any required increase or decrease allocated under specified rules.

questions.stem: A partnership has a partner that is a grantor trust treated as owned by an individual. For purposes of the BBA election-out 100-partner count, how is this trust treated?
options: As an ineligible partner that prevents electing out
As multiple partners equal to the number of beneficiaries
As an eligible partner that does not block the election
As a disregarded entity counted as zero partners
questions.rationale: Eligible partners for the BBA election out are limited to individuals, C corporations, eligible foreign entities, S corporations, and estates of deceased partners; any trust as a partner disqualifies the election.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally TRUE about a partner's share of partnership tax-exempt income?
options: It is taxable to the partner
It has no effect on outside basis
It must be added back as a preference item
It increases the partner's outside basis even though it is not taxed
questions.rationale: Section 705 increases a partner's outside basis by the partner's share of both taxable and tax-exempt income to prevent the exempt income from being taxed later on disposition.

questions.stem: A partnership incurs $7,000 of syndication costs (costs of issuing and marketing partnership interests). How are these treated for tax purposes?
options: Capitalized and never deductible or amortizable
Deducted in full in the first year
Amortized over 180 months like organizational costs
Deducted as ordinary business expenses ratably over five years
questions.rationale: Under Section 709(a), syndication expenses are nondeductible and nonamortizable capital costs, distinguishing them from organizational expenses that may be partially deducted and amortized.

questions.stem: A partner sells her entire partnership interest. The partnership holds unrealized receivables and substantially appreciated inventory (hot assets). How does Section 751(a) affect the character of her gain?
options: No gain is recognized until the partnership sells the assets
All gain is ordinary income
All gain is capital gain
The portion attributable to hot assets is recharacterized as ordinary income, with the remainder generally capital
questions.rationale: Section 751(a) bifurcates a sale of a partnership interest: the share of hot assets produces ordinary income and the remaining gain or loss is capital, preventing conversion of ordinary income into capital gain.

questions.stem: A partnership uses the accrual method but qualifies as a small business under Section 448(c). Which accounting method change may it make beginning in 2024?
options: It must use the lower of cost or market for inventory
It must continue using accrual permanently
It must adopt the percentage-of-completion method
It may switch to the cash method of accounting because it meets the gross receipts test and is not a tax shelter
questions.rationale: Small-business taxpayers under Section 448(c) may use the cash method, are exempt from Section 263A, and may treat inventory under simplified rules, subject to a method-change procedure.

questions.stem: Which entity files Form 1065 and issues Schedule K-1s by default?
options: A multi-member LLC that has not elected corporate treatment
A single-member LLC with no election
A C corporation
A sole proprietorship
questions.rationale: By default, a domestic multi-member LLC is taxed as a partnership and files Form 1065; it may elect to be taxed as a corporation by filing Form 8832 (and possibly Form 2553 for S status).

questions.stem: An S corporation has a negative AAA of -$15,000 and accumulated E&P of $30,000. It makes a $20,000 cash distribution. With no special elections, how is the distribution treated?
options: $20,000 capital gain
$15,000 dividend and $5,000 return of basis
$20,000 reduces stock basis tax-free because AAA cannot go more negative from distributions
The entire $20,000 is a taxable dividend from accumulated E&P because AAA is negative
questions.rationale: Distributions reduce AAA but not below zero; when AAA is zero or negative and accumulated E&P exists, distributions are taxable dividends to the extent of E&P under Section 1368.

questions.stem: An S corporation with accumulated E&P wants to distribute current dividends to avoid future dividend treatment. Which election permits it to treat distributions as first coming from accumulated E&P rather than AAA?
options: The Section 338(h)(10) election
The election under Section 1368(e)(3) to distribute accumulated E&P first (bypass election)
The Section 1374 built-in gains election
The Section 444 fiscal-year election
questions.rationale: The Section 1368(e)(3) bypass (or AAA bypass) election lets an S corporation treat distributions as first made from accumulated E&P, often used to eliminate E&P and avoid the passive investment income tax or termination risk.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a PERMITTED shareholder of an S corporation?
options: A C corporation
An electing small business trust (ESBT)
A nonresident alien individual
A partnership
questions.rationale: Eligible S corporation shareholders include U.S. citizens/residents, certain trusts (grantor trusts, QSSTs, ESBTs, testamentary, and voting trusts), estates, and certain tax-exempt organizations; corporations, partnerships, and nonresident aliens are not eligible.

questions.stem: A qualified subchapter S trust (QSST) holds S corporation stock. Which requirement distinguishes a QSST from an ESBT?
options: A QSST may accumulate income at the trust level taxed at trust rates
A QSST may have multiple income beneficiaries
A QSST may hold both S corporation and partnership interests with no restrictions
A QSST must have one income beneficiary who is a U.S. individual and must distribute all income currently; the beneficiary is treated as the owner
questions.rationale: A QSST under Section 1361(d) requires a single U.S. individual income beneficiary, mandatory current income distributions, and a beneficiary election making the beneficiary the deemed owner; an ESBT may have multiple beneficiaries and is taxed at the trust level on its S portion.

questions.stem: A corporation intended to be an S corporation but failed to timely file Form 2553. It otherwise qualified and all shareholders reported consistently as if the S election were valid. Which relief allows a late S election?
options: Rev. Proc. 2013-30, providing simplified late election relief if reasonable cause and other requirements are met
Form 1139 quick refund procedures
Rev. Rul. 99-5
Section 9100 relief only available through a private letter ruling in all cases
questions.rationale: Rev. Proc. 2013-30 consolidates late-election relief for S corporations, QSubs, ESBTs, and QSSTs, allowing simplified relief (often without a PLR) when reasonable cause and consistent reporting requirements are satisfied within set time limits.

questions.stem: Under Rev. Proc. 2013-30, a late S corporation election generally must be filed within what time frame to use the simplified relief?
options: Within 30 days of the intended effective date
Within 3 years and 75 days of the intended effective date of the election
Within 6 months of the original due date of the return
Within 10 years of formation
questions.rationale: Rev. Proc. 2013-30 generally requires that a late S election request be filed within 3 years and 75 days of the intended effective date, with reasonable cause and consistent reporting, to qualify for simplified relief.

questions.stem: An S corporation shareholder has stock basis of $10,000 and loaned the corporation $8,000 (debt basis). The corporation passes through a $15,000 ordinary loss. How much loss may the shareholder deduct, and how is basis affected?
options: $15,000, fully deductible against combined stock and debt basis, reducing stock basis to $0 and debt basis to $3,000
$8,000, limited to debt basis only
$10,000, limited to stock basis only
$18,000, the full combined basis
questions.rationale: Under Section 1366(d), an S corporation shareholder may deduct losses up to the sum of stock and debt basis; losses reduce stock basis first, then debt basis, with any excess suspended.

questions.stem: In a later profitable year, an S corporation shareholder whose debt basis was previously reduced by losses receives full repayment of the shareholder loan. What is the tax consequence if debt basis is less than the loan's face amount?
options: No income; loan repayments are always tax-free
Income is recognized to the extent repayment exceeds the reduced debt basis
The repayment increases stock basis
The repayment is a tax-free return of capital regardless of basis
questions.rationale: Under Section 1367 and related rules, if a shareholder's debt basis was reduced by losses, loan repayments exceeding the reduced basis generate gain; net income first restores debt basis before increasing stock basis.

questions.stem: A formerly C corporation elected S status. Within the recognition period it sells an asset that had a built-in gain at the date of conversion. Which tax may apply at the corporate level?
options: The built-in gains tax under Section 1374
The personal holding company tax
No corporate-level tax ever applies to S corporations
The accumulated earnings tax
questions.rationale: Section 1374 imposes a corporate-level tax on net recognized built-in gains during the 5-year recognition period following S election, taxed at the highest corporate rate, to prevent avoidance of double taxation on appreciated C corporation assets.

questions.stem: An S corporation with accumulated C corporation E&P has passive investment income exceeding 25% of gross receipts for three consecutive tax years. What is the consequence?
options: Nothing; passive income is irrelevant for S corporations
The shareholders lose all loss carryforwards
The corporation must immediately convert to a partnership
The S election terminates at the beginning of the fourth year, and an excess net passive income tax may apply in the interim years
questions.rationale: Under Sections 1362(d)(3) and 1375, an S corporation with accumulated E&P faces an excess net passive income tax when passive investment income exceeds 25% of gross receipts, and the S election terminates after three consecutive such years.

questions.stem: How many shareholders may an S corporation have at most?
options: No limit
questions.rationale: Under Section 1361(b), an S corporation is limited to 100 shareholders; certain family members may elect to be treated as a single shareholder for this count.

questions.stem: An S corporation pays its more-than-2% shareholder-employee health insurance premiums. How are these premiums treated?
options: Treated as a tax-free fringe benefit like for a regular employee
Deductible only by the corporation with no W-2 inclusion
Included in the shareholder-employee's W-2 wages (Box 1) and potentially deductible by the shareholder as self-employed health insurance
Excluded entirely from the shareholder's income
questions.rationale: More-than-2% S corporation shareholders are treated like partners for fringe benefits; health premiums are added to W-2 Box 1 wages and the shareholder may take the above-the-line self-employed health insurance deduction.

questions.stem: An S corporation makes a distribution to a shareholder that exceeds both the AAA and the shareholder's stock basis. The corporation has no accumulated E&P. How is the excess treated?
options: Capital gain from the deemed sale of stock
Ordinary income
Tax-free return of capital with no limit
A dividend
questions.rationale: For an S corporation with no accumulated E&P, distributions are tax-free to the extent of stock basis under Section 1368, and amounts exceeding basis are treated as capital gain from the sale of stock.

questions.stem: An S corporation has a single shareholder who also performs substantial services. The corporation reports $200,000 of net income and pays the shareholder-employee only $20,000 in wages, distributing the rest. What is the primary tax risk?
options: The IRS may reclassify a portion of distributions as reasonable compensation subject to employment taxes
The corporation owes the accumulated earnings tax
The S election automatically terminates
The shareholder owes self-employment tax on the entire $200,000
questions.rationale: Shareholder-employees must receive reasonable compensation for services; the IRS may reclassify distributions as wages, with employment tax, penalties, and interest, where salary is unreasonably low.

questions.stem: An S corporation election is made by filing Form 2553. To be effective for the current tax year, when must a timely election generally be filed?
options: By the extended due date of the corporation's return
By the 15th day of the third month of the tax year the election is to take effect (or any time in the preceding year)
By December 31 of the prior year only
Within 30 days of incorporation
questions.rationale: Under Section 1362(b), Form 2553 must be filed by the 15th day of the third month of the election year or during the preceding tax year; later filings require late-election relief.

questions.stem: Which of the following will cause an inadvertent termination of an S corporation election?
options: Hiring nonresident alien employees (not shareholders)
Having 90 shareholders
Earning passive investment income of 10% of gross receipts
Issuing a second class of stock with different distribution and liquidation rights
questions.rationale: Section 1361(b) permits only one class of stock (differences in voting rights are allowed); a second class with differing economic rights terminates the S election, though differences solely in voting rights are permitted.

questions.stem: A C corporation has taxable income of $500,000 for 2024. What is its federal income tax at the flat corporate rate?
questions.rationale: Since 2018, C corporations are taxed at a flat 21% rate under Section 11, so $500,000 of taxable income yields $105,000 of tax before credits.

questions.stem: A qualified personal service corporation (such as a law firm operating as a C corporation) has taxable income of $300,000 for 2024. What corporate tax rate applies to its income?
options: 0% because PSCs are pass-through entities
The same flat 21% rate that applies to other C corporations
A graduated rate up to 39%
A special 35% flat rate for personal service corporations
questions.rationale: The pre-2018 35% flat rate for personal service corporations was repealed; PSCs taxed as C corporations now pay the flat 21% rate like all other C corporations.

questions.stem: A C corporation makes a charitable contribution of $90,000 in 2024 when its taxable income (before the contribution and certain items) is $700,000. The annual limit is 10% of taxable income. How much may it deduct currently, and what happens to the excess?
options: $90,000 fully deductible this year
$90,000 carried forward entirely to next year
$70,000 deductible; the $20,000 excess is lost
$70,000 deductible this year; $20,000 carried forward for up to 5 years
questions.rationale: Under Section 170(b)(2), a C corporation's charitable deduction is limited to 10% of taxable income (with modifications), and any excess carries forward for up to 5 succeeding tax years.

questions.stem: A C corporation owns 25% of the stock of another domestic C corporation and receives a $40,000 dividend. What is the dividends-received deduction (DRD) percentage and amount, assuming no taxable income limitation issue?
questions.rationale: The DRD under Section 243 is 50% for less than 20% ownership, 65% for 20% to less than 80%, and 100% for 80%-or-more affiliated-group members, subject to a taxable income limitation.

questions.stem: A calendar-year C corporation expects $1,000,000 of tax for 2024. To avoid an estimated tax underpayment penalty under Section 6655, a large corporation generally must base its required installments on what?
options: 100% of the prior year's tax for all four installments
100% of the current year's tax (the prior-year safe harbor is generally unavailable to large corporations except for the first installment)
90% of the prior year's tax
80% of the current year's tax
questions.rationale: Under Section 6655, corporations must pay the lesser of 100% of current-year tax or 100% of prior-year tax, but large corporations (over $1 million taxable income in a test year) generally lose the prior-year safe harbor except for the first installment.

questions.stem: A small C corporation (not a large corporation) wants to use the prior-year safe harbor for 2024 estimated taxes. Its 2023 tax was $30,000 for a full 12-month year. What total estimated payments avoid the Section 6655 penalty under that safe harbor?
options: $0 because corporations are exempt
$27,000 (90% of prior year)
$30,000 (100% of prior year's tax)
$33,000 (110% of prior year)
questions.rationale: Under Section 6655, a corporation generally avoids the underpayment penalty by paying the lesser of 100% of current-year tax or 100% of the prior year's tax (if the prior year was a 12-month year with positive tax), unless it is a large corporation.

questions.stem: What is the due date for a calendar-year C corporation to file Form 1120, absent an extension?
options: March 15
June 15
April 15
May 15
questions.rationale: C corporations generally file Form 1120 by the 15th day of the fourth month after the tax year ends (April 15 for calendar-year filers), with extensions available; note special rules historically applied to June 30 fiscal-year corporations.

questions.stem: A C corporation has a net operating loss (NOL) arising in 2024. Under current law, how may that NOL be used?
options: Carried forward indefinitely but limited to 80% of taxable income in the year used (no carryback)
Carried back 2 years and forward 20 years
Carried back 5 years with no forward limit
Deductible only in the year incurred
questions.rationale: For NOLs arising in tax years beginning after 2017 (outside the temporary CARES Act window), no carryback is allowed, carryforwards are indefinite, and the deduction is capped at 80% of taxable income.

questions.stem: A C corporation accumulates earnings beyond the reasonable needs of the business to avoid shareholder-level tax on dividends. Which penalty tax may apply?
options: The built-in gains tax
The excess net passive income tax
The branch profits tax
The accumulated earnings tax
questions.rationale: The accumulated earnings tax (Section 531) is a penalty on C corporations that retain earnings beyond reasonable needs to shield shareholders from dividend taxation; a $250,000 (or $150,000 for certain PSCs) accumulated earnings credit generally applies.

questions.stem: A corporation with significant passive investment income owned by few shareholders may be subject to the personal holding company (PHC) tax. What is the general purpose of the PHC tax?
options: To replace the corporate income tax for small businesses
To tax foreign-source income only
To encourage corporations to invest in equipment
To prevent closely held corporations from being used as incorporated pockets to shelter passive income from higher individual rates
questions.rationale: The personal holding company tax (Section 541) imposes an additional tax on undistributed PHC income when a corporation meets the closely held ownership test and the passive-income test, to prevent income sheltering.

questions.stem: A C corporation distributes appreciated property (FMV $50,000, basis $30,000) to a shareholder as a dividend. What is the tax consequence to the corporation?
options: No gain to the corporation; only the shareholder is taxed
The corporation recognizes a $30,000 loss
The corporation recognizes $20,000 of gain as if it sold the property at FMV
The corporation deducts the $20,000 appreciation
questions.rationale: Section 311(b) requires a corporation to recognize gain on the distribution of appreciated property as if sold at FMV; losses on nonliquidating distributions of depreciated property are not recognized.

questions.stem: Under Section 351, shareholders transfer property to a newly formed corporation in exchange for stock. For nonrecognition to apply, the transferors must control the corporation immediately after the exchange. What is the control threshold?
options: At least 662/3% of voting power
At least 80% of the total combined voting power and at least 80% of all other classes of stock
More than 50% of the total value
Any amount, as long as stock is received
questions.rationale: Section 368(c) defines control for Section 351 as at least 80% of combined voting power and 80% of each other class of stock; transferors as a group must meet this immediately after the exchange for nonrecognition.

questions.stem: In a Section 351 exchange, a shareholder transfers property (basis $40,000, FMV $100,000) and receives stock worth $80,000 plus $20,000 cash (boot). How much gain does the shareholder recognize?
options: $0 because Section 351 is fully tax-free
$60,000, the full realized gain
$20,000, the lesser of realized gain or boot received
questions.rationale: Under Section 351(b), when boot is received, gain is recognized equal to the lesser of realized gain or the boot; losses are not recognized in a Section 351 exchange.

questions.stem: A C corporation completely liquidates and distributes appreciated property to its shareholders. What is the general tax consequence at the corporate level under Section 336?
options: No gain or loss to the corporation
The corporation recognizes gain (and generally loss) as if it sold the property at FMV
The corporation may deduct the unrealized appreciation
The corporation defers all gain to the shareholders
questions.rationale: Section 336 treats a complete liquidation as a deemed sale of the corporation's assets at FMV, triggering corporate-level gain or loss (with limits on certain related-party loss recognition).

questions.stem: A business with average annual gross receipts of $20 million for 2024 wants to know whether it is subject to the Section 163(j) business interest expense limitation. Which statement is correct?
options: It is exempt under the small-business exception because it meets the gross receipts test and is not a tax shelter
It must capitalize all interest
It is subject to the limitation regardless of gross receipts
It may deduct interest only up to 30% of gross receipts
questions.rationale: The Section 163(j) small-business exemption applies when average annual gross receipts do not exceed the Section 448(c) threshold ($30 million for 2024) and the taxpayer is not a tax shelter.

questions.stem: For a taxpayer subject to Section 163(j) in 2024, the deduction for business interest is generally limited to the sum of business interest income, floor plan financing interest, plus what percentage of adjusted taxable income (ATI)?
options: 30% of ATI
100% of ATI
50% of ATI
20% of ATI
questions.rationale: Section 163(j) limits business interest expense to business interest income, floor plan financing interest, and 30% of adjusted taxable income; disallowed interest carries forward indefinitely.

questions.stem: A small business taxpayer meeting the Section 448(c) gross receipts test is exempt from the UNICAP rules. Which Code section provides the uniform capitalization rules from which it is exempt?
options: Section 1245
Section 263A
Section 469
Section 199A
questions.rationale: Section 263A requires capitalizing certain direct and indirect costs into inventory and self-constructed property; small-business taxpayers under the Section 448(c) gross receipts test are exempt from UNICAP.

questions.stem: A small business taxpayer that meets the Section 448(c) gross receipts test and does not keep an inventory for financial accounting purposes may, under Section 471(c), treat inventory in which of the following ways?
options: It must use FIFO for all inventory
It may treat inventory as non-incidental materials and supplies or follow its applicable financial statement (or books) method
It must capitalize inventory under full absorption costing
It may never deduct inventory costs
questions.rationale: Section 471(c) allows small-business taxpayers (meeting the Section 448(c) test) to either treat inventory as non-incidental materials and supplies or conform to their applicable financial statement or books-and-records method.

questions.stem: What is the gross receipts threshold (indexed) under Section 448(c) that generally defines a small-business taxpayer for 2024?
options: $30 million
$25 million
$5 million
$10 million
questions.rationale: The Section 448(c) gross receipts test threshold, originally $25 million in 2018, is indexed for inflation and is $30 million for 2024; meeting it unlocks the cash method, and exemptions from 263A, 163(j), and 471.

questions.stem: A taxpayer sells nonresidential real property (Section 1250) at a gain after taking straight-line depreciation. For a C corporation, what additional recapture rule may apply under Section 291?
options: No recapture because straight-line was used
100% of depreciation is recaptured as ordinary income
The full gain is ordinary income
20% of the amount that would have been recaptured if the property were Section 1245 property is treated as ordinary income
questions.rationale: Section 291 requires corporations to treat 20% of the additional amount that would be recaptured under Section 1245 (over the Section 1250 amount) as ordinary income on dispositions of depreciable real property.

questions.stem: A business places a passenger automobile (used 100% for business) in service in 2024 and elects bonus depreciation. The vehicle is subject to the luxury auto depreciation caps. What limits the first-year depreciation despite bonus depreciation?
options: No limit applies once bonus depreciation is elected
The vehicle must be fully expensed under Section 179 with no cap
The Section 280F luxury auto first-year cap (increased by the bonus depreciation amount) limits the deduction
Depreciation is barred entirely for autos
questions.rationale: Section 280F imposes annual dollar caps on depreciation for passenger automobiles; bonus depreciation increases only the first-year cap by a fixed amount, so a large purchase price is still subject to the limitation.

questions.stem: A new business incurs $52,000 of start-up costs before opening. Under Section 195, how much may it deduct in the first year, given the phase-out?
options: $5,000 reduced by the amount over $50,000, so $3,000; the remainder is amortized over 180 months
$52,000 in full
questions.rationale: Under Section 195, up to $5,000 of start-up costs is deductible in year one, reduced by the amount total costs exceed $50,000; the balance is amortized ratably over 180 months beginning when the business starts.

questions.stem: A taxpayer elects Section 179 expensing on qualifying equipment. The Section 179 deduction cannot exceed which of the following?
options: The taxpayer's gross receipts
The cost of the property regardless of income
The aggregate taxable income from the active conduct of any trade or business
Three times the depreciation otherwise allowable
questions.rationale: Section 179 expensing is limited to the annual dollar cap, phased out above the investment threshold, and further limited to taxable income from the active conduct of a trade or business, with carryforward of disallowed amounts.

questions.stem: Bonus depreciation under Section 168(k) is being phased down. For qualified property placed in service in 2024, what is the bonus depreciation percentage?
questions.rationale: Section 168(k) bonus depreciation phases down 20 points per year: 100% (2022 and prior), 80% (2023), 60% (2024), 40% (2025), 20% (2026), then 0%.

questions.stem: An employer withholds federal income tax and the employee share of FICA from wages but fails to remit these amounts to the IRS. Which tax is considered a trust fund tax for which a responsible person may be personally liable?
options: Federal unemployment tax (FUTA)
The withheld income tax and employee share of FICA (trust fund taxes)
State sales tax
The employer share of FICA only
questions.rationale: Under Section 6672, withheld income tax and the employee portion of FICA are trust fund taxes; a responsible person who willfully fails to collect or pay them is liable for the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty equal to 100% of the unpaid trust fund tax.

questions.stem: The Trust Fund Recovery Penalty (TFRP) under Section 6672 can be imposed on a responsible person who acts willfully. Which two elements must both be present?
options: Being a responsible person AND willful failure to collect, account for, or pay over the trust fund taxes
Negligence and a large tax balance
Filing late and underpaying estimated tax
Ownership of more than 50% of the company and a felony conviction
questions.rationale: Section 6672 imposes the 100% penalty when a responsible person (one with the duty and authority to collect, account for, and pay trust fund taxes) willfully fails to do so; willfulness means a voluntary, intentional disregard of a known duty.

questions.stem: For 2024, an employer pays an employee $180,000 in wages. The Social Security wage base is $168,600. On how much of the wages is the 6.2% employer Social Security tax imposed?
questions.rationale: For 2024 the Social Security taxable wage base is $168,600; the 6.2% employer and 6.2% employee Social Security tax applies only up to that base, while the 1.45% Medicare tax applies to all wages.

questions.stem: The Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% applies to wages above a threshold. What is the employer's obligation regarding this tax?
options: The employer must withhold the additional 0.9% on wages paid to an employee in excess of $200,000, with no employer match
The employer pays a matching 0.9%
The employer is exempt from withholding it
The employer withholds it only if the employee requests
questions.rationale: Employers must withhold the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on wages exceeding $200,000 per employee, with no employer match; the employee reconciles the actual liability (which may use different filing-status thresholds) on the individual return.

questions.stem: For 2024, the FUTA tax rate is 6.0% on the first $7,000 of each employee's wages, but employers generally receive a credit for state unemployment taxes paid. What is the typical net FUTA rate after the maximum credit?
questions.rationale: FUTA is 6.0% on the first $7,000 of each employee's annual wages; a credit of up to 5.4% for state unemployment taxes generally reduces the effective FUTA rate to 0.6% (subject to credit reductions in certain states).

questions.stem: Which form does an employer use to report quarterly federal income tax withholding and FICA taxes?
options: Form 940
Form 941
Form W-3
Form 944
questions.rationale: Employers report federal income tax withholding and the employee and employer FICA taxes quarterly on Form 941; small employers may file annually on Form 944 if notified by the IRS.

questions.stem: A worker is classified by a business as an independent contractor, but the business controls when, where, and how the work is performed and provides all tools. Under the common-law test, this worker is most likely a(n):
options: Independent contractor because a contract says so
Partner in the business
Employee, because the business has the right to control the details of how the work is done
Statutory nonemployee regardless of control
questions.rationale: Worker classification turns on the common-law right-to-control test (behavioral control, financial control, and relationship of the parties); substance over the contractual label controls, and misclassification can trigger back employment taxes and penalties.

questions.stem: A business wants relief from employment tax reclassification of workers it treated as independent contractors. Which provision may provide safe-harbor relief if the business had a reasonable basis and consistently treated the workers (and similar workers) as contractors and filed all required Forms 1099?
options: Section 199A
The Trust Fund Recovery Penalty
Circular 230
Section 530 of the Revenue Act of 1978
questions.rationale: Section 530 of the Revenue Act of 1978 provides safe-harbor relief from employment tax reclassification when the employer had a reasonable basis, was consistent in treatment, and filed required information returns (such as Forms 1099).

questions.stem: For payments made in calendar year 2024, a third-party settlement organization (such as a payment app or online marketplace) must issue Form 1099-K when a payee's gross payments exceed what threshold under the IRS's transition relief?
options: $20,000 and more than 200 transactions only
$10,000 regardless of transactions
$5,000 (the IRS transition threshold for 2024)
$600 with no transaction minimum
questions.rationale: The American Rescue Plan lowered the statutory 1099-K threshold to $600, but the IRS phased in the change; for 2024 the reporting threshold is $5,000 under transition relief, regardless of the number of transactions.

questions.stem: A business pays an unincorporated independent contractor $1,200 for services during 2024. Which information return must it generally file?
options: Form 1099-K
Form 1099-NEC for nonemployee compensation of $600 or more
Form W-2
No form is required for amounts under $5,000
questions.rationale: Businesses must file Form 1099-NEC for payments of $600 or more for services to non-employees who are not corporations; the form is due to recipients and the IRS by January 31.

questions.stem: A simple trust is required to distribute all of its income currently. For 2024 it has trust accounting income of $20,000 and distributable net income (DNI) of $18,000. How much can the beneficiaries be taxed on, and what is the distribution deduction limit?
options: $0 because trusts pay all the tax
$18,000, limited to DNI; the trust's distribution deduction is also limited to DNI
$38,000, the sum of both amounts
$20,000 because that is trust accounting income
questions.rationale: DNI serves as both the ceiling on the trust's distribution deduction and the maximum amount taxable to beneficiaries, preserving the character of the income passed through (Sections 651-652).

questions.stem: A complex trust has DNI of $30,000, which includes $5,000 of tax-exempt interest. It distributes $30,000 to its sole beneficiary. What amount of the distribution is taxable to the beneficiary?
options: $25,000, because the tax-exempt portion retains its character and is not taxable
questions.rationale: Under the conduit principle, distributions carry out DNI retaining each item's character; tax-exempt income remains exempt in the beneficiary's hands, so only the taxable portion of DNI ($25,000) is taxed.

questions.stem: What is the difference between trust accounting income (TAI) and distributable net income (DNI)?
options: DNI always includes capital gains, while TAI never does
They are always identical
TAI is a federal tax figure and DNI is a state-law figure
TAI is determined under the governing instrument and state law to allocate between income and principal, while DNI is a tax concept limiting the distribution deduction and beneficiary taxation
questions.rationale: Trust accounting income governs how much must or may be distributed under the instrument and state law; DNI is the tax measure that limits the distribution deduction and the amount taxable to beneficiaries, and generally excludes capital gains allocated to corpus.

questions.stem: Which form is used to report the income, deductions, and distributions of an estate or trust?
options: Form 1065
Form 990
Form 1040
Form 1041
questions.rationale: Fiduciaries report estate and trust income, deductions, gains, losses, and distributions to beneficiaries on Form 1041, issuing Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) to beneficiaries.

questions.stem: An estate has a fiscal year ending June 30. Which statement about estate tax years is correct?
options: An estate must use the decedent's prior tax year
An estate must use a calendar year like trusts generally must
An estate has no tax year
An estate may elect a fiscal year ending on the last day of any month
questions.rationale: Unlike trusts (which generally must use a calendar year), an estate may elect a fiscal year ending on the last day of any month, allowing flexibility in timing income and distributions.

questions.stem: A trust instrument permits the trustee, in its discretion, to allocate capital gains to income or to consistently treat them as distributed. Under the regulations, when may capital gains be included in DNI?
options: Never; capital gains are always excluded from DNI

When, pursuant to the governing instrument and local law or the fiduciary's reasonable and consistent exercise of discretion, capital gains are allocated to income or treated as part of a distribution
Only if the trust is a grantor trust
Only in the year of termination
questions.rationale: Generally capital gains are allocated to corpus and excluded from DNI, but Reg. 1.643(a)-3 allows their inclusion when allocated to income, consistently treated as distributed, or actually distributed under a reasonable and consistently applied policy.

questions.stem: A trust or estate is allowed an exemption on Form 1041. What is the exemption amount for a simple trust versus an estate?
options: A simple trust receives $300 and an estate receives $600
Both receive $4,700
Both receive $600
A complex trust receives $600 and an estate receives $100
questions.rationale: Under Section 642(b), the personal exemption is $600 for an estate, $300 for a simple trust (required to distribute all income), and $100 for a complex trust.

questions.stem: A trust has high undistributed taxable income. Compared to individuals, trust income tax brackets are:
options: Identical to single individuals
Highly compressed, reaching the top marginal rate at a relatively low income level
Flat at 21%
Wider, reaching the top rate only at very high income
questions.rationale: Estates and nongrantor trusts face compressed brackets that reach the top ordinary rate (and the net investment income tax threshold) at a low income level, incentivizing distributions to beneficiaries in lower brackets.

questions.stem: Which form does a tax-exempt organization with gross receipts normally over $200,000 or total assets over $500,000 generally file?
options: Form 990-N (e-Postcard)
Form 990
Form 1065
Form 1120
questions.rationale: Exempt organizations file in the 990 series based on size: Form 990-N (e-Postcard) for very small organizations, Form 990-EZ for mid-size, and full Form 990 for larger organizations exceeding the gross receipts/asset thresholds.

questions.stem: A tax-exempt organization conducts a regularly carried-on trade or business unrelated to its exempt purpose, generating $25,000 of net income. What is the tax consequence?
options: The organization loses its exemption automatically
No tax because the organization is exempt
The income is taxed at individual rates
The income is unrelated business taxable income (UBTI), reported on Form 990-T and taxed at corporate rates after a $1,000 specific deduction
questions.rationale: Sections 511-513 impose the unrelated business income tax on net income from a trade or business regularly carried on that is not substantially related to the exempt purpose, reported on Form 990-T with a $1,000 specific deduction.

questions.stem: A private foundation fails to distribute the required minimum amount (generally about 5% of net investment asset value) for charitable purposes by the end of the following year. Which excise tax applies?
options: The Section 4942 tax on undistributed income (failure to meet the distribution requirement)
The Section 4941 self-dealing tax
The Section 511 UBIT
The Section 4940 tax on net investment income
questions.rationale: Private foundations must meet a minimum distribution requirement (generally 5% of investment assets); failure triggers the Section 4942 excise tax on undistributed income, which increases if not corrected.

questions.stem: A private foundation pays an excise tax on its net investment income. Under current law (post-2019), what is the rate?
options: A flat 5% rate
A flat 21% rate
A two-tier rate of 1% or 2%
A flat 1.39% rate on net investment income
questions.rationale: The Taxpayer Certainty and Disaster Tax Relief Act of 2019 replaced the two-tier (1%/2%) excise tax with a single flat 1.39% tax on a private foundation's net investment income under Section 4940.

questions.stem: A disqualified person engages in a sale of property with a private foundation. Which excise tax regime applies to this transaction?
options: Section 4941 self-dealing excise tax on the disqualified person
No tax because related-party sales are permitted
Section 4942 undistributed income tax
Section 4940 net investment income tax
questions.rationale: Section 4941 imposes excise taxes on acts of self-dealing (such as sales, leases, or loans) between a private foundation and a disqualified person, applying even when terms are fair, with initial and additional taxes for failure to correct.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a private foundation from a public charity for federal tax purposes?
options: Private foundations are taxable entities while public charities are not
Public charities must file Form 990-PF
Public charities have broad public support or perform specific public functions, while private foundations are typically funded by a single source and are subject to additional excise taxes
Private foundations cannot receive deductible contributions
questions.rationale: An organization described in Section 501(c)(3) is presumed a private foundation unless it qualifies as a public charity (through public support or function); private foundations face additional excise taxes and file Form 990-PF.

questions.stem: A new organization seeking recognition of exemption under Section 501(c)(3) generally applies using which form?
options: Form 1023 (or Form 1023-EZ for eligible small organizations)
Form 990
Form 8832
Form SS-4 only
questions.rationale: To be recognized as exempt under Section 501(c)(3), an organization files Form 1023 (or Form 1023-EZ for small eligible organizations); after recognition it files annual 990-series returns.

questions.stem: An exempt organization fails to file a required annual return (Form 990 series) for three consecutive years. What is the consequence?
options: Automatic revocation of tax-exempt status
A small monetary penalty only
Conversion to a private foundation
A one-year suspension of activities
questions.rationale: Section 6033(j) provides for automatic revocation of exempt status when an organization fails to file the required Form 990-series return or notice for three consecutive years; reinstatement requires a new application.

questions.stem: A farmer uses the cash method and elects income averaging. Which schedule is used to report farm income and expenses for a sole proprietor farmer?
options: Schedule F
Form 4835 only
Schedule E
Schedule C
questions.rationale: Sole proprietor farmers report farm operating income and expenses on Schedule F (Form 1040); farm income averaging is computed on Schedule J.

questions.stem: An employer must deposit employment taxes on either a monthly or semiweekly schedule based on a lookback period. What determines the deposit schedule for a given year?
options: Whether the employer is a corporation
The total employment tax liability reported during the lookback period (generally the four quarters ending the prior June 30)
The number of employees only
The current year's actual deposits
questions.rationale: Employers determine their Form 941 deposit schedule by the aggregate employment tax liability in the lookback period; $50,000 or less means monthly, more than $50,000 means semiweekly, with a next-day rule for $100,000 accumulations.

questions.stem: An employer accumulates $120,000 of employment tax liability on a single payday. What deposit rule applies?
options: It may wait until the end of the quarter
The next-day deposit rule requires deposit by the next business day because accumulated liability reached $100,000
Annual deposit on Form 944 is allowed
Monthly deposit is sufficient
questions.rationale: Under the $100,000 next-day deposit rule, any employer (monthly or semiweekly) that accumulates $100,000 or more of employment taxes on any day must deposit by the next business day, and a monthly depositor then becomes semiweekly.

questions.stem: Which form is used to report and pay annual federal unemployment (FUTA) tax?
options: Form 945
Form 943
Form 940
Form 941
questions.rationale: Employers report and pay FUTA annually on Form 940, generally due January 31 (or February 10 if all deposits were timely).

questions.stem: A business reimburses employee travel under an accountable plan. To qualify, the plan must meet which requirements?
options: Have a business connection, require substantiation, and require return of excess advances
Reimburse a flat monthly stipend regardless of expenses
Be limited to executives
Pay reimbursements only at year-end
questions.rationale: Under Reg. 1.62-2, accountable plan reimbursements (business connection, substantiation, and return of excess) are excluded from wages; failing any requirement makes the payments taxable wages subject to withholding.

questions.stem: An estate makes a distribution to a beneficiary in its final tax year, and the estate has excess deductions and a net operating loss carryover. What happens to these excess deductions on termination?
options: They convert to capital losses for the estate only
They must be carried back by the estate
They are lost permanently
They pass through to the beneficiaries succeeding to the property, who may deduct them
questions.rationale: Section 642(h) provides that on the termination of an estate or trust, unused NOL carryovers, capital loss carryovers, and excess deductions are passed through to the beneficiaries succeeding to the property.

questions.stem: A sole proprietor reports net profit of $100,000 on Schedule C. For self-employment tax, the net earnings from self-employment are first multiplied by what factor before applying the SE tax rate?
options: 100% (no adjustment)
92.35% (to account for the deduction equivalent of the employer-share)
questions.rationale: Self-employment tax is computed by multiplying net SE earnings by 92.35%, then applying 12.4% Social Security (up to the wage base) and 2.9% Medicare; one-half of the SE tax is deductible above the line.

questions.stem: A C corporation has a short tax year because it was newly formed on March 1 and elected a calendar year, so its first return covers March 1 through December 31. How is its tax generally computed for a short period due to a change in accounting period (not initial year)?
options: By ignoring the short period
By annualizing the short-period income, computing tax on the annualized amount, then prorating that tax back to the short period
By prorating the annual tax evenly
By using the prior owner's tax
questions.rationale: When a short period results from a change in accounting period, Section 443 requires annualizing the short-period income, computing the tax on the annualized figure, and then multiplying by the ratio of short-period months to 12; an initial or final short year generally does not require annualization.

questions.stem: A business pays a worker who is a statutory employee (such as certain full-time life insurance sales agents). How are the worker's earnings treated?
options: Treated identically to a partner
No reporting is required
Reported on Form W-2 with Social Security and Medicare withheld, but the worker deducts business expenses on Schedule C
Reported only on Form 1099-NEC with no FICA
questions.rationale: Statutory employees (e.g., certain drivers, full-time life insurance agents, home workers, traveling salespersons) receive Form W-2 with FICA withheld but may deduct trade or business expenses on Schedule C.

questions.stem: Which return does a single-member LLC owned by an individual that has not elected corporate treatment use to report its business income?
options: Form 1065
Schedule C on the owner's Form 1040
Form 990
Form 1120-S
questions.rationale: A domestic single-member LLC defaults to a disregarded entity; an individual owner reports the LLC's trade or business on Schedule C (or Schedule E/F as applicable) of Form 1040.

questions.stem: A trust distributes appreciated property to a beneficiary in satisfaction of a specific dollar bequest. What is the general tax consequence to the trust absent a Section 643(e)(3) election?
options: The trust always recognizes gain
No gain is ever recognized on in-kind distributions
The beneficiary recognizes the trust's gain
The trust recognizes gain because distributing property to satisfy a pecuniary (fixed-dollar) obligation is treated as a sale; the beneficiary takes FMV basis
questions.rationale: Distributing appreciated property to satisfy a pecuniary (specific dollar) bequest is treated as a sale by the fiduciary, triggering gain; non-pecuniary in-kind distributions generally are tax-free with carryover basis unless a Section 643(e)(3) election is made.

questions.stem: A 65-day rule election is available to certain trusts and estates. What does this election permit?
options: Treating distributions made within the first 65 days of the following tax year as if made on the last day of the prior tax year
Extending the trust's tax year by 65 days
Deferring all income for 65 days
Filing the return 65 days late without penalty
questions.rationale: The Section 663(b) 65-day rule lets a complex trust or estate elect to treat distributions made within 65 days after the close of the tax year as paid on the last day of that prior year, aiding income shifting to beneficiaries.

questions.stem: An employer fails to deposit $10,000 of payroll taxes that were due. The deposit is made 12 days late. Which penalty tier under Section 6656 generally applies?
options: 2% for deposits 1-5 days late
10% for deposits 16 or more days late
5% for deposits 6-15 days late
15% for amounts not paid within 10 days of an IRS notice
questions.rationale: Section 6656 sets graduated failure-to-deposit penalties: 2% (1-5 days late), 5% (6-15 days late), 10% (16+ days late or not deposited via required EFT), and 15% (unpaid 10+ days after notice or demand).

questions.stem: A trust has rental real estate that produces a passive loss. The trust materially participates through its fiduciary's activities. How are the passive activity rules generally applied to the trust?
options: The passive activity loss rules apply to trusts; material participation is generally determined by the activities of the trustee acting in a fiduciary capacity
Trusts are exempt from the passive activity rules
Beneficiaries always determine material participation
Only grantor trusts are subject to passive activity rules
questions.rationale: Section 469 applies to trusts and estates; courts and the IRS generally measure a trust's material participation by the activities of the fiduciary acting in that capacity, affecting whether losses are passive.

questions.stem: A business hires its first employee and must obtain identification for payroll tax purposes. Which number must the business have to file employment tax returns?
options: An Employer Identification Number (EIN)
An Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN)
The owner's Social Security number only
A Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN)
questions.rationale: Any business with employees must have an EIN, obtained on Form SS-4, to report wages, withhold and deposit employment taxes, and file Forms 941/940 and W-2.

questions.stem: A grantor establishes an irrevocable trust but retains a reversionary interest worth more than 5% of the trust's value at inception. What is the income tax effect?
options: The reversion is ignored for income tax
Income is split among beneficiaries
The trust is a separate taxpayer taxed at trust rates
The grantor is treated as the owner of the portion subject to the reversion, so that income is taxed to the grantor
questions.rationale: Section 673 treats the grantor as owner of any portion of a trust in which the grantor holds a reversionary interest exceeding 5% of that portion's value (measured at inception), making the income taxable to the grantor.

questions.stem: A partnership or S corporation pays state taxes under a state pass-through entity tax (PTET) election. What is the general federal benefit of such an election?
options: It exempts the owners from self-employment tax
It eliminates all federal tax on the entity
It converts the entity to a C corporation
The entity deducts the state taxes at the entity level, effectively working around the individual $10,000 SALT cap for the owners
questions.rationale: IRS Notice 2020-75 blessed state pass-through entity taxes; the entity deducts the state tax in computing pass-through income, providing a federal deduction not subject to the $10,000 individual SALT cap.

questions.stem: By what date must an employer furnish Form W-2 to employees and file copies with the Social Security Administration?
options: January 31
April 15
March 15
February 28
questions.rationale: Employers must furnish Form W-2 to employees and file with the Social Security Administration by January 31; Form 1099-NEC has the same January 31 deadline.

questions.stem: A complex trust has DNI of $50,000 and makes a first-tier distribution (required) of $30,000 and a second-tier distribution (discretionary) of $40,000. How is DNI allocated between the tiers?
options: All DNI to first-tier distributions regardless of amount
All $50,000 to second-tier distributions
Equally, $25,000 to each tier
First-tier distributions are deemed to carry out DNI first ($30,000), and the remaining $20,000 of DNI is allocated to second-tier distributions
questions.rationale: Under the tier system, first-tier (required) distributions carry out DNI first; any remaining DNI is allocated to second-tier (discretionary) distributions, with beneficiaries taxed on their share of DNI carried out.

questions.stem: An employer offers a dependent care assistance program. For 2024, what is the maximum amount of employer-provided dependent care benefits generally excludable from an employee's income (married filing jointly)?
questions.rationale: Under Section 129, up to $5,000 of employer-provided dependent care assistance is excludable from income ($2,500 if married filing separately); the temporary $10,500 limit applied only to 2021.

questions.stem: A business provides an employee a qualified transportation fringe benefit (transit pass). Under current law, how is the employer's deduction affected?
options: Generally nondeductible by the employer, though excludable from the employee's income up to the monthly limit
Fully deductible by the employer
Deductible only if the employee includes it in income
Deductible at 50%
questions.rationale: The 2017 tax law disallowed employer deductions for qualified transportation fringe benefits (such as transit and parking), although employees may still exclude amounts up to the indexed monthly limit.

questions.stem: A trust has a charitable contribution made from gross income pursuant to the governing instrument. How does the charitable deduction for a trust differ from that of an individual?
options: Trusts cannot deduct charitable contributions
A trust may deduct charitable contributions without percentage limits if paid from gross income pursuant to the governing instrument under Section 642(c)
Trusts deduct charitable contributions only up to 60% of AGI
Charitable deductions for trusts are limited to $300
questions.rationale: Section 642(c) allows estates and trusts an unlimited charitable deduction for amounts paid (or, in some cases, permanently set aside) for charitable purposes from gross income pursuant to the governing instrument, unlike the percentage limits for individuals.

questions.stem: An employer reimburses an employee's qualified moving expenses in 2024. How are these reimbursements treated for a non-military employee?
options: Excludable from income as a qualified moving expense reimbursement
Taxable wages, because the moving expense exclusion is suspended for non-military taxpayers through 2025
Deductible above the line by the employee
Excludable up to $5,000
questions.rationale: The 2017 tax law suspended the moving expense deduction and exclusion for 2018-2025 except for members of the Armed Forces on qualifying moves; non-military employer reimbursements are taxable wages.

questions.stem: Which schedule of Form 1041 reports the beneficiary's share of income, deductions, and credits from an estate or trust?
options: Schedule K-1 (Form 1065)
Schedule C
Schedule SE
Schedule K-1 (Form 1041)
questions.rationale: Estates and trusts pass income to beneficiaries on Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), which beneficiaries use to report their share on their own returns, preserving the character of the income.

questions.stem: An accrual-basis C corporation accrues a year-end bonus to a cash-basis employee who is NOT a related party. To deduct the bonus in the accrual year, by when must it generally be paid?
options: Within 12 months
It is never deductible until paid
Within 2.5 months after the close of the tax year, satisfying the all-events test and economic performance
By the end of the accrual year
questions.rationale: Under Reg. 1.404(b)-1T, accrued compensation paid within 2.5 months after year-end is not deferred compensation and is deductible in the accrual year if the all-events test is met; bonuses to related cash-basis owners are deductible only when paid under Section 267.

questions.stem: An accrual-basis corporation owes a year-end accrued salary to a more-than-50% shareholder who is a cash-basis taxpayer. When may the corporation deduct it?
options: Only when the amount is actually paid and includible in the shareholder's income, under the related-party matching rule of Section 267
Never
Within 2.5 months after year-end
When accrued, regardless of payment
questions.rationale: Section 267 requires matching: when a corporation owes an accrued expense to a related cash-basis taxpayer (such as a more-than-50% shareholder), the deduction is deferred until the amount is paid and the payee includes it in income.

questions.stem: A business uses a vehicle and chooses the standard mileage rate rather than actual expenses for the first year the vehicle is placed in service. What does this election allow in later years?
options: It generally permits switching to the actual expense method in later years (using straight-line depreciation thereafter)
It bars any depreciation forever
It requires using actual expenses going forward
It locks the business into the standard mileage rate permanently
questions.rationale: To preserve the option to switch methods, a taxpayer must use the standard mileage rate in the first year the vehicle is placed in service; in later years they may switch to actual expenses but must then use straight-line depreciation.

questions.stem: A trust is required to make estimated tax payments. Unlike most individuals, when is a trust or estate generally exempt from estimated tax requirements?
options: An estate (and certain grantor trusts receiving the residue) is exempt from estimated tax for any tax year ending within 2 years of the decedent's death
Only foreign trusts are exempt
Trusts are always exempt for their first three years
Trusts are never required to make estimated payments
questions.rationale: Under Section 6654(l), estates and certain testamentary trusts are not required to make estimated tax payments for any tax year ending before the date two years after the decedent's death.

questions.stem: A small employer wants to claim a credit for providing health insurance. The small business health care tax credit is generally available to employers with fewer than how many full-time equivalent employees?
questions.rationale: Under Section 45R, the small business health care tax credit is for employers with fewer than 25 FTEs, average annual wages below the indexed threshold, that pay at least 50% of employee premiums through a SHOP plan.

questions.stem: A nonprofit with annual gross receipts normally $50,000 or less may satisfy its annual filing requirement by submitting which item?
options: Form 990-N (the electronic e-Postcard)
The full Form 990
Form 1120
Nothing is required
questions.rationale: Form 990-N (e-Postcard) satisfies the annual filing requirement for small exempt organizations with gross receipts normally $50,000 or less, avoiding automatic revocation under Section 6033(j).

questions.stem: A business pays an attorney $5,000 for legal services and also pays the attorney $40,000 in settlement proceeds on behalf of a claimant. How are these reported?
options: Both amounts on Form 1099-NEC
Both on Form W-2
The $5,000 legal fee on Form 1099-NEC and the $40,000 gross proceeds to the attorney on Form 1099-MISC (Box 10)
Neither requires reporting
questions.rationale: Payments for an attorney's services ($600+) are reported on Form 1099-NEC, while gross proceeds paid to an attorney (e.g., settlements) are reported in Box 10 of Form 1099-MISC regardless of the attorney's services to the payer.

questions.stem: A trust makes a distribution that exceeds DNI. The excess distribution above DNI is generally treated how to the beneficiary?
options: As additional taxable income
As a capital gain
As a deductible loss
As a tax-free distribution of corpus (principal) to the extent it exceeds DNI
questions.rationale: Beneficiary taxation is capped by DNI; distributions exceeding DNI represent a return of trust principal and are generally tax-free to the beneficiary, with the trust's distribution deduction also limited to DNI.

questions.stem: An employer in a credit reduction state pays FUTA. What happens to the FUTA credit in such a state?
options: The credit increases above 5.4%
The maximum 5.4% state credit is reduced, increasing the employer's effective FUTA rate
FUTA is waived entirely
The state pays the difference
questions.rationale: When a state has outstanding federal unemployment loans, it becomes a credit reduction state, and employers there receive a reduced FUTA credit, increasing their effective FUTA tax on the first $7,000 of wages.

questions.stem: A simple trust is defined for tax purposes by which characteristics?
options: It may accumulate income and make charitable contributions
It is always a grantor trust
It must distribute all income currently, make no charitable contributions, and distribute no corpus during the year
It has only one beneficiary
questions.rationale: A simple trust is one that is required to distribute all income currently, makes no charitable contributions, and distributes no principal; any trust failing these tests is a complex trust for that year.

questions.stem: A C corporation has an excess charitable contribution carryover from 5 years ago that will expire this year and a current-year contribution. In what order are contributions deducted against the 10% limit?
options: Only current-year contributions are deductible
Carryovers never expire
Carryovers are used before current-year contributions
Current-year contributions are deducted first, then carryovers from earliest years, with the oldest carryover used first
questions.rationale: A C corporation deducts current-year charitable contributions first against the 10% taxable income limit, then applies carryovers oldest-first; carryovers unused after 5 years are lost.

questions.stem: An estate has gross income of $700 for the year. Is it required to file Form 1041?
options: No, estates never file
Only if it distributes to beneficiaries
No, because gross income is under $1,000
Yes, an estate must file Form 1041 if it has gross income of $600 or more for the tax year
questions.rationale: A domestic estate must file Form 1041 if it has gross income of $600 or more for the tax year (or any beneficiary is a nonresident alien); a trust generally files if it has any taxable income or gross income of $600 or more.

questions.stem: A business owner contributes to a SEP-IRA for employees. For 2024, the maximum employer contribution per employee is generally limited to the lesser of 25% of compensation or what dollar amount?
questions.rationale: For 2024, employer SEP-IRA contributions are limited to the lesser of 25% of an employee's compensation or $69,000 (the Section 415(c) defined contribution limit), with compensation capped at $345,000.

questions.stem: Mateo and Priya form a general partnership. Mateo contributes cash of $40,000 and Priya contributes equipment with a fair market value of $40,000 and an adjusted basis of $25,000. What is Priya's initial outside basis in her partnership interest, assuming no liabilities?
questions.rationale: Under Section 722, a partner's basis in a partnership interest acquired by contribution equals the money plus the adjusted basis of any property contributed.

questions.stem: A two-member LLC taxed as a partnership distributes $10,000 cash to partner Dana, whose outside basis just before the distribution is $6,000. The distribution is a current (nonliquidating) distribution. What are the tax consequences to Dana?
options: No gain; basis reduced to a negative $4,000
$10,000 ordinary income
$4,000 capital gain; basis reduced to zero
No gain; basis reduced to zero and $4,000 carried forward
questions.rationale: Under Section 731(a)(1), a partner recognizes gain only to the extent money distributed exceeds outside basis; basis cannot fall below zero.

questions.stem: A calendar-year partnership has three equal partners, all individuals with December 31 tax years. The partnership wants to use a fiscal year ending June 30 without a business-purpose justification. Which statement is correct about its required tax year?
options: It must generally use a December 31 year-end to match its majority/principal partners absent a valid Section 444 election or business purpose
It may freely elect any fiscal year it chooses
Partnerships have no required tax year
It must use a September 30 year-end
questions.rationale: Section 706(b) requires a partnership to use the tax year of its majority partners, then principal partners, then the least-aggregate-deferral year, unless a business purpose or Section 444 election applies.

questions.stem: Partner Quinn has an outside basis of $20,000. In a single liquidating distribution she receives $5,000 cash and inventory with a partnership inside basis of $9,000 and fair market value of $14,000. What basis does Quinn take in the inventory?
questions.rationale: Under Section 732(b) and (c), in a liquidating distribution the partner reduces basis by cash, and unrealized receivables and inventory take a carryover basis (limited to remaining outside basis).

questions.stem: A guaranteed payment of $30,000 is paid to partner Sora for services, determined without regard to partnership income. How is this treated?
options: A nondeductible distribution of profits
Tax-free return of capital to Sora
A distribution that reduces only Sora's capital account with no income
Deductible by the partnership (if otherwise deductible) and ordinary income to Sora
questions.rationale: Section 707(c) treats guaranteed payments for services or capital as ordinary income to the partner and, if otherwise deductible, as a partnership deduction.

questions.stem: A partnership makes a valid Section 754 election. Partner Wei buys an interest from a departing partner for $80,000 when his share of inside basis of partnership assets is $50,000. What is the effect of the election?
options: Wei's outside basis is reduced to $50,000
