No basis adjustment is permitted
The partnership recognizes $30,000 of gain
A positive Section 743(b) basis adjustment of $30,000 is made to inside basis for Wei's benefit
questions.rationale: A Section 754 election triggers a Section 743(b) adjustment on the transfer of an interest, equal to the difference between the transferee's outside basis and his share of inside basis.

questions.stem: An S corporation has a single shareholder. The corporation owns 100% of a subsidiary that is a qualified subchapter S subsidiary (QSub). For federal income tax purposes, how is the QSub treated?
options: As a disregarded entity whose assets and activities are treated as the parent S corporation's
As a partnership with the parent
As a tax-exempt entity
As a separate C corporation filing its own return
questions.rationale: A QSub election causes the subsidiary to be disregarded, with its items treated as belonging to the parent S corporation.

questions.stem: A partnership distributes property (not money) to a partner whose outside basis is $12,000. The property has a partnership inside basis of $18,000 and fair market value of $25,000 in a nonliquidating distribution. What basis does the partner take in the distributed property?
questions.rationale: Under Section 732(a), distributed property generally takes a carryover basis, but in a current distribution that basis is capped at the partner's outside basis.

questions.stem: A husband and wife jointly operate an unincorporated business and file a joint return. They have elected qualified joint venture treatment. How is the business generally reported?
options: On Form 1120 as a corporation
On two Schedules C, one for each spouse based on their respective interests
On a single Form 1065 partnership return
On a single Schedule C in one spouse's name only
questions.rationale: Under Section 761(f), spouses materially participating in a jointly owned unincorporated business can elect out of partnership treatment and file two Schedules C.

questions.stem: Partner Ravi has a basis in his partnership interest of $0 at year-end and is allocated a $5,000 ordinary loss. He has no amount at risk beyond his basis and is a passive investor. What portion of the loss may he currently deduct?
questions.rationale: Section 704(d) limits a partner's deductible losses to outside basis; disallowed amounts carry forward until basis is restored (at-risk and passive limits may further apply).

questions.stem: A partner contributes property with a built-in gain (FMV $50,000, basis $30,000) to a partnership. Three years later the partnership sells the property for $55,000. Under Section 704(c), how is the $20,000 precontribution built-in gain allocated?
options: Allocated to the non-contributing partners
Allocated equally among all partners by profit ratio
Allocated entirely to the contributing partner
Not recognized because it is a partnership asset
questions.rationale: Section 704(c) requires that built-in gain or loss on contributed property be allocated to the contributing partner to prevent shifting of tax consequences.

questions.stem: What is the due date (without extension) of a calendar-year partnership's Form 1065 for tax year 2024?
options: October 15, 2025
April 15, 2025
March 17, 2025
questions.rationale: Partnership returns are due the 15th day of the third month after the close of the tax year, with weekend/holiday adjustments.

questions.stem: A partnership contributes appreciated property to the partnership; later, the same property is distributed to a different partner within seven years of contribution. What rule may apply?
options: No special rule applies after one year
The constructive ownership rules of Section 318
The disguised sale rules under Section 707
The Section 704(c)(1)(B) mixing-bowl rule, possibly triggering gain to the contributing partner
questions.rationale: Under Section 704(c)(1)(B), distributing 704(c) property to a non-contributing partner within seven years triggers recognition of the remaining built-in gain or loss by the contributor.

questions.stem: An LLC with two members has not filed any entity classification election. For 2024 it wants to be taxed as a C corporation effective January 1, 2024. What must it do?
options: Nothing; multi-member LLCs are corporations by default
File Form SS-4 to change classification
File Form 8832 electing association status, generally effective no more than 75 days before filing
File Form 2553 only
questions.rationale: Form 8832 is used to elect association (corporation) status; effective dates are limited to 75 days retroactive or 12 months prospective from the filing date.

questions.stem: A partner receives a current distribution of two parcels of land. The total basis to be allocated to the parcels (after reducing for any cash) is $10,000, but the parcels have partnership inside bases of $7,000 and $8,000 (total $15,000). How is the $10,000 allocated between the parcels using the required rules?
options: Allocate based on relative inside bases: $4,667 and $5,333
$10,000 to the higher-basis parcel only
$7,000 and $3,000 based on contribution order
$5,000 to each parcel equally
questions.rationale: Under Section 732(c), if remaining basis is less than total inside basis, the decrease is allocated among the properties in proportion to their adjusted bases.

questions.stem: For 2024, a C corporation has taxable income of $400,000. What is its regular federal income tax before credits?
questions.rationale: Since the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, C corporations pay a flat 21% federal income tax rate.

questions.stem: A C corporation receives $100,000 of dividends from a domestic corporation in which it owns 25% of the stock. What is its dividends-received deduction for 2024?
questions.rationale: Section 243 allows a 50% DRD for under-20% ownership, 65% for 20%-to-under-80%, and 100% for 80%-or-more affiliated dividends.

questions.stem: In 2024 a business places in service $3,200,000 of qualifying Section 179 property. The 2024 Section 179 dollar limit is $1,220,000 and the phase-out threshold is $3,050,000. What is the maximum Section 179 deduction (before any taxable income limit)?
questions.rationale: Section 179 reduces the dollar limit by the amount total qualifying purchases exceed the investment threshold, dollar for dollar.

questions.stem: What is the MACRS recovery period for nonresidential real property placed in service in 2024 (using the general depreciation system)?
options: 15 years
40 years
39 years
27.5 years
questions.rationale: Under MACRS GDS, nonresidential real property uses a 39-year straight-line recovery period; residential rental uses 27.5 years.

questions.stem: Which depreciation convention generally applies to MACRS personal property (5- or 7-year) when more than 40% of property is not placed in service in the last quarter?
options: Half-year convention
Mid-quarter convention
Full-year convention
Mid-month convention
questions.rationale: MACRS personal property uses the half-year convention by default, switching to mid-quarter only if more than 40% of basis is placed in service in the fourth quarter.

questions.stem: A business sells Section 1245 property (machinery) for $40,000. Its original cost was $50,000 and accumulated depreciation was $35,000 (adjusted basis $15,000). How much of the $25,000 gain is recaptured as ordinary income under Section 1245?
questions.rationale: Section 1245 recaptures gain as ordinary income to the extent of the lesser of the recognized gain or prior depreciation; here gain ($25,000) is less than depreciation, so all is ordinary.

questions.stem: A taxpayer sells depreciable real property (Section 1250) used in a business at a gain. Straight-line depreciation was used. For an individual, how is the portion of gain equal to depreciation generally taxed?
options: Fully excluded from income
As short-term capital gain
As unrecaptured Section 1250 gain taxed at a maximum 25% rate
All as ordinary income under Section 1250 recapture
questions.rationale: For real property depreciated straight-line, there is no ordinary 1250 recapture, but the depreciation-related gain is unrecaptured Section 1250 gain taxed up to 25%.

questions.stem: A business trades in a delivery truck used 100% for business for a new truck in 2024. Both are tangible personal property. How are like-kind exchange rules applied?
options: No gain or loss is ever recognized on trade-ins
Section 1031 no longer applies to personal property; the exchange is generally a taxable sale and purchase
Gain is deferred under Section 1031 like-kind exchange treatment
The truck qualifies for tax-free treatment under Section 351
questions.rationale: Since 2018, Section 1031 like-kind exchange deferral applies only to real property; personal property exchanges are fully taxable.

questions.stem: What MACRS recovery period applies to qualified improvement property (QIP) placed in service in 2024 under GDS?
options: 39 years
7 years
15 years
27.5 years
questions.rationale: The CARES Act corrected QIP to a 15-year GDS recovery period (straight-line), allowing bonus depreciation eligibility.

questions.stem: A business places amortizable Section 197 intangibles (purchased goodwill) in service. Over what period is goodwill amortized?
options: 39 years straight-line
5 years straight-line
15 years straight-line
Not amortizable
questions.rationale: Section 197 requires straight-line amortization of acquired goodwill and similar intangibles over 15 years.

questions.stem: A new business incurs $4,000 of qualifying start-up costs before opening. For 2024, how much may it generally elect to deduct in the first year (assuming total start-up costs are under $50,000)?
options: Up to $5,000, so the full $4,000 is deductible currently
$0; all must be capitalized
$2,000 only
$1,000 only
questions.rationale: Section 195 permits a first-year deduction of up to $5,000 of start-up costs (phased out dollar-for-dollar above $50,000), with the remainder amortized over 180 months.

questions.stem: For 2024, what is the gross-receipts threshold (3-year average) below which a C corporation may generally use the cash method of accounting and is exempt from the UNICAP and interest-limitation small-business rules?
options: $30 million
$50 million
$10 million
$1 million
questions.rationale: Under Section 448(c), the 2024 inflation-adjusted average gross receipts threshold is $30 million for cash method eligibility and related small-business exceptions.

questions.stem: An accrual-method business performs services and bills a customer $8,000 in December 2024; payment is received in February 2025. When is the $8,000 included in income?
options: 2024, when the right to income is fixed and the amount is determinable
Split evenly between 2024 and 2025
Only when the customer's check clears
2025, when cash is received
questions.rationale: Accrual-method taxpayers include income when all events have occurred fixing the right to receive it and the amount is determinable.

questions.stem: A taxpayer sells business real property on the installment method, recognizing gain as payments are received. The property had been depreciated and is subject to Section 1245 recapture of $20,000. How is the recapture reported?
options: Recognized in full in the year of sale as ordinary income, regardless of payments received
Deferred until the final payment
Treated as capital gain over the installment period
Spread over the installment period as payments are received
questions.rationale: Section 453(i) requires that Section 1245/1250 recapture be recognized in the year of an installment sale, not spread over payments.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has a net Section 1231 gain of $15,000 for 2024. In the prior five years she had $9,000 of unrecaptured net Section 1231 losses. How is the current-year gain characterized?
options: All $15,000 is ordinary income
$9,000 is long-term capital gain and $6,000 is ordinary income
$9,000 is ordinary income and $6,000 is long-term capital gain
All $15,000 is long-term capital gain
questions.rationale: The Section 1231(c) lookback rule recharacterizes net 1231 gain as ordinary income to the extent of nonrecaptured net 1231 losses from the preceding five years.

questions.stem: Property held primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of business is best classified as what for tax purposes?
options: Inventory (ordinary income property)
A capital asset
Section 1231 property
Section 1250 property
questions.rationale: Inventory and property held primarily for sale to customers are excluded from capital asset treatment and produce ordinary income.

questions.stem: A sole proprietor reports business income on Schedule C. The business has net profit of $80,000. For self-employment tax purposes, what amount is multiplied by 92.35% to compute net earnings from self-employment?
options: The gross receipts
The net profit reduced by the standard deduction
The $80,000 net profit
The net profit plus health insurance
questions.rationale: Schedule SE applies the 92.35% factor to net profit to arrive at net earnings from self-employment subject to the 15.3% SE tax (with the wage base cap on the Social Security portion).

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an eligible shareholder of an S corporation?
options: A resident alien individual
A U.S. citizen individual
A qualifying single-member LLC owned by an eligible individual (disregarded)
A partnership
questions.rationale: Under Section 1361, S corporation shareholders are limited to U.S. individuals, estates, certain trusts, and certain tax-exempt organizations; partnerships and corporations cannot be shareholders.

questions.stem: An S corporation may have only one class of stock. Which of the following violates the single-class-of-stock requirement?
options: Shares carrying different rights to distributions and liquidation proceeds
Differences in voting rights among common shares
Stock with identical economic rights but different par values
Stock held by different types of eligible shareholders
questions.rationale: Under Section 1361(b)(1)(D), an S corporation can have only one class of stock based on identical rights to distribution and liquidation; voting differences are allowed.

questions.stem: A calendar-year C corporation wants to be an S corporation effective January 1, 2025. By when must it file a timely Form 2553?
options: By March 15, 2025 (within 2 months and 15 days of the start of the tax year)
By December 31, 2024
By April 15, 2025
By January 1, 2026
questions.rationale: An S election is timely if filed by the 15th day of the third month of the tax year it is to take effect, or any time in the prior tax year.

questions.stem: An S corporation shareholder has stock basis of $10,000 and debt basis of $4,000 (a direct loan to the corporation). The corporation allocates a $12,000 ordinary loss to her. How much loss may she deduct currently?
questions.rationale: Under Section 1366(d), an S shareholder deducts losses to the extent of stock basis plus basis in direct loans to the corporation; here the full $12,000 is allowed.

questions.stem: An S corporation pays a reasonable salary to its sole shareholder-employee and also makes distributions. Why is the reasonable-compensation requirement important to the IRS?
options: Distributions are subject to self-employment tax
S corporations cannot pay any salary
Salary is subject to employment taxes, while distributions generally are not, so understating salary avoids payroll tax
Salary is exempt from all payroll taxes
questions.rationale: Because S corporation distributions escape FICA tax, the IRS requires reasonable wages for shareholder-employees who provide services to prevent payroll tax avoidance.

questions.stem: An S corporation shareholder begins the year with $15,000 stock basis. The corporation passes through $8,000 of ordinary income, $2,000 of tax-exempt income, and a $5,000 distribution. What is the shareholder's year-end stock basis?
questions.rationale: Stock basis increases by income (taxable and tax-exempt) and decreases by distributions: $15,000 + $8,000 + $2,000 - $5,000 = $20,000.

questions.stem: Which form does an S corporation file to report its income and the shareholders' distributive shares?
options: Form 1065
Form 1120-S with Schedules K-1
Form 1041
Form 1120
questions.rationale: Form 1120-S is the S corporation income tax return, accompanied by Schedules K-1 reporting each shareholder's pro rata share.

questions.stem: How is an S corporation's income generally allocated among shareholders?
options: Based on services performed
Entirely to the majority shareholder
Per share, per day (pro rata based on stock ownership)
By special allocations agreed in an operating agreement
questions.rationale: Section 1377 requires S corporation items to be allocated pro rata on a per-share, per-day basis; special allocations are not permitted.

questions.stem: Xavier transfers property with a basis of $40,000 and FMV of $100,000 to a newly formed corporation solely in exchange for 100% of its stock. He controls the corporation immediately after. What gain does Xavier recognize?
questions.rationale: Section 351 provides nonrecognition when property is transferred to a corporation solely for stock and the transferors are in control (80%) immediately afterward.

questions.stem: In a Section 351 transfer, the transferor contributes property (basis $30,000, FMV $50,000) and receives stock worth $40,000 plus $10,000 cash (boot). How much gain does the transferor recognize?
questions.rationale: Under Section 351(b), when boot is received, gain is recognized to the extent of the lesser of realized gain or the boot received.

questions.stem: A C corporation has current E&P of $20,000 and accumulated E&P of a deficit of $50,000. It distributes $30,000 cash to shareholders. How much is treated as a taxable dividend?
questions.rationale: A distribution is a dividend to the extent of current E&P first; a negative accumulated E&P does not net against positive current E&P for this purpose.

questions.stem: A corporation completely liquidates, distributing assets to its sole individual shareholder. The assets have FMV of $200,000; the shareholder's stock basis is $120,000. How does the shareholder treat the liquidation?
options: As a sale of stock, recognizing $80,000 gain
As a tax-free return of capital
As an ordinary dividend of $200,000
As a $120,000 loss
questions.rationale: Section 331 treats a complete corporate liquidation as a sale or exchange of stock by the shareholder, producing capital gain or loss.

questions.stem: Which corporation may be subject to the personal holding company (PHC) tax?
options: A closely held corporation deriving most income from passive sources such as dividends, interest, and rents
A widely held public corporation with diverse operations
An S corporation
A tax-exempt charity
questions.rationale: The PHC tax applies to closely held C corporations where 5 or fewer individuals own more than 50% and at least 60% of income is PHC income (passive).

questions.stem: What is the employee and employer Social Security tax rate (each) on wages up to the wage base for 2024?
questions.rationale: The OASDI (Social Security) rate is 6.2% for the employee and 6.2% for the employer on wages up to the annual wage base.

questions.stem: An employer pays an employee wages of $250,000 in 2024 (single). Beyond the regular Medicare tax, what additional withholding applies once wages exceed $200,000?
options: An extra 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax withholding on wages above $200,000
An extra 6.2% Social Security tax
An extra 3.8% net investment income tax withholding
No additional withholding
questions.rationale: Employers withhold an additional 0.9% Medicare tax on an employee's wages over $200,000, without regard to filing status.

questions.stem: A business willfully fails to remit withheld payroll taxes (trust fund taxes) to the IRS. Which penalty may be assessed against a responsible person individually?
options: The accuracy-related penalty
The failure-to-file penalty only
No personal liability is possible
The Trust Fund Recovery Penalty equal to 100% of the unpaid trust fund taxes
questions.rationale: The Section 6672 Trust Fund Recovery Penalty imposes personal liability equal to 100% of the unpaid withheld taxes on responsible persons who willfully fail to remit them.

questions.stem: A worker classification dispute arises. Which factor most strongly indicates that a worker is an employee rather than an independent contractor?
options: The worker provides services to multiple clients
The worker can realize a profit or loss
The worker provides his own tools
The business controls how, when, and where the work is performed (behavioral control)
questions.rationale: The IRS evaluates behavioral control, financial control, and the relationship of the parties; strong behavioral control indicates an employee.

questions.stem: Which form is used to report nonemployee compensation of $600 or more paid to an independent contractor for 2024?
options: Form 1099-MISC
Form W-2
Form 1099-DIV
Form 1099-NEC
questions.rationale: Since 2020, nonemployee compensation of $600 or more is reported on Form 1099-NEC rather than Form 1099-MISC.

questions.stem: An employer files Form 941 and accumulates more than $50,000 in employment tax liability during the lookback period. Which deposit schedule generally applies?
options: Semiweekly deposit schedule
Monthly deposit schedule
No deposits required
Annual deposit schedule
questions.rationale: Employment tax deposit frequency depends on the lookback period: $50,000 or less is monthly, and more than $50,000 is semiweekly.

questions.stem: Which income tax return is generally used by a domestic estate or trust?
options: Form 1041
Form 1040
Form 1065
Form 990
questions.rationale: Estates and trusts report income on Form 1041, with beneficiaries receiving Schedule K-1 for distributed amounts.

questions.stem: A trust has gross income of $5,000 for the year. What is the filing threshold that generally requires a trust to file Form 1041?
options: Gross income of $10,000 or more
Trusts never have to file
Gross income of $100 or more
Gross income of $600 or more (or any taxable income)
questions.rationale: A trust must file Form 1041 if it has any taxable income, gross income of $600 or more, or a nonresident alien beneficiary.

questions.stem: A complex trust has distributable net income (DNI) of $40,000 and distributes $50,000 to its sole beneficiary. How much is taxable to the beneficiary, and how does the trust treat the distribution?
options: $0 to the beneficiary; the trust pays all the tax
$40,000 to the beneficiary; trust's distribution deduction is limited to DNI of $40,000
$10,000 to the beneficiary; trust deducts $10,000
$50,000 to the beneficiary; trust deducts $50,000
questions.rationale: DNI sets the ceiling on the trust's distribution deduction and on the income taxable to beneficiaries; distributions exceeding DNI are generally a return of corpus.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of distributable net income (DNI) for trusts and estates?
options: To set the trustee's compensation
To limit and characterize the income distribution deduction and the amount taxable to beneficiaries
To compute the alternative minimum tax exemption
To determine the entity's gross estate
questions.rationale: DNI under Section 643 limits the distribution deduction and allocates the character of income passed through to beneficiaries.

questions.stem: A simple trust is required to distribute all of its income currently. Which statement is correct?
options: A simple trust pays tax on all its income at the trust level
A simple trust may accumulate income
A simple trust may distribute corpus and still remain simple
A simple trust must distribute all accounting income currently and may not make charitable contributions
questions.rationale: A simple trust must distribute all income currently, make no charitable gifts, and distribute no principal; otherwise it is treated as a complex trust.

questions.stem: An estate has income in respect of a decedent (IRD) of $15,000 collected after death. How is IRD treated?
options: It is excluded from gross income entirely
It is taxed only on the decedent's final return
It is always tax-free to the estate
It is taxable to the recipient (estate or beneficiary) with the same character it would have had to the decedent
questions.rationale: Income in respect of a decedent is taxed to the estate or beneficiary who receives it, keeping its original character (e.g., ordinary or capital).

questions.stem: An estate has a tax year that need not be a calendar year. What flexibility does an estate have that a trust generally does not?
options: An estate may elect a fiscal year-end
An estate may avoid filing entirely
An estate may use a 16-month tax year
An estate is exempt from income tax
questions.rationale: Estates may choose a fiscal year-end, but trusts (other than certain charitable trusts) generally must use a calendar year.

questions.stem: A Section 501(c)(3) organization operates an unrelated business regularly that is not substantially related to its exempt purpose. What may result?
options: Automatic loss of exempt status
A penalty equal to the gross receipts
No tax because charities are always exempt
Unrelated business income tax (UBIT) on the net income from the unrelated activity
questions.rationale: Unrelated business taxable income is taxed under Sections 511-514; the organization files Form 990-T and pays tax at corporate or trust rates.

questions.stem: How much of unrelated business gross income may an exempt organization deduct as a specific deduction before computing UBIT?
questions.rationale: Section 512(b)(12) allows a $1,000 specific deduction in computing unrelated business taxable income.

questions.stem: A small tax-exempt organization with gross receipts normally $50,000 or less is generally required to file what?
options: Form 990-EZ
Form 990
Form 990-N (e-Postcard)
Nothing at all
questions.rationale: Form 990-N (e-Postcard) is the annual electronic notice for the smallest exempt organizations; failure to file for three consecutive years revokes exemption.

questions.stem: An estate is in its final tax year and has excess deductions on termination. How are these treated for the beneficiaries?
options: They are lost permanently
They pass through to the beneficiaries succeeding to the estate property
They convert to a charitable deduction
They become a carryover to the estate's nonexistent next year
questions.rationale: Under Section 642(h), excess deductions and certain carryovers on the termination of an estate or trust pass through to the beneficiaries.

questions.stem: For tax years beginning in 2022 and later, how is adjusted taxable income (ATI) computed for the Section 163(j) limitation with respect to depreciation and amortization?
options: ATI equals gross receipts
ATI adds back depreciation and amortization
ATI is computed without adding back depreciation and amortization (a stricter EBIT-based measure)
ATI ignores all interest expense
questions.rationale: Beginning in 2022, depreciation and amortization are no longer added back in computing ATI, tightening the Section 163(j) limitation.

questions.stem: Business meals provided at a restaurant in 2024 that are ordinary and necessary are generally deductible at what percentage?
questions.rationale: After the temporary 100% restaurant deduction expired, business meals reverted to the general 50% limitation for 2024.

questions.stem: Under current law, how are business entertainment expenses (e.g., tickets to a sporting event for clients) treated for 2024?
options: Fully deductible
50% deductible
Generally nondeductible
Deductible only if over $25
questions.rationale: Since the TCJA, entertainment expenses are generally nondeductible, although certain business meals remain 50% deductible.

questions.stem: A business gives holiday gifts to its clients. What is the maximum deductible amount per recipient per year for business gifts?
questions.rationale: Under Section 274(b), deductions for business gifts are limited to $25 per recipient per year.

questions.stem: The qualified business income (QBI) deduction under Section 199A generally allows eligible taxpayers to deduct up to what percentage of qualified business income?
questions.rationale: The QBI deduction is generally 20% of qualified business income, subject to taxable income thresholds, W-2 wage/UBIA limits, and SSTB rules.

questions.stem: Above the taxable income thresholds, the QBI deduction for a non-SSTB business is limited to the greater of 50% of W-2 wages, or 25% of W-2 wages plus what?
options: 25% of gross receipts
2.5% of net income
10% of payroll taxes
2.5% of the unadjusted basis of qualified property (UBIA)
questions.rationale: For high-income taxpayers, the QBI deduction is limited to the greater of 50% of W-2 wages, or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of qualified property UBIA.

questions.stem: For a high-income taxpayer above the thresholds, income from a specified service trade or business (SSTB) such as law or accounting is treated how for QBI purposes?
options: Always fully eligible regardless of income
Phased out and generally not eligible for the QBI deduction
Eligible only at 10%
Eligible for the full 20% deduction
questions.rationale: For SSTBs, the QBI deduction phases out as taxable income rises through the threshold range and is fully disallowed above the upper limit.

questions.stem: A self-employed individual establishes a SEP-IRA. For 2024, the maximum deductible contribution is generally the lesser of 25% of net self-employment earnings (with adjustments) or what dollar amount?
questions.rationale: For 2024, SEP contributions are limited to the lesser of 25% of compensation (net earnings adjusted) or $69,000.

questions.stem: A small employer establishes a SIMPLE IRA plan. What is the general employer contribution requirement?
options: A contribution equal to 25% of each employee's salary
Either a matching contribution up to 3% of compensation or a 2% nonelective contribution for eligible employees
A flat 10% of payroll
No employer contribution is required
questions.rationale: SIMPLE IRA employers must either match up to 3% of compensation (with limited reductions) or contribute 2% nonelective for eligible employees.

questions.stem: An employer provides group-term life insurance to employees. How much coverage is generally excludable from an employee's income?
options: All coverage regardless of amount
None; it is always taxable
The first $50,000 of coverage
The first $25,000 of coverage
questions.rationale: Section 79 excludes the cost of up to $50,000 of group-term life insurance; the cost of excess coverage is taxable using IRS uniform premium tables.

questions.stem: Which of the following employer-provided benefits is generally excludable from an employee's gross income as a working condition fringe benefit?
options: Business use of an employer-provided vehicle
Cash bonuses
Gift cards redeemable for cash
Personal vacation paid by the employer
questions.rationale: A working condition fringe benefit (Section 132) is property or services that would be deductible by the employee if paid personally, such as business use of a company car.

questions.stem: A business suffers a federally declared disaster loss to business property with an adjusted basis of $40,000 and decline in FMV of $30,000, fully destroyed. No insurance recovery. What is the deductible casualty loss for the fully destroyed business property?
options: $30,000 (decline in FMV)
$35,000 (average)
$40,000 (adjusted basis)
questions.rationale: For completely destroyed business property, the loss equals adjusted basis; for partial destruction it is the lesser of basis or decline in FMV (less any recovery).

questions.stem: A merchant uses the LIFO inventory method. In a period of rising prices, what is the general effect on taxable income compared with FIFO?
options: LIFO and FIFO produce identical income
LIFO produces lower taxable income because newer, higher costs are matched against revenue
LIFO eliminates cost of goods sold
LIFO produces higher taxable income
questions.rationale: In an inflationary environment, LIFO assigns the latest higher costs to COGS, reducing gross profit and taxable income relative to FIFO.

questions.stem: Under the uniform capitalization (UNICAP) rules of Section 263A, certain costs must be capitalized into inventory. Which type of business is generally exempt under the small-business exception for 2024?
options: Any C corporation
A business with more than 500 employees
Only sole proprietorships
A business with average annual gross receipts of $30 million or less (3-year average)
questions.rationale: The Section 263A small-business exception applies to taxpayers meeting the Section 448(c) gross-receipts test ($30 million for 2024).

questions.stem: The standard mileage rate for business use of an automobile in 2024 is 67 cents per mile. A sole proprietor drives 10,000 business miles. What is the standard mileage deduction?
questions.rationale: The 2024 business standard mileage rate is 67 cents per mile; 10,000 x $0.67 = $6,700.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who uses the actual expense method for a business vehicle in the first year it is placed in service generally may NOT do what in a later year?
options: Deduct business parking and tolls
Switch to the standard mileage rate for that vehicle
Claim depreciation
Continue using actual expenses
questions.rationale: Choosing the standard mileage rate must occur in the first year a vehicle is used for business; using actual expenses (with depreciation) in year one locks the taxpayer out of the standard mileage rate later.

questions.stem: A C corporation pays estimated tax. To avoid an underpayment penalty, a corporation (not a large corporation) must generally pay the lesser of 100% of the current year's tax or what?
options: 110% of the prior year's tax
80% of the current year's tax
90% of the prior year's tax
100% of the prior year's tax (if it filed a return showing tax for a full 12-month year)
questions.rationale: Corporations generally must pay the lesser of 100% of the current year's tax or 100% of the prior year's tax; large corporations may only use the prior-year safe harbor for the first installment.

questions.stem: Which form does a C corporation use to figure and pay estimated tax penalties or to determine required installments?
options: Form 2220
Form 2210
Form 1120-W worksheet only
Form 8862
questions.rationale: Form 2220 computes the corporate underpayment of estimated tax penalty.

questions.stem: For 2023 and later tax years, the corporate alternative minimum tax (CAMT) imposes a 15% minimum tax on the adjusted financial statement income of which corporations?
options: Applicable corporations with average annual adjusted financial statement income over $1 billion
All C corporations
S corporations only
Corporations with gross receipts over $30 million
questions.rationale: The Inflation Reduction Act CAMT imposes a 15% tax on adjusted financial statement income of corporations averaging over $1 billion in such income.

questions.stem: An S corporation incurs organizational expenditures of $3,000 in its first year. How may these costs generally be treated?
options: Added to shareholder basis directly
Elect to deduct up to $5,000 in the first year (with the rest amortized over 180 months)
Capitalized and never deducted
Deducted only when the corporation dissolves
questions.rationale: Section 248 allows a first-year deduction of up to $5,000 of organizational expenditures, with the balance amortized over 15 years.

questions.stem: A partner contributes services (not property) to a partnership in exchange for a capital interest. What is the tax consequence to the service partner?
options: Tax-free under Section 721
The fair market value of the capital interest received is ordinary compensation income
No income; services are never taxable
A capital gain equal to the interest's value
questions.rationale: A capital interest received for services is taxable as ordinary compensation equal to its fair market value; Section 721 does not protect contributions of services.

questions.stem: A partnership has a technical termination concern when a sale of partnership interests occurs. Under current law (post-TCJA), what is the rule regarding technical terminations under former Section 708(b)(1)(B)?
options: Technical terminations were repealed; a sale of 50% or more of interests no longer terminates the partnership
Technical terminations apply only to LLCs
A sale of 50% or more of interests within 12 months terminates the partnership
Any sale of an interest terminates the partnership
questions.rationale: Effective 2018, the technical termination rule of former Section 708(b)(1)(B) was repealed; partnerships terminate only when no part of any business continues to be carried on by any partners.

questions.stem: A partner sells equipment to his own partnership in which he owns a 60% interest, recognizing a loss. How is the loss treated under the related-party rules?
options: Carried back two years
Deductible only as a capital loss
Fully deductible
Disallowed because the partner owns more than 50% of the partnership
questions.rationale: Section 707(b) disallows losses on transactions between a partnership and a partner owning, directly or indirectly, more than 50% of the capital or profits interest.

questions.stem: A C corporation makes a loan to its sole shareholder at no interest. What tax issue may arise?
options: No issue; interest-free loans are always permitted
Below-market loan rules may impute interest income to the corporation and a dividend to the shareholder
The corporation may deduct the foregone interest
The shareholder recognizes a capital gain
questions.rationale: Section 7872 recharacterizes below-market shareholder loans, imputing interest income to the lender corporation and a dividend (and deemed interest payment) involving the shareholder.

questions.stem: For 2024, at what taxable income level does a trust or estate reach the top 37% ordinary income tax bracket (approximately)?
questions.rationale: Trusts and estates have highly compressed brackets, reaching the 37% rate at roughly $15,200 of taxable income for 2024.

questions.stem: A trust has undistributed net investment income and adjusted gross income exceeding the threshold for the net investment income tax (NIIT). The 2024 trust NIIT threshold is the dollar amount at which the top bracket begins (about $15,200). What rate applies to the lesser of undistributed NII or the excess AGI?
questions.rationale: The 3.8% NIIT applies to trusts on the lesser of undistributed net investment income or AGI exceeding the top-bracket threshold.

questions.stem: A charitable remainder trust (CRT) is generally what for income tax purposes during its term?
options: Fully taxable on all income annually
A grantor trust always
Generally exempt from income tax, with distributions taxed to the income beneficiary under a tiered system
Taxed as a C corporation
questions.rationale: Qualifying charitable remainder trusts are generally exempt from income tax; payouts to beneficiaries carry out income under the four-tier system of Section 664(b).

questions.stem: A partnership distributes only cash of $7,000 to a partner with an outside basis of $7,000 in a nonliquidating distribution. What gain does the partner recognize?
options: An amount equal to the partner's profit share
questions.rationale: Under Section 731(a), a cash distribution produces gain only to the extent it exceeds outside basis; an equal amount is a tax-free return of capital.

questions.stem: A partnership has a Section 754 election in effect and distributes property to a partner, creating a basis disparity. Which Code section governs the resulting adjustment to the basis of remaining partnership property?
options: Section 743(b)
Section 734(b)
Section 704(c)
Section 751(b)
questions.rationale: With a Section 754 election, distributions trigger Section 734(b) adjustments to the basis of the partnership's remaining property; transfers of interests trigger Section 743(b).

questions.stem: A corporation makes a Section 1244 stock election. An individual original shareholder sells the stock at a loss. What benefit does Section 1244 provide?
options: The loss is disallowed entirely
Up to $50,000 ($100,000 for married filing jointly) of the loss may be treated as an ordinary loss
The entire loss is tax-free
The loss must be a long-term capital loss
questions.rationale: Section 1244 lets original holders of qualifying small business corporation stock deduct losses as ordinary (up to $50,000/$100,000 MFJ), beyond which capital loss treatment applies.

questions.stem: An individual holds qualified small business stock (QSBS) under Section 1202 acquired in 2024 and held more than five years. What is the general gain exclusion percentage on a later sale?
questions.rationale: Section 1202 allows a 100% exclusion of gain on QSBS acquired after September 27, 2010 and held more than five years, subject to the greater of $10 million or 10x basis per-issuer cap.

questions.stem: Which entity files Schedule C as part of an individual's Form 1040?
options: An S corporation
A single-member LLC treated as a disregarded entity owned by an individual
A multi-member LLC
A C corporation
questions.rationale: A disregarded single-member LLC owned by an individual reports its trade or business on Schedule C of the owner's Form 1040.

questions.stem: A controlled group of corporations must share certain tax benefits. Which of the following must generally be apportioned among members of a controlled group?
options: The cost of goods sold
The 21% flat corporate tax rate
The dividends-received deduction percentage
The accumulated earnings credit and certain other limited amounts
questions.rationale: Controlled groups under Section 1561 must share specified tax benefits, including the accumulated earnings credit and certain minimum amounts, to prevent multiplication of benefits.

questions.stem: A partnership reports on the cash method and a partner's K-1 shows a guaranteed payment of $40,000 and an ordinary loss share of $10,000. How does the partner treat these on his return?
options: Ignore the guaranteed payment
Net them to $30,000 of ordinary income
Report $40,000 of ordinary income (guaranteed payment) and separately deduct the $10,000 loss if basis allows
Report $40,000 as capital gain
questions.rationale: A guaranteed payment is ordinary income to the partner; the distributive share of loss is a separate item subject to the loss limitation rules.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a requirement for an S corporation to be valid?
options: It must have at least 200 shareholders
It must be a foreign corporation
It must be publicly traded
It must be a domestic corporation with only allowable shareholders and one class of stock
questions.rationale: Section 1361 requires an S corporation to be a domestic eligible corporation with no more than 100 allowable shareholders and a single class of stock.

questions.stem: Under MACRS, which method is generally used for 5-year and 7-year property (such as computers and office furniture)?
options: 150% declining balance only
Straight-line over the recovery period
Units of production
200% declining balance, switching to straight-line
questions.rationale: MACRS GDS uses 200% declining balance for 3-, 5-, 7-, and 10-year property, switching to straight-line when advantageous.

questions.stem: An S corporation shareholder loaned money to the corporation. The corporation repays part of the loan when the shareholder's debt basis has been reduced below the loan's face amount by prior pass-through losses. What is the consequence?
options: The repayment is a nondeductible dividend
The shareholder may recognize income to the extent the repayment exceeds debt basis
No income; loan repayments are always tax-free
The corporation recognizes gain
questions.rationale: If pass-through losses reduced a shareholder's debt basis, repayments of that debt exceeding the reduced basis are taxable to the shareholder.

questions.stem: A C corporation accrues a bonus to a more-than-50% shareholder-employee but does not pay it within 2.5 months after year-end. When is the bonus deductible?
options: In the accrual year regardless of payment
Half in the accrual year, half when paid
Never
Only when the bonus is actually paid (matching rule for related parties)
questions.rationale: Section 267(a)(2) matches the deduction for accrued amounts owed to related parties to the year the recipient includes the amount in income.

questions.stem: An estate must file Form 706 (estate tax return) if the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts exceeds the basic exclusion amount. The 2024 federal estate tax basic exclusion amount is approximately what?
options: $1 million
$13.61 million
$5.49 million
$11.7 million
questions.rationale: For 2024 the basic exclusion amount is about $13.61 million; estates exceeding that (plus adjusted taxable gifts) must file Form 706.

questions.stem: An estate elects the alternate valuation date for estate tax purposes. When may property generally be valued under that election?
options: On the decedent's birthday
One year after the date of death
Six months after the date of death (or earlier date of disposition)
On the date the return is filed
questions.rationale: Section 2032 permits valuing estate property six months after death (or on the date of disposition if sooner), but only if it reduces both the gross estate and the estate tax due.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally a deductible ordinary and necessary business expense?
options: Bribes or kickbacks
A fine paid to a government for violating the law
Federal income taxes
Salaries paid to employees for services rendered
questions.rationale: Section 162 allows deductions for ordinary and necessary business expenses such as reasonable employee compensation, while fines, bribes, and federal income tax are nondeductible.

questions.stem: A C corporation distributes property subject to a liability greater than the property's fair market value to a shareholder. For gain recognition under Section 311(b), what value is used?
options: The property's fair market value, treated as not less than the liability assumed
The shareholder's basis
Zero
The property's basis
questions.rationale: Section 311(b)(2) provides that if a liability exceeds FMV, the FMV of distributed property is deemed to be at least the amount of the liability for gain computation.

questions.stem: A partnership distributes inventory to one partner and only cash to others, causing a shift in the partners' interests in hot assets. Which rule may recharacterize the transaction?
options: Section 751(b) disproportionate distribution rules
Section 721 nonrecognition
Section 731(c) marketable securities rule
Section 704(b) substantial economic effect
questions.rationale: Section 751(b) recharacterizes distributions that change partners' relative shares of hot assets as a deemed sale or exchange to the extent of the shift.

questions.stem: A partnership distributes marketable securities to a partner. For purposes of the gain rules, how are the securities generally treated?
options: As inventory in all cases
As money (cash), potentially triggering gain if value exceeds basis
As nondepreciable property only
As tax-free under Section 721
questions.rationale: Section 731(c) treats distributed marketable securities as money (with certain reductions), which can cause gain recognition when value exceeds outside basis.

questions.stem: What is the corporate tax treatment of dividends a C corporation pays to its shareholders?
options: A tax credit to the corporation
Deferred until shareholders sell their stock
Not deductible by the corporation; paid from after-tax earnings
Deductible by the corporation
questions.rationale: Corporate dividends are nondeductible distributions of after-tax earnings, resulting in taxation at both the corporate and shareholder levels.

questions.stem: A private foundation must generally distribute a minimum amount for charitable purposes each year or face an excise tax. This requirement is known as what?
options: The unrelated business income rule
The minimum distribution (payout) requirement
The accumulated earnings requirement
The conformity requirement
questions.rationale: Under Section 4942, private foundations must distribute approximately 5% of the value of net investment assets annually for charitable purposes or face an excise tax on undistributed income.

questions.stem: A sole proprietor materially participates in the business. How are the business profits treated for self-employment tax purposes?
options: Subject only to the 3.8% net investment income tax
Treated as wages with FICA withholding
Subject to self-employment tax as net earnings from self-employment
Exempt from self-employment tax
questions.rationale: A sole proprietor's net profit from an active business is subject to self-employment tax (Social Security and Medicare) computed on Schedule SE.

questions.stem: A corporation reconciles book income to taxable income. On which schedule of Form 1120 is this reconciliation generally reported for smaller corporations?
options: Schedule D
Schedule PH
Schedule UTP
Schedule M-1
questions.rationale: Schedule M-1 reconciles financial statement (book) income with taxable income; larger corporations use the more detailed Schedule M-3.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes a partnership's federal income tax liability?
options: A partnership is generally a pass-through entity and pays no entity-level federal income tax on its operating income
A partnership is taxed twice like a C corporation
A partnership pays tax at individual rates
A partnership pays federal income tax at 21%
questions.rationale: Partnerships generally do not pay entity-level federal income tax; income passes through to partners who report it on their own returns.

questions.stem: An S corporation has accumulated adjustments account (AAA) and no accumulated E&P. It distributes $25,000 cash to a shareholder with stock basis of $18,000. How is the distribution treated?
options: $25,000 ordinary income
$18,000 capital gain and $7,000 tax-free
$18,000 tax-free return of basis and $7,000 capital gain
$25,000 taxable dividend
questions.rationale: For an S corporation with no accumulated E&P, distributions reduce stock basis (tax-free) and any excess over basis is treated as gain from the sale of stock.

questions.stem: For a calendar-year partnership, what is the late-filing penalty structure under Section 6698 for failing to file Form 1065 on time?
options: A flat $500 penalty per return
A penalty per partner per month (up to 12 months) the return is late
A penalty equal to 25% of partnership income
No penalty applies to partnerships
questions.rationale: Section 6698 imposes a monthly penalty (a set dollar amount per partner, indexed annually) for up to 12 months when a partnership return is filed late.

questions.stem: Which type of organization is described in Section 501(c)(3)?
options: Religious, charitable, scientific, and educational organizations
Social welfare organizations
Labor organizations
Business leagues and chambers of commerce
questions.rationale: Section 501(c)(3) describes organizations organized and operated exclusively for charitable, religious, educational, scientific, and similar purposes.

questions.stem: A 501(c)(3) public charity engages in substantial lobbying without making a Section 501(h) election. What risk does it face?
options: Loss of exempt status for engaging in a substantial amount of lobbying
Automatic conversion to a 501(c)(4)
No risk; charities may lobby without limit
A reduction in the standard deduction
questions.rationale: Substantial lobbying can jeopardize 501(c)(3) status; the Section 501(h) election provides safe-harbor expenditure limits instead of the vague 'substantial part' test.

questions.stem: A corporation pays an officer compensation that the IRS determines is unreasonably high in a closely held company. How may the excess be recharacterized?
options: As additional deductible salary
As tax-exempt income
As a charitable contribution
As a nondeductible constructive dividend to the officer-shareholder
questions.rationale: Compensation must be reasonable to be deductible; the excess paid to a shareholder-employee is typically treated as a nondeductible dividend.

questions.stem: A partnership has $50,000 of recourse debt that is refinanced into $50,000 of nonrecourse debt. For the general partner who previously bore the full economic risk of loss, what is the likely basis effect?
options: No change to basis
A potential deemed distribution as the partner's share of liabilities decreases, possibly triggering gain
Conversion of capital gain to ordinary income
An automatic increase in basis
questions.rationale: A decrease in a partner's share of liabilities is treated as a deemed cash distribution under Section 752(b), reducing basis and potentially triggering gain.

questions.stem: Which item increases an S corporation shareholder's stock basis?
options: Nondeductible expenses
The shareholder's share of losses
Distributions to the shareholder
The shareholder's share of separately stated and nonseparately stated income
questions.rationale: Stock basis increases for income items (taxable and tax-exempt) and capital contributions, and decreases for distributions, losses, and nondeductible expenses.

questions.stem: What is the order in which an S corporation shareholder's stock basis is adjusted at year-end?
options: Losses first, then income, then distributions
Increased by income, decreased by distributions, then decreased by losses and deductions
Decreased by distributions first, then increased by income
All adjustments occur simultaneously with no ordering
questions.rationale: The ordering rules increase basis for income, then reduce for distributions, then reduce for nondeductible expenses and losses, which can limit loss deductions.

questions.stem: An estate distributes a specific bequest of $20,000 cash to a beneficiary in a lump sum, as required by the will. How does this affect DNI and the beneficiary?
options: It carries out DNI to the beneficiary
It increases the estate's distribution deduction
A specific bequest of a sum of money paid in not more than three installments does not carry out DNI and is not taxable to the beneficiary
It is taxable as ordinary income
questions.rationale: Section 663(a)(1) excludes specific bequests of a sum of money (paid all at once or in not more than three installments) from the distribution deduction and DNI carryout rules.

questions.stem: A corporation has a built-in gain asset and is subject to the Section 1374 BIG tax. What is the rate of the built-in gains tax?
options: 21% (the corporate rate)
questions.rationale: The Section 1374 built-in gains tax is computed at the highest corporate tax rate (21%) on net recognized built-in gain during the recognition period.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally a nondeductible expense for a business?
options: Advertising costs
Employee health insurance premiums
Office rent
Lobbying expenses to influence federal legislation
questions.rationale: Section 162(e) disallows deductions for lobbying and political expenditures, while ordinary operating costs like rent, advertising, and employee benefits are deductible.

questions.stem: A C corporation distributes $100,000 to a 30% shareholder. The corporation has no current or accumulated E&P, and the shareholder's stock basis is $40,000. How is the distribution treated to the shareholder?
options: $40,000 tax-free return of capital and $60,000 capital gain
$100,000 capital gain
$100,000 tax-free
$100,000 dividend
questions.rationale: Distributions with no E&P reduce stock basis tax-free; amounts exceeding basis are treated as gain from the sale of the stock.

questions.stem: A partnership's tax matters are handled under the BBA by a designated individual or entity. What is this person called?
options: The managing member
The partnership representative
The general counsel
The tax matters partner
questions.rationale: The BBA regime replaced the TEFRA 'tax matters partner' with the 'partnership representative,' who has sole authority to bind the partnership in IRS proceedings.

questions.stem: A small partnership wants to elect out of the BBA centralized audit regime. Which requirement must it meet?
options: It must have 100 or fewer eligible partners, none of which is a partnership or certain ineligible entity
It must have only foreign partners
It must be a publicly traded partnership
It must have more than 100 partners
questions.rationale: Under Section 6221(b), partnerships with 100 or fewer eligible partners (no partnership or certain ineligible partners) may elect out of the centralized audit regime annually.

questions.stem: A trust pays $4,000 of trustee fees and $1,000 of expenses allocable to tax-exempt income. How much of the trustee fee related to taxable income is generally deductible by the trust?
options: None of the fees
Only the portion allocable to taxable income; the part allocable to tax-exempt income is nondeductible
All $5,000 of expenses
The full $4,000 plus the $1,000
questions.rationale: Under Section 265, expenses allocable to tax-exempt income are nondeductible; only the portion related to taxable income is deductible by the trust.

questions.stem: When does an S corporation election generally take effect if Form 2553 is filed after the 15th day of the third month of the tax year (and no relief applies)?
options: Immediately on filing
The following tax year
Retroactively to the start of the current year
It is permanently denied
questions.rationale: An untimely Form 2553 (without relief under Rev. Proc. 2013-30) is effective for the following tax year rather than the current one.

questions.stem: A taxpayer disposes of MACRS 5-year property in a year before the recovery period ends. Which depreciation convention generally affects the depreciation allowed in the year of disposition?
options: Depreciation is recaptured in full with no current deduction
No depreciation is allowed in the disposition year
The applicable convention (e.g., half-year) allows a partial year of depreciation in the disposition year
Full-year depreciation is always allowed
questions.rationale: On disposition, the applicable MACRS convention determines the partial-year depreciation allowed in the year the property is sold.

questions.stem: A C corporation has a tax year ending June 30. When is its Form 1120 due (without extension), and does a special rule apply to June 30 fiscal-year filers?
options: The 15th day of the fourth month after year-end generally, but June 30 fiscal-year corporations had a special later deadline for a transition period
The last day of the year
Always April 15
The 15th day of the third month after year-end
questions.rationale: C corporation returns are generally due the 15th day of the fourth month after year-end, with a long-standing special transition rule for corporations with a June 30 year-end.

questions.stem: A taxpayer elects to expense research and experimental (R&E) costs. Under current law for amounts paid or incurred after 2021, how must domestic R&E expenditures be treated?
options: Deducted currently in full
Capitalized over 39 years
Never deductible
Capitalized and amortized over 5 years (15 years for foreign research)
questions.rationale: Since 2022, Section 174 requires capitalizing and amortizing R&E expenditures over 5 years (domestic) or 15 years (foreign) rather than immediate expensing.

questions.stem: A C corporation contributes inventory to a qualified charity for the care of the ill, needy, or infants. What enhanced deduction may apply?
options: An enhanced deduction up to basis plus one-half of the appreciation, not exceeding twice basis
The full fair market value with no limit
Only the inventory's basis is deductible
No deduction is allowed for inventory contributions
questions.rationale: Section 170(e)(3) provides an enhanced charitable deduction for C corporations donating qualifying inventory: basis plus half the appreciation, capped at twice basis.

questions.stem: What is the basis to a partnership of property contributed by a partner in a tax-free Section 721 transaction?
options: The contributing partner's adjusted basis (carryover basis)
Zero
The property's original cost when first purchased by the partner
The property's fair market value at contribution
questions.rationale: Section 723 gives the partnership a carryover basis in contributed property equal to the contributing partner's adjusted basis.

questions.stem: A new corporation issues stock in exchange for services performed by a founder. How does the founder treat the stock received?
options: As tax-free under Section 351
As a tax-free gift
As ordinary compensation income equal to the stock's fair market value
As a capital contribution with no income
questions.rationale: Under Section 83, stock received in exchange for services is ordinary compensation income equal to its fair market value when substantially vested; such stock does not count toward Section 351 control by property transferors.

questions.stem: A trust makes a distribution to a beneficiary that carries out DNI consisting of both ordinary income and tax-exempt interest. How is the character determined on the beneficiary's K-1?
options: All as tax-exempt income
The distribution carries out a proportionate share of each class of income making up DNI
All as ordinary income
The trustee chooses the character
questions.rationale: Under Section 662(b), distributions retain the character of the underlying classes of income in DNI on a proportionate basis.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of years over which a C corporation may carry forward an unused general business credit?
options: Indefinitely
20 years
5 years
10 years
questions.rationale: Under Section 39, unused general business credits are carried back 1 year and forward up to 20 years.

questions.stem: A partnership distributes property with a basis of $5,000 to a partner whose outside basis is $30,000 in a current distribution. What basis does the partner take in the property and what is the partner's remaining outside basis?
options: $30,000 property basis; $0 remaining
$5,000 property basis; $25,000 remaining outside basis
$0 property basis; $30,000 remaining
$5,000 property basis; $30,000 remaining
questions.rationale: In a nonliquidating distribution, distributed property generally takes a carryover basis (capped at outside basis), and the partner's outside basis is reduced by that amount.

questions.stem: What is the basis of property received by a corporation in a tax-free Section 351 transfer from a shareholder?
options: Fair market value
Zero
The corporation's cost
The transferor's adjusted basis, increased by any gain recognized by the transferor
questions.rationale: Section 362 gives the corporation a carryover basis in Section 351 property, increased by any gain recognized by the transferor.

questions.stem: A decedent's final individual income tax return (Form 1040) covers what period?
options: Only the month of death
A full 12 months regardless of death date
The entire year following death
From January 1 through the date of death
questions.rationale: The decedent's final return includes income earned from the beginning of the tax year through the date of death; post-death income goes on the estate's return.

questions.stem: A disguised sale is suspected when a partner contributes property and receives a related distribution. Within what time frame are a contribution and distribution presumed to be a disguised sale (rebuttable)?
options: Five years
Two years
6 months
Seven years
questions.rationale: Reg. 1.707-3 creates a rebuttable presumption that a contribution and related distribution within two years constitute a disguised sale.

questions.stem: A corporation makes nondeductible expenditures that reduce E&P. Which of the following reduces E&P even though it is not a deductible expense?
options: Tax-exempt municipal bond interest received
Issuance of new stock
A capital contribution received
Federal income taxes paid
questions.rationale: E&P is adjusted for economic items not reflected in taxable income; federal income taxes paid reduce E&P, while tax-exempt interest increases it.

questions.stem: A partnership has a single corporate partner and one individual partner. Which tax year must it generally use under the least-aggregate-deferral rule if there is no majority or principal partner with a common year?
options: Always a calendar year
The year that produces the least aggregate deferral of income to the partners
Any year it chooses
Always the corporate partner's year
questions.rationale: Section 706(b) applies the majority-interest, then principal-partner, then least-aggregate-deferral tests to determine a partnership's required tax year.

questions.stem: A complex trust accumulates income in the current year. In a later year it makes a distribution that includes previously accumulated income. What rule may apply to the beneficiary?
options: The accumulated income is always tax-free
The throwback rule has been largely repealed for most domestic trusts
The trust must dissolve
The beneficiary must amend prior-year returns
questions.rationale: The throwback rules generally no longer apply to domestic trusts; distributions are taxed under the current-year DNI rules, with the throwback regime mainly affecting foreign trusts.

questions.stem: A corporation redeems a shareholder's stock. When is a redemption treated as a sale or exchange (capital gain) rather than a dividend?
options: When the redemption is substantially disproportionate, completely terminates the interest, or is not essentially equivalent to a dividend
Only if the shareholder owns 100% of the stock
Whenever the corporation has E&P
Never; redemptions are always dividends
questions.rationale: Section 302 provides exchange (capital gain) treatment for redemptions that are substantially disproportionate, complete terminations, or not essentially equivalent to a dividend.

questions.stem: For depreciation purposes, when is property considered placed in service?
options: When it is ready and available for its intended use
When it is purchased
When it is fully paid for
When it is first sold
questions.rationale: Depreciation begins when property is placed in service, meaning it is ready and available for its intended use, regardless of when it is actually used or paid for.

questions.stem: A parent corporation and its 100%-owned subsidiary file a consolidated return. An intercompany sale of inventory at a profit occurs between them. How is the gain generally treated until the inventory leaves the group?
options: Recognized immediately by the seller
Recognized only by the buyer
Deferred under the consolidated return intercompany transaction rules until the property is sold outside the group
Never recognized
questions.rationale: Consolidated return rules defer intercompany transaction gains until a triggering event, such as sale of the property outside the affiliated group.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the tax treatment of a single-member LLC that elects to be taxed as an S corporation?
options: It is automatically a C corporation
It remains disregarded
It files Form 1120-S and the owner is a shareholder-employee
It files Form 1065
questions.rationale: A single-member LLC may elect to be taxed as an S corporation, filing Form 1120-S with the owner as a shareholder-employee.

questions.stem: An estate's administrative expenses (such as attorney fees) may be deducted on which return at the executor's election?
options: Either on the estate tax return (Form 706) or the estate's income tax return (Form 1041), but not both
Only on the decedent's final Form 1040
On none of the returns
Only on the beneficiaries' returns
questions.rationale: Under Section 642(g), administration expenses may be claimed on the estate tax return or the estate's income tax return, but not both.

questions.stem: A partner abandons a worthless partnership interest with no distribution and no liability relief. How is the resulting loss generally characterized?
options: A Section 1231 loss
A nondeductible personal loss
An ordinary loss, because there is no sale or exchange and no deemed distribution
Always a capital loss
questions.rationale: If a partner abandons an interest without any actual or deemed distribution (no liability relief), the loss is ordinary because no sale or exchange occurs; any liability relief would convert it to a capital loss.

questions.stem: How long is the recognition period for the built-in gains tax under current law?
options: 10 years
7 years
5 years
Indefinite
questions.rationale: The Section 1374 recognition period is permanently set at 5 years for the built-in gains tax.

questions.stem: A new partnership wants to amortize its organizational expenses. What is the treatment under Section 709?
options: Deduct over 5 years only
Deduct all costs immediately with no limit
Capitalize permanently with no deduction
Elect to deduct up to $5,000 of organizational costs (phased out over $50,000) and amortize the rest over 180 months
questions.rationale: Section 709 allows a first-year deduction of up to $5,000 of partnership organizational expenses, with the balance amortized over 180 months; syndication costs are not deductible.

questions.stem: A C corporation makes a charitable contribution that exceeds the 10% taxable income limit. What happens to the excess?
options: It may be carried back 3 years
It may be carried forward for up to 5 years
It converts to an ordinary deduction
It is permanently lost
questions.rationale: Corporate charitable contributions over the 10% limit carry forward for up to five years, subject to the limit in each year.

questions.stem: A partnership has a special allocation of depreciation to one partner. For the allocation to be respected, it must have substantial economic effect. Which is a core requirement?
options: Capital accounts must be maintained under the Section 704(b) rules and liquidating distributions made according to positive capital account balances
The allocation must match the profit-sharing ratio
The allocation must be approved by the IRS in advance
The allocation must be temporary
questions.rationale: Substantial economic effect under Reg. 1.704-1(b) requires proper capital account maintenance, liquidation per capital accounts, and either a deficit restoration obligation or a qualified income offset, plus substantiality.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a separately stated item on an S corporation Schedule K-1?
options: Salaries paid to non-shareholder employees
Section 1231 gains and losses
Cost of goods sold
Office supplies expense
questions.rationale: Items that could affect a shareholder's tax differently, such as Section 1231 gains, capital gains, and charitable contributions, are separately stated on Schedule K-1.

questions.stem: A partnership distributes cash that reduces a partner's basis to zero, then later allocates income to the partner. What happens to a loss that was suspended in a prior year due to insufficient basis?
options: It converts to a capital loss
It may be deducted when the partner's basis is restored by the income allocation
It must be carried back
It is permanently lost
questions.rationale: Losses suspended under the Section 704(d) basis limitation carry forward and become deductible when the partner's outside basis is restored.

questions.stem: A charity receives a contribution of appreciated long-term capital gain property from a corporation. For the corporation, special rules limit the deduction for contributions of ordinary income property to what amount?
options: Fair market value
The property's basis (reduced by the ordinary income that would result on sale)
Twice the basis always
Zero
questions.rationale: Under Section 170(e), the deduction for ordinary income property is reduced by the gain that would not have been long-term capital gain if sold, generally limiting it to basis.

questions.stem: A shareholder contributes property with a liability that exceeds basis in a Section 351 transfer. What is the consequence of the liability assumed by the corporation exceeding the basis of the transferred property?
options: Gain is recognized to the extent the liabilities assumed exceed the total adjusted basis of property transferred
The corporation recognizes the gain
No gain is ever recognized
The transfer fails Section 351 entirely
questions.rationale: Section 357(c) requires a transferor to recognize gain when liabilities assumed by the corporation exceed the total adjusted basis of the property transferred.

questions.stem: A partnership's ordinary business income is reported on which line item that flows to the partners' Schedules K-1?
options: As a dividend on Form 1099-DIV
As wages on Form W-2
As ordinary business income (loss) on Schedule K and box 1 of Schedule K-1
As interest on Form 1099-INT
questions.rationale: A partnership reports ordinary business income (loss) on Schedule K, with each partner's share appearing in box 1 of Schedule K-1.

questions.stem: A corporation distributes its own stock as a stock dividend that is pro rata to all common shareholders. How is this generally treated?
options: Generally nontaxable, with the shareholder's basis spread over old and new shares
Always taxable as a dividend
Deductible by the corporation
Taxable as capital gain
questions.rationale: Under Section 305(a), pro rata stock dividends are generally nontaxable, and basis is reallocated among the shares; certain disproportionate or elective distributions can be taxable.

questions.stem: A taxpayer placed in service qualifying property and wants to maximize the current-year deduction. In what order are Section 179 expensing and bonus depreciation generally applied?
options: Section 179 first, then bonus depreciation, then regular MACRS on the remaining basis
Regular MACRS first, then Section 179
They cannot be combined
Bonus depreciation first, then Section 179, then regular MACRS
questions.rationale: To maximize first-year cost recovery, taxpayers apply Section 179 first, then bonus depreciation on the remaining basis, and finally regular MACRS.

questions.stem: A calendar-year corporation wants its S election to be effective for the current tax year. By what date must Form 2553 be filed?
options: By the 15th day of the 4th month after the end of the tax year
Within 30 days after the first shareholder meeting
By April 15 of the following year
No later than 2 months and 15 days after the start of the tax year
questions.rationale: A timely filed election needs consent of all shareholders, and eligibility at all times during the period before the election.

questions.stem: Which of the following may be a shareholder of an S corporation?
options: A C corporation
A nonresident alien individual
An estate of a deceased shareholder
A partnership
questions.rationale: Violating eligibility ends the election on the date the ineligible shareholder acquires stock.

questions.stem: An S corporation has two shareholders. One receives a $20,000 distribution, and the other receives $5,000 in the same year. The governing documents give both identical rights. What is the effect on the S election?
options: The election terminates because of two classes of stock
The distribution is taxed as a dividend to the first shareholder
No termination occurs, though the IRS may recharacterize the timing differences
The election terminates only if the difference exceeds 50%
questions.rationale: Voting differences are permitted. Differences in distribution or liquidation rights are not.

questions.stem: At the start of the year, an S corporation shareholder has stock basis of $10,000. The corporation allocates her $15,000 of ordinary income and makes a $20,000 distribution to her. In what order are these adjusted, and what is the effect of the distribution?
options: The distribution is taxable up to $5,000 as ordinary income
Basis rises to $25,000, then falls to $5,000; nothing is taxable
Basis falls to $0 first, and she recognizes $10,000 of capital gain
The income is ignored, and the $20,000 is a taxable dividend
questions.rationale: A distribution in excess of stock basis is treated as capital gain.

questions.stem: An S corporation that was formerly a C corporation sells an appreciated asset 3 years after converting. The asset's built-in gain existed at the conversion date. What tax may apply?
options: The 20% accumulated earnings tax on retained earnings
The §1374 built-in gains tax, imposed at the corporate rate
No corporate-level tax, since an S corporation is a pass-through
The personal holding company tax on passive income
questions.rationale: The recognition period is 5 years from the first day of the first S year.

questions.stem: A partner contributes land with an adjusted basis of $40,000 and a fair market value of $100,000 to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest. What are the consequences?
options: Her basis in the partnership interest is $100,000
She recognizes $60,000 of gain on the contribution
No gain is recognized; her basis in the interest is $40,000
The partnership takes a $100,000 basis in the land
questions.rationale: The built-in gain is allocated back to the contributing partner under §704(c).

questions.stem: A partner's outside basis is $30,000. The partnership assumes a $10,000 liability of the partner in connection with the contribution. How is the partner's basis affected by the liability relief?
options: Basis is reduced by the part of the liability shifted to others
Basis increases by the full $10,000 of liability assumed
Basis is reduced to zero, whatever the amount shifted
Basis is unaffected, since liabilities never change basis
questions.rationale: A reduction below zero causes gain recognition.

questions.stem: Which statement about guaranteed payments to a partner is correct?
options: Deductible by the partnership only in years it has a profit
Taxed to the partner as long-term capital gain
Deductible by the partnership; ordinary income to the partner, win or lose
A distribution of profits that is not subject to SE tax
questions.rationale: Report guaranteed payments on Schedule K-1 (Box 4) of Form 1065.

questions.stem: A limited partner of a partnership receives a $10,000 guaranteed payment for services and a $30,000 distributive share of ordinary income. What portion is generally subject to self-employment tax?
options: The $30,000 distributive share only
The $10,000 guaranteed payment only
The entire $40,000
Neither amount
questions.rationale: General partners include both their distributive share and guaranteed payments in SE earnings.

questions.stem: A calendar-year partnership files Form 1065. When is the return due, and what extension is available?
options: April 15, with an automatic six-month extension on Form 4868
April 15, with a three-month extension
March 15, with no extension available
March 15, with an automatic six-month extension on Form 7004
questions.rationale: Penalties apply per partner or shareholder per month for late returns.
