options: The IRS Independent Office of Appeals only
A U.S. District Court or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims, after paying the tax and filing a timely refund claim
The U.S. Court of Appeals as a trial court
The U.S. Tax Court before paying the disputed amount
questions.rationale: Refund suits (tax already paid) are brought in U.S. District Court or the Court of Federal Claims; Tax Court is the prepayment forum for deficiencies.

questions.stem: The Taxpayer Bill of Rights includes which of the following as one of the enumerated rights?
options: The right to deduct all personal expenses
The right to retain representation
The right to a guaranteed refund within 10 days
The right to never be audited more than once
questions.rationale: The Taxpayer Bill of Rights enumerates ten rights, including the right to retain representation and the right to a fair and just tax system.

questions.stem: During an examination, a taxpayer being interviewed (other than under summons) generally has the right to do what if the taxpayer clearly states a desire to consult with a representative?
options: Have the IRS pay the representative's fee
Suspend the interview to consult an authorized representative
Refuse to ever be re-interviewed
Continue the interview only if the IRS agent agrees
questions.rationale: Under the taxpayer's rights during examinations, a taxpayer who states a desire to consult a representative may generally suspend a non-summons interview to do so.

questions.stem: Under §7521, the IRS generally may not require a taxpayer to accompany an authorized representative to an interview in the absence of what?
options: A power of attorney on file
A written request from the taxpayer
An administrative summons issued to the taxpayer
A signed engagement letter
questions.rationale: Section 7521 lets a taxpayer with an authorized representative avoid attending IRS interviews unless the IRS issues a summons to compel attendance.

questions.stem: Under §7525, a limited confidentiality privilege exists between a taxpayer and a federally authorized tax practitioner. This privilege applies to what?
options: All state tax disputes
Tax shelter promotion communications
Criminal tax matters and the preparation of returns
Noncriminal tax matters before the IRS and noncriminal tax proceedings in federal court brought by or against the United States
questions.rationale: The §7525 privilege covers noncriminal tax matters before the IRS and noncriminal federal tax litigation, but not criminal matters, return preparation, or tax shelter promotion communications.

questions.stem: A Taxpayer Assistance Order (TAO) issued by the National Taxpayer Advocate may direct the IRS to do what?
options: Take or refrain from a specified action, such as releasing a levy, to relieve a significant hardship
Disbar the assigned revenue officer
Reverse a Tax Court decision
Permanently forgive the taxpayer's tax liability
questions.rationale: A Taxpayer Assistance Order can direct the IRS to take or stop a specified action to relieve a significant hardship, though it does not forgive the liability itself.

questions.stem: Audit reconsideration is generally available to a taxpayer in which situation?
options: The taxpayer has new information not previously considered, did not appear for the original audit, or disagrees with an assessment from an examination
The taxpayer missed the Tax Court petition deadline and wants to relitigate the same facts already decided by the court
The taxpayer simply wants a different examiner
The taxpayer agreed to and fully paid the assessment and signed a closing agreement
questions.rationale: Audit reconsideration lets a taxpayer ask the IRS to reevaluate an examination assessment based on new information or a missed audit, but not where there is finality (closing agreement, paid in full, or a court decision).

questions.stem: Fast Track Settlement (FTS) is a program that allows certain taxpayers to do what?
options: Obtain an automatic 50% penalty reduction
Bypass the Tax Court
Resolve disputes while the case is still in the examination function, with an Appeals official acting as a neutral facilitator
Skip the examination entirely
questions.rationale: Fast Track Settlement uses a trained Appeals mediator to help resolve issues while the case is still in examination, retaining the taxpayer's other appeal rights if no agreement is reached.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who has received a Notice of Federal Tax Lien filing and a notice of intent to levy may request which type of hearing to dispute the collection action?
options: A whistleblower award hearing
A Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing using Form 12153
A jeopardy assessment hearing
A passport revocation hearing
questions.rationale: A Collection Due Process hearing (Form 12153) lets a taxpayer challenge a lien filing or proposed levy and propose collection alternatives before Appeals.

questions.stem: Under the Collection Appeals Program (CAP), which statement is correct?
options: CAP requires payment of the full liability first
CAP determinations can be appealed to the U.S. Tax Court
CAP is available only after a Tax Court petition is filed
CAP allows a broad range of collection actions to be appealed, but the taxpayer cannot challenge the underlying tax liability and cannot seek judicial review of the CAP decision
questions.rationale: CAP provides faster Appeals review of various collection actions but, unlike CDP, does not allow disputing the underlying liability and offers no judicial review of the outcome.

questions.stem: An offer in compromise based on doubt as to collectibility asks the IRS to do what?
options: Forgive the liability because the taxpayer denies owing it
Convert the liability to a nondischargeable debt
Accept less than the full amount owed because the taxpayer's reasonable collection potential is less than the liability
Suspend interest indefinitely
questions.rationale: A doubt-as-to-collectibility OIC is based on the taxpayer's reasonable collection potential being less than the assessed liability, justifying acceptance of a lesser amount.

questions.stem: Which form is generally used to submit an offer in compromise?
options: Form 12153
Form 656
Form 433-F only
Form 9465
questions.rationale: An offer in compromise is submitted on Form 656, supported by the appropriate collection information statement (Form 433-A (OIC) or 433-B (OIC)).

questions.stem: When the IRS accepts a doubt-as-to-collectibility OIC, the taxpayer generally must do what to remain in compliance for the offer to stand?
options: Waive all future appeal rights forever
Pay double the offered amount
Surrender the taxpayer's passport
Timely file and pay all required taxes for a five-year period following acceptance
questions.rationale: An accepted OIC requires the taxpayer to stay in full compliance (file and pay timely) for five years; default can reinstate the original liability.

questions.stem: Under §6159, an installment agreement may be terminated or modified by the IRS for which of the following reasons?
options: The taxpayer provided materially inaccurate or incomplete information, or fails to pay an installment or another tax liability when due
The taxpayer requested a transcript
The taxpayer moved to a different state
Interest rates changed nationally
questions.rationale: Section 6159 allows the IRS to modify or terminate an installment agreement for default, providing inaccurate information, failing to pay another liability, or a significant change in financial condition (with notice).

questions.stem: Which collection alternative is appropriate for a taxpayer who cannot pay anything at all without suffering economic hardship?
options: Currently Not Collectible (CNC) status (hardship), which temporarily suspends active collection
A transferee assessment
Immediate full payment by levy
A jeopardy assessment
questions.rationale: Currently Not Collectible (hardship) status pauses active collection when paying would prevent meeting basic living expenses, though interest and penalties continue to accrue and the debt remains.

questions.stem: When a taxpayer files for bankruptcy, the automatic stay under the Bankruptcy Code generally does what to IRS collection?
options: Stops most IRS collection actions, such as levies and lien filings, during the bankruptcy
Permanently discharges all federal taxes
Requires the IRS to refund all prior payments
Has no effect on the IRS as a sovereign
questions.rationale: The bankruptcy automatic stay generally suspends IRS collection actions during the case; whether the taxes are ultimately discharged depends on the type of tax and timing rules.

questions.stem: Certain older income taxes may be dischargeable in bankruptcy if specific timing rules are met. Which of the following is one such common requirement?
options: The tax must be a trust fund recovery penalty
The return was due (including extensions) more than three years before the bankruptcy petition
The taxpayer must have a current installment agreement
The tax must be a payroll tax
questions.rationale: Income tax discharge in bankruptcy generally requires meeting timing tests, including the 3-year (return due date), 2-year (return filed), and 240-day (assessment) rules, and the tax must not be fraud-related.

questions.stem: Under §6901, transferee liability allows the IRS to collect a transferor's unpaid tax from a transferee. This generally applies when what occurs?
options: Property is transferred for less than adequate consideration, leaving the transferor unable to pay the tax (often a fraudulent or constructive-fraud transfer)
The transferee requested a transcript
The transferor died testate
The transferee filed a joint return
questions.rationale: Section 6901 lets the IRS assess and collect a transferor's tax from a transferee who received property for less than adequate consideration, generally limited to the value of property received.

questions.stem: A jeopardy assessment or termination assessment allows the IRS to do what?
options: Permanently waive penalties
Grant an automatic installment agreement
Refer the case to the Taxpayer Advocate
Assess and immediately collect tax when collection is determined to be in jeopardy, bypassing normal deficiency procedures
questions.rationale: Jeopardy and termination assessments permit immediate assessment and collection when normal delay would endanger collection; the taxpayer has expedited post-assessment review rights.

questions.stem: After a jeopardy or termination assessment, the taxpayer's expedited review rights include what?
options: No review at all
A right to a jury trial within 10 days
Administrative review by the IRS and, if still dissatisfied, judicial review in U.S. District Court (or Tax Court for jeopardy levies) within statutory deadlines
Automatic abatement after 30 days
questions.rationale: Jeopardy and termination assessments carry expedited review: administrative review first, then prompt judicial review of the reasonableness of the assessment and the amount.

questions.stem: Under §7345, when the IRS certifies a taxpayer as having a 'seriously delinquent tax debt,' what consequence may follow?
options: The taxpayer loses the right to file returns
The taxpayer's wages are automatically garnished at 100%
The State Department may deny, revoke, or limit the taxpayer's passport
The taxpayer is immediately arrested
questions.rationale: Section 7345 allows the IRS to certify seriously delinquent tax debts to the State Department, which may deny or revoke the taxpayer's passport.

questions.stem: For purposes of §7345 passport certification, a 'seriously delinquent tax debt' is generally an unpaid, legally enforceable, assessed federal tax liability exceeding a threshold (indexed for inflation, over $50,000 base) for which what condition is also met?
options: The taxpayer has filed for bankruptcy
A notice of federal tax lien has been filed (with administrative rights exhausted/lapsed) or a levy has been issued
The debt is less than 30 days old
The taxpayer is in an accepted installment agreement
questions.rationale: A seriously delinquent tax debt for §7345 requires an assessed, enforceable liability above the indexed threshold with a filed lien (rights exhausted) or issued levy; debts in installment agreements, OICs, CDP, or innocent-spouse requests are excluded.

questions.stem: Which of the following debts is excluded from §7345 passport certification even if it exceeds the dollar threshold?
options: A debt the taxpayer simply refuses to pay
A debt with a levy already issued
A debt being timely paid under an IRS-accepted installment agreement
A debt with a filed lien and exhausted appeal rights
questions.rationale: Debts being paid under installment agreements or accepted OICs, or subject to pending CDP hearings or innocent-spouse requests, are excluded from passport certification.

questions.stem: The IRS uses private collection agencies (PCAs) for certain inactive tax receivables. Which of the following actions may a PCA NOT take?
options: Discuss payment options with the taxpayer
File a notice of federal tax lien or issue a levy
Set up an installment agreement consistent with IRS guidelines
Identify themselves and the IRS authorization
questions.rationale: Private collection agencies can locate taxpayers and arrange payments within IRS rules, but they cannot take enforcement actions like liens or levies, which only the IRS can do.

questions.stem: Under §6672, the trust fund recovery penalty (TFRP) may be assessed against whom?
options: Only the corporation that failed to remit the taxes
Only the company's outside auditor
Any person responsible for collecting, accounting for, and paying over trust fund taxes who willfully fails to do so
Only the IRS revenue officer
questions.rationale: The §6672 trust fund recovery penalty reaches responsible persons who willfully fail to pay over trust fund taxes; it equals 100% of the unpaid trust fund amount.

questions.stem: Before assessing the trust fund recovery penalty, the IRS generally must do what?
options: Issue Letter 1153 proposing the TFRP, giving the responsible person 60 days to appeal
Wait 10 years
Get the corporation's written consent
Obtain a court judgment
questions.rationale: The IRS proposes the TFRP with Letter 1153/Form 2751, allowing a 60-day appeal to the Independent Office of Appeals before the penalty is assessed against the responsible person.

questions.stem: The distinction between an 'injured spouse' and an 'innocent spouse' is best described as which of the following?
options: They are identical and interchangeable
Both apply only to separately filed returns
An injured spouse seeks to recover their share of a joint refund offset for the other spouse's separate debt; an innocent spouse seeks relief from liability for an understatement on a joint return
An innocent spouse files Form 8379 and an injured spouse files Form 8857
questions.rationale: Injured spouse (Form 8379) protects a refund share offset for a spouse's separate debt; innocent spouse (Form 8857) relieves a spouse of liability for the other's erroneous items on a joint return.

questions.stem: A whistleblower who provides information leading to IRS collection may receive an award under §7623(b) of generally what range, when the amount in dispute exceeds the statutory threshold (over $2 million and, for individuals, gross income over $200,000)?
options: A flat $10,000 award
15% to 30% of the collected proceeds attributable to the information
50% to 75% of collected proceeds
1% to 5% of collected proceeds
questions.rationale: Section 7623(b) provides a mandatory award of 15%–30% of collected proceeds for cases meeting the dollar thresholds; smaller cases fall under the discretionary §7623(a) program (up to 15%).

questions.stem: Which form does a whistleblower file to claim an award for reporting tax noncompliance?
options: Form 211, Application for Award for Original Information
Form 656
Form 3949-A, Information Referral
Form 14039, Identity Theft Affidavit
questions.rationale: Whistleblowers seeking an award submit Form 211 to the IRS Whistleblower Office; Form 3949-A merely reports suspected noncompliance without claiming an award.

questions.stem: Which form must be completed to document due diligence for returns claiming the EITC, the child tax credit/additional child tax credit/credit for other dependents, the American opportunity tax credit, and head of household filing status?
options: Form 8867, Paid Preparer's Due Diligence Checklist
Form 8948, Preparer Explanation for Not Filing Electronically
Form 8879, IRS e-file Signature Authorization
Form 2848
questions.rationale: Form 8867 documents the paid preparer's due diligence for the EITC, CTC/ACTC/ODC, AOTC, and head of household filing status.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under §6695(g), what is the penalty (as adjusted for inflation) for each failure by a preparer to comply with the EITC/CTC/AOTC/HOH due diligence requirements?
options: $5,000 per return
$50 per failure, not adjusted
An inflation-adjusted amount (commonly cited around $635 per failure for recent years) for each credit or HOH determination
10% of the disallowed credit
questions.rationale: Section 6695(g) imposes an inflation-adjusted penalty (recently about $635) for EACH failure to meet due diligence—and it applies separately to each of EITC, CTC/ACTC/ODC, AOTC, and HOH on the same return.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: The four requirements of due diligence under the §6695(g) regulations include completing Form 8867, computing the credit, keeping records, and what fourth requirement?
options: The knowledge requirement—making reasonable inquiries when information appears incorrect, inconsistent, or incomplete
Charging a contingent fee
Obtaining a power of attorney from the taxpayer
Filing the return electronically
questions.rationale: The four due-diligence requirements are: complete Form 8867, compute the credits (worksheets), the knowledge requirement (reasonable inquiries), and record retention.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: How long must a preparer retain the records supporting EITC/CTC/AOTC/HOH due diligence (including Form 8867 and worksheets)?
options: Indefinitely
7 years
1 year from the filing date
3 years from the latest of the return's due date, the date filed, or the date the preparer gave the return to the taxpayer to sign
questions.rationale: Due-diligence records (Form 8867, worksheets, and a record of inquiries) must be retained three years from the latest of the due date (no extensions), filing date, or date presented for signature.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Section 6695 lists several preparer penalties. Which of the following is one of them?
options: Failure to obtain a CPA license
Failure to pay the taxpayer's tax
Failure to sign the return as preparer
Failure to win an audit
questions.rationale: Section 6695 covers preparer failures such as not furnishing a copy (a), not signing (b), not furnishing the preparer's identifying number (c), not retaining records (d), and not filing correct information returns (e).
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under §6694(a), the first-tier penalty for an understatement due to an unreasonable position is generally the greater of $1,000 or what?
options: 10% of the tax shown on the return
50% of the income derived (or to be derived) by the preparer with respect to the return or claim
$5,000 flat
100% of the understatement
questions.rationale: Section 6694(a) penalizes an unreasonable-position understatement at the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived by the preparer from the return.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under §6694(b), the penalty for an understatement due to willful or reckless conduct is generally the greater of $5,000 or what?
options: 10% of the understatement
$1,000 flat
75% of the income derived (or to be derived) by the preparer with respect to the return or claim
50% of the income derived (or to be derived) by the preparer with respect to the return
questions.rationale: Section 6694(b) penalizes willful or reckless understatements at the greater of $5,000 or 75% of the income derived by the preparer, offset by any §6694(a) penalty already paid.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: A preparer can avoid the §6694(a) penalty for a position that is not a tax shelter or reportable transaction if the position met what standard and, where required, was disclosed?
options: More likely than not in all cases
Substantial authority, or reasonable basis if adequately disclosed (and the disclosure requirements are met)
Any standard, as long as the client agreed
A frivolous standard
questions.rationale: Under §6694(a), a non-disclosed position needs substantial authority, while a disclosed position needs a reasonable basis; tax shelters and reportable transactions require the 'more likely than not' standard.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Form 8879 is best described as which of the following?
options: A power of attorney
The IRS e-file Signature Authorization, by which the taxpayer authorizes the ERO to enter or generate the taxpayer's PIN to e-file the return
An extension request
An offer in compromise
questions.rationale: Form 8879 authorizes an Electronic Return Originator (ERO) to enter or generate the taxpayer's personal identification number to electronically sign and file the taxpayer's return.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: An Electronic Return Originator (ERO) must receive a completed and signed Form 8879 from the taxpayer when?
options: Before the ERO transmits the return (or releases it for transmission)
After the IRS accepts the return
Within 30 days after transmission
Only if the return is rejected
questions.rationale: The ERO must have a completed, signed Form 8879 in hand before electronically transmitting the taxpayer's return.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under the e-file mandate, a specified tax return preparer who reasonably expects to file (or whose firm reasonably expects to file in the aggregate) how many or more covered individual income tax returns in a calendar year must generally e-file?
options: 11 or more
100 or more
25 or more
5 or more
questions.rationale: The preparer e-file mandate applies to specified preparers expecting to file 11 or more covered returns (individual, estate, and trust income tax returns) in a calendar year.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: If an individual taxpayer chooses to have their return filed on paper rather than electronically by a preparer subject to the e-file mandate, the preparer documents this with which form?
options: Form 8879
Form 8948, Preparer Explanation for Not Filing Electronically
Form 2848
Form 8867
questions.rationale: Form 8948 documents an allowable reason (such as a taxpayer's choice) for a mandated preparer to file a paper return instead of e-filing.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: A taxpayer who wants to file a paper return despite their preparer being subject to the e-file mandate generally must do what?
options: File Form 656
Request a CDP hearing
Choose paper filing and have the preparer attach Form 8948 (a taxpayer statement choosing paper may be kept by the preparer)
Obtain a private letter ruling
questions.rationale: A taxpayer can opt out of e-file; the preparer then files the paper return with Form 8948 explaining the taxpayer's choice, and may keep a signed taxpayer statement.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: A taxpayer who needs more time to file an individual income tax return may obtain an automatic six-month extension by filing which form?
options: Form 2350
Form 7004
Form 1127
Form 4868
questions.rationale: Form 4868 grants an automatic six-month extension to FILE an individual return, but it does not extend the time to PAY the tax due.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: An extension of time to file (Form 4868) does what with respect to the payment of tax due?
options: It extends the time to pay by six months as well
It eliminates all penalties
It does not extend the time to pay; tax is still due by the original due date and interest/penalties may accrue on unpaid amounts
It converts the balance to an installment agreement
questions.rationale: An extension to file does not extend the time to pay; interest and a potential failure-to-pay penalty accrue on any unpaid tax from the original due date.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under the math-error procedure, when the IRS corrects a clerical or mathematical error on a return, the taxpayer generally has how long to request abatement of the resulting assessment?
options: 10 days
1 year
90 days
60 days from the notice to request abatement, after which the IRS may assess and collect
questions.rationale: Under §6213(b), a math-error assessment can be made without a deficiency notice, but the taxpayer has 60 days to request abatement, after which the IRS must use normal deficiency procedures.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under §6020(b), if a taxpayer fails to file a required return, the IRS may prepare a Substitute for Return (SFR). Which statement about an SFR is correct?
options: An SFR eliminates the failure-to-file penalty
The SFR claims all deductions and credits the taxpayer could have taken
An SFR cannot be replaced by a later taxpayer-filed return
The SFR generally uses filing status and limited information available to the IRS and does not include most deductions or credits the taxpayer might otherwise claim
questions.rationale: Under §6020(b), the IRS may prepare a Substitute for Return using available data; it generally excludes beneficial deductions and credits, so filing an actual return often lowers the liability.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under §6651, the failure-to-file penalty is generally what rate, and how does it interact with the failure-to-pay penalty in the same month?
options: 5% per month up to 25%, reduced by the 0.5% failure-to-pay penalty for any month both apply
1% per month with no maximum
25% per month up to 100%
10% one-time only
questions.rationale: Section 6651 imposes a 5% per month failure-to-file penalty (max 25%), reduced by the 0.5% failure-to-pay penalty in any overlapping month; minimum penalties apply for very late returns.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: The failure-to-pay penalty under §6651(a)(2) is generally what rate per month?
options: 0.5% per month (up to 25%), with the rate adjusted in certain circumstances
5% per month
20% one-time
1% per day
questions.rationale: The §6651(a)(2) failure-to-pay penalty is 0.5% of unpaid tax per month (max 25%); the rate can drop for accepted installment agreements or rise after a levy notice.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: First-time abatement (FTA) penalty relief is generally available for which penalties, and under what condition?
options: Any penalty, regardless of prior compliance
Only fraud penalties
Only the accuracy-related penalty
Failure-to-file, failure-to-pay, and failure-to-deposit penalties, generally if the taxpayer has a clean compliance history for the prior three years and is current on filing/payment
questions.rationale: First-time abatement relieves failure-to-file, failure-to-pay, and failure-to-deposit penalties for taxpayers with a clean three-year compliance history who are current on filing and payment.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: A taxpayer who can show reasonable cause for failing to file or pay may have the related penalty abated. Reasonable cause is generally based on what?
options: Facts showing the taxpayer exercised ordinary business care and prudence but was nevertheless unable to comply
The size of the refund expected
The taxpayer's disagreement with the tax law
The taxpayer's lack of funds to pay, standing alone
questions.rationale: Reasonable cause requires showing ordinary business care and prudence with an inability to comply; it does not include mere lack of funds or disagreement with the law.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under the recordkeeping rules, how long should a taxpayer generally keep records that support items on a tax return (the basic limitations period)?
options: 30 days after filing
Forever, in all cases
Generally 3 years from the date the return was filed (or due), tied to the assessment statute of limitations
1 year after filing
questions.rationale: Taxpayers generally keep records for three years (the standard assessment statute), with longer retention for property basis, 6-year substantial-omission cases, and 7 years for certain bad-debt/loss claims.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under §6501, the IRS generally has how long to assess additional tax after a return is filed, and what extends that period to six years?
options: Ten years; no extension applies
Five years; extended to ten for late filing
Three years; extended to six years if there is a substantial omission of gross income (generally more than 25% of gross income stated)
Two years; doubled if the return is amended
questions.rationale: Section 6501 gives the IRS three years to assess (six for a substantial 25%+ omission of gross income), with no time limit for a false/fraudulent return or a failure to file.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: There is no statute of limitations on assessment in which situation under §6501(c)?
options: When the taxpayer requests an installment agreement
When the taxpayer files an amended return
When a refund claim is pending
When the taxpayer files a false or fraudulent return with intent to evade tax, or fails to file a return at all
questions.rationale: Section 6501(c) imposes no assessment statute of limitations for fraudulent returns filed to evade tax or where no return is filed.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: The collection statute of limitations under §6502 generally allows the IRS to collect an assessed tax for how long after assessment?
options: Indefinitely
20 years
3 years
10 years from the date of assessment (the Collection Statute Expiration Date), subject to suspension/extension events
questions.rationale: Under §6502, the IRS generally has 10 years from assessment to collect (the CSED); certain events (bankruptcy, pending OIC, CDP, time abroad) suspend or extend that period.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: A taxpayer requesting copies of IRS records may use the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). FOIA generally allows access to what?
options: Another taxpayer's confidential return information
Agency records, subject to statutory exemptions (such as those protecting third-party confidential information and certain law-enforcement materials)
Only records created after the request
Unlimited access with no exemptions
questions.rationale: FOIA grants access to existing agency records subject to exemptions; it cannot be used to obtain another person's confidential return information protected by §6103.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under the Privacy Act and §6103, a taxpayer generally has the right to do what regarding their own IRS records?
options: Demand deletion of all assessment records
Prevent the IRS from ever sharing data with state tax agencies
Access records the IRS maintains about them and request correction of inaccurate personal information, subject to exemptions
Obtain any other person's tax records on request
questions.rationale: The Privacy Act lets individuals access and seek correction of their own records (with exemptions), while §6103 governs confidentiality and the limited authorized disclosures of return information.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Which form is used to amend an individual income tax return?
options: Form 843
Form 1040-X
Form 8857
Form 9465
questions.rationale: Form 1040-X is used to correct or amend a previously filed individual income tax return.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: A preparer who endorses the importance of recordkeeping should advise that records substantiating the basis of property be kept for how long?
options: Only one year
Exactly three years from purchase
Until the period of limitations expires for the year in which the property is disposed of
Until the return is filed
questions.rationale: Basis records should be retained until the statute of limitations runs for the year the property is disposed of, because basis determines gain or loss reported in that year.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: When a paid preparer prepares a return but is not required to sign it electronically, the preparer must still do which of the following under §6695?
options: Charge a contingent fee
Waive the taxpayer's appeal rights
File the return only on paper
Sign the return (manual or authorized) and include the PTIN, furnish a copy to the taxpayer, and retain required records
questions.rationale: A paid preparer's core §6695 duties include signing, providing a PTIN, furnishing the taxpayer a copy of the return, and retaining records or a list of returns prepared.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under §6107, a return preparer must retain a completed copy of each return (or a list of taxpayers and identifying numbers) for what minimum period?
options: 10 years after assessment
1 year after the close of the return period
5 years after filing
3 years after the close of the return period in which the return was signed
questions.rationale: Section 6107 requires a preparer to keep a copy of each return prepared, or a list of taxpayers, for three years after the close of the return period; failure is penalized under §6695(d).
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: An ERO who is also the paid preparer of an e-filed return generally must do what regarding the preparer signature requirement?
options: Send a paper signature page to the IRS
Have the taxpayer sign on the preparer's behalf
Skip signing because e-filing exempts preparers
Sign as the paid preparer (using the practitioner PIN method or appropriate signature) in addition to acting as the ERO
questions.rationale: An ERO who is also the paid preparer must satisfy the preparer signature requirement (e.g., the practitioner PIN method) and retain the required authorizations.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: If an e-filed return is rejected by the IRS and cannot be corrected for retransmission, the ERO should generally do what to ensure timely filing?
options: Take reasonable steps to inform the taxpayer and, if the return cannot be e-filed, file a paper return by the later of the due date or within the perfection period (e.g., 5 or 10 days)
Take no action; rejection counts as filing
Wait until the next tax year
Convert the return to an installment agreement
questions.rationale: When an e-filed return is rejected and cannot be perfected, the ERO informs the taxpayer and files a paper return; the transmission perfection period gives a short grace window for timely filing.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Which statement about a Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN) is correct?
options: A PTIN is the same as a CAF number
A PTIN never needs renewal
A PTIN is required only for attorneys
Anyone who prepares or substantially helps prepare a federal return for compensation must have a valid PTIN
questions.rationale: Every paid federal tax return preparer must obtain a PTIN and renew it annually; it is distinct from a CAF number used for third-party authorizations.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: A preparer who fails to be diligent and signs a return claiming a credit the taxpayer is clearly not entitled to may face which combination of consequences?
options: Only a warning letter
No consequences if the taxpayer agreed
Automatic criminal prosecution only
Penalties under §6694 (understatement) and §6695(g) (due diligence), plus potential Circular 230 sanctions
questions.rationale: Signing a return with an unsupported credit can expose a preparer to §6694 and §6695(g) penalties and Circular 230 discipline; client agreement is not a defense.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: When a taxpayer makes a payment with an extension or return, the IRS applies payments in a general order. Voluntary payments may be designated by the taxpayer to be applied to what?
options: Future estimated taxes only
A specific tax, period, and type of liability the taxpayer designates (e.g., trust fund portion)
Only the oldest tax year automatically
The preparer's fee
questions.rationale: Taxpayers may designate how voluntary payments are applied (specific tax, period, and type, such as the trust fund portion); the IRS applies involuntary payments (e.g., levies) in its own best interest.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under §6511(b)(2), the amount of a refund is limited by a 'look-back' rule. If a claim is filed within the 3-year period, the refund is limited to the tax paid within how long before the claim (plus any extension period)?
options: 2 years only
10 years
3 years plus the period of any extension of time to file
1 year plus extensions
questions.rationale: Under §6511(b)(2), a claim filed within the 3-year period can recover only tax paid in the 3 years (plus extensions) before the claim; a claim filed only within the 2-year period is limited to tax paid in the prior 2 years.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: When a preparer obtains information from a taxpayer that appears incorrect or incomplete and bears on a refundable credit, the knowledge requirement obligates the preparer to do what?
options: Ignore it and rely solely on the taxpayer's word
Refuse the engagement automatically
Make reasonable inquiries to obtain correct and complete information and contemporaneously document those inquiries and responses
Report the taxpayer to the IRS
questions.rationale: Under the §6695(g) knowledge requirement, a preparer must make and document reasonable inquiries whenever the information furnished appears incorrect, inconsistent, or incomplete.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Which form does a business entity (such as a partnership or corporation) generally use to request an automatic extension of time to file its return?
options: Form 4868
Form 7004
Form 8857
Form 2350
questions.rationale: Form 7004 provides an automatic extension to file many business returns (e.g., 1065, 1120, 1120-S), while individuals use Form 4868.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: An accuracy-related penalty under §6662 is generally imposed on the taxpayer at what rate for a substantial understatement or negligence?
options: 100% of the tax
20% of the portion of the underpayment attributable to the misconduct (40% for certain gross valuation misstatements or undisclosed noneconomic substance/foreign transactions)
75% of the underpayment
5% of the understatement
questions.rationale: The §6662 accuracy-related penalty is generally 20% of the underpayment attributable to negligence or substantial understatement, rising to 40% for certain valuation and undisclosed transactions; §6663 imposes a 75% civil fraud penalty.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: The civil fraud penalty under §6663 is imposed at what rate on the portion of an underpayment attributable to fraud, and who bears the burden of proof?
options: 20%; the taxpayer bears the burden
100%; the taxpayer must disprove fraud
75% of the underpayment attributable to fraud; the IRS bears the burden of proving fraud by clear and convincing evidence
50%; neither party bears a burden
questions.rationale: The §6663 civil fraud penalty is 75% of the fraud-attributable underpayment, with the IRS bearing the burden to prove fraud by clear and convincing evidence.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: A representative who wishes to withdraw from a power of attorney already on file with the IRS may do so by sending the IRS what?
options: A copy of the Form 2848 with 'WITHDRAW' written across the top, signed and dated by the representative
A new Form 8821
A verbal notice to the revenue agent
Form 9465
questions.rationale: A representative withdraws from a Form 2848 by submitting a copy marked 'WITHDRAW' (signed and dated) or a signed statement; the taxpayer revokes by marking a copy 'REVOKE.'

questions.stem: Form 2848 generally allows a taxpayer to authorize a representative to perform most acts the taxpayer can perform, EXCEPT which of the following, unless specifically authorized?
options: Signing the taxpayer's return (allowed only in limited circumstances such as disease/injury, continuous absence from the U.S., or other authorized situations) and substituting/adding representatives or receiving (not endorsing) refund checks
Requesting a transcript
Representing the taxpayer in an examination
Receiving confidential tax information
questions.rationale: Form 2848 grants broad authority, but signing returns (only in limited situations), substituting representatives, and similar acts must be specifically authorized; a representative can receive but never endorse a refund check.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230 §10.6, an enrolled agent who fails to satisfy the continuing education requirements or fails to file a timely renewal application may be placed in what status?
options: Inactive enrollment status, during which the individual may not practice before the IRS as an enrolled agent
Automatic disbarment
Permanent termination with no reinstatement
Active status with a warning
questions.rationale: Section 10.6 allows placing an enrolled agent in inactive status for failing CE or renewal, barring practice until the requirements are met and the individual is returned to active status.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, an OPR proceeding for disbarment or suspension is initiated by a complaint and is decided after a hearing before whom?
options: The Tax Court
An Administrative Law Judge (ALJ), whose decision may be appealed to the Secretary or delegate
A jury in U.S. District Court
The Return Preparer Office
questions.rationale: Circular 230 disciplinary cases proceed by complaint and answer, are heard by an Administrative Law Judge, and may be appealed to the Secretary or delegate, with possible judicial review afterward.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230 §10.7, which of the following is generally permitted WITHOUT being an enrolled or otherwise authorized practitioner?
options: Representing a client in a complex Appeals conference
Practicing as an unlimited representative for unrelated clients
An individual representing themselves before the IRS, or a regular full-time employee representing their employer
Endorsing a client's refund check
questions.rationale: Section 10.7 allows certain limited practice without enrollment, including self-representation, an employee representing the employer, and family members representing immediate family.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230 §10.8, a person who prepares (and signs, or prepares all or substantially all of) a tax return for compensation must do what?
options: Be admitted to the Tax Court bar
Possess a law degree
Have a valid PTIN and be subject to the duties and restrictions in Circular 230
Be a U.S. citizen
questions.rationale: Section 10.8 brings compensated return preparers within Circular 230's scope and requires a valid PTIN, subjecting them to its standards of conduct.

questions.stem: A taxpayer may designate a third party on the return itself (the 'Third Party Designee' checkbox) to discuss the processing of that specific return. This designee authority is limited in scope and generally expires when?
options: After 30 days
Never; it is permanent
When the taxpayer dies
One year from the original due date of the return (without regard to extensions)
questions.rationale: The return's Third Party Designee checkbox grants narrow authority to discuss processing of that specific return and generally expires one year from the original due date (without extensions).

questions.stem: An offer in compromise based on 'effective tax administration' (ETA) may be accepted even when the taxpayer could full-pay, when what is true?
options: The taxpayer disputes owing the tax
Collection in full would create economic hardship, or exceptional circumstances make full collection inequitable or detract from voluntary compliance
The taxpayer simply prefers to pay less
The statute of limitations has expired
questions.rationale: An effective tax administration OIC is used when the tax is owed and collectible but full collection would cause economic hardship or be unfair/inequitable under exceptional circumstances.

questions.stem: An offer in compromise based on doubt as to liability is appropriate when what is true?
options: There is a genuine dispute as to the existence or amount of the correct tax liability under the law
The taxpayer cannot afford to pay the tax
The taxpayer wants to stop interest from accruing
The taxpayer prefers an installment agreement
questions.rationale: A doubt-as-to-liability OIC (Form 656-L) is based on a genuine dispute about whether the assessed tax is legally owed or its correct amount.

questions.stem: The IRS must release a federal tax lien within how many days after the liability is fully satisfied or becomes legally unenforceable?
options: 30 days
90 days
60 days
10 days
questions.rationale: Under §6325, the IRS must release a federal tax lien within 30 days after the underlying liability is satisfied or becomes legally unenforceable.

questions.stem: A taxpayer may request a 'certificate of discharge' of property from a federal tax lien (e.g., to sell a specific asset). Which statement is correct?
options: A certificate of discharge removes the lien from a specific piece of property while the lien remains on the taxpayer's other property
A discharge eliminates the underlying tax debt
A discharge removes the lien from all of the taxpayer's property
A discharge is automatic upon any sale
questions.rationale: A certificate of discharge (Form 14135) removes the lien from a specific property to facilitate a sale, but the lien remains on the taxpayer's other assets and the debt remains.

questions.stem: A 'subordination' of a federal tax lien differs from a discharge because subordination does what?
options: Transfers the lien to a co-owner
Allows another creditor to move ahead of the IRS's lien position on specific property (e.g., to refinance), without removing the IRS lien
Removes the lien entirely
Forgives the tax debt
questions.rationale: A lien subordination (Form 14134) allows another creditor to take priority over the IRS lien on certain property (commonly for refinancing), while the IRS lien stays in effect.

questions.stem: Before levying on a taxpayer's property, the IRS generally must provide a Final Notice of Intent to Levy and notice of the right to a CDP hearing at least how many days before the levy?
options: 30 days
60 days
10 days
90 days
questions.rationale: Under §6330, the IRS must provide a final notice of intent to levy and CDP hearing rights at least 30 days before levy, subject to narrow exceptions like jeopardy or state-refund levies.

questions.stem: Certain property is exempt from IRS levy under §6334. Which of the following is generally exempt?
options: A limited amount of wages, salary, and other income based on the taxpayer's standard deduction and exemptions, plus items like necessary tools of a trade up to a limit and certain personal effects
All bank accounts
All of the taxpayer's wages
Vacation homes
questions.rationale: Section 6334 lists property exempt from levy, including a limited amount of wages, certain personal effects and tools of a trade (up to limits), unemployment benefits, and certain pensions.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230 §10.2, the term 'practice before the IRS' includes which of the following activities?
options: Auditing a client's financial statements
Communicating with the IRS for a taxpayer, representing a taxpayer at conferences/hearings/meetings, and preparing/filing documents with the IRS
Providing investment advice
Only preparing and filing tax returns
questions.rationale: Section 10.2 defines practice before the IRS broadly to include representing taxpayers, communicating with the IRS, and preparing and filing documents on a taxpayer's behalf.

questions.stem: A non-IRS attorney or CPA who is not yet recognized but wants to represent a taxpayer may sometimes appear without a power of attorney by what limited means?
options: Endorsing the refund check
Filing the appropriate Declaration of Representative and, where needed, a power of attorney; without these, recognition to represent is generally not granted
Simply telling the agent they are an attorney
Submitting a properly executed Form 2848 is never required
questions.rationale: Recognition as a representative requires the proper Declaration of Representative and, where applicable, a Form 2848 power of attorney; without them, the IRS generally will not recognize the representative.

questions.stem: Under §6107(b), failing to retain the required copy of returns or the list of taxpayers can result in a penalty under which provision?
questions.rationale: Section 6695(d) penalizes a preparer's failure to retain the copies or list of returns required by §6107.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, an enrolled agent who is suspended may be reinstated only after the period of suspension ends and what additional showing, if required?
options: No showing is ever required
Payment of a flat $1,000 fee with no other conditions
Re-taking the entire SEE in all cases
A demonstration that the practitioner is not likely to again engage in disreputable conduct and that reinstatement is not contrary to the public interest
questions.rationale: After a suspension or disbarment period, reinstatement generally requires a showing that the practitioner will not resume misconduct and that reinstatement is consistent with the public interest.

questions.stem: If a taxpayer wants their representative to receive original notices and other written communications from the IRS, the taxpayer must indicate this on Form 2848 by doing what?
options: Nothing; representatives automatically receive all originals
Endorsing the notices
Filing a separate Form 911
Checking the appropriate box; otherwise the representative generally receives copies, and original notices still go to the taxpayer
questions.rationale: On Form 2848, the taxpayer can have copies of notices sent to the representative, but original notices generally still go to the taxpayer; the box selection controls this delivery.

questions.stem: A taxpayer in an examination disagrees with the revenue agent and the case is unagreed. To pursue Appeals while preserving rights, the taxpayer generally files what in response to a 30-day letter for cases over the small-case threshold?
options: A formal written protest requesting an Appeals conference
Form 656
Form 911
A Tax Court petition
questions.rationale: In response to a 30-day letter, larger cases require a formal written protest to obtain an Appeals conference, while smaller cases may use a brief small-case request.

questions.stem: Which form does a taxpayer use to request a copy of a previously filed tax return (an exact copy, for a fee)?
options: Form 4506-T, Request for Transcript of Tax Return
Form 4506, Request for Copy of Tax Return
Form 8821
Form 1040-X
questions.rationale: Form 4506 obtains an exact copy of a filed return (for a fee); Form 4506-T obtains a transcript of return information at no charge.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: A return transcript and an account transcript differ in that a return transcript shows what?
options: The taxpayer's bank account details
All adjustments and payments after filing
Most line items from the return as originally filed (and certain forms/schedules), but not later adjustments
Only the balance due
questions.rationale: A return transcript reflects the return as originally filed, while an account transcript shows subsequent activity such as payments, penalties, and adjustments.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Circular 230 is officially published as which of the following?
options: The Internal Revenue Manual
Treasury Department Circular No. 230, found in 31 C.F.R. Part 10, governing practice before the IRS
Title 26 of the Internal Revenue Code
A revenue ruling
questions.rationale: Circular 230 (31 C.F.R. Part 10) sets the rules governing those who practice before the IRS, including attorneys, CPAs, enrolled agents, and other preparers.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's representative learns mid-engagement that two clients they jointly represent now have directly adverse interests regarding which spouse caused an understatement. Under §10.29, the representative should generally do what?
options: Continue representing both without disclosure since they are spouses

Evaluate the conflict, and continue only if the representative reasonably believes they can competently and diligently represent each, it is legal, and each affected client gives informed written consent
Immediately report both clients to the IRS
Endorse any joint refund check to resolve the dispute
questions.rationale: Section 10.29 requires conflict analysis and, to proceed, the reasonable belief of competent/diligent representation, legality, and informed written consent from each affected client (retained 36 months).

questions.stem: When a return claims the Earned Income Tax Credit and the preparer relies on a client's statement about a qualifying child's residency, the preparer satisfies due diligence by doing what?
options: Accepting the statement without question in all cases
Requiring the client to provide a DNA test
Asking reasonable questions when the information seems incomplete or inconsistent and documenting the inquiries and answers
Reporting the client to the IRS
questions.rationale: The §6695(g) knowledge requirement obligates the preparer to make and document reasonable inquiries when EITC residency information appears incomplete or inconsistent.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a 'partial payment installment agreement' (PPIA)?
options: An installment agreement under which the monthly payments will not fully pay the liability before the collection statute expires, subject to periodic financial review
An agreement to pay the full balance in equal monthly amounts
An agreement that forgives the tax immediately
A short-term agreement of 120 days or less
questions.rationale: A partial payment installment agreement lets a taxpayer make smaller payments that will not fully pay the debt before the collection statute expires, with periodic reviews of ability to pay.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, a practitioner who knowingly gives false or misleading information to the Department of the Treasury or any officer is engaging in what?
options: An act outside Circular 230
A protected First Amendment activity
Disreputable conduct subject to sanction under §10.51
Permissible advocacy
questions.rationale: Section 10.51 treats knowingly giving false or misleading information to Treasury or IRS officials as disreputable conduct warranting sanction.

questions.stem: Under §6651(f), the penalty for fraudulent failure to file a return is increased from the standard 5% per month to what rate?
options: 10% per month, up to 50%
15% per month (up to 75% maximum)
0.5% per month
20% per month, up to 100%
questions.rationale: Section 6651(f) raises the failure-to-file penalty to 15% per month (maximum 75%) when the failure to file is fraudulent.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: If a taxpayer and the IRS reach a final agreement that conclusively settles a tax matter and is binding on both parties, which document is generally used?
options: A Form 2848
A Form 4506
A closing agreement (Form 866 or Form 906)
A Form 8821
questions.rationale: A closing agreement (Form 866 or 906) under §7121 is a final, binding settlement of a tax matter that generally cannot be reopened absent fraud, malfeasance, or misrepresentation of a material fact.

questions.stem: A closing agreement under §7121 may be set aside only upon a showing of what?
options: A new revenue ruling
The taxpayer's later change of mind
The representative's withdrawal
Fraud, malfeasance, or misrepresentation of a material fact
questions.rationale: Section 7121 closing agreements are conclusive and may be reopened only for fraud, malfeasance, or misrepresentation of a material fact.

questions.stem: An Appeals officer evaluating a case considers the 'hazards of litigation.' This means the Appeals officer may do what?
options: Impose additional penalties automatically
Decide cases solely on the IRS's litigating position
Ignore the strength of the taxpayer's evidence
Settle a case for less than the full amount based on the probability that the IRS would not prevail if the matter were litigated
questions.rationale: Appeals settlements may reflect the hazards of litigation, compromising issues based on the probability of the IRS prevailing in court, a flexibility examination personnel lack.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who relied on the written advice of a competent tax professional, after providing complete and accurate information, may have an accuracy-related penalty abated based on what?
options: Reasonable cause and good-faith reliance on professional advice
The advice being free of charge
The amount of the refund
The professional's PTIN status alone
questions.rationale: Reasonable, good-faith reliance on a competent professional's advice (with complete and accurate facts disclosed) can support reasonable-cause relief from the accuracy-related penalty.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, which section specifically governs the requirements a practitioner must meet when giving written advice concerning a federal tax matter?
options: Section 10.37
Section 10.21
Section 10.35
Section 10.34
questions.rationale: Circular 230 Section 10.37 governs written advice, requiring the practitioner to base advice on reasonable assumptions, consider all relevant facts, and not consider the likelihood of audit. The 2014 amendments eliminated the detailed covered-opinion rules of former 10.35.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the reasonableness factors a practitioner must consider when rendering written advice under Circular 230 Section 10.37?
options: Whether the practitioner evaluated the likelihood the return would be audited
Whether the practitioner considered all relevant facts the practitioner knew or reasonably should have known
Whether the practitioner relied on the advice of another person with adequate basis for that reliance
Whether the practitioner relied on representations the practitioner knew were incorrect
questions.rationale: Section 10.37 forbids the practitioner from considering the likelihood of audit (the audit lottery) when giving written advice. The other items are genuine factors used to judge whether written advice was reasonable.

questions.stem: The Office of Professional Responsibility may seek expedited suspension of a practitioner under Circular 230 Section 10.82 in which situation?
options: The practitioner charged an unconscionable fee
The practitioner failed to return client records
The practitioner's license to practice as an attorney or CPA was suspended or revoked by a state for cause
The practitioner gave a written opinion lacking substantial authority
questions.rationale: Expedited suspension under Section 10.82 applies in limited circumstances such as loss of a state professional license for cause, certain criminal tax convictions, or demonstrated failure to file personal returns. Most violations proceed through the regular complaint-and-hearing process.

questions.stem: After the Office of Professional Responsibility files a complaint under Circular 230, the respondent practitioner generally must file an answer within how many days from the date the complaint is served?
options: 60 days
30 days
15 days
10 days
questions.rationale: Section 10.64 requires the respondent to answer the OPR complaint within 30 days of service unless a longer time is specified. Failure to answer can result in a default decision.

questions.stem: In a Circular 230 disciplinary proceeding, which standard of proof applies to establish a violation when censure, suspension, or disbarment is sought?
options: Substantial evidence
Beyond a reasonable doubt
Clear and convincing evidence
Preponderance of the evidence
questions.rationale: Under Section 10.76, the OPR must prove a violation warranting censure, suspension, or disbarment by clear and convincing evidence. This is higher than the ordinary preponderance standard.

questions.stem: An administrative law judge issues a decision in a Circular 230 case. A party who wishes to appeal that decision to the Secretary's delegate (the Treasury Appellate Authority) generally must file an appeal within how many days?
options: 30 days
45 days
10 days
90 days
questions.rationale: Section 10.77 gives a party 30 days to appeal the administrative law judge's decision to the appellate authority. The agency decision becomes final if no timely appeal is taken.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230 Section 10.50(c), a monetary penalty imposed on a firm or practitioner for conduct may be in an amount up to:
options: $10,000 regardless of fees earned
The gross income derived or to be derived from the conduct giving rise to the penalty
$1,000 per violation
Twice the unpaid tax liability
questions.rationale: Section 10.50(c) allows the IRS to impose a monetary penalty up to the gross income derived (or to be derived) from the conduct, and it can be imposed on the individual, the firm, or both. It may be in addition to or instead of suspension or disbarment.

questions.stem: Circular 230 Section 10.27 generally prohibits contingent fees. Which of the following is a permitted exception?
options: Any matter before the IRS if the client agrees in writing
Promoting a tax shelter for a percentage of tax saved
Preparing an original income tax return for a contingent fee
Services rendered in connection with an IRS examination of, or challenge to, an original return
questions.rationale: Section 10.27 permits contingent fees in narrow circumstances, including services connected with an IRS examination or challenge to an original return, certain timely amended returns or claims, claims for refund involving statutory interest or penalties, and judicial proceedings. Original return preparation for a contingent fee is barred.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230 Section 10.27, a contingent fee is also permitted for a claim for refund filed in connection with which item?
options: A claim for refund of penalties or interest determined under the Internal Revenue Code
A claim for refund relating solely to additional tax owed on an original return
Preparation of an amended return filed before any IRS contact
A request for a private letter ruling
questions.rationale: Among the narrow exceptions in Section 10.27 is a claim for refund filed in connection with the determination of statutory interest or penalties. Routine amended returns filed before IRS contact do not qualify.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230 Section 10.29, when a practitioner represents two clients with a conflict of interest but obtains valid informed written consent from each, how long must the written consents be retained?
options: 1 year from the date consent was obtained
30 days after the engagement ends
At least 36 months from the date the representation concludes
Permanently
questions.rationale: Section 10.29 permits conflict-of-interest representation only with each affected client's informed written consent. The practitioner must keep those consents for at least 36 months after the representation ends and produce them to the IRS upon request.

questions.stem: Which Circular 230 section establishes a practitioner's duty to exercise due diligence in preparing and filing tax returns and other documents?
options: Section 10.25
Section 10.23
Section 10.24
Section 10.22
questions.rationale: Section 10.22 imposes the due-diligence duty, requiring practitioners to be accurate in returns and documents and in representations to clients and the IRS. A practitioner may generally rely on another's work if reasonable care was used in selecting that person.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230 Section 10.3, which of the following individuals is NOT included in the definition of a practitioner authorized to practice before the IRS?
options: An enrolled retirement plan agent
A certified public accountant
An enrolled agent
An unenrolled return preparer with no Annual Filing Season Program record
questions.rationale: Section 10.3 lists attorneys, CPAs, enrolled agents, enrolled actuaries, and enrolled retirement plan agents as practitioners. Unenrolled preparers are not practitioners, though AFSP participants gain limited representation rights for returns they prepared and signed.

questions.stem: Under Section 10.34(a) of Circular 230, a practitioner may not sign a tax return or advise a position unless there is, at minimum, a reasonable basis and the position is not frivolous. What additional standard applies if the position would not be disclosed?
options: More likely than not is required
Substantial authority is required for an undisclosed position to avoid the standard being violated
Only a good-faith belief is needed
No additional standard applies once reasonable basis exists
questions.rationale: Section 10.34 ties signing and advising standards to the preparer-penalty thresholds: reasonable basis with disclosure, substantial authority without disclosure, and the higher more-likely-than-not standard for tax shelters and reportable transactions.

questions.stem: Circular 230 Section 10.51 lists incompetence and disreputable conduct. Which of the following is specifically listed as disreputable conduct?
options: Charging a reasonable hourly fee
Maintaining a client trust account
Advising a client to disclose an uncertain position
Willfully failing to file the practitioner's own federal tax returns
questions.rationale: Section 10.51 enumerates disreputable conduct, including conviction of certain crimes, giving false information, willful failure to file returns, misappropriation of funds, and willfully assisting tax evasion. Willfully failing to file one's own returns is a classic example.

questions.stem: A former IRS employee who personally and substantially participated in a particular matter while in government service is, under Circular 230 Section 10.25, subject to which restriction?
options: A permanent bar from representing or assisting anyone in that same particular matter
No restriction once enrolled as an agent
A two-year cooling-off period for all IRS practice
A one-year bar from any IRS contact
questions.rationale: Section 10.25 imposes a permanent bar on representing or knowingly assisting in the specific matter in which the former employee personally and substantially participated, plus a two-year restriction for matters that were under their official responsibility, and a one-year restriction on certain rule-development matters.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230 Section 10.36, a firm that has a practice involving federal tax matters must take which step regarding its members?
options: Obtain malpractice insurance for each member
Require all members to be enrolled agents
Personally review every return prepared by any member
Take reasonable steps to ensure the firm has adequate procedures for all members to comply with Circular 230
questions.rationale: Section 10.36 makes those with principal authority over a firm's tax practice responsible for ensuring the firm has adequate procedures so members comply with Circular 230. A failure to take reasonable steps can itself be a violation.

questions.stem: Circular 230 Section 10.30 governs solicitation and advertising. Which practice does it specifically prohibit?
options: Advertising on the internet
Publishing a written fee schedule
Listing areas of practice
Using false, fraudulent, or coercive statements or claims in advertising
questions.rationale: Section 10.30 bars false, fraudulent, coercive, or misleading advertising and solicitation. Practitioners may advertise fees and must honor published fee information for at least 30 days after the last publication.

questions.stem: Under IRC Section 6694(a), the penalty for an unreasonable position by a tax return preparer applies when the position lacked which standard and there was no reasonable basis with disclosure?
options: A more-likely-than-not belief for every position
Substantial authority for an undisclosed position
Clear and convincing evidence
Proof beyond a reasonable doubt
questions.rationale: Section 6694(a) penalizes understatements from unreasonable positions: an undisclosed non-shelter position needs substantial authority, a disclosed position needs reasonable basis, and tax shelters or reportable transactions need a more-likely-than-not standard.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the components of the IRC Section 6695 preparer penalties?
options: Failure to have substantial authority for a position
Failure to furnish a copy of the return to the taxpayer
Failure to furnish the preparer's identifying number (PTIN)
Failure to sign the return as preparer
questions.rationale: Section 6695 imposes procedural penalties: failure to furnish a copy, sign, furnish a PTIN, retain records, file information returns, negotiate a refund check, and meet EITC/due-diligence requirements. Substantial-authority issues fall under Section 6694.

questions.stem: Under IRC Section 6695(f), a tax return preparer who endorses or otherwise negotiates a refund check issued to a taxpayer is subject to a penalty. This rule is intended to prevent:
options: Taxpayers from claiming the EITC
Preparers from diverting clients' refund checks to themselves
Preparers from e-filing returns
Preparers from charging contingent fees
questions.rationale: Section 6695(f) imposes a penalty per check on a preparer who endorses or negotiates a taxpayer's refund check, except for depositing into the taxpayer's own account. This protects taxpayers from preparers diverting refunds.

questions.stem: IRC Section 6700 imposes a penalty for which of the following?
options: Promoting abusive tax shelters
Aiding and abetting an understatement of tax liability
Failing to sign a return
Disclosing taxpayer return information without authorization
questions.rationale: Section 6700 targets promoters of abusive tax shelters. Section 6701 addresses aiding and abetting understatements; Sections 6713 and 7216 address unauthorized disclosure of return information.

questions.stem: IRC Section 6701 imposes a penalty for aiding and abetting an understatement of tax liability. The per-document penalty amount is generally:
options: $1,000, or $10,000 if the document relates to a corporation's tax
10% of the understatement
$5,000 per document for all taxpayers
$500 per document with no exceptions
questions.rationale: Section 6701 penalizes aiding, assisting, or advising in preparing a document known to result in an understatement. The penalty is $1,000 per person per period, rising to $10,000 when the document relates to a corporation's tax.

questions.stem: IRC Section 7216 makes it a criminal offense for a tax return preparer to:
options: Charge an unreasonable fee
Knowingly or recklessly disclose or use tax return information without authorization
Fail to keep continuing education records
Sign a return without a PTIN
questions.rationale: Section 7216 imposes criminal penalties (a misdemeanor) on preparers who knowingly or recklessly disclose or use return information without the taxpayer's consent. Section 6713 is the parallel civil penalty.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between IRC Section 6713 and Section 7216 regarding unauthorized disclosure of taxpayer information?
options: Both require willful intent
Section 7216 applies only to attorneys
Section 6713 is a civil penalty with no intent requirement; Section 7216 is a criminal misdemeanor requiring knowing or reckless conduct
Section 6713 is criminal; Section 7216 is civil
questions.rationale: Section 6713 imposes a $250 civil penalty per disclosure (capped at $10,000 per year) without regard to intent, while Section 7216 is a criminal statute requiring knowing or reckless unauthorized disclosure or use.

questions.stem: A tax preparer who is a specified tax return preparer expecting to file 11 or more covered returns must e-file, but a client insists on a paper return. The preparer should file:
options: Form 8948 to explain the paper-filing exception
Form 8821 to authorize disclosure
Form 8867 with the return
Form 2848 for the client
questions.rationale: Form 8948, Preparer Explanation for Not Filing Electronically, accompanies a paper return when a specified preparer is otherwise subject to the e-file mandate, such as when the taxpayer chose to file on paper.

questions.stem: An Electronic Return Originator (ERO) signs returns for e-filing. The ERO's responsibility includes which of the following?
options: Guaranteeing the IRS will accept the return
Representing the taxpayer in an audit automatically
Paying any balance due for the taxpayer
Verifying taxpayer identity and obtaining required signature authorizations such as Form 8879
questions.rationale: EROs originate the electronic submission of returns and must verify taxpayer identity and obtain proper signature authorization, such as Form 8879. The ERO also retains records and follows IRS e-file program rules.

questions.stem: The per-failure penalty for not meeting the due-diligence requirements under IRC Section 6695(g) is indexed for inflation. For a return claiming the EITC, CTC, and AOTC, a preparer who fails the requirements for all three credits could be penalized:
options: Only at year end as a single aggregate penalty
Once, regardless of the number of credits
Per credit, so up to three separate penalties on the same return
Only if the IRS proves willfulness
questions.rationale: Section 6695(g) assesses the due-diligence penalty separately for each applicable credit and for head of household status. A return claiming several covered items can therefore generate several penalties.

questions.stem: Under IRC Section 6694, a preparer can avoid the unreasonable-position penalty by showing reasonable cause and good faith. Which factor is most relevant to that defense?
options: The dollar amount of the refund claimed
Whether the client was audited
The preparer's years of experience alone
The nature of the error, the frequency of errors, and reliance on advice of another preparer or the taxpayer
questions.rationale: The reasonable-cause-and-good-faith defense to the Section 6694(a) penalty considers the nature and materiality of the error, its isolated nature, the preparer's normal office practices, and reasonable reliance on the advice of others or the taxpayer's information.

questions.stem: Which form must a paid preparer keep, along with worksheets, to document compliance with the EITC due-diligence knowledge requirement?
options: Form 1040-X
Form W-7
Form 8867 and the computation worksheets, plus a record of how eligibility information was obtained
Form 4506
questions.rationale: To satisfy due diligence, a preparer keeps Form 8867, the credit computation worksheets, and contemporaneous records showing how eligibility information was gathered and any inquiries made. These must be retained for three years.

questions.stem: A tax shelter or reportable transaction position taken by a preparer must meet which standard to avoid the Section 6694 penalty?
options: Substantial authority
More likely than not that the position would be sustained on its merits
Reasonable basis with disclosure
A non-frivolous argument
questions.rationale: Section 6694 imposes the elevated more-likely-than-not standard for positions involving tax shelters and reportable transactions, reflecting the heightened scrutiny Congress applied to such transactions.

questions.stem: Who is considered the signing tax return preparer for purposes of the preparer penalties when multiple preparers work on a return?
options: The individual preparer who has primary responsibility for the overall substantive accuracy of the return
The client who signs the return
The most senior person in the firm
Every person who touched any line of the return
questions.rationale: The signing tax return preparer is the one with primary responsibility for the overall substantive accuracy of the return. A nonsigning preparer is someone who prepares a substantial portion but does not sign, and is subject to penalties under different rules.

questions.stem: Under the IRS e-file program, an ERO who is suspended from participation may be subject to sanctions. The IRS categorizes e-file infractions into levels. A Level Three infraction generally results in:
options: Immediate criminal referral in all cases
No action
Suspension from the e-file program for two years
A written reprimand only
questions.rationale: IRS e-file monitoring categorizes infractions into three levels, with Level Three being the most serious and typically resulting in a two-year suspension or expulsion from the program. Lesser infractions draw reprimands or one-year suspensions.

questions.stem: A preparer who fails to retain a completed copy of each return or a list of taxpayers for whom returns were prepared is subject to a penalty under which provision?
options: Section 6700
Section 6694(a)
Section 6695(d)
Section 7216
questions.rationale: Section 6695(d) imposes a penalty for failing to retain a completed copy of each return or claim, or a list of taxpayers and return information, for the three-year retention period.

questions.stem: A preparer obtains taxpayer consent to use tax return information to solicit additional business. Under the Section 7216 regulations, the consent must:
