options: Be in writing, signed and dated by the taxpayer, before the disclosure or use, and meet specific content requirements
Be obtained only after the return is filed
Be implied from the engagement letter
Be obtained orally and noted in the file
questions.rationale: The Section 7216 regulations and Revenue Procedure guidance require a signed, dated, written consent obtained before any use or disclosure not otherwise permitted, with specified content. Consent cannot be implied or oral.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants a third party to receive and inspect confidential tax information but NOT to advocate or represent before the IRS. Which authorization is appropriate?
options: Form 911, Taxpayer Advocate request
Form 2848, Power of Attorney
Form 8821, Tax Information Authorization
Form 56, Notice Concerning Fiduciary Relationship
questions.rationale: Form 8821 permits a designee to inspect and receive confidential return information but confers no authority to represent the taxpayer. Form 2848 is required to actually represent and advocate before the IRS.

questions.stem: The Third Party Designee checkbox on Form 1040 allows the named person to do which of the following?
options: Receive the taxpayer's refund check
Discuss the processing of that specific return with the IRS, provide missing information, and respond to certain notices for that year
Represent the taxpayer in an audit and sign agreements
Bind the taxpayer to an installment agreement
questions.rationale: The Third Party Designee authority is narrow and limited to the processing of the specific return for one year. It expires automatically one year after the return's due date and does not allow representation, signing agreements, or receiving refunds.

questions.stem: The IRS Centralized Authorization File (CAF) unit processes which documents?
options: Powers of attorney (Form 2848) and tax information authorizations (Form 8821)
Audit reconsideration requests
Only Form 1040 returns
Offers in compromise
questions.rationale: The CAF unit enters Forms 2848 and 8821 into the Centralized Authorization File, assigning a CAF number so the IRS can confirm a representative's scope of authority during interactions.

questions.stem: On Form 2848, if a representative wants the IRS to send copies of original notices and communications to the representative, the representative must:
options: File a separate Form 8821
Check the box on the form indicating they wish to receive copies of notices and communications
Automatically receive all notices once the CAF is updated
Request it by phone after each notice issues
questions.rationale: Form 2848 lets a representative elect to receive copies of notices and communications by checking the appropriate box. Without that election, the IRS sends originals to the taxpayer and may not copy the representative.

questions.stem: A taxpayer receives a Notice of Federal Tax Lien filing under IRC Section 6320. The taxpayer wishes to request a Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing. The request must be filed within:
options: 60 days after the lien filing
90 days after the lien filing
30 days after the end of the 5-business-day period in which the IRS must notify the taxpayer of the lien filing
30 days after the day of the lien filing
questions.rationale: Section 6320 requires the IRS to notify the taxpayer of a lien filing within 5 business days, after which the taxpayer has 30 days to request a CDP hearing. A late request may still qualify for an equivalent hearing.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a key difference between a Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing and an Equivalent Hearing?
options: Both suspend the collection statute identically
An equivalent hearing provides Tax Court review; a CDP hearing does not
A CDP hearing decision may be appealed to the Tax Court, while an equivalent hearing decision cannot
An equivalent hearing must be requested within 30 days
questions.rationale: A CDP hearing requested within 30 days suspends levy action and the collection statute and results in a determination subject to Tax Court review. An equivalent hearing (requested within one year of a missed CDP deadline) gives a similar Appeals review but no Tax Court appeal and no statutory suspension.

questions.stem: The Collection Appeals Program (CAP) differs from a CDP hearing in that under CAP:
options: There is no right to judicial review of the Appeals decision
Only the IRS, not the taxpayer, can initiate it
The taxpayer has more time to request the hearing
The taxpayer may dispute the underlying tax liability
questions.rationale: CAP allows quick Appeals review of a broad range of collection actions (liens, levies, seizures, installment agreement decisions) but does not permit challenging the underlying liability and provides no judicial review. CDP is narrower in scope but offers Tax Court review.

questions.stem: The Collection Statute Expiration Date (CSED) is generally how long after assessment, absent tolling?
options: 6 years
3 years
20 years
10 years
questions.rationale: Section 6502 provides a 10-year collection period from the date of assessment. Certain events such as bankruptcy, OIC pendency, CDP hearings, and installment agreement requests can toll or extend the CSED.

questions.stem: Which of the following events does NOT generally toll (suspend) the Collection Statute Expiration Date?
options: A bankruptcy automatic stay plus six months
The taxpayer moving to a different state
The pendency of a properly filed offer in compromise
The pendency of a timely CDP hearing request
questions.rationale: Tolling events include a pending OIC, a pending CDP hearing, bankruptcy (stay plus six months), being outside the country for at least six months, and certain installment agreement actions. Merely relocating does not toll the CSED.

questions.stem: An offer in compromise based on effective tax administration (ETA) requires the taxpayer to show:
options: That the taxpayer has no assets at all
That the tax is legally incorrect
That the collection statute has expired
That, although the tax is correct and collectible, requiring full payment would create economic hardship or be detrimental to voluntary compliance and equity
questions.rationale: ETA offers are available when the tax is valid and collectible but full collection would cause economic hardship or be unfair and inequitable given the taxpayer's circumstances. The liability and ability to pay are not in dispute.

questions.stem: The Trust Fund Recovery Penalty under IRC Section 6672 may be assessed against:
options: Only the company's outside accountant
Only the corporation that failed to remit the taxes
Any employee of the business regardless of authority
Any responsible person who willfully failed to collect, account for, or pay over trust fund taxes
questions.rationale: The TFRP applies to responsible persons who willfully fail to remit withheld income and the employee share of FICA (the trust fund taxes). Both responsibility (authority and duty) and willfulness must be present.

questions.stem: For Trust Fund Recovery Penalty purposes, willfulness generally means:
options: A voluntary, conscious, and intentional decision to pay other creditors instead of the United States, knowing the taxes were due
An intent to defraud the government
Failing to file the corporation's income tax return
Gross negligence only
questions.rationale: TFRP willfulness does not require bad motive or fraud. It is met when a responsible person knowingly uses available funds to pay other creditors instead of the withheld trust fund taxes, or acts with reckless disregard of an obvious risk.

questions.stem: The Trust Fund Recovery Penalty equals what portion of the unpaid employment taxes?
options: The entire employment tax including the employer's share and penalties
50% of the total employment tax liability
100% of the trust fund portion (withheld income tax and the employee share of FICA)
The employer's matching share of FICA only
questions.rationale: The TFRP recovers 100% of the trust fund taxes, which are the income tax withheld and the employee portion of FICA. The employer's matching share is not a trust fund tax and is not part of the penalty.

questions.stem: The IRS may collect an assessed tax from a person who received property from the taxpayer for less than full value. This person is referred to as a:
options: Fiduciary protector
Whistleblower
Transferee
Power of attorney
questions.rationale: Transferee liability under IRC Section 6901 lets the IRS pursue someone who received the taxpayer's property without adequate consideration, up to the value of the assets received, when the transfer left the taxpayer unable to pay.

questions.stem: An alter-ego theory allows the IRS to collect a taxpayer's liability from:
options: Any business in the same industry
The taxpayer's tax preparer
A wholly unrelated third party
An entity that is so controlled by and intermingled with the taxpayer that it is effectively the same as the taxpayer
questions.rationale: Alter-ego (and nominee) theories let the IRS reach assets held in the name of an entity or person that is, in substance, the taxpayer. Courts examine control, commingling of funds, and lack of corporate formalities.

questions.stem: Innocent spouse relief under IRC Section 6015(b) generally requires that:
options: Only one of the spouses signed the return
The requesting spouse pays the full liability first
The understatement is due to an erroneous item of the other spouse, the requesting spouse did not know and had no reason to know, and it would be inequitable to hold them liable
The spouses are still married
questions.rationale: Section 6015(b) relief requires a joint return with an understatement attributable to the other spouse's erroneous item, the requesting spouse's lack of actual or constructive knowledge, and inequity in imposing liability.

questions.stem: Relief by separation of liability under IRC Section 6015(c) is available only to a requesting spouse who:
options: Filed separate returns
Earned no income during the year
Is divorced, legally separated, widowed, or not a member of the same household as the other spouse for the 12 months before the request
Is still married and living with the other spouse
questions.rationale: Section 6015(c) allocates the deficiency between the spouses as if separate returns had been filed, but it is limited to those divorced, legally separated, widowed, or not members of the same household for the prior 12 months.

questions.stem: Equitable relief under IRC Section 6015(f) differs from relief under 6015(b) and (c) because it:
options: Requires an understatement only
Can apply to an underpayment of properly reported tax, not just an understatement, when other relief is unavailable and it would be inequitable to hold the spouse liable
Requires payment in full before relief
Is available only to married couples
questions.rationale: Section 6015(f) is the catch-all equitable relief provision. Unlike (b) and (c), it can address underpayments of properly reported tax and is granted based on all facts and circumstances when other relief does not apply.

questions.stem: Regarding the time limit to request innocent spouse relief, which statement is correct under current IRS practice?
options: All three types of relief require a request within 2 years of the first collection activity

Relief under 6015(b) and (c) must generally be requested within 2 years of the first collection activity, while equitable relief under 6015(f) is allowed within the collection or refund limitations period
There is no time limit for any innocent spouse relief
Equitable relief must be requested within 90 days
questions.rationale: The statutory 2-year period from the first collection activity applies to 6015(b) and (c). For equitable relief under 6015(f), the IRS expanded the period so a request is timely if made while the collection statute is open or within the refund limitations period.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who disagrees with the results of a prior audit and has new information may request which of the following without amending the return?
options: A jeopardy assessment
An offer in compromise
A whistleblower claim
Audit reconsideration
questions.rationale: Audit reconsideration is an informal process allowing the IRS to reconsider a previous audit assessment when the taxpayer presents new information or did not participate. It does not require an amended return, though the liability must remain unpaid or be eligible for a refund claim.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes audit reconsideration from filing an amended return (Form 1040-X)?
options: Audit reconsideration always requires Tax Court approval
An amended return can never claim a refund
They are identical procedures
Audit reconsideration asks the IRS to reconsider an existing audit assessment, while an amended return is a taxpayer-initiated correction subject to the refund statute of limitations
questions.rationale: Audit reconsideration is an administrative reexamination of an existing audit assessment, usually where tax is unpaid. An amended return is the taxpayer's own correction and, when seeking a refund, must comply with the Section 6511 limitations period.

questions.stem: The Fast Track Settlement program is designed to:
options: Resolve disputes more quickly while a case is still in Examination, using Appeals as a mediator
Eliminate the need to pay any tax
Replace the entire audit process
Provide automatic penalty abatement
questions.rationale: Fast Track Settlement uses an Appeals officer as a mediator while the case is still in Examination, allowing many disputes to be resolved within a target of roughly 60 to 120 days while preserving the taxpayer's appeal rights if no agreement is reached.

questions.stem: Under IRC Section 7345, the State Department may deny, revoke, or limit a passport when a taxpayer has a:
options: Any unpaid tax balance over $100
Seriously delinquent tax debt that has been certified to the State Department (an assessed, unpaid liability above an indexed threshold with a lien or levy)
Pending audit
Late-filed return
questions.rationale: Section 7345 requires the IRS to certify seriously delinquent tax debts (assessed, unpaid amounts above an indexed threshold with a filed lien or issued levy) to the State Department, which can deny or revoke a passport. Certain debts in installment agreements, accepted OICs, or CDP hearings are excluded.

questions.stem: Which of the following would generally cause the IRS to reverse a seriously delinquent tax debt certification under Section 7345?
options: The taxpayer moving abroad
The taxpayer requesting an extension to file
The taxpayer entering into and remaining current on an installment agreement
The taxpayer renewing a driver's license
questions.rationale: Certification is reversed when the debt is fully satisfied or becomes legally unenforceable, or ceases to be seriously delinquent, such as when the taxpayer enters an installment agreement or accepted OIC, makes a timely CDP election, or obtains innocent spouse relief.

questions.stem: The IRS may correct a clearly erroneous mathematical or clerical error on a return using a math error notice. The taxpayer who disagrees must request abatement within how many days to have the assessment handled under normal deficiency procedures?
options: 120 days
30 days
60 days
90 days
questions.rationale: Section 6213(b) allows summary assessment of math or clerical errors, but the taxpayer has 60 days to request abatement. A timely request forces the IRS to use regular deficiency procedures, including a notice of deficiency, before reassessing.

questions.stem: When the IRS prepares a Substitute for Return (SFR) under IRC Section 6020(b) for a nonfiler, which consequence applies?
options: The SFR cannot later be replaced by the taxpayer's own return
The SFR starts the refund statute of limitations
The SFR generally uses standard deduction and single or married-filing-separately status, omitting most credits and itemized deductions, often producing a higher liability
The SFR is filed with the most favorable deductions for the taxpayer
questions.rationale: An SFR under Section 6020(b) is prepared without the taxpayer's beneficial deductions, credits, or filing status, so it usually overstates tax. The taxpayer can file an original return to correct it, and the SFR does not start the assessment statute the way a filed return does.

questions.stem: An IRS Substitute for Return (SFR) has a notable effect on bankruptcy dischargeability. Generally, taxes assessed from an SFR where the taxpayer never filed their own return are:
options: Automatically forgiven
Always dischargeable after three years
Treated the same as a timely filed return
Generally not dischargeable, because the taxpayer did not file a return
questions.rationale: Filing a return is a prerequisite for discharging income taxes in bankruptcy. Where the IRS prepared an SFR and the taxpayer never filed, the taxes are generally nondischargeable, which is one reason filing the actual return matters even after an SFR assessment.

questions.stem: Under the IRS Whistleblower program (IRC Section 7623(b)), a whistleblower whose information leads to collected proceeds may receive an award when the amounts in dispute exceed:
options: $200,000 in gross income and the tax, penalties, and interest in dispute exceed $2,000,000 (for individual taxpayers)
questions.rationale: Section 7623(b) provides a mandatory award of 15% to 30% of collected proceeds when amounts in dispute exceed $2,000,000 (and individual gross income exceeds $200,000). Smaller cases fall under the discretionary 7623(a) program.

questions.stem: Under the mandatory whistleblower award provisions of IRC Section 7623(b), the award generally ranges from:
options: 1% to 5% of collected proceeds
50% to 75% of collected proceeds
A flat 10% regardless of contribution
15% to 30% of the collected proceeds
questions.rationale: The mandatory whistleblower award under 7623(b) is 15% to 30% of collected proceeds, with the percentage depending on the significance of the whistleblower's contribution. Discretionary awards under 7623(a) can be up to 15%.

questions.stem: A claim for refund must generally be filed within the later of which periods under IRC Section 6511?
options: 3 years from filing the return or 2 years from paying the tax
5 years from filing the return
1 year from paying the tax only
10 years from assessment
questions.rationale: Section 6511 sets the refund claim deadline at the later of 3 years from filing the return or 2 years from paying the tax. The amount recoverable is also limited by the corresponding lookback period.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files a refund claim 3 years after timely filing the return. Under the Section 6511(b)(2) lookback rule, the refund is limited to:
options: No refund at all
Only the tax paid in the last 6 months
All tax paid in the prior 10 years
Tax paid within the 3 years immediately preceding the claim (plus the extension period), which generally includes withholding and estimated taxes deemed paid on the return due date
questions.rationale: Section 6511(b)(2) caps the refund to amounts paid within the lookback period. For a claim filed within the 3-year window, the lookback is 3 years plus any extension, and withholding and estimated payments count as paid on the original due date.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's installment agreement request, while pending, generally has what effect on IRS levy action?
options: It extends the assessment statute by 5 years
It forgives the underlying tax
No effect; levies continue
Levy action is generally prohibited while the installment agreement request is pending, plus 30 days after rejection, and during any timely appeal
questions.rationale: Section 6331(k) prohibits levy while an installment agreement proposal is pending, for 30 days after rejection or termination, and during any timely appeal. The collection statute may be affected by certain related actions, but the tax is not forgiven.

questions.stem: A taxpayer qualifies for a guaranteed installment agreement under IRC Section 6159 if the liability is income tax of $10,000 or less and certain conditions are met. Which condition is required?
options: The taxpayer must be a corporation
In the past 5 years, the taxpayer filed and paid on time, did not have an installment agreement, and agrees to full payment within 3 years
The taxpayer must pay a 20% down payment
The taxpayer must waive all appeal rights
questions.rationale: A guaranteed installment agreement is available when an individual's income tax liability is $10,000 or less, the taxpayer was compliant in the prior 5 years with no prior agreement, can pay within 3 years, and agrees to remain compliant. The IRS must accept it.

questions.stem: A taxpayer in financial hardship may have their account placed in Currently Not Collectible (CNC) status. While in CNC status:
options: The collection statute stops running entirely forever
The taxpayer no longer needs to file returns
Active collection is suspended, but interest and penalties continue to accrue and the IRS may keep refunds and file a lien
The tax debt is permanently canceled
questions.rationale: Currently Not Collectible status pauses active collection due to hardship, but it does not eliminate the debt. Interest and penalties continue, refunds can be applied to the balance, a lien may be filed, and the collection statute keeps running, so the debt can expire at the CSED.

questions.stem: Innocent spouse relief is requested on which form, and to which judicial forum can a denial generally be appealed?
options: Form 8857; the United States Tax Court
Form 911; the Court of Federal Claims
Form 656; the District Court
Form 843; the Supreme Court
questions.rationale: Form 8857 requests innocent spouse relief under Section 6015. If denied, the requesting spouse may petition the Tax Court, generally within 90 days of the final determination.

questions.stem: Under IRC Section 6330(d), after the IRS Independent Office of Appeals issues a Notice of Determination following a CDP hearing, the taxpayer who disagrees must petition the Tax Court within:
options: 1 year
30 days from the date of the determination
90 days
60 days
questions.rationale: After a CDP Notice of Determination, the taxpayer has 30 days to petition the Tax Court for review under Section 6330(d). Missing this deadline forfeits judicial review of the determination.

questions.stem: Form 843 is generally used to:
options: Apply for an ITIN
Request an installment agreement
Claim a refund or request abatement of certain taxes, penalties, interest, or fees (other than income tax already reported on a return)
Request innocent spouse relief
questions.rationale: Form 843 is used to claim a refund or abatement of penalties, interest, and certain taxes and fees. Income tax overpayments are generally claimed on the original or amended income tax return (Form 1040-X), not Form 843.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: A first-time penalty abatement (FTA) waiver may be available for a failure-to-file or failure-to-pay penalty if the taxpayer:
options: Owes more than $100,000
Is currently under criminal investigation
Has never filed a return before
Was compliant with filing requirements and had no penalties for the prior 3 tax years (and has filed or filed an extension and paid or arranged to pay any tax due)
questions.rationale: First-time abatement is an administrative waiver for a single period when the taxpayer has a clean compliance history for the prior three years, is current on filing (or has an extension), and has paid or arranged to pay any tax due. It applies to failure-to-file, failure-to-pay, and failure-to-deposit penalties.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Reasonable cause for penalty abatement is generally established by showing:
options: The penalty is small
The taxpayer simply forgot the deadline
The taxpayer disagreed with the tax law
The taxpayer exercised ordinary business care and prudence but was nevertheless unable to comply due to circumstances beyond their control
questions.rationale: Reasonable cause turns on whether the taxpayer exercised ordinary business care and prudence but was still unable to comply due to events beyond their control. Examples include serious illness, death, unavoidable absence, or a natural disaster.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under the Boyle case, reliance on an agent to file a return by the deadline is generally:
options: Always reasonable cause if the agent is a CPA
Reasonable cause only for corporations
Not reasonable cause for a late-filed return, because the duty to file timely is nondelegable, although reliance on professional advice about a substantive tax position may be reasonable cause
Reasonable cause for late filing
questions.rationale: United States v. Boyle held that a taxpayer cannot establish reasonable cause for late filing by relying on an agent to file on time, because meeting a clear deadline is nondelegable. Reasonable reliance on professional advice about substantive tax questions, however, can constitute reasonable cause.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: The accuracy-related penalty under IRC Section 6662 generally equals what percentage of the underpayment attributable to negligence or a substantial understatement?
questions.rationale: The accuracy-related penalty under Section 6662 is 20% of the underpayment for negligence, substantial understatement, or substantial valuation misstatement, rising to 40% for gross valuation misstatements and certain undisclosed foreign asset understatements.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: The civil fraud penalty under IRC Section 6663 is generally equal to:
options: 50% of the interest
75% of the portion of the underpayment attributable to fraud
20% of the underpayment
100% of the tax owed
questions.rationale: Section 6663 imposes a 75% penalty on the part of an underpayment attributable to fraud. Once the IRS proves any portion is due to fraud, the entire underpayment is presumed fraudulent unless the taxpayer shows otherwise.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: The failure-to-file penalty under IRC Section 6651(a)(1) is generally:
options: 0.5% per month, up to 25%
20% one-time
5% per month (or part of a month) up to a maximum of 25% of the unpaid tax
75% of the tax
questions.rationale: The failure-to-file penalty is 5% of the unpaid tax per month or part of a month, up to 25%. When both failure-to-file and failure-to-pay apply in the same month, the failure-to-file penalty is reduced by the failure-to-pay penalty.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: When a return is more than 60 days late, the minimum failure-to-file penalty under IRC Section 6651 is the lesser of a specified inflation-adjusted dollar amount or:
options: The full balance plus interest
100% of the amount of tax required to be shown on the return
10% of the tax required to be shown on the return
25% of the refund
questions.rationale: If a return is over 60 days late, Section 6651 imposes a minimum penalty equal to the lesser of an inflation-adjusted dollar amount or 100% of the tax required to be shown on the return. If no tax is due, this minimum does not apply.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to pay a disputed tax and then sue for a refund in U.S. District Court or the Court of Federal Claims. A prerequisite is that the taxpayer must:
options: Obtain an OIC
First petition the Tax Court
Have a CAF number
Fully pay the assessed tax and file an administrative claim for refund that is denied or remains unaddressed for 6 months
questions.rationale: Refund litigation in District Court or the Court of Federal Claims requires full payment of the tax, a timely administrative refund claim, and either denial of that claim or the passage of six months without action. The Tax Court, by contrast, is a prepayment forum.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under IRC Section 6511, a refund claim based on a bad debt or worthless security has an extended limitations period of:
options: 3 years
10 years
7 years from the due date of the return for the year the debt or security became worthless
2 years
questions.rationale: Section 6511(d) extends the refund claim period to 7 years for claims attributable to worthless securities or bad debts, recognizing the difficulty in pinpointing the year of worthlessness.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: The general statute of limitations on assessment under IRC Section 6501 is 3 years, but it extends to 6 years when:
options: The taxpayer claims any credit
The taxpayer omits gross income exceeding 25% of the gross income reported on the return
The return is e-filed
The taxpayer files late
questions.rationale: Section 6501(e) provides a 6-year assessment statute for a substantial omission of more than 25% of gross income. The statute is unlimited for a false or fraudulent return or for failure to file.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: The statute of limitations on assessment is unlimited (never expires) when:
options: The taxpayer claims a large refund
The taxpayer underpays estimated tax
The taxpayer files an extension
The taxpayer files a false or fraudulent return with intent to evade tax, or fails to file a return
questions.rationale: Section 6501(c) removes the assessment limitations period entirely for fraudulent returns filed to evade tax and for failures to file. In those cases the IRS can assess at any time.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Form 872 and Form 872-A both relate to the assessment statute of limitations. The key difference is that Form 872-A:
options: Is an open-ended (indefinite) consent that remains in effect until terminated by either party, while Form 872 extends the statute to a fixed date
Applies only to estate tax
Cannot be revoked
Shortens the statute to one year
questions.rationale: Form 872 is a fixed-date consent extending the assessment statute, while Form 872-A is an open-ended consent that stays in effect until terminated by either party (Form 872-T) or by the issuance of a notice of deficiency.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: A taxpayer who needs to correct a previously filed return to report additional income should file:
options: Form 990
Form 4868
Form 1040-X, Amended U.S. Individual Income Tax Return
Form 2553
questions.rationale: Form 1040-X amends a previously filed Form 1040. To claim a resulting refund, it must be filed within the Section 6511 limitations period; additional tax should be paid to limit interest and penalties.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: Under IRC Section 6404(g), the IRS must generally suspend interest and certain penalties on a timely filed individual return if it does not provide a notice stating the taxpayer's liability and the basis for it within:
options: 6 months of the later of the filing date or the due date
5 years
18 months of the later of the original due date or the date the return was timely filed
3 years
questions.rationale: Section 6404(g) suspends interest and certain penalties for individuals if the IRS does not notify the taxpayer of the liability and its basis within the applicable period (generally 18 months) after the later of the due date or timely filing. Exceptions apply, including fraud and listed transactions.
questions.source: Part 3 – Completion of the Filing Process

questions.stem: An enrolled agent is representing two business partners, Dana and Rey, in an examination of their partnership. During the exam the IRS proposes adjustments that would benefit Dana but increase Rey's tax. What does Circular 230 require the practitioner to do?
options: Represent only Dana since she benefits and drop Rey without notice
Determine whether a conflict of interest exists and, if so, obtain informed written consent from each affected client
Continue representing both because partners always share identical interests
Withdraw immediately because any joint representation is automatically prohibited
questions.rationale: Under Circular 230 section 10.29, a practitioner may represent clients with conflicting interests only if the practitioner reasonably believes competent representation can be provided, it is not prohibited by law, and each client gives informed written consent.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, how long must a practitioner retain the written consents obtained when representing clients with a conflict of interest?
options: No retention is required once consent is signed
At least 36 months from the date the representation concludes
Until the next filing season ends
Indefinitely, with no defined retention period
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.29 requires written conflict-of-interest consents to be retained for at least 36 months from the date the conflicted representation concludes, and they must be provided to the IRS on request.

questions.stem: A client asks an enrolled agent to charge a fee equal to 30% of any refund the EA can obtain by filing an amended return for a year already filed, where no examination or written IRS challenge is pending. Under Circular 230, this contingent fee arrangement is:
options: Permitted only if the client agrees orally
Required to be at least 50% to be enforceable
Generally prohibited for preparing an original or amended return in these circumstances
Permitted because amended returns always justify contingent fees
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.27 generally bars contingent fees for preparing returns, with narrow exceptions such as fees charged in connection with an IRS examination or a claim filed within 120 days of receiving a written notice of examination.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent prepares a return and later discovers the client omitted significant income on a prior-year return the EA did not prepare. The client refuses to correct it. Under Circular 230, the EA must:
options: Advise the client of the error and the consequences of not correcting it
File an amended return on the client's behalf despite the refusal
Immediately notify the IRS of the client's error without the client's permission
Withdraw from all representation and report the client to the state board
questions.rationale: Under Circular 230 section 10.21, when a practitioner knows a client has not complied or has made an error or omission, the practitioner must advise the client of the noncompliance and the consequences, but is not required to disclose it to the IRS.

questions.stem: A practitioner receives a written request from the IRS for records and information needed to determine a client's correct tax liability. The records are in the client's possession, not the practitioner's. Under Circular 230, the practitioner must:
options: Refuse to respond because the records belong to the client
Promptly notify the IRS that the records are not in the practitioner's possession and provide any information about who has them
Ignore the request unless a subpoena is issued
Demand a summons before providing any response
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.20 requires a practitioner to promptly submit records or information lawfully requested by the IRS, and if the practitioner does not have them, to notify the IRS and provide information about the person believed to possess them, unless the practitioner believes in good faith the request is privileged.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent issues written advice to a client about a transaction. Under the Circular 230 written advice standard, the practitioner may NOT:
options: Apply the relevant legal authorities to the facts
Take into account the possibility that the return will not be audited
Consider all relevant facts the practitioner knows or reasonably should know
Rely on the representations of the client if reliance is reasonable
questions.rationale: Under Circular 230 section 10.37, a practitioner giving written advice must base it on reasonable factual and legal assumptions and must not take into account the likelihood that the return will be audited or an issue raised.

questions.stem: The Office of Professional Responsibility proposes to sanction an enrolled agent for a pattern of willful violations of Circular 230. Which sanction is the most severe that OPR may impose after a proceeding?
options: A private reprimand
Censure
A monetary penalty capped at $1,000
Disbarment from practice before the IRS
questions.rationale: Under Circular 230 section 10.50, OPR may censure, suspend, disbar, or impose monetary penalties; disbarment is the most severe sanction available.

questions.stem: A disbarred practitioner wants to be reinstated to practice before the IRS. Under Circular 230, a disbarred practitioner may petition for reinstatement after how long?
options: Immediately, because disbarment is always temporary
Never; disbarment is permanent and irreversible
After 5 years from the date of disbarment
After 1 year from the date of disbarment
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.81 permits a disbarred or suspended practitioner to petition OPR for reinstatement, but no earlier than 5 years after the date of disbarment or suspension.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent supervises three staff preparers and is responsible for the firm's tax practice. Under Circular 230 section 10.36, the EA with principal authority must:
options: Take reasonable steps to ensure the firm has adequate procedures for compliance with Circular 230
Guarantee that no staff member ever makes an error
Eliminate all supervisory responsibility by delegating to staff
Personally review every return before it is filed
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.36 places responsibility on the practitioner with principal authority over a firm's tax practice to take reasonable steps to ensure adequate procedures are in place for compliance and to address known noncompliance.

questions.stem: A practitioner takes a position on a client's return that is contrary to a Treasury regulation. To avoid a Circular 230 violation under the standards for advising on return positions, the position must:
options: Be supported by the client's oral statement alone
Be agreed to in writing by the IRS in advance
Have at least a 20% chance of success
Represent a good-faith challenge to the validity of the regulation and be adequately disclosed where required
questions.rationale: Under Circular 230 section 10.34, a practitioner may advise a position contrary to a regulation only if the position is not frivolous, represents a good-faith challenge to the regulation, and is adequately disclosed when required to avoid penalties.

questions.stem: Which document governs the rules of practice for representatives before the Internal Revenue Service?
options: Publication 17
The Taxpayer Bill of Rights brochure
The Internal Revenue Manual
Treasury Department Circular No. 230
questions.rationale: Treasury Department Circular No. 230 contains the regulations governing practice before the IRS, including who may practice and the standards of conduct for practitioners.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent learns that an employee in the firm has been incompetently preparing returns in violation of Circular 230, and the EA has principal authority over the practice. The EA does nothing to correct the situation. Under section 10.36, the EA may be subject to discipline if:
options: Any single error occurred regardless of the EA's knowledge
The employee was an independent contractor
Through willfulness, recklessness, or gross incompetence the EA failed to take reasonable steps to ensure compliance
The EA personally prepared each defective return
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.36 subjects the individual with principal authority to discipline if, through willfulness, recklessness, or gross incompetence, they fail to take reasonable steps to ensure firm compliance or to correct known noncompliance.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, which of the following best describes a practitioner's duty of due diligence under section 10.22?
options: The practitioner must personally verify the client's bank records
The practitioner is responsible only for arithmetic accuracy
The practitioner must exercise due diligence in preparing and filing documents and in determining the correctness of representations to the client and IRS
The practitioner must audit every figure provided by the client
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.22 requires practitioners to exercise due diligence in preparing and filing tax documents and in determining the correctness of representations made to the Department of the Treasury and to clients.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent receives a notice of suspension from the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility. The EA wishes to contest it. The proceeding to determine the sanction is conducted before:
options: An Administrative Law Judge
A U.S. District Court judge
The U.S. Tax Court
A jury of practitioners
questions.rationale: Under Circular 230 sections 10.60 through 10.76, disciplinary proceedings against practitioners are conducted before an Administrative Law Judge, whose decision may be appealed to the Secretary or delegate.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, a practitioner may NOT charge an unconscionable fee. This requirement is found in which area of practitioner conduct?
options: Continuing education requirements
E-file mandates
Rules on advertising only
Standards regarding fees
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.27 prohibits a practitioner from charging an unconscionable fee in connection with any matter before the IRS and restricts contingent fees.

questions.stem: A practitioner publishes a fee schedule in an advertisement. Under Circular 230 section 10.30, the practitioner must honor the published fees for how long after the last date of publication?
options: At least 90 calendar days
At least one year
At least 30 calendar days
No minimum period applies
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.30 requires a practitioner who publishes a fee schedule to honor the published fees for at least 30 days after the date of the last publication.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of disreputable conduct for which a practitioner may be sanctioned under Circular 230 section 10.51?
options: Advising a client of an error on a prior return
Retaining client records as required
Giving false or misleading information to the Department of the Treasury
Promptly responding to an IRS information request
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.51 defines incompetence and disreputable conduct, including giving false or misleading information, conviction of certain crimes, and willfully evading tax, among others.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent reasonably believes a client's position lacks substantial authority and is not adequately disclosed. Under Circular 230, advising the client to take that position on the return would:
options: Be required to maximize the client's refund
Be acceptable because audit risk is low
Violate section 10.34 because the practitioner should not advise a position lacking a reasonable basis or that would subject the client to penalty without disclosure
Be permissible if the client insists in writing
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.34 prohibits a practitioner from advising a return position unless it satisfies applicable standards, and the practitioner cannot justify a weak position based on the chance the return will not be examined.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent's enrollment lapses because the EA failed to renew. While the enrollment is inactive, the individual may NOT:
options: Apply to renew enrollment
Prepare tax returns if they hold a valid PTIN
Take continuing education courses
State or imply that they are eligible to represent taxpayers before the IRS as an enrolled agent
questions.rationale: When an enrolled agent's status is inactive or lapsed, the individual may not practice before the IRS or represent that they are an enrolled agent eligible to do so until enrollment is reinstated.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, a practitioner who knows that a client has not filed required returns and the client refuses to file should:
options: File the returns without the client's signature
Report the client to the IRS Criminal Investigation division
Continue representing the client and ignore the unfiled returns
Advise the client of the noncompliance and the potential consequences, and consider whether to continue the representation
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.21 requires the practitioner to advise the client of noncompliance and its consequences; the practitioner must also evaluate ethical obligations regarding continued representation but is not required to report the client to the IRS.

questions.stem: A practitioner is negotiating an offer in compromise and tells the revenue officer that the client has no other bank accounts, knowing the client has an undisclosed offshore account. This conduct most directly violates Circular 230 because it:
options: Constitutes giving false or misleading information to the Treasury
Is a continuing education deficiency
Is an advertising violation
Is only a state bar matter
questions.rationale: Knowingly giving false or misleading information to the Department of the Treasury, such as concealing assets during an offer in compromise, is incompetence and disreputable conduct under Circular 230 section 10.51 and may result in sanctions.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, who has the authority to investigate complaints and propose sanctions against practitioners?
options: The Taxpayer Advocate Service
The Appeals Office
The Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR)
The Criminal Investigation division
questions.rationale: The Office of Professional Responsibility administers and enforces Circular 230, investigating allegations of misconduct and proposing or imposing sanctions on practitioners.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent wants to use the designation 'EA' and advertise services. Under Circular 230 section 10.30, which statement about solicitation and advertising is correct?
options: A practitioner is barred from all forms of advertising
A practitioner may use any false or misleading claim if disclosed in fine print
A practitioner must obtain IRS pre-approval of all advertisements
A practitioner may not use false, fraudulent, or coercive statements or claims in advertising
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.30 allows advertising and solicitation but prohibits false, fraudulent, coercive, or misleading statements, and restricts certain fee-related claims.

questions.stem: A practitioner is asked to provide written advice that the practitioner knows will be used to promote a tax shelter to many investors. Under Circular 230, the practitioner's written advice standard requires that the practitioner:
options: Disregard facts because marketing materials are not returns
Not rely on representations the practitioner knows are unreasonable, incorrect, or incomplete
Take into account that most investors will not be audited
Assume the best-case outcome for marketing appeal
questions.rationale: Under Circular 230 section 10.37, written advice must be based on reasonable factual and legal assumptions, must not rely on representations the practitioner knows are unreasonable or incorrect, and must not consider audit likelihood.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, a practitioner who is suspended from practice before the IRS may, during the suspension period:
options: Continue to use the title 'enrolled agent' freely
Sign tax returns as a paid preparer with full representation rights
Represent clients at an IRS examination
Not practice before the IRS in any capacity requiring practitioner status
questions.rationale: A practitioner who is suspended under Circular 230 may not practice before the IRS during the suspension period and may not represent that they are eligible to do so.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent receives a referral fee from a financial advisor for sending clients who then buy investment products. Regarding the client relationship, Circular 230 most directly addresses this through the rules on:
options: Conflicts of interest and the duty to act in the client's best interest
E-file participation
Continuing education credits
PTIN renewal
questions.rationale: A referral or kickback arrangement can create a conflict of interest under Circular 230 section 10.29 because the practitioner's personal financial interest may be adverse to the client's; informed written consent may be required.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, the standard a practitioner must meet before signing a tax return as a preparer regarding undisclosed positions is generally that the position has:
options: Any nonzero chance of success
A reasonable basis only
Substantial authority, unless the position is disclosed and has a reasonable basis
Frivolous-level support if the client insists
questions.rationale: Consistent with section 6694 and Circular 230 section 10.34, an undisclosed return position generally requires substantial authority, while a disclosed position requires at least a reasonable basis.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files an individual income tax return on the April 15 due date showing tax due but does not pay. The IRS assesses the tax. Generally, how long does the IRS have to collect the assessed tax by levy or court proceeding?
options: 10 years from the assessment date
Forever, because tax debts never expire
3 years from the assessment date
6 years from the assessment date
questions.rationale: Under section 6502, the IRS generally has 10 years from the date of assessment to collect tax by levy or a court proceeding; this period is the Collection Statute Expiration Date (CSED) and can be extended or suspended in certain circumstances.

questions.stem: A taxpayer owes $18,000 and cannot pay in full but can pay $300 per month. The taxpayer requests a guaranteed installment agreement. Which condition is generally required for a guaranteed installment agreement under section 6159?
options: The liability is $10,000 or less (excluding penalties and interest) and other conditions are met
The taxpayer has unfiled returns
The liability exceeds $100,000
The taxpayer is in bankruptcy
questions.rationale: A guaranteed installment agreement is available when the tax owed is $10,000 or less excluding penalties and interest, the taxpayer has timely filed and paid for the prior 5 years, agrees to full payment within 3 years, and meets other conditions; the $18,000 liability would instead require a different agreement type.

questions.stem: What is the maximum individual liability threshold for a streamlined installment agreement that generally does not require a financial statement (Form 433-F)?
questions.rationale: Individuals who owe $50,000 or less in combined tax, penalties, and interest can generally obtain a streamlined installment agreement payable within 72 months without submitting a detailed financial statement.

questions.stem: The IRS files a Notice of Federal Tax Lien against a taxpayer. The taxpayer wants to challenge the filing. The taxpayer's primary administrative remedy is to request:
options: An automatic discharge of the lien
A refund suit in district court
A private letter ruling
A Collection Due Process hearing within 30 days of the notice of the lien filing
questions.rationale: After the IRS files a Notice of Federal Tax Lien, it must notify the taxpayer, who may request a Collection Due Process hearing within 30 days following the end of the 5-business-day notification period to contest the filing and propose collection alternatives.

questions.stem: A taxpayer requests an installment agreement but later defaults by missing payments. Before terminating the agreement, the IRS generally must:
options: Provide notice and a 30-day period before terminating or altering the agreement
Refer the case to Criminal Investigation
Reduce the balance owed
Levy immediately without notice
questions.rationale: Under section 6159, the IRS must provide 30 days' notice before terminating or modifying an installment agreement (other than for jeopardy), and the taxpayer may appeal the proposed termination.

questions.stem: A business fails to remit withheld payroll taxes. The IRS seeks to hold a responsible person liable for the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty. The TFRP equals:
options: A flat $10,000 per quarter
The full amount of employment tax including the employer's share
50% of the total payroll tax liability
100% of the unpaid trust fund taxes (the withheld income and employee FICA)
questions.rationale: The Trust Fund Recovery Penalty under section 6672 equals 100% of the trust fund taxes (withheld income tax and the employee portion of FICA) that a responsible person willfully failed to collect, account for, or pay over.

questions.stem: Which two elements must the IRS establish to impose the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty on an individual?
options: Criminal intent and conviction
Bankruptcy and insolvency
Responsibility (a duty to collect, account for, and pay over) and willfulness
Negligence and a large balance due
questions.rationale: The TFRP applies to a responsible person who willfully fails to collect, account for, and pay over trust fund taxes; both responsibility and willfulness must be established.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is experiencing economic hardship and cannot pay any amount toward a tax debt without being unable to meet basic living expenses. The IRS may place the account in:
options: A criminal referral
An immediate levy program
Currently Not Collectible (CNC) status
A frivolous filer list
questions.rationale: When collection would create economic hardship leaving the taxpayer unable to meet necessary living expenses, the IRS may report the account as Currently Not Collectible, though penalties and interest continue to accrue and the lien may still be filed.

questions.stem: A taxpayer submits an offer in compromise based on doubt as to collectibility. The IRS generally calculates the minimum acceptable offer as the taxpayer's:
options: Reasonable Collection Potential (net realizable equity in assets plus future income)
Monthly disposable income for 6 months only
Total tax debt regardless of assets
Annual gross income only
questions.rationale: For a doubt-as-to-collectibility offer, the IRS evaluates Reasonable Collection Potential, which is net realizable equity in assets plus future income (generally 12 months of disposable income for lump-sum offers or 24 months for periodic-payment offers).

questions.stem: If the IRS does not act on an offer in compromise within 24 months of the date it is received, the offer is:
options: Deemed accepted by operation of law
Converted to an installment agreement
Automatically rejected
Returned without consideration
questions.rationale: Under section 7122(f), if the IRS does not reject an offer in compromise within 24 months after the date it is submitted, the offer is deemed accepted; certain periods, such as when liability is disputed in court, are excluded from the 24 months.

questions.stem: A federal tax lien arises automatically when which three events occur?
options: The taxpayer files for bankruptcy, dies, and moves
The taxpayer is audited, appeals, and loses
Tax is assessed, a notice and demand for payment is made, and the taxpayer neglects or refuses to pay
The taxpayer requests an installment agreement, defaults, and refiles
questions.rationale: The general federal tax lien under section 6321 arises automatically when the tax is assessed, the IRS sends notice and demand for payment, and the taxpayer neglects or refuses to pay; it attaches to all the taxpayer's property and rights to property.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants the IRS to make its lien secondary to another creditor's interest so the taxpayer can refinance a mortgage. The taxpayer should request:
options: A certificate of nonattachment
A certificate of subordination
Withdrawal of the lien
A certificate of discharge
questions.rationale: Under section 6325(d), the IRS may issue a certificate of subordination making the federal tax lien secondary to another interest, which can enable a taxpayer to refinance and ultimately increase the government's collection prospects.

questions.stem: After full payment of the underlying tax liability, the IRS must release a federal tax lien within:
options: 90 days
6 months
30 days
60 days
questions.rationale: Under section 6325(a), the IRS must issue a certificate of release of a federal tax lien within 30 days after the liability is fully satisfied or becomes legally unenforceable, or after a bond is accepted.

questions.stem: The IRS issues a levy on a taxpayer's wages. A continuous wage levy attaches to:
options: The taxpayer's wages on a continuing basis until the levy is released
Only the first $1,000 of monthly wages
Only future bonuses, not regular wages
Only the wages earned on the single day of the levy
questions.rationale: A levy on salary or wages is continuous under section 6331(e), attaching to the taxpayer's pay until the levy is released, subject to a statutory exempt amount the taxpayer retains.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally exempt from an IRS levy under section 6334?
options: Necessary schoolbooks and certain personal effects up to a statutory amount
A taxpayer's brokerage account
A taxpayer's vacation home
A taxpayer's second vehicle
questions.rationale: Section 6334 lists property exempt from levy, including necessary schoolbooks, certain wearing apparel and household effects up to a statutory amount, unemployment benefits, certain pensions, and tools of a trade up to limits.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's wage levy is causing economic hardship. The taxpayer asks the IRS to release the levy. Under section 6343, the IRS must release a levy if:
options: The levy is creating an economic hardship due to the taxpayer's financial condition
The taxpayer changes jobs
The taxpayer has filed an extension
The taxpayer simply disagrees with the assessment
questions.rationale: Under section 6343, the IRS must release a levy if it determines the levy is creating an economic hardship, the liability is satisfied or unenforceable, an installment agreement is in effect, or release would facilitate collection.

questions.stem: A taxpayer disagrees with the results of a Collection Due Process hearing. To seek judicial review, the taxpayer generally petitions:
options: The U.S. Tax Court within 30 days of the Notice of Determination
The U.S. Court of Federal Claims within 6 months
A U.S. District Court within 2 years
The IRS Commissioner directly
questions.rationale: After a Collection Due Process Notice of Determination, the taxpayer may petition the U.S. Tax Court for review within 30 days of the determination.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to challenge an IRS collection action but missed the 30-day deadline for a Collection Due Process hearing. The taxpayer may instead request an:
options: Automatic abatement of the entire debt
Extension of the CSED
Immediate refund of all payments
Equivalent hearing within one year, though Tax Court review of the result is not available
questions.rationale: If a taxpayer misses the 30-day CDP window, they may request an equivalent hearing within one year, which provides Appeals review but does not include the right to judicial review in Tax Court.

questions.stem: A taxpayer enters into a partial payment installment agreement (PPIA). A distinguishing feature of a PPIA is that:
options: No financial disclosure is required
Penalties stop accruing immediately
The agreement may result in part of the liability not being fully paid before the collection statute expires
The full balance must be paid before the CSED
questions.rationale: A partial payment installment agreement allows a taxpayer to make smaller payments that may not fully satisfy the liability before the CSED; it requires financial disclosure and is subject to periodic review.

questions.stem: Which IRS form is generally used by an individual wage earner to provide a Collection Information Statement when requesting a non-streamlined installment agreement?
options: Form 8821
Form 2848
Form 433-A
Form 1040-X
questions.rationale: Form 433-A is the Collection Information Statement for wage earners and self-employed individuals, used to evaluate ability to pay for installment agreements, offers in compromise, or CNC status.

questions.stem: A levy on a bank account is generally subject to a holding period before the bank surrenders the funds. That holding period is:
options: 45 calendar days
21 calendar days
10 business days
30 calendar days
questions.rationale: Under section 6332(c), a bank receiving a levy must hold the funds for 21 calendar days before surrendering them, giving the taxpayer time to resolve issues or claim the levy was in error.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's federal tax debt is being collected and the taxpayer believes the collection statute has already expired. The taxpayer can verify the CSED by:
options: Filing a new tax return
Reviewing the IRS account transcript for the assessment date and any tolling events
Checking the state tax website
Asking the local court clerk
questions.rationale: The CSED is generally 10 years from assessment but is extended by tolling events such as pending offers, CDP requests, bankruptcy, and time abroad; the IRS account transcript documents the assessment date and these events.

questions.stem: What is the general statute of limitations for the IRS to assess additional tax on a timely filed individual income tax return with no fraud or substantial omission?
options: 6 years from the filing date
No limitation period applies
3 years from the filing date or due date, whichever is later
10 years from the filing date
questions.rationale: Under section 6501, the IRS generally must assess additional tax within 3 years after the return is filed or its due date, whichever is later, absent fraud or a substantial omission of income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer omits from gross income an amount that exceeds 25% of the gross income reported on the return. The IRS assessment statute of limitations is extended to:
options: Unlimited
6 years
10 years
3 years
questions.rationale: Under section 6501(e), if a taxpayer omits gross income exceeding 25% of the gross income reported, the IRS has 6 years to assess additional tax.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files a fraudulent return with the intent to evade tax. The statute of limitations for the IRS to assess tax is:
options: Unlimited; there is no assessment statute of limitations for fraud
6 years
3 years
1 year after discovery
questions.rationale: Under section 6501(c), there is no statute of limitations on assessment in the case of a false or fraudulent return filed with the intent to evade tax, or where no return was filed.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files a claim for refund. Generally, the claim must be filed within the later of:
options: 1 year from filing or 1 year from payment
10 years from filing or 5 years from payment
3 years from the time the return was filed or 2 years from the time the tax was paid
6 years from filing or 1 year from payment
questions.rationale: Under section 6511, a refund claim must be filed within 3 years from the time the return was filed or 2 years from the time the tax was paid, whichever period expires later; if no return was filed, the 2-year rule applies.

questions.stem: During an examination, the IRS asks the taxpayer to sign Form 872 to extend the assessment statute. Form 872 generally provides for:
options: A waiver of all taxpayer appeal rights
A fixed expiration date to which both parties agree
An automatic 10-year extension
An indefinite extension with no end date
questions.rationale: Form 872 is a consent to extend the time to assess tax to a specific agreed-upon date, whereas Form 872-A is an open-ended consent that continues until terminated by either party; signing does not waive appeal rights.

questions.stem: If a taxpayer never files a required tax return, the statute of limitations for the IRS to assess that year's tax:
options: Expires after 3 years from the due date
Does not begin to run until a return is filed
Is fixed at 6 years
Begins on the original due date regardless of filing
questions.rationale: When no return is filed, section 6501(c)(3) provides that tax may be assessed at any time; the statute of limitations does not begin until a return is filed.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files a return reporting a basis overstatement that causes a gross income omission. Under current law for substantial omissions of income, an overstatement of basis that understates gross income:
options: Reduces the period to 2 years
Is always ignored for statute purposes
Can trigger the 6-year assessment period as an omission of gross income
Triggers an unlimited assessment period
questions.rationale: Congress amended section 6501(e) to provide that an overstatement of basis that results in an omission of gross income exceeding 25% can trigger the 6-year assessment statute of limitations.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files an original return three months before the due date. For statute of limitations purposes, the return is generally treated as filed on:
options: The due date of the return
The actual early filing date
The first day of the tax year
The date the IRS processes it
questions.rationale: Under section 6501(b)(1), a return filed before its due date is deemed filed on the due date, so the assessment statute of limitations begins to run from the due date rather than the earlier filing date.

questions.stem: Which IRS office offers an independent forum to resolve tax disputes without litigation after an examination?
options: The Office of Professional Responsibility
The Taxpayer Advocate Service
Criminal Investigation
The IRS Independent Office of Appeals
questions.rationale: The IRS Independent Office of Appeals provides taxpayers an opportunity to resolve disputes arising from examinations and collection actions impartially without going to court.

questions.stem: A taxpayer disagrees with proposed audit adjustments documented in a 30-day letter. To request consideration by the IRS Independent Office of Appeals, the taxpayer generally must:
options: Pay the full proposed deficiency first
Submit a written protest (or small case request) within the time stated in the letter
Request a private letter ruling
File a petition in Tax Court immediately
questions.rationale: In response to a 30-day letter, a taxpayer requests Appeals consideration by filing a written protest within the time stated; a small case request may be used when the disputed amount is at or below the threshold.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to litigate a tax dispute but prefers a forum where a jury trial is available. The taxpayer should generally pay the tax, file a refund claim, and then sue in:
options: The U.S. Supreme Court
The IRS Independent Office of Appeals
U.S. District Court
U.S. Tax Court
questions.rationale: To obtain a jury trial in a tax case, a taxpayer must pay the tax, file a refund claim, and upon denial sue in U.S. District Court; the Tax Court and Court of Federal Claims do not provide juries.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes Tax Court from refund litigation?
options: Tax Court requires full payment of the disputed tax before filing
In Tax Court the taxpayer generally need not pay the deficiency first, while refund suits require prior payment
Refund suits do not require filing a claim with the IRS
Tax Court provides jury trials
questions.rationale: The U.S. Tax Court allows taxpayers to contest a deficiency without first paying it, whereas refund litigation in District Court or the Court of Federal Claims requires payment of the tax and a denied or unaddressed refund claim before suit.

questions.stem: The Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) is most appropriately used when a taxpayer:
options: Wants to avoid filing a return
Is experiencing a significant hardship or has been unable to resolve a problem through normal IRS channels
Disagrees with the tax law itself
Wants to commit fraud without detection
questions.rationale: The Taxpayer Advocate Service is an independent organization within the IRS that helps taxpayers experiencing financial hardship or who have been unable to resolve their issues through normal IRS channels, and it can issue Taxpayer Assistance Orders.

questions.stem: A taxpayer requests that the Taxpayer Advocate Service intervene because an IRS levy threatens immediate hardship. The instrument TAS may issue to direct the IRS to take or cease an action is a:
options: Taxpayer Assistance Order (TAO)
Private letter ruling
Notice of Deficiency
Closing agreement
questions.rationale: Under section 7811, the National Taxpayer Advocate may issue a Taxpayer Assistance Order directing the IRS to release a levy or take other action when a taxpayer is suffering or about to suffer a significant hardship.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is selected for a correspondence audit questioning a charitable contribution deduction. The most appropriate response is to:
options: Ignore the notice since correspondence audits are not binding
Provide the requested documentation substantiating the deduction by the deadline
Immediately petition the Tax Court
File an amended return removing all deductions
questions.rationale: A correspondence audit is conducted by mail and asks the taxpayer to substantiate specific items; the taxpayer should respond by the deadline with documentation supporting the questioned deduction.

questions.stem: Under the Taxpayer Bill of Rights, which right ensures that taxpayers can expect the IRS to consider facts and circumstances that might affect their liabilities and ability to pay?
options: The right to a fair and just tax system
The right to confidentiality only
The right to advertise
The right to unlimited appeals
questions.rationale: The Taxpayer Bill of Rights includes the right to a fair and just tax system, which entitles taxpayers to expect the IRS to consider facts and circumstances affecting their liabilities, ability to pay, or ability to timely provide information.

questions.stem: In an IRS examination, the burden of proof for substantiating deductions generally rests with the:
options: IRS in all cases
Appeals officer
Taxpayer, who must keep records to support items claimed
Tax preparer
questions.rationale: Deductions and credits are a matter of legislative grace, and taxpayers generally bear the burden of keeping adequate records and substantiating the items claimed, though section 7491 can shift the burden in limited circumstances.

questions.stem: For the burden of proof to shift to the IRS under section 7491 in a court proceeding, the taxpayer must, among other conditions:
options: Hire an enrolled agent
Refuse to provide any records
Introduce credible evidence, comply with substantiation requirements, maintain records, and cooperate with reasonable IRS requests
Pay the disputed tax in full
questions.rationale: Under section 7491, the burden of proof may shift to the IRS on factual issues if the taxpayer introduces credible evidence, complies with substantiation and recordkeeping requirements, and cooperates with reasonable IRS requests for information.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants an enrolled agent to represent them before the IRS, including arguing the case and receiving confidential information. Which form authorizes this representation?
options: Form 2848, Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative
Form 4506, Request for Copy of Tax Return
Form 8821, Tax Information Authorization
Form W-9
questions.rationale: Form 2848 is the IRS Power of Attorney that authorizes an eligible representative to act on the taxpayer's behalf before the IRS, while Form 8821 only authorizes access to information without representation rights.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent files Form 2848 for a client. Which statement about the Centralized Authorization File (CAF) number is correct?
options: Each taxpayer receives a unique CAF number
The CAF number expires every year
The CAF number is assigned to the representative to track authorizations on file with the IRS
The CAF number replaces the EA's PTIN on all returns
questions.rationale: The Centralized Authorization File number is a unique identifier the IRS assigns to a representative; it is recorded on Forms 2848 and 8821 so the IRS can track and verify the representative's authorizations.

questions.stem: A Form 2848 lists a specific tax matter and tax periods. Generally, the representative's authority under that power of attorney is:
options: Valid only for criminal matters
Automatically extended to future years
Unlimited across all tax types and years
Limited to the matters and periods specified on the form
questions.rationale: Form 2848 grants authority only for the tax matters and periods specifically listed; a representative cannot act on matters or years not described, although the form permits listing certain future periods within a limited window.

questions.stem: A taxpayer signs a new Form 2848 naming a different representative for the same tax matter and periods, without checking the box to retain prior representatives. The effect on a prior Form 2848 for those matters is generally that the prior authorization is:
options: Revoked for the overlapping matters and periods unless retention is indicated
Still fully effective
Converted into a Form 8821
Suspended for 60 days
questions.rationale: A newly filed Form 2848 generally revokes any earlier power of attorney for the same matters and periods unless the taxpayer specifically indicates that the prior representative is to be retained.

questions.stem: To become an enrolled agent by examination, a candidate must pass all three parts of the Special Enrollment Examination and then:
options: Apply for enrollment and pass a suitability check including a tax compliance review
Pass a state bar exam
Obtain a CPA license first
Work for the IRS for five years
questions.rationale: A candidate who passes all three parts of the SEE applies for enrollment on Form 23 and must pass a suitability check, which includes a review of personal and business tax compliance and background.

questions.stem: Any individual who is paid to prepare or assist in preparing federal tax returns must obtain and use a:
options: Centralized lien number
CAF number
Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN)
Social Security number only
questions.rationale: Under section 6109, all paid tax return preparers must obtain a PTIN and include it on returns they prepare for compensation; the PTIN must be renewed annually.

questions.stem: A preparer fails to comply with the due diligence requirements for the Earned Income Tax Credit on a return. The penalty under section 6695(g) is generally:
options: No penalty if the credit was correct
10% of the credit claimed
An inflation-adjusted amount (about $600) per failure, per credit or filing status
A flat $50 per return regardless of year
questions.rationale: Section 6695(g) imposes a penalty, adjusted annually for inflation (approximately $600 in recent years), for each failure to comply with due diligence requirements, assessed separately for each applicable credit and for head of household status.

questions.stem: A tax preparer prepares a return with an understatement due to an unreasonable position for which there was no substantial authority and no disclosure. The first-tier preparer penalty under section 6694(a) is generally the greater of $1,000 or:
options: 50% of the income derived by the preparer with respect to the return
100% of the tax understatement
A flat $5,000
10% of the client's total tax
questions.rationale: Under section 6694(a), the penalty for an understatement due to an unreasonable position is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived (or to be derived) by the preparer for preparing the return.

questions.stem: A preparer willfully attempts to understate a client's tax liability or recklessly disregards rules. The section 6694(b) penalty is the greater of $5,000 or:
options: 10% of the understatement
75% of the income derived by the preparer with respect to the return
A flat $1,000
50% of the income derived by the preparer with respect to the return
questions.rationale: Under section 6694(b), for willful or reckless conduct the preparer penalty is the greater of $5,000 or 75% of the income the preparer derived (or will derive) with respect to the return, reduced by any 6694(a) penalty paid.

questions.stem: An Electronic Return Originator (ERO) originates the electronic submission of returns. To become an ERO, an applicant must:
options: Be a U.S. Tax Court practitioner
Apply to the IRS e-file program and become an Authorized IRS e-file Provider
Obtain a CAF number
Pass the bar exam
questions.rationale: To become an ERO, an applicant must complete the IRS e-file application, pass a suitability check, and be accepted as an Authorized IRS e-file Provider; EROs originate the electronic transmission of returns to the IRS.

questions.stem: How long must an ERO generally retain Form 8879 after a return is filed?
options: 6 years
3 years from the return due date or the IRS received date, whichever is later
Until the end of the calendar year
Indefinitely
questions.rationale: Per IRS e-file rules, the ERO must retain Form 8879 and supporting documents for 3 years from the return due date or the IRS received date, whichever is later, and make them available to the IRS on request.

questions.stem: A married taxpayer files a joint return. The spouse later discovers that the other spouse understated income, and the requesting spouse did not know and had no reason to know of the understatement. The requesting spouse may seek relief by filing:
options: Form 8857, Request for Innocent Spouse Relief
Form 4562
Form 1045
Form 8832
questions.rationale: Under section 6015, a spouse who filed jointly may request innocent spouse relief on Form 8857 if there is an understatement attributable to the other spouse and the requesting spouse did not know and had no reason to know of it, and it would be inequitable to hold them liable.

questions.stem: Which type of relief under section 6015 allocates the deficiency between spouses as if they had filed separate returns, generally for taxpayers who are divorced, legally separated, or living apart?
options: Injured spouse relief
Innocent spouse relief based only on fraud
Separation of liability relief
Currently Not Collectible status
questions.rationale: Section 6015(c) provides separation of liability relief, allocating the understatement between spouses as if separate returns had been filed, and is generally available to taxpayers who are divorced, widowed, legally separated, or not living together for the prior 12 months.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who is a confirmed victim of tax-related identity theft may be issued an Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN). The IP PIN:
options: Replaces the taxpayer's Social Security number
Is a permanent number that never changes
