Is a six-digit number that helps verify the taxpayer's identity and is generally renewed annually
Is shared publicly to prevent fraud
questions.rationale: An Identity Protection PIN is a six-digit number the IRS provides to help prevent misuse of a taxpayer's SSN on fraudulent returns; it is generally valid for one calendar year and must be entered on the return.

questions.stem: A taxpayer discovers that someone filed a fraudulent return using their Social Security number. To report the identity theft to the IRS and request marker placement on the account, the taxpayer generally files:
options: Form 14039, Identity Theft Affidavit
Form 2848
Form 1040-X only
Form 656
questions.rationale: Form 14039, the Identity Theft Affidavit, is used to notify the IRS that a taxpayer is or may be a victim of identity theft so the IRS can mark the account and take protective action.

questions.stem: A taxpayer requests abatement of a failure-to-file penalty, asserting that a serious illness prevented timely filing. The IRS may abate the penalty if the taxpayer demonstrates:
options: That the taxpayer used an enrolled agent
Any reason at all, since abatement is automatic
That the tax was small
Reasonable cause and an absence of willful neglect
questions.rationale: The failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties may be abated if the taxpayer shows the failure was due to reasonable cause, such as serious illness, and not due to willful neglect; the IRS evaluates all facts and circumstances.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has a clean compliance history and is assessed a failure-to-file penalty for one year. The taxpayer may qualify for relief under the:
options: Offer in compromise program only
Statute of limitations on collection
Innocent spouse provisions
First-Time Abatement (FTA) administrative waiver
questions.rationale: The First-Time Abatement administrative waiver allows the IRS to remove certain failure-to-file, failure-to-pay, and failure-to-deposit penalties for taxpayers with a clean compliance history for the prior three years and who are otherwise current.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files a return 4 months late and owes tax. The failure-to-file penalty is generally:
options: 0.5% per month up to 25%
10% flat
1% per month with no maximum
5% per month, up to a maximum of 25% of the unpaid tax
questions.rationale: Under section 6651(a)(1), the failure-to-file penalty is generally 5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part of a month the return is late, up to a maximum of 25%, reduced by the failure-to-pay penalty in months both apply.

questions.stem: A taxpayer relied in good faith on the written advice of a competent tax professional, disclosed all relevant facts, and the advice turned out to be wrong, resulting in an underpayment. Regarding the accuracy-related penalty, the taxpayer may:
options: Only reduce the penalty by half
Never avoid the penalty because reliance is irrelevant
Avoid the penalty by establishing reasonable cause and good-faith reliance on professional advice
Avoid the penalty only by paying interest
questions.rationale: Under section 6664(c), the accuracy-related penalty does not apply to a portion of an underpayment for which the taxpayer had reasonable cause and acted in good faith, which can include reasonable reliance on the advice of a competent tax professional given full and accurate facts.

questions.stem: A preparer fails to sign a return prepared for compensation and fails to furnish a copy to the taxpayer. These omissions may trigger penalties under:
options: Section 7201 for tax evasion
Section 6695 for failure to sign and failure to furnish a copy
Section 6015 innocent spouse rules
Section 6662 accuracy-related penalty
questions.rationale: Section 6695 imposes assessable penalties on paid preparers for, among other things, failing to sign the return, failing to furnish a copy to the taxpayer, and failing to include their identifying number.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent represents a client under a valid Form 2848 during an examination. The agent disagrees with the examiner and wants the case sent to Appeals. The EA's authority to do so generally:
options: Requires a separate Form 8821
Does not exist because only attorneys can go to Appeals
Exists, because EAs have unlimited practice rights and can represent clients before Appeals
Requires the client to appear personally at all conferences
questions.rationale: Enrolled agents have unlimited rights to practice before the IRS and, under a valid Form 2848, may represent the taxpayer at examination, before the Independent Office of Appeals, and in collection matters.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, a practitioner who has been retained must exercise competence. Competence requires:
options: The appropriate level of knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation necessary for the matter
That the practitioner guarantee a favorable result
Only that the practitioner hold a valid credential
That the practitioner never decline an engagement
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.35 requires practitioners to possess the necessary competence, which is the appropriate level of knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation for the matter, and competence may be achieved through study or consultation with others.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent prepared a client's return and the client is later examined. The IRS asserts the EA negligently overlooked a clear legal authority. For the EA to defend against a Circular 230 competence allegation, the most relevant inquiry is whether the EA:
options: Used commercial tax software
Filed the return electronically
Had the requisite knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation, including any reasonable consultation
Charged a low fee
questions.rationale: Competence under Circular 230 section 10.35 is assessed by whether the practitioner had the requisite knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation; a practitioner may become competent through research or by consulting with a knowledgeable professional.

questions.stem: A taxpayer requests a Collection Appeals Program (CAP) hearing rather than a CDP hearing. A key difference is that a CAP decision:
options: Requires payment of the full tax first
Is generally binding and cannot be appealed to court
May be appealed to the Tax Court
Always suspends the collection statute for two years
questions.rationale: The Collection Appeals Program offers a faster Appeals review of certain collection actions, but unlike a CDP hearing, the CAP determination is binding and cannot be appealed to the Tax Court.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who cannot pay in full and owes a balance may avoid the failure-to-pay penalty increasing during an approved installment agreement by:
options: The penalty being eliminated entirely
Paying no interest
Having the failure-to-pay penalty rate reduced while the installment agreement is in effect for an individual
Stopping all accruals
questions.rationale: While an individual is under an approved installment agreement, the failure-to-pay penalty rate is reduced from 0.5% to 0.25% per month, although interest and the reduced penalty continue to accrue until the balance is paid.

questions.stem: A revenue officer determines that collection of a tax is in jeopardy. The IRS may make a jeopardy levy. The taxpayer's protection in this situation includes the right to:
options: Request administrative and judicial review of whether the jeopardy levy was reasonable
No review whatsoever
Convert the levy into an installment agreement automatically
Automatically void the levy by objecting
questions.rationale: When the IRS makes a jeopardy or termination assessment or levy, section 7429 gives the taxpayer the right to expedited administrative review and then judicial review of whether the action was reasonable and the amount appropriate.

questions.stem: During an office audit, the examiner expands the scope to additional issues and tax years. The taxpayer's representative should recognize that:
options: The representative must consent in writing to any expansion
The IRS can never expand an audit beyond the original notice
The IRS may examine other open years and issues within the statute, subject to limits on repetitive audits
Expanding the audit voids the assessment statute
questions.rationale: The IRS may examine any open tax year and additional issues, subject to the statute of limitations and protections against repetitive examinations of the same items; the representative should manage the scope and ensure proper procedures.

questions.stem: A taxpayer prevails in a dispute with the IRS and seeks to recover litigation and administrative costs. Under section 7430, recovery generally requires that the taxpayer:
options: Simply win the case on any issue
Be the prevailing party, exhaust administrative remedies, and meet net worth and substantial justification conditions
Have used an attorney rather than an EA
File the claim within 10 years
questions.rationale: Under section 7430, a taxpayer who substantially prevails may recover reasonable administrative and litigation costs if they exhausted administrative remedies, did not unreasonably protract the proceeding, meet net worth requirements, and the IRS position was not substantially justified.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent prepares a return claiming a large charitable deduction. The client hands over a one-line note saying 'donated artwork, worth about $40,000.' The EA enters the figure without asking for an appraisal or any further detail. Which Circular 230 standard has the practitioner most likely violated?
options: Section 10.27 fee rules
Section 10.30 advertising restrictions
Section 10.22 due diligence as to accuracy by relying on the client's bare statement without making reasonable inquiry into information that appears incomplete
Section 10.34(b) on willful understatement of liability only
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.22 requires due diligence as to the accuracy of representations to clients and to the IRS; a practitioner may rely on a client's information in good faith but must make reasonable inquiries when the information appears incorrect, inconsistent, or incomplete.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, when may a practitioner endorse or otherwise negotiate a refund check issued to a client?
options: Whenever the client verbally authorizes it
When the refund is deposited into the practitioner's trust account
Only if the practitioner deducts the preparation fee first
Never; a practitioner may not endorse or negotiate a taxpayer's refund check
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.31 prohibits a practitioner from endorsing or otherwise negotiating any check issued to a client in respect of a federal tax liability, including directing a refund into an account the practitioner controls.

questions.stem: An EA is asked to handle a client's claim for refund of penalties already paid. The client proposes paying the EA 25 percent of any penalty amount recovered. Under Circular 230 section 10.27, is this contingent fee permissible?
options: Yes, but only if the client is an individual
Yes, a contingent fee is permitted for services in connection with a claim for refund filed in connection with the determination of penalties
No, because all contingent fees are prohibited in every IRS matter
No, contingent fees are allowed only for original return preparation
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.27 generally bars contingent fees but expressly allows them for an IRS examination of an original return, certain amended returns or refund claims filed within 120 days of a notice, judicial proceedings, and claims for refund filed in connection with the determination of interest or penalties.

questions.stem: A taxpayer discovers an EA omitted a $9,000 item of income on a prior-year return the EA prepared. The EA realizes the omission while preparing the current year's return. What does Circular 230 require?
options: The EA may ignore it because the prior year is closed once filed
The EA must immediately amend the prior return without telling the client
The EA must report the client to the IRS
The EA must advise the client promptly of the error or omission and the consequences of not correcting it
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.21 requires a practitioner who knows a client has not complied with the law or has made an error or omission to advise the client promptly of the noncompliance, error, or omission and the consequences of failing to correct it.

questions.stem: An EA who is also a financial planner runs a radio ad stating 'IRS-Enrolled Agent: guaranteed to cut your tax bill in half or your money back.' Which Circular 230 advertising rule does this violate?
options: Section 10.27, because it sets a fee
Section 10.51, because it is only an incompetence issue
None, because radio ads are exempt from Circular 230
Section 10.30, because the ad contains a false, fraudulent, or misleading representation through a guaranteed result
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.30 forbids practitioners from using any form of public communication or private solicitation that contains a false, fraudulent, coercive, or misleading claim, such as guaranteeing a specific tax outcome.

questions.stem: An EA repeatedly misses filing deadlines, prepares returns with recurring math and law errors, and does not keep current on tax law changes. The Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) wants to act. Which Circular 230 basis best fits this conduct?
options: Section 10.51(a)(13) incompetence and disreputable conduct demonstrated by a pattern of willful or reckless conduct or gross incompetence
Section 10.6 enrollment renewal
Section 10.27 contingent fees
Section 10.31 negotiating checks
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.35 requires practitioners to be competent, and section 10.51 defines incompetence and disreputable conduct, including reckless or grossly incompetent conduct, as a basis for OPR sanctions.

questions.stem: After OPR proposes to censure, suspend, or disbar a practitioner, what is the practitioner generally entitled to before the sanction becomes final?
options: A hearing before an Administrative Law Judge
A jury trial in U.S. District Court
An immediate disbarment with no review
A meeting only with the IRS Commissioner
questions.rationale: Under Circular 230 sections 10.60 through 10.76, OPR files a complaint and the practitioner is entitled to a hearing before an Administrative Law Judge, whose decision can be appealed to the Secretary's delegate.

questions.stem: An ALJ has issued a decision disbarring an enrolled agent. The EA disagrees. To whom may the EA appeal the ALJ's decision under Circular 230?
options: Directly to the U.S. Supreme Court
No appeal is available from an ALJ decision
To the local IRS Taxpayer Advocate
To the Secretary of the Treasury or his or her delegate (the Treasury Appellate Authority)
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.77 provides that an ALJ's decision may be appealed to the Secretary of the Treasury or delegate, and after that final agency decision a practitioner may seek judicial review.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a monetary sanction that OPR may impose under Circular 230 in addition to or instead of censure, suspension, or disbarment?
options: Garnishment of the practitioner's wages by OPR
A monetary penalty up to the gross income derived or to be derived from the conduct subject to the sanction
Automatic restitution to all affected clients
A flat $500 fine regardless of the conduct
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.50 authorizes censure, suspension, disbarment, and a monetary penalty up to the gross income derived or to be derived from the conduct giving rise to the penalty, which may also be imposed on an employer who knew of the conduct.

questions.stem: What is the lowest level of formal discipline OPR may impose, consisting of a public reprimand?
options: Permanent injunction
Disbarment
Suspension
Censure
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.50 lists censure (a public reprimand) as the least severe sanction, followed by suspension, disbarment, and monetary penalty.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent maintains an enrollment cycle ending in a year tied to the last digit of the SSN. Over the three-year enrollment cycle, what is the minimum total continuing education an EA must complete, and how much must be ethics?
options: 72 hours total, including 6 hours of ethics, with a minimum of 16 hours per year (2 of which are ethics)
40 hours total, including 4 hours of ethics
100 hours total, including 10 hours of ethics
24 hours total with no ethics requirement
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.6 requires enrolled agents to complete 72 hours of CE over the three-year enrollment cycle, including 6 hours of ethics or professional conduct, with a minimum of 16 hours (including 2 ethics hours) in each year.

questions.stem: An organization wants to offer continuing education to enrolled agents. Before its programs can count toward an EA's CE, what must the organization generally do?
options: Get approval from the state bar association
Simply mail the IRS a list of attendees after each course
Register as an IRS-approved continuing education provider and obtain a provider number
Nothing; any course on tax counts automatically
questions.rationale: To deliver qualifying CE for enrolled agents, an organization must become an IRS-approved continuing education provider, obtain a provider number, and ensure programs meet the standards in Circular 230 section 10.9 and related guidance.

questions.stem: An EA completes a 4-hour 'ethics and professional conduct' webinar from an IRS-approved provider. How does this count toward the EA's annual ethics requirement?
options: It counts only if the EA also passes a separate ethics exam
It satisfies the 2-hour annual ethics minimum and the extra 2 hours count toward total CE
It does not count because ethics CE must be in person
Only 2 of the 4 hours count for anything
questions.rationale: Qualifying ethics CE from an IRS-approved provider satisfies the 2-hour annual ethics minimum, and hours beyond the minimum still apply to the overall 16-hour annual and 72-hour cycle totals.

questions.stem: How long must an enrolled agent retain records demonstrating completion of continuing education in case of an IRS audit of CE compliance?
options: For 4 years following the date of renewal of enrollment
No retention is required
For 10 years
For 1 year only
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.6(j) requires enrolled agents to retain documentation of CE completion (certificates, provider records, etc.) for four years following the date of renewal of enrollment.

questions.stem: An EA's enrollment lapses because the EA failed to renew and pay the renewal fee on time. While the enrollment is inactive, may the individual represent taxpayers before the IRS as an enrolled agent?
options: Yes, lapsed status has no effect on practice
Only in collection matters
No, an individual whose enrollment is inactive or lapsed may not practice before the IRS or hold out as an enrolled agent
Yes, for 90 days after lapse
questions.rationale: Failure to timely renew enrollment places the individual in inactive status; under Circular 230 section 10.6, such a person may not practice before the IRS or hold out as an enrolled agent until reinstated.

questions.stem: An EA gives written tax advice on a partnership structure. Under the current Circular 230 section 10.37 written advice standards, which is required?
options: The EA may rely on the taxpayer's representations even if clearly false to save time
The advice must satisfy the old 'covered opinion' disclaimer rules and include a boilerplate disclaimer
The EA must base the advice on reasonable factual and legal assumptions, consider all relevant facts the EA knows or should know, and not rely on unreasonable representations
The EA must guarantee the position will survive audit
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.37 sets standards for written advice: base it on reasonable assumptions, consider all relevant facts the practitioner knows or should know, relate law to facts, and do not rely on representations the practitioner knows or should know are incorrect or incomplete.

questions.stem: A taxpayer asks an EA to delay producing records that the IRS has lawfully requested, hoping the auditor will give up. What does Circular 230 require of the EA?
options: Destroy the records to protect the client
Refuse all contact with the IRS
Comply with the client to keep the engagement

Exercise due diligence and not unreasonably delay; section 10.20 requires prompt submission of records or information lawfully requested unless the practitioner believes in good faith they are privileged
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.20 requires a practitioner to promptly submit records or information lawfully requested by an IRS officer or employee unless the practitioner believes in good faith and on reasonable grounds that the material is privileged.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, who within the IRS is responsible for matters related to practitioner conduct and discipline?
options: The Criminal Investigation Division
The Taxpayer Advocate Service
The Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR)
The Office of Appeals
questions.rationale: The Office of Professional Responsibility administers and enforces Circular 230, including investigating allegations of misconduct and pursuing sanctions against practitioners.

questions.stem: An EA who heads a tax department fails to put in place any procedures to ensure staff comply with Circular 230, and a subordinate willfully prepares fraudulent returns. Under section 10.36, the EA with principal authority may be sanctioned if which condition is met?
options: The EA, through willfulness, recklessness, or gross incompetence, failed to take reasonable steps to ensure adequate procedures and the firm engaged in a pattern of noncompliance
The EA personally signed every return
The subordinate was an enrolled agent too
Any single error occurred, regardless of procedures
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.36 requires individuals with principal authority over a firm's tax practice to take reasonable steps to ensure adequate procedures for Circular 230 compliance; failure through willfulness, recklessness, or gross incompetence, combined with a pattern of noncompliance, can result in sanctions.

questions.stem: An EA wants to use the designation in marketing. Which statement about holding out is consistent with Circular 230?
options: An EA may call themselves a 'certified IRS specialist'
An EA may claim to be employed by the IRS
An EA may state 'enrolled to represent taxpayers before the Internal Revenue Service' or 'enrolled agent,' but may not imply an employment relationship with the IRS
An EA may use the IRS seal in advertising
questions.rationale: Circular 230 permits enrolled agents to describe themselves as such or as 'enrolled to represent taxpayers before the IRS,' but they may not use the term in a misleading way, imply an IRS employment relationship, or use IRS insignia.

questions.stem: An EA's client refuses to correct a return error the EA flagged. After advising the client of the consequences, what must the EA do regarding future work for that client?
options: Always withdraw from all engagements
Immediately notify the IRS of the client's refusal
Correct the return without consent
Decide whether continued representation is consistent with Circular 230; the EA is not required to withdraw but should consider professional standards and may not assist in perpetuating the error
questions.rationale: Under section 10.21 the EA must advise the client of the error and consequences; the EA need not report the client but must not assist in perpetuating noncompliance and should weigh whether to continue the engagement.

questions.stem: An EA takes a return position that has a reasonable basis but lacks substantial authority and is not disclosed. Under Circular 230 section 10.34(a), when may the practitioner sign such a return?
options: Only for corporate clients
Only if the client signs a waiver
Never; positions must always have substantial authority

The practitioner may not willfully, recklessly, or through gross incompetence sign a return with an unreasonable position as defined under section 6694; a non-tax-shelter position generally needs a reasonable basis with adequate disclosure or substantial authority
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.34(a) prohibits willfully, recklessly, or through gross incompetence signing or advising a position that the practitioner knows or reasonably should know is an unreasonable position under section 6694, which generally requires substantial authority, or reasonable basis with adequate disclosure for non-shelter positions.

questions.stem: Which of the following individuals is generally NOT permitted to practice before the IRS under Circular 230 as a 'practitioner'?
options: An unenrolled preparer who did not participate in the Annual Filing Season Program, for full representation rights
A certified public accountant in good standing
An enrolled agent in active status
An attorney in good standing
questions.rationale: Practitioners with unlimited practice rights include attorneys, CPAs, enrolled agents, enrolled actuaries, and enrolled retirement plan agents; unenrolled preparers have limited rights, and only AFSP participants have limited representation before certain IRS personnel for returns they prepared.

questions.stem: An AFSP record-of-completion holder (unenrolled preparer) prepared a return that is now under examination. What may this preparer do?
options: Represent the taxpayer only before revenue agents, customer service representatives, and similar IRS employees regarding the return they prepared and signed
Nothing; only attorneys, CPAs, and EAs may represent in any capacity
Represent any taxpayer in any IRS matter
Represent the taxpayer before Appeals and Counsel
questions.rationale: Annual Filing Season Program participants have limited representation rights, allowing them to represent taxpayers before IRS revenue agents, customer service representatives, and similar employees regarding returns they prepared and signed, but not before Appeals, Collection, or Counsel.

questions.stem: An EA is suspended from practice for two years. During the suspension, the EA arranges for a colleague to file representation paperwork while the suspended EA does the substantive work behind the scenes. What is the status of this arrangement?
options: Prohibited; a suspended practitioner may not practice before the IRS directly or indirectly, and assisting others to circumvent the suspension is also a violation
Permissible if the colleague is also an EA
Permissible for collection matters only
Permissible, because the suspended EA is not signing anything
questions.rationale: A suspended or disbarred practitioner may not practice before the IRS in any manner, directly or indirectly, and both the suspended practitioner and any practitioner who knowingly assists in circumventing the sanction can be disciplined.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, when a client requests their records, which records may a practitioner withhold pending payment of a disputed fee?
options: None; everything must be kept by the practitioner
All records, including the client's original documents
Only the client's W-2s

The practitioner must return the client's records necessary for the client to comply with federal tax obligations, even if a fee dispute exists, though the practitioner may keep certain work product if state law permits a retaining lien
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.28 requires a practitioner to promptly return any client records necessary for the client to comply with federal tax obligations, even in a fee dispute; if state law permits a retaining lien on the practitioner's own work product, only those documents may be withheld.

questions.stem: Which of the following is considered 'practice before the IRS' under Circular 230?
options: Communicating with the IRS on a taxpayer's behalf regarding rights, privileges, or liabilities, including representation at conferences and preparing documents
Only appearing in U.S. Tax Court
Only preparing tax returns
Only providing investment advice
questions.rationale: Practice before the IRS comprises all matters connected with a presentation to the IRS relating to a taxpayer's rights, privileges, or liabilities, including preparing and filing documents, corresponding, communicating, and representing a client at conferences and meetings.

questions.stem: An EA discovers that a former client's return, which the EA did not prepare, contains a clearly fraudulent deduction. The current engagement is unrelated. What does Circular 230 require regarding the fraudulent prior return?
options: The EA must withdraw from the current engagement
The EA must amend the prior return
The EA must report the former client to OPR
Circular 230 imposes no duty to act on a return the EA did not prepare and is not engaged to address, but the EA should not knowingly assist in furthering the fraud
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.21 obligations attach to returns the practitioner prepared or to a client's noncompliance the practitioner learns of in the engagement; the practitioner must never knowingly further fraud but has no affirmative duty to correct an unrelated return the EA did not prepare.

questions.stem: OPR sends a practitioner a 'pre-allegation notice' inviting a response before deciding whether to pursue formal action. What is the practical significance of responding at this stage?
options: It waives all defenses
It gives the practitioner an opportunity to provide an explanation and possibly resolve the matter before a formal Circular 230 complaint is filed
It automatically results in censure
It transfers the case to Tax Court
questions.rationale: Before filing a formal complaint, OPR typically contacts the practitioner, allowing a response; engaging at this stage can lead to closure without sanction, a soft notice, or a negotiated resolution short of formal discipline.

questions.stem: A practitioner who is disbarred wants to be reinstated. Under Circular 230, when may a disbarred practitioner petition for reinstatement?
options: Immediately after disbarment
After 1 year

After the expiration of 5 years following disbarment, and reinstatement may be granted if the practitioner is not likely to again engage in disqualifying conduct and reinstatement is not contrary to the public interest
Never; disbarment is always permanent
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.81 permits a disbarred or suspended practitioner to petition for reinstatement after five years, and OPR may grant it if satisfied the practitioner is unlikely to engage in conduct contrary to the regulations and reinstatement is in the public interest.

questions.stem: What form does a taxpayer use to authorize an enrolled agent to represent them before the IRS, granting the EA power to receive confidential information and act on the taxpayer's behalf?
options: Form 8821, Tax Information Authorization
Form 4506
Form 2848, Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative
Form W-9
questions.rationale: Form 2848 grants a representative the authority to represent the taxpayer before the IRS and to receive confidential information; Form 8821 only authorizes disclosure of information without representation rights.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files Form 8821 naming an EA to receive copies of IRS notices but does not file Form 2848. The EA later wants to attend an audit conference and argue the taxpayer's position. Can the EA do so based on the Form 8821?
options: Yes, Form 8821 fully authorizes representation
Yes, if the audit is by mail
Only if the EA also signs the return
No, Form 8821 only authorizes the inspection and receipt of information; representation requires Form 2848
questions.rationale: A Form 8821 tax information authorization permits a designee to receive and inspect confidential tax information but confers no authority to represent, advocate, or sign on the taxpayer's behalf; that requires a Form 2848 power of attorney.

questions.stem: On a Form 2848, a taxpayer wants the representative to be able to substitute or add another representative. What must the taxpayer do?
options: Specifically authorize the act of substituting or adding representatives on the Form 2848, because that authority is not granted by default
Call the IRS to grant it verbally
Nothing; substitution is automatic
File a separate Form 8821
questions.rationale: By default a Form 2848 does not permit the representative to substitute or add another representative; the taxpayer must specifically authorize that act on the form for the representative to delegate authority.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files a new Form 2848 for the 2023 tax year naming a different representative, but wants the prior representative for 2022 to remain. What is the effect of the new Form 2848?
options: It revokes all prior powers of attorney for all years automatically
It has no effect on prior authorizations
It only adds the new representative and never revokes anyone
A new Form 2848 revokes a prior POA for the same matters and periods unless the taxpayer checks the box to retain the prior representative and attaches a copy of the prior authorization
questions.rationale: A newly filed Form 2848 automatically revokes any earlier power of attorney for the same matters and tax periods unless the taxpayer specifically checks the retention box and attaches a copy of the authorization to be retained.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of obtaining a CAF (Centralized Authorization File) number when an EA submits a Form 2848?
options: It is the taxpayer's account number
It is a unique number the IRS assigns to track a representative's authorizations on file
It is the EA's enrollment number
It replaces the EA's PTIN on returns
questions.rationale: The Centralized Authorization File number is a unique identifier the IRS assigns to a representative to track powers of attorney and tax information authorizations associated with that representative.

questions.stem: A representative wants to immediately revoke an existing Form 2848 without naming a new representative. What is the proper method?
options: Call the local IRS office only
File a new return
Send a copy of the previously filed Form 2848 with 'REVOKE' written across the top, signed and dated, to the IRS (or a statement of revocation with required details)
Do nothing; it expires on its own
questions.rationale: To revoke a power of attorney without naming a new representative, the taxpayer (or representative withdrawing) sends the IRS a copy of the Form 2848 with 'REVOKE' (or 'WITHDRAW') written across the top, signed and dated, or a signed statement containing the same information.

questions.stem: A taxpayer receives a CP2000 notice proposing additional tax from unreported 1099 income. The taxpayer disagrees with part of it. What is the CP2000 and the appropriate first response?
options: It is a final bill that must be paid immediately
It is a notice of deficiency that requires a Tax Court petition immediately
It is a refund notice
It is an underreporter notice proposing changes based on third-party data; the taxpayer should respond by the deadline agreeing or disagreeing with explanation and documentation
questions.rationale: A CP2000 is an IRS Automated Underreporter notice proposing adjustments based on mismatches between the return and third-party information returns; the taxpayer should respond by the deadline indicating agreement or disagreement with supporting documentation.

questions.stem: Which type of IRS examination is generally the most limited in scope, conducted entirely through correspondence and focused on specific line items such as a credit or deduction?
options: Office examination
Field examination
Criminal investigation
Correspondence (mail) examination
questions.rationale: Correspondence examinations are conducted by mail, are narrowly focused on specific items such as particular deductions or credits, and are the least complex type of IRS audit; office and field exams are progressively broader.

questions.stem: An examination of a complex business with inventory, multiple entities, and significant assets is most likely to be conducted as which type of audit, and by whom?
options: An automated underreporter review
A field examination by a revenue agent at the taxpayer's place of business or representative's office
A correspondence audit by a tax examiner
An office audit by a tax compliance officer
questions.rationale: Field examinations, conducted by revenue agents, are used for complex returns such as businesses with inventory and multiple entities, and typically take place at the taxpayer's business or the representative's office.

questions.stem: After an examination, the IRS issues a 30-day letter with an examination report. The taxpayer wants to dispute the findings administratively. What does the 30-day letter offer?
options: An automatic refund
The right to file a Tax Court petition
The opportunity to request a conference with the IRS Office of Appeals by filing a written protest within 30 days
A final, non-appealable assessment
questions.rationale: A 30-day letter accompanies the examination report and offers the taxpayer the opportunity to request an Appeals conference within 30 days by filing a written protest; declining or missing it generally leads to a statutory notice of deficiency.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is proposing to appeal an examination of a return showing total proposed additional tax and penalties of $22,000 for one tax period. What format of protest is required to go to Appeals?
options: A formal written protest, because the amount exceeds $25,000
No protest is needed; Appeals is automatic
A small case request, because the amount is $25,000 or less for the period
A Tax Court petition
questions.rationale: For disputes where the total amount of proposed additional tax, penalties, and interest for any tax period is $25,000 or less, the taxpayer may submit a small case request; larger amounts require a formal written protest.

questions.stem: What is a statutory notice of deficiency commonly called, and what key right does it convey?
options: A CP2000; the right to a refund
A 90-day letter; the right to petition the U.S. Tax Court within 90 days (150 days if addressed outside the U.S.) before assessment
A 30-day letter; the right to an Appeals conference
A levy notice; the right to a hearing
questions.rationale: A statutory notice of deficiency, or 90-day letter, gives the taxpayer 90 days (150 days if the notice is addressed to a person outside the United States) to file a petition with the U.S. Tax Court, which is the only forum that allows litigation before paying the tax.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a notice of deficiency dated and mailed March 3. The 90th day falls on Sunday, June 1. When is the last day to file a Tax Court petition?
options: Monday, June 2, because if the last day falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day
There is no fixed deadline
March 3 plus 60 days
Sunday, June 1, regardless of the weekend
questions.rationale: The 90-day period to petition the Tax Court is strict, but if the last day falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday in the District of Columbia, the deadline is extended to the next succeeding business day.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to use the Tax Court's simplified 'S case' procedures. What is the dollar limit for small tax cases, and what is the trade-off?
options: $50,000 or less in dispute per year; the decision cannot be appealed
$10,000 or less in dispute; the decision can be appealed
There is no limit
$100,000 or less; full appeal rights
questions.rationale: The Tax Court's small tax case (S case) procedures are available when the amount in dispute is $50,000 or less for any one tax year or period; proceedings are less formal, but the decision is final and may not be appealed.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid an assessed tax in full and now wants to litigate to recover it. Which courts have jurisdiction over a refund suit, and what is the prerequisite?
options: The U.S. District Court or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims, after full payment of the tax and timely filing of a claim for refund that is disallowed or unanswered
Only the U.S. Supreme Court
Any state court
Only the U.S. Tax Court, with no payment required
questions.rationale: To sue for a refund, a taxpayer must first pay the tax in full and file a timely administrative claim for refund; if denied or not acted upon within six months, suit may be brought in U.S. District Court or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims.

questions.stem: An IRS examiner adjusts a return by correcting an obvious arithmetic mistake and issues a 'math error' notice that summarily assesses additional tax. What special right does the taxpayer have regarding a math error assessment?
options: None; math error assessments are final
The taxpayer can only pay and file a refund claim
The taxpayer must immediately file in Tax Court
The taxpayer has 60 days to request abatement of the math error assessment, after which the IRS must follow normal deficiency procedures to pursue the amount
questions.rationale: Math or clerical error assessments are summary assessments, but section 6213(b) gives the taxpayer 60 days to request abatement; if requested, the IRS must follow normal deficiency procedures, issuing a notice of deficiency to pursue the tax.

questions.stem: A taxpayer never filed a return, and the IRS prepared a Substitute for Return (SFR) under section 6020(b). How does the SFR generally treat the taxpayer's filing status and deductions?
options: It always uses married filing jointly
It uses the most favorable status and all available deductions
It cannot be prepared without taxpayer consent
It typically uses the least favorable filing status (e.g., single or married filing separately) and standard deduction with no itemized deductions or dependents the IRS is unaware of
questions.rationale: Under section 6020(b), the IRS may prepare a substitute for return when a taxpayer fails to file; the SFR typically uses the least favorable filing status and standard deduction only, so filing an accurate original return usually reduces the liability.

questions.stem: After the IRS files a substitute for return and assesses tax, the taxpayer files an accurate original return showing a lower liability. What will the IRS generally do?
options: Reject the original return because the SFR is final
Treat the original return as an amended return only
Process the original return as the taxpayer's return and adjust the account, generally reducing the SFR-based assessment
Ignore the original return entirely
questions.rationale: Filing an accurate original return after an SFR assessment lets the taxpayer claim the correct filing status, deductions, and credits; the IRS will process the original return and adjust the account, typically lowering the SFR-based liability.

questions.stem: A taxpayer agreed to and paid an audit assessment but later finds new documentation that would have changed the result. The assessment period and deficiency procedures have passed. What administrative remedy may be available?
options: None; the matter is permanently closed
A collection due process hearing
Audit reconsideration, an informal IRS process to reevaluate an assessment when the taxpayer presents new information not previously considered
A section 6213 deficiency petition
questions.rationale: Audit reconsideration is an informal process allowing the IRS to reevaluate the results of a prior audit or SFR assessment when the taxpayer provides new information not previously considered, did not appear for the original audit, or moved and never received correspondence.

questions.stem: During an office examination, the revenue agent requests the EA to extend the statute of limitations on assessment by signing Form 872. What should the EA consider before advising the client to sign?
options: Always refuse, because extensions never help the taxpayer
Sign only if the client gets paid
Always sign, because the IRS requires it
Weigh whether more time benefits the client (e.g., to gather records or pursue Appeals) versus letting the statute expire, and consider a restricted (Form 872) versus open-ended consent
questions.rationale: Consenting to extend the assessment statute (Form 872 for a fixed date or Form 872-A open-ended) is voluntary; the representative should weigh the benefit of more time to develop facts and pursue Appeals against the risk, and may seek a restricted consent.

questions.stem: A taxpayer owes $48,000 in assessed individual income tax and wants an installment agreement without submitting detailed financial statements. The taxpayer can pay it off within 72 months. Which agreement likely applies?
options: A streamlined installment agreement, generally available for assessed balances of $50,000 or less payable within 72 months without a full financial disclosure
A guaranteed installment agreement
A partial payment installment agreement
An offer in compromise
questions.rationale: A streamlined installment agreement generally applies to individuals with assessed balances of $50,000 or less who can pay within 72 months (and within the collection statute), and it does not require a Collection Information Statement.

questions.stem: Which installment agreement must the IRS accept if the taxpayer owes $10,000 or less, has filed and paid on time for the prior 5 years, agrees to pay within 3 years, and meets other conditions?
options: Currently not collectible status
Guaranteed installment agreement
Offer in compromise
Partial payment installment agreement
questions.rationale: Under section 6159, the IRS must grant a guaranteed installment agreement when the aggregate tax liability is $10,000 or less, the taxpayer has filed and paid timely for the past five years, agrees to full payment within three years, and meets the other statutory conditions.

questions.stem: A taxpayer owes $90,000 but, based on a full financial analysis, can only pay $400 per month, which will not full-pay before the collection statute expires. Which arrangement fits?
options: Automatic 120-day extension
Guaranteed installment agreement
Streamlined installment agreement
Partial payment installment agreement (PPIA), with periodic financial review
questions.rationale: A partial payment installment agreement is used when a taxpayer cannot full-pay the liability before the collection statute expiration date; the IRS sets payments based on ability to pay, requires a Collection Information Statement, and periodically reviews the taxpayer's financial condition.

questions.stem: Which of the following is one of the three grounds on which the IRS may accept an offer in compromise?
options: Doubt as to collectibility (the taxpayer cannot pay the full amount)
Convenience to the taxpayer
The taxpayer's preference to settle
A change in tax rates
questions.rationale: The IRS may accept an offer in compromise on three grounds: doubt as to liability, doubt as to collectibility, and effective tax administration (where collection would create economic hardship or be unfair and inequitable).

questions.stem: A taxpayer could technically full-pay the tax by liquidating retirement savings, but doing so would leave the elderly, disabled taxpayer unable to meet basic living expenses. Which OIC basis is most applicable?
options: There is no applicable basis
Doubt as to liability
Doubt as to collectibility
Effective tax administration (economic hardship or public policy/equity grounds)
questions.rationale: An effective tax administration offer in compromise may be accepted when there is no doubt the tax is owed and could be collected, but requiring full payment would create economic hardship or, due to exceptional circumstances, would be detrimental to voluntary compliance and unfair.

questions.stem: A taxpayer submits a lump-sum cash offer in compromise. What payment must accompany the offer (absent a low-income certification)?
options: 50 percent of the offer amount
The entire offer amount up front
Nothing until the IRS accepts
A 20 percent down payment of the offer amount plus the application fee
questions.rationale: For a lump-sum cash offer in compromise, the taxpayer must submit a 20 percent nonrefundable down payment with the offer along with the application fee, unless the taxpayer certifies low-income status, which waives the fee and initial payment requirements.

questions.stem: A taxpayer selects the periodic payment offer in compromise option. What must the taxpayer do with payments while the offer is pending?
options: Continue making the proposed monthly installment payments while the offer is under consideration
Stop all payments until the IRS decides
Pay only after acceptance
Pay 20 percent down and nothing more
questions.rationale: Under the periodic payment offer in compromise option, the taxpayer submits the first proposed installment with the offer and must continue making the proposed monthly payments while the IRS considers the offer; missing payments can cause the offer to be returned.

questions.stem: After the IRS accepts an offer in compromise, the taxpayer must comply with which condition to keep the OIC from defaulting?
options: Waive all future refunds permanently
Pay double the offer amount
Never file another return
Remain in full filing and payment compliance for the next 5 years (or until the offer terms are met)
questions.rationale: As a condition of an accepted offer in compromise, the taxpayer must remain in compliance by timely filing returns and paying all taxes for five years; default during that period can reinstate the full original liability less payments made.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a Notice of Federal Tax Lien filing and a Final Notice of Intent to Levy. To preserve the right to a Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing on the levy, by when must the taxpayer request it?
options: Within 90 days
Within 1 year
Within 30 days of the date of the Final Notice of Intent to Levy and right to a hearing
Anytime before the levy is executed
questions.rationale: To obtain a timely Collection Due Process hearing, the taxpayer must request it within 30 days after the date of the Final Notice of Intent to Levy and Notice of Your Right to a Hearing (Letter 1058 or LT11); a timely CDP request also suspends levy and the collection statute and preserves Tax Court review.

questions.stem: A taxpayer missed the 30-day CDP deadline by 45 days. What alternative hearing may still be available, and what is the key difference?
options: An equivalent hearing, which is available within one year but does not give the right to judicial review in Tax Court and does not suspend the collection statute
An automatic levy release
No hearing of any kind
A formal CDP hearing with full Tax Court review
questions.rationale: If a taxpayer misses the 30-day CDP deadline, an equivalent hearing may be requested within one year of the CDP notice; it offers similar Appeals consideration but no right to Tax Court review and does not suspend the collection statute or levy action.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally exempt from an IRS levy?
options: All bank account funds
A statutory minimum amount of wages, salary, and certain other income based on the taxpayer's filing status and number of dependents
All wages without limit
All real property
questions.rationale: Section 6334 lists property exempt from levy, including a minimum amount of wages and salary (calculated from the standard deduction and number of dependents), certain personal effects, unemployment benefits, and certain pension and public assistance payments.

questions.stem: An IRS levy is served on a taxpayer's employer for unpaid taxes. How does a wage levy differ from a levy on a bank account?
options: A wage levy is continuous, attaching to future wages each pay period until released, while a bank levy generally reaches only funds on deposit on the day the levy is served (plus a 21-day hold)
Both are one-time levies
Neither requires prior notice
A bank levy is continuous and a wage levy is one-time
questions.rationale: A wage levy under section 6331(e) is continuous and attaches to a taxpayer's salary and wages until released, while a bank levy is a one-time event reaching only the balance on deposit when served, which the bank holds for 21 days before remitting.

questions.stem: When a bank receives an IRS levy on a taxpayer's account, how long must it hold the funds before sending them to the IRS?
options: 6 months
60 days
21 calendar days, to allow time to resolve disputes such as misidentification or ownership issues
Immediately remit with no holding period
questions.rationale: A bank served with a levy must hold the funds on deposit for 21 calendar days before sending them to the IRS, allowing the taxpayer time to address errors such as mistaken identity or to arrange a release.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to sell their home, but a federal tax lien is attached and the sale proceeds will not fully pay the tax. To allow the sale to close with clear title to the buyer, which lien relief applies to that specific property?
options: Lien subordination
Certificate of discharge of property from the federal tax lien
Offer in compromise
Lien withdrawal
questions.rationale: A certificate of discharge (section 6325(b)) removes the federal tax lien from specific property, allowing a sale or transfer with clear title; it is commonly used when selling a home, with the IRS receiving its interest from the proceeds.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to refinance a mortgage, but the federal tax lien is ahead of the new lender, who will not lend unless its mortgage has priority. Which lien relief lets the new lender's interest take priority over the IRS lien?
options: Discharge
Withdrawal
Subordination
Release
questions.rationale: Subordination (section 6325(d)) does not remove the lien but allows another creditor, such as a refinancing lender, to move ahead of the IRS lien in priority, which can facilitate a refinance that ultimately helps the taxpayer pay the tax.

questions.stem: A taxpayer fully paid the tax liability. What document should the IRS issue regarding the federal tax lien, and within what general timeframe?
options: Nothing; liens never get released
A Certificate of Release of Federal Tax Lien, generally within 30 days after the liability is fully satisfied or becomes unenforceable
A discharge within 1 year
A subordination certificate within 90 days
questions.rationale: Under section 6325(a), the IRS must issue a Certificate of Release of Federal Tax Lien within 30 days after the tax liability is fully paid or becomes legally unenforceable (such as when the collection statute expires).

questions.stem: The collection statute expiration date (CSED) is generally 10 years from assessment. Which of the following events suspends (tolls) the running of the CSED?
options: A pending offer in compromise (plus 30 days), a pending installment agreement request, a CDP hearing, bankruptcy (plus 6 months), or time the taxpayer is out of the country for at least 6 months
Filing the next year's return
The taxpayer moving to another state
The taxpayer hiring a new representative
questions.rationale: Various events suspend the 10-year collection statute, including a pending offer in compromise (plus 30 days), pending installment agreement requests, CDP hearings, bankruptcy stays (plus six months), taxpayer assistance order requests, and continuous absence from the U.S. for six months or more.

questions.stem: A business failed to pay over withheld employment taxes. The IRS seeks to assess the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty (TFRP) personally against the bookkeeper. What two elements must be established?
options: That the person owned the company
That the person was a responsible person who had the duty to collect, account for, and pay over the taxes, and that the person willfully failed to do so
Only that the person was an employee
That the business was profitable
questions.rationale: The Trust Fund Recovery Penalty under section 6672 applies to any person who was responsible for collecting, accounting for, and paying over withheld taxes and who willfully failed to do so; both responsibility and willfulness must be present.

questions.stem: The IRS proposes a Trust Fund Recovery Penalty against a client by issuing Letter 1153 and Form 2751. What is the deadline and method to appeal the proposed TFRP administratively?
options: There is no appeal right for the TFRP
90 days to petition Tax Court
30 days to file a protest with Appeals; failure to respond allows the IRS to assess the penalty
1 year to request an equivalent hearing
questions.rationale: When the IRS proposes the TFRP with Letter 1153 and Form 2751, the responsible person may agree, or file a written protest to the IRS Office of Appeals within the time stated (generally 60 days); if no response is made, the IRS may assess the penalty, after which a refund suit requires paying a divisible portion.

questions.stem: A taxpayer cannot pay anything toward a tax debt because their income barely covers necessary living expenses. What status might the IRS grant to temporarily stop active collection?
options: Innocent spouse relief
Lien discharge
Offer in compromise acceptance
Currently Not Collectible (CNC) status, which suspends active collection while interest and penalties continue to accrue
questions.rationale: Currently Not Collectible status is granted when collection would create economic hardship; active collection is suspended, but the liability remains, interest and penalties continue to accrue, the CSED keeps running, and the IRS may still file a Notice of Federal Tax Lien.

questions.stem: A divorced taxpayer signed a joint return prepared by her ex-spouse, who omitted significant self-employment income she knew nothing about. She wants relief from the resulting joint liability. Which type of innocent spouse relief is most directly aimed at understatements attributable to the other spouse's erroneous items?
options: Injured spouse relief
Separation of liability election under section 6015(c)
Equitable relief under section 6015(f)
Traditional innocent spouse relief under section 6015(b)
questions.rationale: Section 6015(b) traditional innocent spouse relief applies to understatements attributable to the other spouse's erroneous items where the requesting spouse did not know and had no reason to know of the understatement, and it would be inequitable to hold them liable.

questions.stem: When the IRS evaluates a request for equitable innocent spouse relief under section 6015(f), which factor weighs in favor of granting relief?
options: The requesting spouse significantly benefited from the unpaid tax
The requesting spouse would suffer economic hardship if relief were denied
The requesting spouse failed to comply with later tax laws
The requesting spouse had actual knowledge of the item
questions.rationale: In weighing equitable relief under section 6015(f), favorable factors include economic hardship, divorce or separation, lack of knowledge or reason to know, abuse, and compliance with tax laws; unfavorable factors include significant benefit, actual knowledge, and later noncompliance.

questions.stem: A spouse's portion of a joint refund was applied (offset) to the other spouse's past-due child support. The non-liable spouse wants their share of the refund back. What relief applies?
options: Injured spouse allocation using Form 8379
Offer in compromise
Innocent spouse relief under section 6015
Currently not collectible status
questions.rationale: An injured spouse files Form 8379 to claim their portion of a joint overpayment that was, or will be, applied to the other spouse's separate past-due federal tax, state tax, child support, or federal nontax debt.

questions.stem: What is the general deadline to request traditional innocent spouse relief under section 6015(b)?
options: Within 30 days of the return due date
Anytime, with no deadline
Within 10 years of filing the return
Within 2 years after the IRS begins collection activity against the requesting spouse
questions.rationale: Relief under sections 6015(b) and 6015(c) must be requested within two years after the date the IRS first began collection activities against the requesting spouse; equitable relief under 6015(f) is generally tied to the collection statute period.

questions.stem: A preparer is assessed a section 6694(a) penalty for an understatement due to an unreasonable position. What defense can eliminate the penalty?
options: The return was filed electronically
The understatement was small
The preparer had reasonable cause for the understatement and acted in good faith
The client refused to pay the preparer's fee
questions.rationale: The section 6694(a) penalty for an unreasonable position is not imposed if it is shown the preparer had reasonable cause for the understatement and acted in good faith, considering factors such as the nature of the error and reliance on the taxpayer's information.

questions.stem: A preparer knowingly took a frivolous position to reduce a client's tax, resulting in an understatement. Under section 6694(b), the penalty for willful or reckless conduct is generally the greater of which amounts?
options: 10 percent of the tax understated
$1,000 or 50 percent of the income derived (or to be derived) by the preparer with respect to the return
$50 per return
$5,000 or 75 percent of the income derived by the preparer, with a higher floor
questions.rationale: Section 6694(b) penalizes willful or reckless conduct by a preparer with a penalty equal to the greater of $5,000 or 75 percent of the income derived (or to be derived) from the return, while section 6694(a) (unreasonable position) is the greater of $1,000 or 50 percent.

questions.stem: Under section 6695, a paid preparer who fails to furnish a copy of the return to the taxpayer is subject to which penalty (subject to inflation adjustment)?
options: No penalty applies
A penalty equal to the tax due
A penalty per failure (around $60), up to an annual maximum
A penalty of $10,000 per failure
questions.rationale: Section 6695 imposes per-failure penalties (each indexed for inflation, around $60) for failures such as not furnishing a copy of the return to the taxpayer, not signing the return, not furnishing the preparer's identifying number, and not retaining records, each subject to an annual maximum.

questions.stem: A preparer completed returns claiming the Earned Income Tax Credit, the Child Tax Credit, the American Opportunity Tax Credit, and head of household status. Under section 6695(g), what must the preparer do for each of these to avoid the due diligence penalty?
options: Charge a contingent fee

Meet the paid preparer due diligence requirements, including completing Form 8867, computing the credits, keeping required records, and making reasonable inquiries when information appears incorrect or incomplete
Have the taxpayer sign an affidavit
Nothing special; ordinary care is enough
questions.rationale: Section 6695(g) imposes a per-credit due diligence penalty (indexed, around $600) when a preparer fails to comply with due diligence requirements for the EITC, CTC/ACTC/ODC, AOTC, and head of household status, which include completing Form 8867, the credit worksheets, recordkeeping, and reasonable inquiries.

questions.stem: Who is required to obtain and use a Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN)?
options: Any individual who prepares, or assists in preparing, all or substantially all of a tax return for compensation
Anyone who files their own return
Only enrolled agents
Only attorneys and CPAs
questions.rationale: Every individual who is compensated for preparing, or assisting in preparing, all or substantially all of a federal tax return or claim for refund must obtain and use a PTIN and renew it annually.

questions.stem: A tax firm wants to electronically file returns and must obtain an Electronic Filing Identification Number (EFIN). As part of the application, the IRS conducts a suitability check. What does the suitability check typically include?
options: A simple verification of the firm's address
A vote by other tax professionals
A review of the applicant's CE certificates only
A check that may include a credit check, tax compliance check, criminal background check, and review for prior noncompliance with IRS e-file requirements
questions.rationale: To become an authorized e-file provider and receive an EFIN, applicants undergo a suitability check that may include a tax compliance check, a credit check, a criminal background check (including fingerprinting), and a review of any prior noncompliance with IRS e-file requirements.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's e-filed return is rejected because a dependent's SSN was already used on another return. The error cannot be corrected and the return must be filed on paper. What form must the preparer include to explain why the return is being paper-filed?
options: Form 2848
Form 9465
Form 8867
Form 8948, Preparer Explanation for Not Filing Electronically
questions.rationale: When a specified tax return preparer who is otherwise required to e-file submits a paper return (for example, because the e-filed return was rejected and cannot be corrected), Form 8948 is attached to explain the reason for not filing electronically.

questions.stem: A specified tax return preparer files returns for compensation. Under the e-file mandate, when must such a preparer e-file individual income tax returns?
options: Never; e-filing is optional for all
Only for business returns
Only if the client requests it
When the preparer reasonably expects to file more than 10 covered returns (individual, estate, and trust income tax returns) in a calendar year, unless an exception applies
questions.rationale: A specified tax return preparer is one who reasonably expects to file more than 10 individual, estate, or trust income tax returns in a calendar year and must e-file them, unless a return falls within an exception (such as a taxpayer's documented choice to paper file, supported by Form 8948).

questions.stem: Under section 7216, what is generally required before a preparer may disclose or use a client's tax return information for purposes other than preparing the return?
options: A court order in every case
The taxpayer's prior consent, generally in a specific written form
Nothing; preparers may use the data freely
Approval from the IRS
questions.rationale: Section 7216 makes it a crime for a preparer to knowingly or recklessly disclose or use tax return information other than in connection with preparing the return, unless an exception applies or the taxpayer gives valid written consent meeting Treasury requirements.

questions.stem: A preparer wants to use clients' tax return information to market financial products. The consent form is dated and signed but does not specify the recipients or the particular use. Is this consent valid under section 7216 regulations?
options: Yes, because marketing is always permitted
No, the consent must identify the intended purpose of the disclosure or use, the recipients, and meet specific format and content requirements
Yes, a signature and date are all that is needed
No, because consent can never authorize use for marketing
questions.rationale: Treasury regulations under section 7216 require consents to disclose or use tax return information to be specific, identifying the particular use or disclosure, the recipients, and including mandated language; a non-specific consent does not meet the requirements and is invalid.

questions.stem: A preparer signs a return as the paid preparer. Under section 6695(b), what penalty applies if the preparer fails to sign a return they prepared?
options: A per-failure penalty (indexed, around $60) up to an annual maximum
Loss of PTIN automatically
$10,000 per return
No penalty; signing is optional
questions.rationale: Section 6695(b) penalizes a paid preparer who fails to sign a return or claim for refund they prepared, imposing a per-failure penalty (adjusted for inflation) subject to an annual cap.

questions.stem: How long must a paid preparer retain a copy of each return prepared, or a list of taxpayers and returns, under section 6107?
options: For 3 years after the close of the return period
No retention is required
For 1 year
Indefinitely
questions.rationale: Section 6107 requires a paid preparer to retain a completed copy of each return or claim, or a list of the taxpayers and returns, for three years after the close of the return period; failure is penalized under section 6695(d).

questions.stem: During an Appeals conference, the Appeals Officer raises a 'hazards of litigation' analysis. What does this mean for settlement?
options: Appeals cannot settle on litigation risk
Appeals must always uphold the examiner
Hazards of litigation only apply in Tax Court
Appeals may settle a case based on the probability of the IRS prevailing if the matter were litigated, allowing compromise of factual or legal uncertainties
questions.rationale: The IRS Office of Appeals can resolve disputes by considering the hazards of litigation, settling a case for an amount that reflects the probability of success if the matter were litigated; Examination generally cannot settle on that basis.

questions.stem: What is the primary characteristic that the IRS Office of Appeals is designed to maintain in resolving disputes?
options: Speed over fairness
Maximizing revenue collection
Independence and impartiality, resolving cases without litigation on a basis that is fair to both the government and the taxpayer
Loyalty to the examining agent
questions.rationale: The IRS Independent Office of Appeals resolves tax controversies without litigation on a basis that is fair and impartial to both the government and the taxpayer, maintaining independence from the Examination and Collection functions.

questions.stem: A taxpayer requests a Collection Due Process hearing and, at the hearing, wants to dispute the underlying tax liability. When may the taxpayer raise the underlying liability at a CDP hearing?
options: Never; CDP only addresses collection alternatives
Only if the taxpayer did not receive a statutory notice of deficiency and did not otherwise have a prior opportunity to dispute the liability
Always, regardless of prior opportunities
Only in equivalent hearings
questions.rationale: At a CDP hearing the taxpayer may raise spousal defenses, collection alternatives, and procedural issues, and may contest the underlying liability only if they did not receive a statutory notice of deficiency or otherwise have a prior opportunity to dispute it.

questions.stem: After a CDP hearing, Appeals issues a Notice of Determination the taxpayer disagrees with. What is the taxpayer's recourse and deadline?
options: File a refund suit in District Court within 2 years
Petition the U.S. Tax Court for review of the determination within 30 days of the Notice of Determination
No further review is available
Request another CDP hearing within 90 days
questions.rationale: Following a timely CDP hearing, the taxpayer may seek judicial review by petitioning the U.S. Tax Court within 30 days after the date of the Notice of Determination; this Tax Court review is a key advantage of a timely CDP request over an equivalent hearing.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files for bankruptcy while owing federal income tax. What immediate effect does the bankruptcy filing have on IRS collection?
options: It has no effect on IRS collection
It accelerates the levy process
The automatic stay generally halts IRS collection activity (such as levies) during the bankruptcy, and the collection statute is suspended for the stay period plus six months
It permanently cancels all tax debt
questions.rationale: Filing bankruptcy triggers an automatic stay that generally suspends IRS collection efforts; the collection statute is tolled during the stay plus six months, and whether the tax is discharged depends on bankruptcy rules and the type and age of the tax.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's installment agreement is in default because a payment was missed. The IRS proposes to terminate it. What right does the taxpayer have regarding the proposed termination?
options: The taxpayer must immediately full-pay
The taxpayer can only file bankruptcy
None; termination is immediate
The IRS must generally provide 30 days' notice before altering, modifying, or terminating an installment agreement, and the taxpayer may appeal the termination
questions.rationale: Under section 6159, the IRS must give the taxpayer 30 days' notice before modifying or terminating an installment agreement (absent jeopardy), and the taxpayer has the right to appeal the termination or proposed modification.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to claim a refund for a tax year. Under the general statute of limitations, when must a claim for refund be filed?
options: Within 3 years from the time the return was filed or 2 years from the time the tax was paid, whichever is later
There is no deadline
Within 1 year of filing only
Within 10 years of payment
questions.rationale: Section 6511 provides that a claim for refund must generally be filed within three years from the time the return was filed or two years from the time the tax was paid, whichever is later, with a corresponding limit on the amount refundable.

questions.stem: A taxpayer filed a return reporting and paying tax, then files a refund claim exactly 3 years and 1 day after filing the return but only 1 year after a later payment. Considering the lookback rule, what is the consequence?
options: No refund is ever possible after 3 years
The full refund is allowed without limit
The taxpayer must file in Tax Court
The claim may be timely under the 2-year/payment rule, but the amount refundable is limited to tax paid within the lookback period (2 years here), potentially barring recovery of earlier payments
questions.rationale: Under section 6511(b), the refundable amount is limited by a lookback period: for a claim filed within three years of the return, the limit reaches back three years plus extensions; for a claim under the two-year rule, only tax paid within the two years before the claim can be refunded.

questions.stem: An EA is approached by a prospective client who wants to backdate documents to support a deduction. The EA refuses and the client offers to pay triple the normal fee. What should the EA do under Circular 230?
options: Prepare the documents but not sign the return
Report the client to the FBI before doing anything else
Decline to participate, because assisting in creating false or backdated documents is disreputable conduct and could constitute fraud
Accept the engagement because the fee is reasonable
questions.rationale: Helping a client create false or backdated documentation constitutes disreputable conduct under Circular 230 section 10.51 and potential fraud; the practitioner must decline regardless of the fee offered.

questions.stem: An EA learns that a long-time client has been convicted of a tax crime unrelated to the EA's work. Does this conviction obligate the EA to take any specific action under Circular 230?
options: The EA must immediately resign from all engagements

Circular 230 imposes no automatic duty based solely on the client's unrelated conviction, but the EA must not knowingly assist in any noncompliance and should consider whether continued representation raises competence or conflict concerns
The EA must amend all prior returns
The EA must report the conviction to OPR
questions.rationale: A client's unrelated criminal conviction does not by itself trigger a specific Circular 230 obligation; the practitioner's ongoing duties are to avoid assisting noncompliance, exercise due diligence, and use professional judgment about continued representation.

questions.stem: An EA prepares a return relying on a client's organizer and supporting documents that appear complete and consistent. The EA does not independently audit the figures. Is this acceptable under Circular 230?
options: No, the EA must audit and verify every figure
Yes, even if the information is obviously wrong
No, reliance on client information is never allowed

Yes, a practitioner may generally rely in good faith without verification on information furnished by the client, but must make reasonable inquiries if the information appears incorrect, inconsistent, or incomplete
questions.rationale: Circular 230 section 10.34(d) permits a practitioner to rely in good faith, without verification, on information furnished by the client, but the practitioner cannot ignore the implications of other information known and must make reasonable inquiries if information appears incorrect, inconsistent, or incomplete.

questions.stem: A taxpayer under examination wants to record the in-person interview with the IRS examiner. What does the law allow?
options: The taxpayer may make an audio recording of an in-person interview if they give the IRS advance notice (generally 10 days)
Recording is allowed only with a court order
Recording is prohibited
Only the IRS may record
questions.rationale: Under section 7521, a taxpayer may make an audio recording of an in-person interview with the IRS provided they give advance notice (generally 10 calendar days); the IRS may likewise record if it notifies the taxpayer.

questions.stem: During an interview, an EA representing a taxpayer determines the questioning has turned toward potential criminal issues. Under section 7521, what right does the representative have?
options: The EA must answer all questions personally

The representative may suspend the interview to consult with the taxpayer or seek advice if it appears the examiner is developing a criminal matter, and the taxpayer generally need not attend with a valid representative present
The EA must immediately confess on the client's behalf
None; the interview must continue
questions.rationale: Section 7521 provides that an interview may be suspended to allow consultation with a representative, and a taxpayer represented by a qualified practitioner generally cannot be required to attend the interview unless the IRS issues an administrative summons.

questions.stem: An IRS examiner issues an Information Document Request (IDR) during a field audit. What is the best practice for a representative responding to an IDR?
options: Provide everything in the taxpayer's files regardless of relevance
Respond timely and completely with the requested, relevant records, and communicate with the examiner if more time or clarification is needed
Refuse all requests as overreaching
Ignore it until a summons is issued
questions.rationale: An Information Document Request seeks records relevant to the examination; the representative should respond timely and completely with the relevant materials, seek extensions or clarification when needed, and avoid both stonewalling and over-disclosure.

questions.stem: The IRS issues an administrative summons to a third-party bank for a taxpayer's records. What notice right does the taxpayer generally have?
options: The taxpayer may only object after the records are produced
The taxpayer can never challenge a summons
